𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐍𝐞𝐰𝐬 – 𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟗, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔

Institutional blockchain adoption advanced even as fading spot demand and security failures kept crypto risk firmly in view.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰

Crypto’s institutional buildout gained another concrete use case as JPMorgan expanded its deposit token to Ethereum, allowing approved clients to move bank deposits onchain for payments and settlement while keeping access within its regulated customer network. That progress did not translate into a broad risk-on move: bitcoin remained near $82,000, while weaker spot demand, recent ETF outflows and reduced speculative interest left a recovery dependent on fresh buying rather than infrastructure announcements alone. Equities and bitcoin initially found support as stronger-than-expected Chinese growth and falling oil prices improved risk appetite, but the market’s direction remained exposed to inflation concerns and the week’s US data and earnings.

The contrast was visible across the market. BNB rose as the network completed another scheduled burn, while XRP’s small daily rebound did little to erase its weak weekly trend, and ether continued to face ETF withdrawals and leveraged selling. At the same time, security incidents underscored that adoption brings operational risks: Qubic’s wallet-seed exploit forced a network halt, while Cysic shut its bridge after unauthorized token minting. Regulation also remained unsettled, from South Korea’s debate over a planned crypto tax to the US dispute over state authority for prediction markets. The day’s defining tension was therefore not adoption versus stagnation, but expanding institutional rails against fragile demand, unsettled rules and persistent security exposure.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐧𝐚𝐩𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐭

• $BTC: $81,875, -0.2%
• ETH: $2,406, -0.1%
• BNB: $731.44, +1.2%
• XRP: $1.30, -0.2%
• SOL: $104.98, +0.9%
• Sentiment: Bitcoin sentiment recovered into the greed zone, although the broader market remained cautious amid weak spot demand and ETF outflows.
• Flows: US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded about $229 million in net withdrawals for the week ending October 16; spot Ethereum ETFs saw $319.97 million in outflows for the week ending October 16.
• Macro: Bitcoin and Asian equities rose as China’s third-quarter GDP growth exceeded expectations and falling oil prices supported risk appetite. Upcoming US releases include jobless claims on Thursday and manufacturing and services PMIs, plus the University of Michigan consumer survey, on Friday.
𝐓𝐨𝐩 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬

𝟏. 𝐉𝐏𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐚𝐧 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭 𝐭𝐨𝐤𝐞𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐄𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐮𝐦

JPMorgan expanded JPM Coin, its dollar-denominated deposit token, to Ethereum mainnet, adding the public network to its existing Base deployment. The token represents deposits held at JPMorgan rather than a freely transferable stablecoin, and access remains limited to approved institutional customers. Those clients can use it for onchain payments and, where systems are compatible, settlement of tokenized assets and collateral transfers. Because eligibility and compliance controls remain with the bank, the move does not open JPM Coin to retail users or public DeFi markets. Its significance is instead the addition of another public-chain settlement option within an institutional banking system, illustrating how traditional finance can use public blockchain infrastructure without giving up control over participation.

𝟐. 𝐐𝐮𝐛𝐢𝐜 𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐬 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐰𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐭-𝐬𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐟𝐭

Qubic stopped processing transactions after an attacker used weak randomness in wallet recovery-seed generation to compromise 1,404 accounts and steal about 2.94 trillion QU, worth roughly $1.4 million. The weakness affected wallet credentials, not the network’s consensus protocol, and Qubic says it fixed the seed-generation flaw in version 4.26.4. About 87.1% of the stolen tokens remained on the network when it halted, while MEXC froze the receiving account for the portion sent to its platform. The project is identifying affected wallets and preparing recovery options for a vote by its network operators, known as Computors, but no plan has been approved and no restart date has been announced. A software fix does not secure wallets created with weak seeds, leaving the recovery process and affected holders’ next steps unresolved.

𝟑. 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐡 𝐊𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐚 𝐰𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐜𝐫𝐲𝐩𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐚𝐱

South Korean finance officials are due to meet major cryptocurrency exchanges on October 20 as the industry presses for a delay to the planned tax on qualifying crypto income. The current schedule sets the tax to begin on January 1, 2027, with a combined rate of 22% above a 2.5 million won annual allowance. Exchanges say they still need rules for areas including staking, airdrops, hard forks and DeFi, and argue that they have too little time to prepare systems for reporting and calculating taxable income. A proposed bill would tie implementation to international crypto-asset data sharing under the OECD framework, potentially moving the start to 2029 if sharing begins in 2027. That proposal has not been approved, so the meeting may clarify implementation concerns without changing the deadline; until lawmakers act, exchanges and taxpayers face a 2027 schedule alongside the possibility of another postponement.

𝟒. 𝐂𝐌𝐄 𝐬𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐔𝐍𝐈 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐁𝐂𝐇 𝐟𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬

CME Group scheduled futures tied to Uniswap’s UNI and Bitcoin Cash for launch on October 19, subject to regulatory review. The planned contracts come in standard and micro sizes: 10,000 and 1,000 UNI, and 250 and 25 BCH. They are designed to let traders manage exposure to the tokens without holding them directly, extending CME’s crypto derivatives lineup. A scheduled launch does not itself establish that clearance was granted or that trading began, and futures availability is not an endorsement of the assets or a signal of spot-market demand. For the market, the development adds regulated derivatives access, while its practical significance depends on actual trading activity once the contracts are live.

𝟓. 𝐂𝐲𝐬𝐢𝐜 𝐬𝐮𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐠𝐞 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐮𝐧𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐝 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠

Cysic suspended its cross-chain bridge after an attacker minted 10 million CYS tokens on BNB Smart Chain by exploiting unauthorized database access and a message-processing vulnerability, according to the project’s preliminary findings. About 7.2 million tokens were sold and bridged to Ethereum, yielding roughly 306.6 ETH worth $727,000, while the remaining 2.8 million CYS were frozen after the recipient address was blacklisted. Cysic said its mainnet and existing user assets were unaffected, but the bridge will remain closed during an investigation and an external security review. No reopening date was announced. As with Qubic’s wallet incident, the response is now focused on containment and investigation; the bridge’s return depends on resolving the security weakness, not simply resuming activity.

𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 & 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲

Regulatory developments pointed in different directions: authorities are extending oversight, while key boundaries for crypto taxation and market structure remain contested. The European Banking Authority designated USDC the EU’s first significant e-money token under MiCA, bringing Circle’s European issuer under EBA supervision for prudential matters from November 12, including capital, reserves, liquidity and recovery or redemption planning. France’s ACPR will retain oversight of governance, outsourcing and key personnel, so the designation adds scrutiny rather than a new license or a safety guarantee. In South Korea, the planned 2027 tax remains the effective schedule even as officials prepare to discuss exchanges’ readiness and a proposal that could defer implementation to 2029. In the US, Crypto.com-linked North American Derivatives Exchange and Novig are challenging Missouri’s attempt to apply state gambling rules to sports event contracts, arguing federal commodities law governs; courts have not resolved the dispute. Together, these developments show regulation becoming more specific, but not yet more settled for issuers, exchanges or market operators.

𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 & 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤

The day’s security incidents ranged from compromised wallet creation to bridge controls, reinforcing that risk often lies in the systems around a blockchain as much as in its core protocol. Qubic’s exploit stemmed from weak wallet-seed randomness, while Cysic’s preliminary account points to unauthorized database access and a message-processing vulnerability; the incidents are distinct, but both required emergency containment. Qubic holders whose wallets were created with vulnerable software should treat the seed as potentially compromised and follow verified project guidance for migration rather than relying on the software patch alone. Separately, investigators warned that stolen crypto can become harder to trace after entering Zcash’s shielded pool, making visible onchain movements an important window for exchanges and investigators. With crypto thefts reaching $1.18 billion across 107 incidents in Q3, audits alone are not enough: operational controls, access management and response procedures also matter.

𝐀𝐥𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬 & 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐬

Altcoin performance remained uneven: BNB benefited from a scheduled supply reduction, while XRP’s modest rebound sat against weak weekly momentum and unresolved support tests. BNB Chain completed its 37th quarterly Auto-Burn, removing 1,646,196.44 BNB and leaving total supply at 131,512,085; the burn reduces supply but is not an open-market purchase or proof of future price gains. XRP Ledger’s fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment reached the required validator support to begin its two-week approval period, with activation projected for late October if support holds. The amendment repairs technical issues across network functions but does not activate the separate lending features, which still require their own approvals. On Solana, the Alpenglow consensus upgrade is scheduled for October 21 and targets roughly 150-millisecond finality under normal conditions, while requiring validators to run compatible software. Together, these changes focus on supply mechanics, network maintenance and performance; none removes the need for adoption and market demand to support token value.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐖𝐚𝐭𝐜𝐡

text:
Fellow inmates found her sentence hard to believe. “They had a nickname for me: The Woman with All the Days,” Johnson said. “That’s what they called me: The Woman with All the Days. There were people who had committed real crimes who got out before me.”

In 2016, the state agency that oversees judges charged Hayes with violating Alabama’s code of judicial conduct. According to the Judicial Inquiry Commission, Hayes broke state and federal laws by jailing Johnson and hundreds of other Montgomery residents too poor to pay fines. Among those jailed: a plumber struggling to make rent, a mother who skipped meals to cover the medical bills of her disabled son, and a hotel housekeeper working her way through college.

Hayes, a judge since 2000, admitted in court documents to violating 10 different parts of the state’s judicial conduct code. One of the counts was a breach of a judge’s most essential duty: failing to “respect and comply with the law."

Despite the severity of the ruling, Hayes wasn’t barred from serving as a judge. Instead, the judicial commission and Hayes reached a deal. The former Eagle Scout would serve an 11-month unpaid suspension. Then he could return to the bench.

Until he was disciplined, Hayes said in an interview with Reuters, “I never thought I was doing something wrong.”

This week, Hayes is set to retire after 20 years as a judge. In a statement to Reuters, Hayes said he was “very remorseful” for his misdeeds.

Community activists say his departure is long overdue. Yet the decision to leave, they say, should never have been his to make, given his record of misconduct.

“He should have been fired years ago,” said Willie Knight, pastor of North Montgomery Baptist Church. “He broke the law and wanted to get away with it. His sudden retirement is years too late.”

Hayes is among thousands of state and local judges across America who were allowed to keep positions of extraordinary power and prestige after violating judicial ethics rules or breaking laws they pledged to uphold, a Reuters investigation found.

Judges have made racist statements, lied to state officials and forced defendants to languish in jail without a lawyer – and then returned to the bench, sometimes with little more than a rebuke from the state agencies overseeing their conduct.

Recent media reports have documented failures in judicial oversight in South Carolina, Louisiana and Illinois. Reuters went further.

In the first comprehensive accounting of judicial misconduct nationally, Reuters identified and reviewed 1,509 cases from the last dozen years – 2008 through 2019 – in which judges resigned, retired or were publicly disciplined following accusations of misconduct. In addition, reporters identified another 3,613 cases from 2008 through 2018 in which states disciplined wayward judges but kept hidden from the public key details of their offenses – including the identities of the judges themselves.

All told, 9 of every 10 judges were allowed to return to the bench after they were sanctioned for misconduct, Reuters determined. They included a California judge who had sex in his courthouse chambers, once with his former law intern and separately with an attorney; a New York judge who berated domestic violence victims; and a Maryland judge who, after his arrest for driving drunk, was allowed to return to the bench provided he took a Breathalyzer test before each appearance.

The news agency’s findings reveal an “excessively” forgiving judicial disciplinary system, said Stephen Gillers, a law professor at New York University who writes about judicial ethics. Although punishment short of removal from the bench is appropriate for most misconduct cases, Gillers said, the public “would be appalled at some of the lenient treatment judges get” for substantial transgressions.

Among the cases from the past year alone:

In Utah, a judge texted a video of a man’s scrotum to court clerks. He was reprimanded but remains on the bench.

In Indiana, three judges attending a conference last spring got drunk and sparked a 3 a.m. brawl outside a White Castle fast-food restaurant that ended with two of the judges shot. Although the state supreme court found the three judges had “discredited the entire Indiana judiciary,” each returned to the bench after a suspension.

In Texas, a judge burst in on jurors deliberating the case of a woman charged with sex trafficking and declared that God told him the defendant was innocent. The offending judge received a warning and returned to the bench. The defendant was convicted after a new judge took over the case.

“There are certain things where there should be a level of zero tolerance,” the jury foreman, Mark House, told Reuters. The judge should have been fined, House said, and kicked off the bench. “There is no justice, because he is still doing his job.”

Judicial misconduct specialists say such behavior has the potential to erode trust in America’s courts and, absent tough consequences, could give judges license to behave with impunity.

“When you see cases like that, the public starts to wonder about the integrity and honesty of the system,” said Steve Scheckman, a lawyer who directed Louisiana’s oversight agency and served as deputy director of New York’s. “It looks like a good ol’ boys club.”

That’s how local lawyers viewed the case of a longtime Alabama judge who concurrently served on the state’s judicial oversight commission. The judge, Cullman District Court’s Kim Chaney, remained on the bench for three years after being accused of violating the same nepotism rules he was tasked with enforcing on the oversight commission. In at least 200 cases, court records show, Judge Chaney chose his own son to serve as a court-appointed defense lawyer for the indigent, enabling the younger Chaney to earn at least $105,000 in fees over two years.

In February, months after Reuters repeatedly asked Chaney and the state judicial commission about those cases, he retired from the bench as part of a deal with state authorities to end the investigation.

Tommy Drake, the lawyer who first filed a complaint against Chaney in 2016, said he doubts the judge would have been forced from the bench if Reuters hadn’t examined the case.

“You know the only reason they did anything about Chaney is because you guys started asking questions,” Drake said. “Otherwise, he’d still be there.”

Bedrock of American justice

State and local judges draw little scrutiny even though their courtrooms are the bedrock of the American criminal justice system, touching the lives of millions of people every year.

The country’s approximately 1,700 federal judges hear 400,000 cases annually. The nearly 30,000 state, county and municipal court judges handle a far bigger docket: more than 100 million new cases each year, from traffic to divorce to murder. Their titles range from justice of the peace to state supreme court justice. Their powers are vast and varied – from determining whether a defendant should be jailed to deciding who deserves custody of a child.

Each U.S. state has an oversight agency that investigates misconduct complaints against judges. The authority of the oversight agencies is distinct from the power held by appellate courts, which can reverse a judge’s legal ruling and order a new trial. Judicial commissions cannot change verdicts. Rather, they can investigate complaints about the behavior of judges and pursue discipline ranging from reprimand to removal.

Few experts dispute that the great majority of judges behave responsibly, respecting the law and those who appear before them. And some contend that, when judges do falter, oversight agencies are effective in identifying and addressing the behavior. “With a few notable exceptions, the commissions generally get it right,” said Keith Swisher, a University of Arizona law professor who specializes in judicial ethics.

Others disagree. They note that the clout of these commissions is limited, and their authority differs from state to state. To remove a judge, all but a handful of states require approval of a panel that includes other judges. And most states seldom exercise the full extent of those disciplinary powers.

As a result, the system tends to err on the side of protecting the rights and reputations of judges while overlooking the impact courtroom wrongdoing has on those most affected by it: people like Marquita Johnson.

Reuters scoured thousands of state investigative files, disciplinary proceedings and court records from the past dozen years to quantify the personal toll of judicial misconduct. The examination found at least 5,206 people who were directly affected by a judge’s misconduct. The victims cited in disciplinary documents ranged from people who were illegally jailed to those subjected to racist, sexist and other abusive comments from judges in ways that tainted the cases.

The number is a conservative estimate. The tally doesn’t include two previously reported incidents that affected thousands of defendants and prompted sweeping reviews of judicial conduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about.”

Arthur Grim, retired judge

In Pennsylvania, the state examined the convictions of more than 3,500 teenagers sentenced by two judges. The judges were convicted of taking kickbacks as part of a scheme to fill a private juvenile detention center. In 2009, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court appointed senior judge Arthur Grim to lead a victim review, and the state later expunged criminal records for 2,251 juveniles. Grim told Reuters that every state should adopt a way to compensate victims of judicial misconduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about,” Grim said.

In another review underway in Ohio, state public defender Tim Young is scrutinizing 2,707 cases handled by a judge who retired in 2018 after being hospitalized for alcoholism. Mike Benza, a law professor at Case Western Reserve University whose students are helping identify victims, compared the work to current investigations into police abuse of power. “You see one case and then you look to see if it's systemic,” he said.

The review, which has been limited during the coronavirus pandemic, may take a year. But Young said the time-consuming task is essential because “a fundamental injustice may have been levied against hundreds or thousands of people.”

‘Special rules for judges’

Most states afford judges accused of misconduct a gentle kind of justice. Perhaps no state better illustrates the shortcomings of America’s system for overseeing judges than Alabama.

As in most states, Alabama’s nine-member Judicial Inquiry Commission is a mix of lawyers, judges and laypeople. All are appointed. Their deliberations are secret and they operate under some of the most judge-friendly rules in the nation.

Alabama’s rules make even filing a complaint against a judge difficult. The complaint must be notarized, which means that in theory, anyone who makes misstatements about the judge can be prosecuted for perjury. Complaints about wrongdoing must be made in writing; those that arrive by phone, email or without a notary stamp are not investigated, although senders are notified why their complaints have been summarily rejected. Anonymous written complaints are shredded.

These rules can leave lawyers and litigants fearing retaliation, commission director Jenny Garrett noted in response to written questions.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint,” said Sue Bell Cobb, chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court from 2007 to 2011. In 2009, she unsuccessfully championed changes to the process and commissioned an American Bar Association report that offered a scathing review of Alabama's rules.

In most other states, commission staff members can start investigating a judge upon receiving a phone call or email, even anonymous ones, or after learning of questionable conduct from a news report or court filing. In Alabama, staff will not begin an investigation without approval from the commission itself, which convenes about every seven weeks.

By rule, the commission also must keep a judge who is under scrutiny fully informed throughout an investigation. If a subpoena is issued, the judge receives a simultaneous copy, raising fears about witness intimidation. If a witness gives investigators a statement, the judge receives a transcript. In the U.S. justice system, such deference to individuals under investigation is extremely rare.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint.”

Sue Bell Cobb, former chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court

“Why the need for special rules for judges?” said Michael Levy, a Washington lawyer who has represented clients in high-profile criminal, corporate, congressional and securities investigations. “If judges think it’s fair and appropriate to investigate others for crimes or misconduct without providing those subjects or targets with copies of witness statements and subpoenas, why don’t judges think it’s fair to investigate judges in the same way?”

Alabama judges also are given an opportunity to resolve investigations confidentially. Reuters interviews and a review of Alabama commission records show the commission has met with judges informally at least 19 times since 2011 to offer corrective “guidance.” The identities of those judges remain confidential, as does the conduct that prompted the meetings. “Not every violation warrants discipline,” commission director Garrett said.

Since 2008, the commission has brought 21 public cases against judges, including Hayes, charging two this year.

Two of the best-known cases brought by the commission involved Roy Moore, who was twice forced out as chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court for defying federal court orders.

Another Alabama justice fared better in challenging a misconduct complaint, however. Tom Parker, first elected to the state’s high court in 2004, pushed back when the commission investigated him in 2015 for comments he made on the radio criticizing the U.S. Supreme Court's decision legalizing gay marriage.

Parker sued the commission in federal court, arguing the agency was infringing on his First Amendment rights. He won. Although the commission had dropped its investigation before the ruling, it was ordered to cover Parker’s legal fees: $100,000, or about a fifth of the agency’s total annual budget.

In 2018, the people of Alabama elected Parker chief justice.

These days, Parker told Reuters, Alabama judges and the agency that oversees them enjoy “a much better relationship” that’s less politically tinged. “How can I say it? It’s much more respectful between the commission and the judges now.”

text:
BRANIFF'S HOME TURNS 109 YEARS OLD TODAY - Happy Birthday Dallas Love Field! Dallas Love Field turns 109 years old! On this day, Friday, October 19, 1917, the Dallas airport opened for air operations. The new airport was named for Lieutenant Colonel Moss Lee Love of the 11th Cavalry who was killed in a training accident at San Diego, California, on September 4, 1913. The United States Army named the new army flying field located to the north of the City of Dallas to honor the memory of Lieutenant Colonel Love.

In 1917, the Dallas Chamber of Commerce, in an effort to assist the nation in the World War I effort, began negotiations with the Signal Corps to establish a pilot training facility in Dallas. A 600-acre site was chosen to the south of Bachmann Lake and only seven miles from downtown. The Corps stated they could offer a rental fee of $12.00 USD per acre but local farmers whose land would be taken for the new facility wanted $20.00 USD per acre. The Chamber of Commerce agreed to pay the $8.00 USD difference along with other demands from the farmers after the initial agreement was made.

National Air Transport, the predecessor of United Airlines, Inc., was the first airline to begin mail service at Love Field on May 12, 1926, between Dallas and Chicago. The mail service was followed by the first passenger service over a year later on September 17, 1927, between Dallas and Chicago. Delta Airlines began serving Love Field on June 17, 1929, with service to Jackson/Vicksburg, Mississippi with intermediate stops at Shreveport and Monroe, Louisiana.

Braniff Airways reportedly began serving Dallas Love Field on February 1, 1929, with service to Wichita Falls and Oklahoma City, although timetables do not indicate service began at that time. After Paul R. Braniff, Inc., predecessor of Braniff Airways, Inc., was sold to Universal Aviation Corporation in April 1929, service began at Dallas Love Field, soon after, on July 15, 1929. Braniff service at Love Field operated from Tulsa to Ft Worth with intermediate stops at Oklahoma City and Wewoka, Oklahoma, and Dallas Love Field. Universal was sold to Aviation Corporation of America in April 1929, and the Braniff Division was sold and eventually became a part of American Airways in 1932, the 1934 predecessor of American Airlines.

In November 1930, the Braniff brothers formed Braniff Airways, Incorporated, and began flying between Oklahoma City and Tulsa and Wichita Falls, Texas. While Braniff only flew intermittently to Dallas between 1930 and 1934, it did advertise connection service to the region via Bowen Airlines at Tulsa. On May 17, 1934, Braniff operated its first airmail service at Dallas Love Field. The new airmail contract, AM-9, was awarded to Braniff on May 7, 1934, after heroic congressional lobbying efforts by company cofounder Paul Revere Braniff. The route operated between Chicago and Dallas with intermediate stops at Kansas City, Wichita, Ponca City, Oklahoma City and Ft Worth.

Northbound passenger and express service was inaugurated over the new route on May 30, 1934. The following day, southbound passenger and express service was commenced. Braniff employed a total of 47 employees throughout its growing Midwest system at the time the new airmail contract was awarded.
Early scheduled airline flights operated from the original Love Field Terminal that was located at the north end of the airport on Love Field Drive, to the west side of Runway 13/31 (now Rwy 13L/31R). The new two story terminal housed Braniff, Delta, and American Airlines and served the airport until October 6, 1940, when the new Terminal, located along Lemmon Avenue on the northeast end of the airport, was opened.

Braniff Airways and other carriers began operations at the new Dallas Love Field Cedar Springs Terminal on Monday, January 20, 1958. The terminal was dedicated earlier during a seven-day extravaganza from October 20-27, 1957. The new Love Field Terminal replaced the previous Terminal located on the east side of the airport along Lemmon Avenue, which was torn down in 1962. The original access road (Glenn Curtiss Drive) and traffic-circle style access to the 1940 Terminal still exists today.

The spacious new terminal, dedicated during a grand ceremony and Open House that began on October 20, 1957, was part of a massive $20,000,000 USD Love Field Expansion Program. Airlines had been operating out of the Lemmon Avenue Terminal since 1940, and as airline traffic began growing quickly after World War II the space-limited terminal quickly became overcrowded. The new terminal, at the end of Cedar Springs Road, was accessed via Mockingbird Lane and Cedar Springs.

Dallas Architect Jack Corgan designed the new three-concourse terminal that was paneled in unique red and green square panels that featured a mid century flare. The three concourses were single-story with a total of 26 departure gates. The concourses were delineated by direction and color coding that included the West or Green Concourse, North or Yellow Concourse, and finally the East or Red Concourse.

Braniff Airways occupied Gates 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, and 23 of the North or Yellow Concourse and remained in this area until the new Braniff Terminal of the Future was opened in December 1968, at the south end of the East or Red Concourse. American Airlines operated from Gates 1 through 8 of the North or Green Concourse where Southwest Airlines has operated from until 2013. Delta Airlines also shared the Yellow Concourse with Braniff and used Gates 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, and 22. Local service carrier Central Airlines used Gate 9 at the beginning of the Yellow Concourse.

The East or Red Concourse featured Trans Texas Airways at Gate 24 and Continental Airlines at Gates 25 and 26. All airline boarding was done by ventral air stairs contained aboard aircraft so equipped or via roll up stair ramps. Jetways were not introduced at Love Field until American Airlines expanded the North Concourse in 1967. Braniff did not have Jetway service at Love Field until the beginning of operations from the Terminal of the Future in 1968.

Unique powered dual moving sidewalks connected the Main 1958 Terminal Lobby to the three Concourses ending at the first gate of each concourse. The classic mid century style of the 1958 Terminal Building featured a massive Lobby that measured 150-feet by 185-feet with a large area that featured an open layout with retail shops and seating areas. A beautiful Airport Observation Deck was prominently placed on the displaced second floor that was accessible by two escalators and mid century-styled stairwells placed on either end of the expansive Lobby.

Off the southeast end of the Main Lobby was the Ticket Hall. Braniff International's Main Ticket Counter was the first counter off of the Main Lobby followed by Continental, American, Trans Texas and Delta, Central and finally USOA. Braniff remained in this Ticket Counter space until 1968, when the new Terminal of the Future was opened. On the second floor to the west of the Observation Deck was the Dobb's House Luau Restaurant directly behind and below the Control Tower, which was placed on the top of the Main Terminal annex. An additional Dobbs House was also under the Luau Room accessible from the Main Lobby.

Off of the southwest side of the Main Lobby was the walkway to the Baggage Claim Wing. Administration offices were situated over the walkway to the Baggage Claim Wing. Also off of the Main Lobby to the rear of the Braniff Ticket Counter was a lush outdoor garden. The garden was off of the East Side of the Main Lobby and is now a sculpture garden. A beautiful world map was inlaid into the floor of the Main Lobby and was preserved as part of Love Field Modernization Program in 2013. The Braniff El Dorado Room and VIP Lounge was placed on the second floor of the terminal for easy access by Braniff passengers.

The 1957 Love Field Expansion Plan, in addition to the new Terminal, called for an additional Northwest/Southeast Runway 13R/31L to be built on the west side between the new terminal and Denton Drive. The runway was completed in April 1965 and was 8800-feet in length. The original 1957 Plan called for a length of only 7750-feet. A Braniff BAC-One-11 Fastback Twinjet was the first aircraft to take off from the new west parallel runway.

Additional parts of the 1957 Plan included a new Maintenance and Operations Base for Braniff International Airways on the east side of the field along Lemmon Avenue. Bases for Southwest Airmotive and Delta Airlines were planned to the south of the Braniff base. To the north of the Braniff facility, an American Base was planned as well as a future base for other aviation entities, which was mapped just to the north of the old Lemmon Avenue Terminal.

The 1958 Terminal continued to serve all Dallas airlines until January 1974, when operations were moved to the new Dallas/Ft Worth Regional Airport located centrally between the two cities. Southwest Airlines continued to serve Dallas Love Field and remains the anchor carrier at the airport today. Southwest's Corporate Office and Maintenance Facility are also at Love Field located on the west side of the airfield and the 1958 terminal is still in place but was remodeled in 1989, and extensively in 2013.

Braniff served the close-in Dallas airport until January 13, 1974, when all airlines moved to the new Dallas/Ft Worth Regional Airport. However, Braniff continued to operate limited service to San Antonio and Houston from Love Field until the fall of 1974. Braniff's major overhaul and maintenance operations remained at Love Field until 1989. Braniff's last operations at Love Field on January 12, 1974 were as follows:

Last Departure - Dallas Love Field to Austin and San Antonio

Depart DAL 1040PM Arrive AUS 1122PM Flight 187 Boeing 727

Last Arrival - Portland, Oregon to Dallas Love Field

Depart PDX 655PM Arrive DAL 1259AM Flight 189 Boeing 727

Photo: Looking west at Dallas Love Field, Braniff International's magnificent Boeing 747-127 registered as N601BN is parked on the airside of the Airline's Operations and Maintenance Base located on the east side of the airport. The West/Green Concourse was occupied by American Airlines from 1958, until 1974, while the North or Yellow Concourse was originally occupied by Braniff and Delta, but after December 1968, Braniff moved to its new Terminal of the Future located on the south end of the East or Red Concourse, which is visible on the left side of the photo. Delta, American, Eastern and Braniff all flew Boeing 747s at Love Field but only Braniff's 747 crossed the Pacific Ocean to Hawaii.

A young lady using a Flowstar—I like her style and the music; they fit together. I wish we had these in the late ’90s and early 2000s when I went to raves and clubs. Nowadays I’m too old for it and use a wheelchair when I go out. I did see a raver in a manual wheelchair in the Bronx at Countdown 2K2 in 2002. The last rave I know of up here was the Hijinxs festival at the Philadelphia Civic Center, running until 8 a.m. with Allison Wonderland headlining. She’s a solid trap DJ.

I’m in my 40s. A few years ago I scored New Year’s Eve 2022 tickets for MSG to see Phish—my favorite jam band since the Grateful Dead. It would have been my first time. Tickets were on the 400 level behind the band, Paige/rage side. A friend offered to transfer them after I paid, but two hackers screwed everything up and pulled the wool over my chaperone’s and the buyer’s eyes.

They convinced my chaperone (in his 50s, lives in Virginia) that I was lying about liking jam bands, which makes no sense. Anyone who knows me knows I love jam bands and listen to everything, including rap—mostly rap and rock when I’m angry. I was very angry then. Everything fell apart; I never got the tickets. The buyer claimed he ate the $400 cost, but he went with my chaperone instead. They’re friends (one in Maine, one in Virginia) and both assholes. I still love the band but dislike a handful of the fans. If you believe them over me, you’re an idiot. I’m really disabled. Only a burnout drunk moron would think someone fakes a disability then runs a fundraiser for their favorite band. I rarely get to shows or go out and can’t afford it now. I haven’t been to a concert since 2022. Everyone fucked things up in 2023.

The real heads know I’m legit. Google “Ronald Smith Inglis House”—my old nursing home for 10 years—and an article pops up called “The Music Never Stops,” like the Grateful Dead song, made by their marketing department. I even did a promo YouTube video for them with HD camera and lighting. The article is from 2015, seven years before I ever asked for money. Everyone got refunds for the 2021 Hershey Park shows; the Venmo handler returned the money. A thief would’ve kept it.

I just want my reputation back in the jam band community. A certain Facebook group (with 2014 in the name) seems ashamed and won’t admit it. Hackers can ruin lives. I got screwed over—and so did everyone else—because two drug addicts don’t like me. That’s not fair to anybody. Anyway, this chick has skills—check her out!

Before she became a whispered nightmare, Gothel was a dreamer, a wife, a mother-to-be. Betrayed by the husband she trusted, she was dragged into the frozen wilderness and left to die. Alone and bleeding in the snow, she lost her unborn child.

She should have died there, too.

Instead, a witch offered her immortality wrapped in a bitter curse: an insatiable need for human life essence. To keep her sanity, her memories, and the last fragile fragments of her humanity, Gothel must feed. If she starves, the monster inside takes over forever.

Emerging from the woods, Gothel delivers a slow, merciless reckoning, draining the life from her traitorous ex-husband. But when she turns to his new bride, Seraphine, she discovers the woman is carrying a child.

Haunted by the echo of her own loss, Gothel spares her, making a single, sinister promise: On the child’s eighteenth birthday, she will return to claim the life she is owed.

For years, Gothel hunts in the shadows, clinging to her fraying control. Then she meets Rowan—a centuries-old vampire intimately acquainted with grief and bloodshed. He sees the feral creature lurking behind her eyes, yet he is drawn to it, quietly sweeping away the chaotic trail of bodies she leaves behind.

Gothel feels the dangerous pull, but she refuses to break. Her oath and her survival must come first...because the only thing more lethal than her hunger is letting a vampire into her heart.

text:
New Delaware businesses can now run their state permits and inspections through one coordinated process.

Gov. Matt Meyer launched the Small Business Joint Inspection Pilot on Monday, October 19. It comes from Section 5 of Executive Order 21, which he signed in May and which created the Office of Small Business Access. That office, led by Director Anastasia Jackson, runs the pilot.

The state says a new owner used to have to apply to several agencies and search different websites to learn what each one required. Now owners entering through Delaware One Stop are offered the program, and it's voluntary. The state tells them which permits, licenses, and applications their business needs, and the Office of Small Business Access helps line up the inspection visits. Agencies get an alert as soon as a new business enters the process, so they can plan their reviews. Owners may also get local planning, zoning, and business license contacts for their address.

It's only for owners who haven't opened yet and need to complete applications with participating state agencies. You have to create a https://t.co/7uK5IxKhTy account.

Questions go to osba@delaware.gov.

text:
千米高空夺“双金”：她用脚尖再次刷新江西跳伞历史
Winning Two Gold Medals From a Kilometre High: She Rewrites Jiangxi’s Skydiving History With Her Toes

In the history of skydiving in Jiangxi, China, there had never before been a world champion, nor a single gold medal from the World Championships. Within less than a year, one woman erased both of these “zeros”. Her name is Liao Yuting, a native of Xinyu. She first tried skydiving at 16, and at 28, the seasoned athlete stood on the highest podium of the World Championships.

On September 4, in Slovakia, the 39th FAI World Skydiving Championships unfolded.
China’s women’s skydiving team claimed the top honours. Teaming up with her fellow athletes, Xinyu native Liao Yuting won gold in the women’s team event and women’s formation accuracy landing. Recently, our reporter met Liao Yuting after her triumphant return to China. Dressed in casual clothes, she is modest with a bright smile, just like a girl next door. Yet this young woman has spent 12 years achieving a stunning transformation from a rural girl to a world champion.

## 01 The Running Teenager: Her First Life Choice

Born in 1998 in Liao Village, Zhushan Town, Yushui District, Xinyu City, Liao Yuting had an innate love for running and jumping. After enrolling in Yangjin Primary School, her running talent stood out, and she often took first place in school sports meets.

In June 2010, during the summer after her primary school graduation, Jiang Chunhua, an athletics coach from Xinyu Municipal Sports School, came to Yangjin Primary School to scout talent. Teachers recommended Liao Yuting. Impressed by her long legs and explosive power, Coach Jiang brought her to the municipal sports school.

For a rural child, admission to the city sports school was a chance to leave the countryside — yet it also meant leaving home and enduring hardships she had never known. Driven by her passion for running, young Yuting stepped into the municipal sports school somewhat uncertainly. This was the first choice she ever made for herself.

No exaggeration is needed to describe the toil of student-athletes. On summer tracks in scorching heat, her sweat hit the ground and evaporated in an instant. On frosty winter mornings, even with thick coats for warm-ups, her fingertips turned red with cold, yet she never slacked off.

“Obedient and hardworking, she never cut corners in training,” Jiang Chunhua still remembers young Yuting vividly.
When her mother Li Jinfang visited and asked if she could endure such gruelling training, she simply said she loved it. This pure passion eased her family’s worries, and they fully supported her sporting dream. After two years of training, she built solid physical fitness and forged an unyielding grit, earning her a spot on the athletics team of Jiangxi Provincial Sports School.

## 02 A Brave Switch: From Track and Field to the Blue Sky

Life’s splendour often lies in bold attempts.
In April 2014, the skydiving team of Jiangxi Aviation Sports Administration Center launched a provincial talent recruitment drive. Liao Yuting, with excellent physical condition and a steady mindset, caught the coach’s eye. She was 16 then and had never even boarded a plane. The idea of skydiving athletes piercing through clouds, “flying through the air, so cool”, filled her with curiosity and anticipation.

Switching from track and field to the entirely unfamiliar sport of skydiving meant starting everything from scratch. It was her second brave life choice.

Selection was the first hurdle. At the initial training stage, half of the more than 20 team members were eliminated for failing physical fitness assessments. During trial jumps, many more were weeded out due to panic at altitude and inability to complete required manoeuvres. Only one-third of the original group remained — and Liao Yuting was among them.

“Were you scared on your first jump?” She has been asked this countless times.
She always shakes her head with a smile, yet she is honest: for the first two or three seconds after exiting the aircraft, the air pushes hard against her body, and the sense of weightlessness surges rapidly. She did feel flustered at first, but believes she is naturally braver than most and willing to push herself.

“Once I overcame my fear in the air, I thoroughly enjoyed the free fall. Looking down at the land below, I feel as if the whole sky belongs to me.”

## 03 Precision Embroidery: A Bullseye the Size of a Coin

Liao Yuting specialises in accuracy landing, known as the “precision embroidery” of extreme sports. Jumping from 1,000 metres above the ground, athletes judge wind direction and speed amid shifting air currents, manoeuvre their parachutes, and finally touch the bullseye on the ground with their toes.

- Target disc diameter: 16 centimetres
- Bullseye diameter: 2 centimetres (roughly the size of a coin)

Scores are measured by the distance from the athlete’s toes to the bullseye; the closer, the higher the score. There is a saying in skydiving circles: the hardest part of accuracy landing is the final 10 metres before touchdown. Wind conditions at low altitude change in the blink of an eye, leaving little room for parachute adjustment — this is where the drama of the sport lies.

A full parachute pack weighs over 10 kilograms. Years of repeated donning, jumping, canopy control and landing leave nearly all skydiving athletes with chronic injuries, and Liao Yuting is no exception. On non-jumping days, her training schedule is packed: a 3-kilometre run plus strength and coordination training in the morning, followed by another 3-kilometre run and technical refinement in the afternoon. Through thousands of land-based posture simulations and visual estimation of landing points, she turned every movement into instinct.

This steady accumulation of training earned her a place on China’s national skydiving team in March 2019.

## 04 Fighting Back Against Adversity: Shattering Two “Zero” Records

No athlete in competitive sports enjoys a smooth ride all the way. The years 2023 to 2024 were extremely tough for Liao Yuting. Her form fluctuated wildly, and her performance even declined. Watching younger team members rapidly catch up and overtake her, overwhelming anxiety loomed over her like dark clouds.

At this low point, her coaches and family became her strongest support. Ou Junwu, head coach of the national skydiving training squad, cheered her on. Zhou Pingya, her provincial team coach, held high hopes for her. Her mother offered gentle encouragement: “Hang in there. Whatever the final result, you will always be my pride.”

Fueled by these warm wishes, Liao Yuting regained confidence. She made her third brave life decision: refuse to give up, calmly review her problems, polish her techniques, and gradually recover her competitive edge.

- September 2025: At the National Skydiving Championships, Liao Yuting staged a strong comeback. She claimed gold in women’s individual accuracy landing and bronze in women’s all-round, and won silver in women’s formation accuracy landing alongside her teammates.
- October 2025: The 16th FAI World Canopy Piloting & Accuracy Skydiving World Cup and the 1st Asian Canopy Piloting & Accuracy Skydiving Championships were held in Ji’an, Jiangxi. Competing on home ground, Liao Yuting delivered on expectations, sweeping six gold medals and breaking the Asian record for consecutive bullseye hits in women’s individual accuracy landing. She became the first world champion in Jiangxi skydiving history.
- September 2026: At the 39th World Championships, fighting side by side with her teammates, she secured dual gold medals in women’s team and women’s formation accuracy landing, delivering Jiangxi’s first-ever World Championship gold medals in skydiving.

“The moment we won the championship, all of us were so thrilled and overjoyed!” Right after her victory, Liao Yuting shared the joy with her coaches and family.

## 05 Glory and Inheritance: From High Altitude to Training Ground

“Welcome home, Liao Yuting! Congratulations! Your years of hard work have paid off. You are the first world champion from Zhushan Town!” After returning victorious, the Party Secretary of Zhushan Town, Yushui District, Xinyu, shook her hand warmly. Neighbours gave her thumbs-up and praised her: “Excellent.”

Hearing the familiar local dialect moved Liao Yuting deeply: “Thank you to folks back home for your support and love. I will keep striving!”

With glory upon her shoulders, she keeps moving forward. In May 2026, Liao Yuting was appointed assistant coach of the Jiangxi Skydiving Team. Transitioning from athlete to mentor, her arena stretches from high altitudes to the training ground.

    【在中国江西跳伞的历史上，世界冠军的名字此前一个也没有，世锦赛的金牌此前一枚也没有。这两个“零”，被同一个人在不到一年里先后抹掉。她叫廖玉婷，新余人，16岁第一次接触跳伞，28岁成为站上世锦赛最高领奖台的跳伞老将。】

    9月4日，斯洛伐克，第39届世锦赛。
    中国女子跳伞队站上了最高领奖台——新余姑娘廖玉婷与队友联手摘得女子团体金牌和女子集体定点金牌。近期，记者见到了载誉回国的廖玉婷。一身简单的休闲装，待人谦和，笑容干净，分明就是个邻家小妹。可就是这个姑娘，用整整 12年 时间，完成了从农村女孩到世界冠军的惊艳蜕变。

    01 奔跑的少女：人生第一次选择
    1998年，廖玉婷出生在新余市渝水区珠珊镇的廖家村。小玉婷天生热爱跑跳，就读洋津小学后，她的跑步能力凸显，校运动会经常拿第一名。
    2010年6月，小学毕业的暑假，新余市体校田径教练蒋春华到洋津小学选苗子，学校老师推荐了廖玉婷。蒋教练看这个孩子腿长、爆发力强，就把她带到了新余市体校。
    对农村孩子来说，去市体校是走出农门的机会，也意味着要离开家，吃从没吃过的苦。凭着对奔跑的热爱，小玉婷懵懵懂懂踏进了市体校的大门——这是她人生第一次为自己做的选择。
体育生的苦累，不需要渲染。三伏天的跑道，她跑到汗珠子砸在地上，转眼就蒸干；冬天的清晨哈气成霜，她裹着厚外套热身，指尖冻得通红也从不懈怠。
    “又听话又刻苦，训练从不偷懒。”提及当年的小玉婷，蒋春华至今印象深刻。
    母亲李金芳去体校看她，问她这么辛苦吃得消么，她只说自己喜欢。这份纯粹的热爱，让家人打消顾虑，全力支持她的体育梦想。两年打磨后，她练出了扎实的身体素质，更磨出了一股不服输的韧劲儿，顺利跑进江西省体校田径队。

    02 勇敢的转身：从田径到蓝天
    人生的精彩，总藏在勇敢的尝试里。
    2014年4月，江西省航空运动管理中心跳伞队面向全省选材，身体素质过硬、心态稳定的廖玉婷被教练看中。那年她16岁，之前连飞机都没坐过，只是觉得跳伞运动员穿过云层“像飞一样，特别酷”，她充满好奇和期待。
    从田径转向完全陌生的跳伞运动，等于一切从零开始。这是她人生第二次做出勇敢的选择。
入选是第一道门槛。初训阶段，全队20余人有半数因体能考核不达标被淘汰；到试跳环节，又有不少人因高空紧张、无法完成指定动作被刷掉；最终留下的人数仅为最初的三分之一，廖玉婷便是其中一员。
    “第一次跳怕吗？”这个问题她被问过无数次。
    她总笑着摇头，却也坦诚：刚跳出机舱的两三秒，空气像一只大手狠狠托住身体，失重感急速增加。开始心里也会慌，但她认为自己天生比常人胆量更大些，更肯逼自己。
她说： “克服空中恐惧后，我特别享受坠落的过程。俯瞰大地的时候，感觉整片天空都是自己的。”

    03 精准绣花：靶心只有硬币大小
    廖玉婷主攻的定点跳伞，是极限运动里的“精准绣花”：从1000米的高空跃下，在变幻莫测的气流里判断风向风速，操控降落伞，最终用脚尖去踩地面上的靶心。
    靶盘直径： 16厘米
    靶心直径： 2厘米（差不多一枚硬币大小）
    成绩按脚尖离靶心的距离计算，越近分数越高。跳伞圈内有句话：定点最难的是落地前10米，低空风向风速瞬息万变，手里的伞已经没多少调整余地，这也是这项运动的悬念所在。
而整套伞包重二十多斤，常年反复穿戴、起跳、控伞、落地，跳伞运动员身上几乎都带着劳损旧伤，廖玉婷也不例外。不跳伞的日子里，她的训练表排得密不透风：早上3公里跑加力量、协调性训练，下午又是3公里跑加技术打磨。成千上万次的陆地模拟摆姿、目测落点，她把每一个动作都练成本能。
    这份稳扎稳打的训练积累，让她在 2019年3月 叩开了国家跳伞队的大门。

    04 逆风翻盘：打破两个“零”的纪录
    竞技体育没有谁是一路顺风顺水的。2023到2024年，是廖玉婷无比煎熬的两年。那两年她状态时好时坏，成绩起伏不定，甚至出现下滑。看着年轻队员快速赶超，巨大的焦虑像乌云一样罩着她。
    在这个时刻，教练与家人成为她最坚实的后盾。国家跳伞集训队主教练区俊武给她打气，省队教练周平亚也对她寄予厚望，母亲更是温柔鼓励：“再坚持一下，不管最后结果如何，你永远是妈妈的骄傲。”
    声声期许，让廖玉婷重拾信心。她做出人生第三次勇敢的选择：坚决不放弃，沉下心复盘问题、打磨技术，一点点找回状态。
    2025年9月： 全国跳伞冠军赛上，廖玉婷强势归来，斩获女子个人定点金牌、女子全能铜牌，联手队友拿下女子集体定点银牌。
    2025年10月： 国际航联第十六届特技定点跳伞世界杯暨第一届特技定点跳伞亚锦赛落地江西吉安。“家门口”作战的廖玉婷不负众望，一举包揽 6枚金牌，还打破了女子个人定点连续踩点的亚洲纪录，成为江西跳伞史上首位世界冠军。
    2026年9月： 第39届世锦赛。她和队友并肩作战，成功拿下女子团体、女子集体定点双金牌，实现了江西跳伞世锦赛金牌零的突破。
    “拿到冠军的那一刻，我们所有人都特别激动、特别开心！”夺冠后的廖玉婷，第一时间与教练和家人分享喜悦。

    05 荣光与传承：从高空到训练场
    “廖玉婷，欢迎回来！祝贺你，这么多年拼搏不容易，你是珠珊镇第一个世界冠军！”夺冠回家后，新余渝水区珠珊镇党委书记紧紧握住她的手。邻里见了她都伸出大拇指：“洽噶（优秀）”。
    听到熟悉的乡音，廖玉婷很是激动：“感谢家乡人对我的支持和厚爱，我会继续努力的！”
荣光加身，步履不停。2026年5月，廖玉婷受聘为江西飞机跳伞队助理教练，从运动员到“传帮带”的教练，她的赛道从高空延伸到了训练场。

Charles W. Boatright’s Kindle collection spans faith, adventure, military history, and practical living.

His Biblical titles present faith as perseverance in the style of an Indiana Jones expedition, exploring key figures from both Testaments. They highlight cultural insights into the lineages of King David and Jesus through Abraham, Sarah, Tamar, Rahab, and Salmon, showing how ordinary people achieve extraordinary success. Joshua’s Gauntlet of Divine Providence and The Lost Paradise at Kadesh-Barnea follow Joshua, Caleb, and Moses from Egypt to the Promised Land, emphasizing grit, leadership, spiritual resilience, and unexpected detours that forge faith—while revealing a different reason Moses never entered the land.

Covert-operation titles focus on Israel’s elite Sayeret Matkal, including The Sayeret Warriors of Rephaim and Scar & Sicarius: The Odessa Squad, which parallel real missions such as the 1976 Entebbe raid through high-stakes drama.

Health and fitness books draw from Boatright’s own major waistline reduction and vitality into his late sixties. The Catabolic Diet & Fitness Program and Ironclad Fitness use nutrition scoring, circadian timing, and kinetic-chain training to drop weight and build strength. Golf titles like Golfer’s Power Matrix combine natural mechanics with fitness and diet for lifelong health, supporting homeschoolers and veterans.

Rounding out the collection, The Alpha Male Gentleman offers a practical guide to quiet charisma, high confidence, authentic masculinity, unshakable faith, respect, purpose, and age-defying vitality in a culture that often discourages traditional strength. Together, these accessible, results-oriented titles support spiritual growth and lasting physical vitality.

text:
Global News Brief 
1. Financial Times: China’s economy grew 4.5% year-on-year in the third quarter, beating forecasts of 4.4% and accelerating from 4.3% in the previous quarter, as AI-driven exports offset weak consumer spending and investment. Growth reached 4.6% for the first nine months, within the government’s full-year target of 4.5–5.0%.

2. Sports Illustrated: WNBA semifinal openers drew 1.12 million and 1.17 million viewers, down 44–47% from the 2.11 million who watched Caitlin Clark’s Indiana Fever in their first-round opener. The figures highlight Clark’s drawing power, although different matchups and broadcasters also affect comparisons. Despite Indiana’s elimination, the playoffs began strongly, with first-round viewership averaging a record 1.3 million, up 37% from last year.

3. NY Times: France plans to impose curfews following nationwide unrest described as the country’s worst riots in decades. The prime minister defended the police response and pledged to restore order, while government ministers acknowledged failures in handling the violence.

4. Ynet: Turkish-Israeli woman Claudia Medina Halfon was reportedly surrounded and chased by roughly 20–25 anti-Israel protesters at Istanbul’s Istinye Park mall on Sunday. Demonstrators shouted “terrorist” and “child killer” before a physical scuffle prompted security guards to intervene and escort her to safety. Turkish authorities launched an investigation, while Israel’s Foreign Ministry condemned the harassment and accused Turkey of fueling hostility toward Israelis.

5. Washington Post: Israeli police arrested 11 suspects on Monday following West Bank settler attacks on Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine and European diplomats during the Palestinian olive harvest. Levine suffered broken ribs and vertebrae and required finger surgery after Friday’s assault in Abu Falah; diplomats were attacked the following day in Taybeh. The arrests followed international demands for action, though police did not identify the suspects or specify their alleged roles.

6. Yahoo Sports: Viral claims that Caitlin Clark has received overseas offers worth $50 million to $100 million remain unverified, with no official announcement from Clark, her representatives, the Indiana Fever or a European club. The speculation reflects her global popularity and ongoing debate over WNBA salaries and labor conditions.

7. The Telegraph: Britain’s Chancellor is reportedly considering imposing income tax on transfers of family businesses to the next generation, potentially almost doubling the tax bill. In France, President Emmanuel Macron said public gatherings could be banned “when necessary” to curb unrest after nationwide protests saw government buildings torched and shops looted.

8. Reuters: Kenya has confirmed its eighth Ebola case, a 49-year-old patient attendant believed to have been exposed while caring for the country’s first patient, who returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo and died in Nairobi on October 5. The latest patient tested positive while in quarantine, and authorities say there is no evidence of community transmission. The case comes as Congo’s outbreak spreads to an eighth province, with more than 9,400 cases and 4,500 deaths reported, heightening concerns about regional transmission.

9. 1440 Daily Digest: Japan is scheduled to launch its five-year Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission today.  ET to study Mars’ moons, Phobos and Deimos, and return samples from Phobos to Earth. Due to reach Mars in August 2027, the mission aims to determine whether the moons are captured asteroids or debris from an ancient collision, potentially shedding light on how Mars lost its thick atmosphere and surface water.

10. The Times of Israel:  PM Candidate, Benny Gantz has withdrawn from Israel’s election race eight days before the vote. I couldn’t access the update’s text to confirm further details; earlier reporting said his Blue and White party was polling below the 3.25% electoral threshold and that he had pledged to withdraw rather than waste supporters’ votes.

11. Financial Times: Private equity group Charlesbank has agreed to invest in Los Angeles-based Wood Smith Henning & Berman at a reported valuation of approximately $700 million, marking one of the largest private equity deals involving a U.S. law firm. WSHB has nearly 600 lawyers across 43 U.S. offices and specializes in liability defence, a sector attracting investors for its steady cash flows and consolidation potential. Revenue was not disclosed in the excerpt.

12. Naval News: Denmark is acquiring additional Norwegian Naval Strike Missiles to upgrade its navy’s frigates, expanding an agreement reached in late 2025. The government-to-government purchase includes a contract amendment worth approximately NOK 400 million with Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace to produce and deliver the missiles.

13. The National News-Cairo: Egypt has pledged support for Saudi Arabia amid escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi seeking parliamentary authorization for defensive military assistance if Riyadh requests it. Egypt’s National Defence Council said Saudi security is closely linked to Egyptian and wider Arab security, while calling for diplomatic efforts to ease tensions.

14. Yahoo Finance: Bitcoin rebounded above $82,000 on Monday as falling oil prices lifted investor appetite for riskier assets, reversing some of last week’s roughly 3% decline amid a technology-stock selloff and concerns about heavy spending on artificial intelligence caution.

15.  CNN: Ukraine launched one of its largest drone attacks on Russia this year overnight into Sunday, striking the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal despite President Donald Trump’s calls to halt attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Russia said it intercepted 1,015 drones, while local authorities reported one person killed and five wounded. The strikes came amid growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington, as President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities despite Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire that neither country had publicly confirmed.

16.  Epoch Times: Four Canadian service members lost their lives in the major fire at a military base in Alberta on Saturday evening that also left 39 injured, 19 of whom are in critical condition.

17.  Bloomberg: Boulder mayoral candidate and city council member Taishya Adams has drawn criticism from local Jewish leaders for declining to affirm Israel’s right to exist and refusing to sign the council’s joint condemnation of the June 2025 antisemitic firebombing that killed one person and injured a dozen others. Adams says she condemned the attack separately and withheld her signature because the statement omitted anti-Zionism as a motivation. Facing incumbent Mayor Aaron Brockett, she has also advocated divestment from companies linked to Israel’s military, amid concerns among Jewish residents about antisemitism and safety.

18. People: A kindergarten operator in Tianshui, China, was sentenced to life in prison after lead-containing paint was added to food served to more than 200 children. Principal Zhu Jinglin received 15 years, while four kitchen workers were jailed for six to eight years. Authorities found that management instructed staff to use the inedible pigments to make meals more visually appealing. The poisoning emerged in July 2025, when children and staff were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels.

19.  The Epoch Times:  U.S. Customs and Border Protection reported that fiscal year 2026 was its first full fiscal year with no releases of migrants apprehended at the border into the United States, extending the streak to 17 consecutive months through September. Southwest border apprehensions totaled approximately 98,700, about 95% below the annual average under the Biden administration. The agency credited stronger enforcement and deterrence, while also reporting 250 miles of new border barriers and nearly 1 million pounds of drugs seized 63% above the previous four-year annual average.

20.  NY Times: Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, a Redemptorist Catholic priest, was killed when a heavy wooden crucifix detached from a wall and struck him during a livestreamed evening Mass at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church in Guayaquil, Ecuador. Worshippers rushed to help, but emergency responders confirmed his death at the scene. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed his passing; the cause of the crucifix’s detachment remains undetermined.

text:
In the West, we sit at the precipice of a decadent hill of destruction, in which people and groups who leant nothing to the creation of our world now stand ready to raze it to nothing. 
And the Men of the West are now offered two options: 
1) Sink in to a disposition of dismay, apathy, and fearful complaining while analyzing what was and what could have been. 
or
2) Take up the challenge to embrace resolve, to stand in the fray, fight back, and refuse to accept the zeitgeist of slothful fear. 

But who hopes for what is difficult to believe?
Let us take heart from our ancestors. 

For we in the West stand on the shoulders of giants, who built a world where we are afforded the time to chirp and type away, in the midst of immense, excessive comfort. Yet, they were men like you and me. They were men who stood up when the odds were stacked against them and didn’t fear for their comfort or security. 
In Texas we live by the lore of the Alamo.  A boisterous legend of 185+ Texians, who refused to ride under the cover of darkness through Mexican sentries to safety. Rather, they held fast under sure destruction and odds that were insurmountable—because they didn’t fight for themselves but for the hopes and prayers of liberty, a brighter world for the ones they loved. The ones they were charged to steward and protect. 

So what does their example implore us to do?
This season, this now, is not the time for despair or despondency. 
This life we’ve been granted calls for steadfast resolve, and fraternity, and action. 

And unfortunately for our adversaries, our Forefather Giants of the West, lived for hopes they could not see. Men like Washington, Lewis and Clark, Jefferson, Jackson, Lee, Stonewall, Houston, and TR fought their own barbarians at the gate. And they held fast. Their lives are marked by heroism and extreme sacrifice, but they didn’t live or act for these notions. These men acted out of the abundance of necessity, even when the chips were down. 
And their blood runs through our veins. 

So the mantle now comes to us, and we must choose the latter option from above: of resolute courage in the face of destructive forces. We must recognize the bonds that bind us, tied to centuries of mutual strife and conquest. Now we take those qualities and once again reconquest our continent for liberty and security of those we love. The conflict will not leave us unscathed, but together we will reclaim and preserve what they seek to annihilate. 

And this November is important as we all should vote accordingly: a vote for those that truly love our land alone and especially for those that our God loving founders would have tolerated. 
However, please don’t be naive enough to believe that we will stifle this invasion with ballots. The wolves are already parading as our elected sheep, and they move pieces in darkness to fracture the light. The tree of liberty is not refreshed with campaign promises. 

Our motto at Stonewall is “Stand Strong. Stand Together.“  A man must have a strong constitution and individual character, personal strength  like a stone. Stones, however, are easily fractured alone, but an ordered, conglomerate structure of stones is nearly impenetrable. So be the strong man your family deserves, and simultaneously don’t forsake the bonds that tie us together. Fraternal groups of like minded patriots will save our States, our Nation, and the West. 

Stand Strong. Stand Together.

BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY- On this day, Thursday, October 19, 1961, Braniff International Airways announced that the carrier had chosen the British Aerospace Corporation BAC One-11 203AE Twinjet for the Dallas-based carrier's short-haul local service routes. Braniff, a medium sized trunk carrier, was the first US airline to order the twinjet followed by Mohawk Airlines, a local service carrier, and American Airlines, a large trunk airline.

Powered by Rolls Royce Spey Fanjet engines, the One-11 was the first British Transport Aircraft to debut on US routes since July 25, 1955, when Capital Airlines inaugurated Vickers Viscount four-engine turboprop service. The basic tenet of the BAC One-11 was that it would allow airlines to replace aging piston and turboprop airliners and make it possible to create a profitable operation between two short-haul city pairs because of the lower seat mile costs of pure jet aircraft.

As an example, yearly ground support costs for a Convair or Martin twin were $49,994.50 compared to only $19,228.50 for BAC One-11 aircraft in January 1965, with both figures including $50.00 for a boarding stanchion sign. Braniff President Charles Edmund Beard commented on the efficiency of the new One-11, "We will benefit from the most favorable effect on Braniff's earnings of any fleet we have put into service. The One-11s have a lower seat mile cost than any aircraft in trunkline operations anywhere in the world.”

Braniff ordered twelve new One-11s with the first six delivered in October 1964, and the remaining six in the summer of 1965. Braniff eventually placed an order for a total of 26 BAC Fastback Jets, as Braniff dubbed them, with the first, registered as N1543, delivered to the Dallas Love Field base on March 13, 1965. Company officials accepted the aircraft at Newark, New Jersey, before it continued on to Dallas. The second aircraft delivered was Ship N1544 on April 6, 1965.

With the new BAC order Braniff became the first US airline to order the new short-range jet. Braniff, however, was the second US airline, behind Mohawk Airlines, to receive and operate the new regional jet, which replaced DC-6, DC-7, Electra and Convair aircraft on certain routes. The BAC Jet could seat 69 five abreast passengers in a mixed configuration and cruise at speeds of up to 540-miles-per-hour.

Braniff Airways, Incorporated's, order, announced by President Charles Edmund Beard, cost $35 million USD for the new aircraft, engines and spare parts. A $1 million USD BAC One-11 simulator was later purchased on January 25, 1963, and placed in service in the North Extension at the Dallas Love Field Operations and Maintenance Base at 7701 Lemmon Avenue. Mr. Beard noted that, "We know of no aircraft which has been as thoroughly checked and studied prior to order as the check on cost, both investment and operating, and performance we gave this aircraft. The amount of money involved was substantial for any airline and tremendous for us.”

The initial BAC order was firm for six aircraft with an option for six additional twin jets. On March 6, 1963, Braniff exercised its options for the six additional aircraft bringing the total order to 12 aircraft. Two additional aircraft were ordered on February 13, 1964. These 14 aircraft were the only BAC jets delivered to Braniff even though an additional twelve would be ordered on September 29, 1964.

With the sale of Braniff to Greatamerica Corporation in 1964, and a subsequent management overhaul in 1965, Braniff decided to order Boeing 727 Trijet aircraft and canceled the remaining twelve One-11 jet orders, also in 1965. Braniff had already decided that the purchase of Boeing 727 aircraft should be executed prior to 1965, but the Airline's new management decided that the Boeing jet would be a better choice as the company intended to vacate many of its short-haul low density routes that were more suited to the smaller BAC Fastback Jet. Braniff's intention was to become a large long-haul domestic and international trunk carrier rather than a multi-faceted carrier as it had been for the past several decades. Essentially, at the time of its sale in 1964, Braniff was four airlines in one: a local service carrier; short-haul carrier; long-haul trunk; and finally a long-haul international airline.

On April 25, 1965, Braniff's first two BAC One-11 jets went into regularly scheduled passenger service. The New Jet service was inaugurated between Dallas and Houston; Dallas, Austin, San Antonio, and Corpus Christi; Dallas, Lubbock and Amarillo; Chicago, Kansas City, Wichita, Oklahoma City, Dallas, Houston, Corpus Christi, and Brownsville, Texas; Minneapolis/St Paul, Kansas City and Dallas; and finally Minneapolis, Des Moines and St Louis.

President Beard stated that had Braniff taken delivery of the new One-11s at the beginning of 1964, the airline would have realized an increase of $883,900 in operating income including depreciation for the first six months of operation. This figure was based on the BAC Jets replacing Braniff's entire fleet of DC-6 and DC-7s and 1/3 of the Convair 340/440 piston powered aircraft. Braniff operated 33 flights daily between Dallas and Houston Hobby, a distance of 240 miles using Convairs, Douglas DC-6s, Electras, and Boeing 720s offering a total of 2360 seats each day. The direct operating cost of flying the 33 daily flights was $12,607.00 USD each day. Mr. Beard explained that if this number of seats was provided daily with One-11s then the number of flights would increase to 33 from 38, which would be more appealing to Braniff passengers and cause operating income to increase to $1437.00 USD daily or $523,068.00 USD yearly.

Mr. Beard offered as an additional example, a longer route between Dallas and Amarillo, a distance of 323 miles, to emphasize the cost efficiencies of the BAC Jets. Braniff service featured four daily roundtrips between the two cities using Electra Jets and Convairs. Two of the roundtrips were flown with Electras which featured similarly low seat mile costs. However, when One-11 costs were applied to the two Amarillo Electra flights the costs savings were substantial. Operating income would increase $91,728.00 USD per year because of efficiency of the BAC Jets. Similarly, Braniff operated 19 trips or 992 seats daily between Kansas City and Omaha, a distance of 165 miles, using Electras, Convairs, and DC-6 aircraft. The same number of seats could be provided with only 14 One-11 roundtrips which resulted in an increase in operating income of $180,544.00 USD annually.

Braniff's new regional jets were ordered without the tail cone airstairs to save money and weight. The front airstairs were ordered for operation at airports without jetways. The carrier also saved $10 USD per aircraft by reducing the foam padding in the copilot's seat. Braniff named their BAC jets One-11 Jet and also called them The New Jet as well as Fastback Jet in its various initial advertising and promotional campaigns. The Fastback moniker came about as a result of the jet's engines being aft mounted and fastback automobile styling, which featured a continuous sloping of the roofline down to the rear of the car resulting in a lower drag coefficient.

Braniff operated their BAC jets in scheduled service until 1973, with many of them going first to Mohawk and then to Allegheny as a result of the two carrier's merging. However, Braniff's first BAC One-11 N1543 remained with the carrier until 1977. Ship N1543 was outfitted in a corporate configuration and was leased to companies in need of executive transportation.

Photo: A beautiful Braniff International Airways BAC One-11 203AE is parked on the ramp at Braniff’s Operations and Maintenance Base at Dallas Love Field in 1965. The little British Aircraft Corporation Twinjet is painted in the 1959 Red and Blue El Dorado Super Jet Color Scheme.
