News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Monday, October 19, 2026 · 11:59 PM ET

Two teams took big leads on Monday night. One kept adding to its lead and is going to the World Series. The other stopped adding, started holding, and needed a fourth-down breakup at the goal line and a sack on the last snap to get out of its own building with a win.

That was the whole day. Some people build a lead and then protect it. Other people build a lead and then keep building. The first group calls it being careful. The second group calls it Monday.

Adding versus holding. Here is how Monday made the case.

Sunday was the gun versus the clock, and it gets one echo, and this is it: Sunday said the teams that own the clock rarely need the gun. Monday added a footnote. Owning the clock only works if you keep spending it. The moment you start sitting on it, the clock starts working for the other side.

Start in St. Petersburg, because the Rays wrote the cleanest version of the argument at Tropicana Field.

The Tampa Bay Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 7–3 in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series. They won the series 4–2. They are going to the World Series for the third time in the franchise's 29 seasons.

They will play the Milwaukee Brewers. Neither franchise has ever won a World Series. The Associated Press noted it is the first matchup in which both teams are chasing their first title since 1980, when the Phillies beat the Royals. Game 1 is Friday night in Milwaukee.

"We got one more bite!" Kevin Cash told his team as the clubhouse celebration started.

Now look at how they got there, inning by inning, because the line score is the essay.

Second inning. Junior Caminero led off with a single off opener Shawn Armstrong. Tim Herrin came in. Chandler Simpson reached on a fielder's choice and stole second. Victor Mesa Jr. walked. Simpson took third on a Jonny DeLuca flyout. Mesa stole second. Richie Palacios looped a double into right-center. Two runs. Rays 2, Guardians 0.

Third inning. DeLuca hit a sacrifice fly off Joey Cantillo. Rays 3, Guardians 0.

Here is the honest part, because a thesis that hides its own counterevidence is just a slogan. In the third, the Rays loaded the bases with nobody out and did not break it open. AP said it plainly: they missed an opportunity to put the game away. For a few innings, Tampa Bay looked like a team that had built a lead and was now going to sit on it.

Sixth inning. Nathaniel Lowe singled in Cleveland's first run. Rays 3, Guardians 1. The lead was still there, but it was getting thinner, and thinner leads make managers nervous and make crowds quiet.

Then came the seventh, and the Rays did the thing this whole essay is about. They did not hold. They added.

Caminero, who hit 42 home runs in the regular season, had gone 32 October at-bats without a home run. With a man on in the seventh, in his 33rd, he faced Cade Smith, Cleveland's All-Star closer, and Smith threw him a splitter. Caminero sent it off the left-field foul pole. Two runs. Rays 5, Guardians 1. AP reported he became the first player to homer off a Smith splitter.

He did not jog. He turned around before he reached first base, looked toward his dugout, and pounded his chest with both arms. He cupped his ear rounding second. He stopped before the plate, pointed into the stands, and crossed his arms before he touched home. You are allowed to do all of that when you have just turned a two-run lead into a four-run lead in the seventh inning of a pennant clincher.

And here is why adding matters, proven by the very next half-inning.

The Guardians did not quit. They loaded the bases against Tyler Wells and Ian Seymour on two singles and a walk with two outs. Seymour walked Patrick Bailey to force in a run. Then he hit Angel Martínez with a pitch to force in another. Rays 5, Guardians 3. The go-ahead run was standing at first base.

Do the math the other way. If Caminero's ball hooks foul, if the Rays had held at 3–1 instead of adding, that eighth inning is not a scare. It is a tie game or a Cleveland lead, with the bases loaded and a sellout crowd watching its season turn.

Instead, Kevin Kelly came in and struck out Brayan Rocchio on three changeups. Bases loaded, inning over.

"Credit to our guys," Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said. "It's a gut punch there in the seventh. And our guys came right back. Our guys never quit. They never stopped fighting. That's who they are."

He was right about his team. They came right back. They just came back against a lead that had already been padded, and padding is the difference between a rally and a comeback.

Then the Rays added again.

Yandy Díaz had guaranteed a Game 6 win through an interpreter on Sunday. In the bottom of the eighth, he hit a two-run homer off Hunter Gaddis. Rays 7, Guardians 3. The four-run cushion that Cleveland had just spent two outs and two forced runs shrinking was back, whole, in one swing.

That is the pattern. Two in the second. One in the third. Two in the seventh. Two in the eighth. Every time Cleveland took something away, Tampa Bay put more back. The Rays never asked their bullpen to protect a margin that was getting smaller. They kept making it bigger.

Closer Bryan Baker finished it. He was on the mound for the final out, and the image of the night is him with both arms in the air and his glove raised high, the dugout spilling onto the field behind him. That is the photo on this post: Baker, number 17, ALCS and Postseason signage behind him, a building that had a roof shredded by a hurricane two years ago now full and screaming.

Freddy Peralta was named ALCS MVP. He threw 5 1/3 gritty innings on Monday and allowed one run and five hits. It was his second win of the series in his third appearance. He threw six scoreless innings to win Game 2 and got two outs in relief in Game 4. Three appearances, every one of them asked to do a different job, every one of them done.

Now the building, because the building is part of the argument.

A sellout crowd of 40,230 waved yellow-and-blue rally towels, rang cowbells, and chanted "Let's go Rays!" all night at Tropicana Field. Hurricane Milton shredded that roof two years ago and caused damage throughout the stadium. The Rays played their 2025 home games across the bay in Tampa, at the Yankees' spring training complex. They got new ownership before this season. They secured a deal for a new stadium near the Buccaneers, to be ready in 2029. Then they came back to the Trop and won 55 games at home in the regular season. Only the Brewers won that many at home.

Read that list again. Every item is an addition. A team that lost its building did not spend the year protecting what was left. It added owners, added a stadium plan, added home wins, and on Monday added runs in four different innings.

"This is for you!" Caminero yelled into a microphone on the field after the game. "Let's go! I can't hear you!"

And the date. Monday was the 18-year anniversary of the Rays' first American League pennant, in 2008. Same franchise, same building, same October night, 18 years apart. Anniversaries are usually about holding on to a memory. The Rays used theirs to add a new one on top of it.

The series itself followed the same shape. After sweeping the Yankees in the Division Series, the Rays fell behind Cleveland 0–1 and then 1–2. They did not try to steady themselves. They won three straight.

There is a technical footnote that belongs here too, because it shows what the other side was forced into. Shawn Armstrong, who was also Cleveland's opener in Game 4, faced the first four batters on Monday. AP reported he became the first pitcher in postseason history to start a game after pitching on both of the previous two days. That is what holding looks like from the trailing side. You are not building anything. You are patching, with the same arms, three days running.

The loss extended Cleveland's World Series championship drought to 78 years.

"I couldn't be more proud of our group," Vogt said. "It just hurts. It stings. Really felt like we had a team to go and just weren't able to get there."

That quote deserves to be read without a joke attached. Cleveland fought back in the sixth and again in the eighth. It is not a team that quit. It ran into a team that refused to stop adding.

Now go west, to Santa Clara, where the other half of the argument happened, and where it nearly flipped.

The San Francisco 49ers beat the Washington Commanders 23–17 on Monday Night Football. The 49ers are 6–0. Washington is 1–4–1.

For a half, this was the most complete adding performance of the season.

San Francisco scored touchdowns on its first two drives. Brock Purdy hit Mike Evans for 24 yards on the third play of the game and finished that drive with an 11-yard touchdown pass to George Kittle. Christian McCaffrey ran one in from a yard out. Then, with 13 seconds left in the half, McCaffrey ran in another from a yard out, at the end of a 14-play, 69-yard drive that took 6:13. The 49ers led 20–3 at halftime.

The first-half numbers look like a typo. Pro Football Talk had the Commanders at 17 plays, two first downs, and 90 yards. The 49ers had 41 plays, 17 first downs, and 303 yards. AP put it the most memorable way: San Francisco gained as many first downs in the first half as Washington ran plays.

Washington's best first-half chance at a touchdown ended when Jayden Daniels threw the ball away on fourth-and-2 from the 13.

In the third quarter, Eddy Piñeiro hit a 33-yard field goal at the end of an 11-play, 65-yard drive that took 6:05. San Francisco 23, Washington 3.

Pause on that drive, because it was the last real addition the 49ers made all night.

From that point, San Francisco stopped adding and started holding. Pro Football Talk tallied it: the 49ers' last three drives were three-and-outs that gained a total of 7 yards. Washington outgained San Francisco 224 to 72 in the second half.

And the other side added.

With 15 seconds left in the third quarter, Daniels hit Diggs from a yard out to finish an 11-play, 65-yard drive. San Francisco 23, Washington 10. With 9:22 left in the game, Daniels found running back R. White for a 9-yard touchdown at the end of a 10-play, 80-yard drive. San Francisco 23, Washington 17.

A 20-point lead had become a six-point lead, and the team holding it was not moving the ball.

Then came the part of the night where holding nearly failed outright.

On Washington's next-to-last possession, Romello Height sacked Daniels with 2:55 left, and the 49ers looked like they had the stop. But Ashtyn Davis was flagged for illegal contact. PFT counted four defensive penalties by San Francisco that handed Washington first downs.

Washington drove to a fourth down at the San Francisco 17. Daniels threw for Treylon Burks in the end zone. Burks had it, briefly, before Malik Mustapha knocked it loose as Burks hit the ground. Incomplete, with 1:54 to play.

That should have been the end. It wasn't, because a team that is holding cannot also add, and San Francisco went three-and-out again.

On the punt, 49ers gunner Siran Neal was called for fair catch interference. Fifteen yards. Washington got the ball at its own 46 with 52 seconds left. A second chance at a miracle, gifted.

The Commanders moved to the San Francisco 28. Then Daniels was called for intentional grounding, which pushed them back to the 40 for one last snap. Keion White and Ogbo Okoronkwo got to Daniels before he could throw the desperation pass. Sack. Game over. It was one of four 49ers sacks on the night.

So yes, the 49ers held. They are 6–0. ESPN's AP recap noted it is their best start since they won their first eight games in 2019 on the way to a Super Bowl appearance. A win is a win and an unbeaten record is an unbeaten record.

But look at how differently the two leads behaved.

The Rays led 3–1 and then added four. Their lead got bigger in the late innings, so when the opponent rallied, the rally hit a wall.

The 49ers led 23–3 and then added nothing. Their lead got smaller in every late possession, so when the opponent rallied, the rally reached the 17 and then the 28, and the game came down to a hand on a ball and a pass rush on the final snap.

The Rays never needed a miracle stop. The 49ers needed two.

There is a history lesson sitting on the sideline that makes this almost too neat.

Kyle Shanahan spent two years as Dan Quinn's offensive coordinator in Atlanta. That run included the Super Bowl after the 2016 season, when the Falcons blew a 28–3 lead to New England. Monday night, Shanahan's team led Quinn's team 23–3. Same two men, a lead of almost exactly the same shape, and the trailing side clawing back in the second half.

This time the lead held. Barely. And it held on defense, after the offense stopped adding. The lesson of 28–3 was never that big leads are fragile. It was that leads stop growing the moment you start trying to protect them, and a lead that stops growing is already shrinking.

To be fair to San Francisco, there were reasons the offense stalled. Mike Evans left late in the first half with an Achilles injury after three catches for 94 yards. He had missed practice during the week with soreness in the tendon and broken ribs. Washington lost Terry McLaurin to a left knee injury in the first quarter; he left on a cart in an air cast. Javon Kinlaw also left Washington's line with a knee injury. Both teams lost their best receiver. Only one of them kept finding plays without him: Daniels finished 29 of 40 for 300 yards and two touchdowns, and nine different Washington receivers caught a pass.

The individual line that will outlive this game belongs to Purdy. He went 21 of 29 for 264 yards and a touchdown. In doing so he passed the 1,500-attempt threshold, and according to the AP recap he officially became the highest-rated passer in NFL history, at 105.6, ahead of Lamar Jackson's 102.7.

Think about what passer rating actually rewards. It is a career of adding: completions, yards per attempt, touchdowns, without giving it back in interceptions. Purdy crossed into first place all-time on the same night his offense went three-and-out three times in a row. Both things are true. A career is the long version of adding. A fourth quarter is where you find out whether you remember how.

McCaffrey rushed 16 times for 64 yards and two touchdowns and caught nine passes for 53 yards. Kittle had five catches for 69 yards and the opening touchdown. The 49ers are 6–0 and 4–0 at home, and they visit Atlanta on Sunday. Washington goes into a bye and hosts Philadelphia on November 1, a week after a tie with the Giants in which, AP noted, it mismanaged the overtime clock and cost itself a shot at a winning field goal. That is Sunday's lesson again, from the other direction: Washington spent last week losing the clock and this week losing a 20-point first half.

Now leave the stadiums, because Monday made the same argument in places with no scoreboard.

In Tehran, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived on Monday for his first visit since the Middle East war broke out. Al Arabiya reported he was scheduled to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and hold talks with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Lavrov has said Moscow's efforts are "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war." The trip follows Vladimir Putin telling Pezeshkian in early October that Russia was ready to help mediate.

At a joint press conference, Araghchi blamed Washington for the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz. "The war imposed by the United States and the Zionist regime, combined with the economic blockade, constitutes the principal source of insecurity in our region," he said. Reuters, via Dawn, reported he called on regional countries to work toward a joint security arrangement and said, "We welcome any initiative that leads to security from within without the presence of foreign forces." Those are his claims, quoted, not endorsed.

The offer on the table has not changed, and that is the point. On Sunday in Baghdad, at a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, Araghchi said Iran's seven-day plan to reopen the strait was "still on the table." If Washington meets Iran's conditions, he said, the strait reopens on day six and negotiations resume on day seven. Reuters reported those conditions include lifting the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports, lifting sanctions on Iran's oil exports, and ending hostilities on all regional fronts. Iran first presented the plan in mid-September after an interim ceasefire collapsed.

Washington's position has not changed either. Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity. Reuters described the central disagreement as Washington wanting the nuclear program addressed from the start, while Tehran wants talks to begin with reopening the strait.

So here is the diplomatic version of a lead nobody is adding to. Both sides are holding a position. Neither is building on it. Iran adds a visitor, Russia, and a new venue for the same offer. The United States holds the blockade. Al Arabiya reported Iran claims control over the waterway and regularly targets ships that cross without its authorization, and that the U.S. maintains a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports. The war began in February with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. There was a ceasefire in April and a U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding in June, and hostilities around the strait never stopped. Reuters put the war at eight months. Before it, about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas moved through that water.

When both sides are only holding, nobody's lead grows, and the thing in the middle stays shut. That is not a prediction. It is just what holding produces.

Then there is the one story on Monday about someone who spent 43 years adding.

Christiane Amanpour, CNN's chief international anchor, said Monday she will leave the network next June. "After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" she said in a statement reported by CNN's Brian Stelter.

She is 68. AP noted she started at CNN as an entry-level assistant and rose to become one of the most visible correspondents in television. She has hosted her own interview program on CNN International since 2009. In January 2025 she scaled back to a few days a week. In January 2027 the show moves to once a week, and it ends in May. She will keep reporting and traveling for CNN through June. "Amanpour & Company," her PBS program, ends in December.

Her own list of what she added is the résumé of the last four decades of war: "From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between." It is the teams and camaraderie that counted, she said, as they "battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity."

CNN chairman Mark Thompson announced it in a memo Monday morning and said the two had been discussing it for months. "I'm very sorry to see her go," he wrote, "but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally."

She did not give a reason. CNN reported she said she "will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism." The Los Angeles Times and The Guardian have reported on her earlier public concern about the Paramount Skydance acquisition of CNN's parent company. Connect those dots yourself or don't; she didn't.

Her closing line was the cleanest sentence anyone said all day: "Remember: always be truthful, not neutral."

Notice what she did not say. She did not say she was protecting a legacy. She said there are "interesting new projects down the line." Forty-three years in and she is still talking like someone adding, not someone holding.

So line the day up.

The Rays led and kept adding: two, one, two, two. They are going to the World Series, on the anniversary of the first time they went.

The 49ers led by 20 and stopped adding. They held on by a forced-out football at the goal line and a sack on the last snap. They are unbeaten, and they know how close Monday came to being the night that ended it.

Iran and the United States are each holding a position. The strait stays shut and Moscow flies in to add a voice to a conversation that is not moving.

And a 68-year-old journalist with 43 years of additions behind her announced her exit by talking about what comes next.

Here is the lesson, and it is the same in every one of those rooms. A lead is not a thing you have. It is a thing you are doing. The second you stop doing it, it starts getting smaller, and the other side, which has nothing to protect, gets to spend every remaining minute adding.

The Rays understood that on Monday. Every time Cleveland took a run off the margin, Tampa Bay put two back. That is why their closer was standing on the mound with both arms up and the dugout pouring out behind him, instead of standing at the goal line hoping a defensive back could get a hand on it.

Sunday said own the clock. Monday said keep spending it.

The World Series starts Friday in Milwaukee. Two franchises that have never won it. Both of them got there by adding.

Adding versus holding. Pick a side before Friday.

If this was worth your night, follow Grok Man. Tomorrow's lead is already being built.

text:
Alberta’s long-running separatist movement holds another vote today. Votes will be hand-counted overnight, with results expected by mid-morning tomorrow.

The movement has roots going back decades (Western alienation, equalization, resource control) and has waxed and waned with federal politics—stronger under Liberal governments in Ottawa, quieter under Conservatives.

“Let the Eastern bastards freeze in the dark.” This famous bumper sticker became a symbol of Alberta anger during Pierre Trudeau’s National Energy Program (NEP) in the early 1980s. The NEP tried to keep Canadian oil prices below world levels and increase federal revenue from Alberta’s oil boom; many Albertans saw it as Ottawa “milking” the province. Support for separation spiked around this time but later faded.

Alberta would be an oil superpower—but landlocked. The province holds the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves (mostly oil sands), after Venezuela, Saudi Arabia, and Iran. Roughly 90% of its crude exports already go to the United States. An independent Alberta would still be landlocked, so any pipelines to tidewater would require deals with Canada or the U.S.

Separatists have shopped their case in Washington. Leaders of groups like the Alberta Prosperity Project met U.S. State Department officials multiple times to discuss what an independent Alberta could offer (including energy). Some in the movement have floated joining the U.S. as a state or territory; most mainstream supporters prefer full independence or a western Canadian union.

Support used to be tiny. In the 1970s, surveys in Calgary found only 2.7–4% of people even cautiously supportive of independence. The modern surge is often traced to Justin Trudeau’s 2015 election, later energy policies, and the Freedom Convoy era. Former Premier Jason Kenney has said the pandemic and convoy “radicalized” people and gave the movement a new cause after earlier fringe parties struggled.

Today’s vote is historic, with unusually high advance turnout. Albertans are voting on whether the province should remain in Canada or start the legal process toward a future binding separation referendum (plus nine other questions on immigration, provincial powers, etc.).

The result is non-binding and pre-vote polls consistently showed roughly 70–78% favouring staying in Canada. Let’s see how the results compare, but this historic poll will surely kickstart a long list of reforms regardless of what Albertans choose tonight.

text:
Happy Birthday Bela Lugosi

Lugosi was a legendary film star, best known for portraying Count Dracula in the iconic movie “Dracula” (1931), and appearing in numerous classic horror films in the ‘30s and ‘40s. Lugosi was born in 1882 in Lugos, Hungary. In 1920, he emigrated to the States, where his first film role was in the silent melodrama “The Command” (1923). Other parts followed, in which he played villains and continental types (which were seen as the same thing). In 1927, Lugosi was approached to star in a Broadway production of “Dracula”, adapted from Bram Stoker's novel. He opened to much fanfare and rave reviews. Despite this, Lugosi was not Universal’s first choice for the role when the studio began its film production in 1930. Paul Muni, Chester Morris and Conrad Veidt were all considered. Lugosi lobbied furiously and eventually won studio executives over, thanks in part to his acceptance of a "paltry" salary of $3,500. “Dracula” made him an international star, but it was as much a curse as a blessing. In the film, he appeared with minimal makeup, using his natural, heavily accented voice. Disdaining suggestions that he learn proper English and give up his tendency to surround himself with sycophantic Hungarians, dancing girls and goulash, Lugosi found himself typecast in films such as “Murders in the Rue Morgue” (1932). Characterised by an overweening arrogance, he auditioned for other roles, and was astounded when he didn’t get them because no one could understand what he was saying. Five films at Universal, including the fascinating and sexually deviant “The Black Cat” (1934), and “Son of Frankenstein” (1939), as well as two at RKO, “You'll Find Out” (1940) and the superb “The Body Snatcher” (1945), paired him with Boris Karloff. Lugosi inevitably received second billing. There are contradictory reports about his attitude towards Karloff, with most claiming he was openly resentful of the latter’s long-term success and ability to play roles outside the horror genre. Allegedly, the English actor’s insistence that the cast break for afternoon tea enraged the Magyar, who once threw a cucumber sandwich at a cameraman while uttering a string of curses. Lugosi played one conventional role in Sol Lesser's “The Return of Chandu”(1934), but his self-inflicted difficulties made his films dull and repetitive. He also developed chronic sciatica. The actor was treated with asparagus juice, but was eventually prescribed opiates, and his increasing dependence on morphine led to a decline in offers of work. However his profile rose in 1938, when a California theatre owner revived “Dracula” and “Frankenstein” as a double feature. Lugosi made a personal appearance, which thrilled new audiences who had never seen him before. Universal took note and rehired him. He appeared in “Son of Frankenstein” (1939), as Ygor, a mad blacksmith with a broken neck, in a splendid performance, and was relatively busy during the 1940s, working in three pictures for RKO and one for Columbia. He played Dracula for a second and final time in Abbott and Costello’s “Meet Frankenstein” (1948), which was his last "A" movie. The ageing actor was persuaded to seek treatment for his drug addiction, but had virtually no money. When Frank Sinatra heard of Lugosi's problems, he visited him in hospital and gave him a $1,000 cheque. Sinatra recalled Lugosi's astonishment, as the two men had never met before. Bela Lugosi died of a heart attack on August 16, 1956, aged 73. He was buried in his full Dracula costume and ring. Since his death he has become a cult figure, particularly among the young, something that one hopes would please him.

Amy’s Kitchen is bringing the debate over ultra-processed food into its latest national marketing campaign. Founded in 1987, the family-owned California company built its business around organic prepared food and now offers more than 150 varieties of frozen and packaged products, including vegan and gluten-free options. Its products are sold across the United States and in more than 11 other countries.

The new campaign puts Amy’s Non-UPF Verified certification from the Non-GMO Project at the center of its message. According to the company, nearly 90% of its product range has earned the designation. Amy’s wants shoppers to better understand how their food is made and reconsider assumptions about frozen meals. A survey of 2,000 Americans commissioned by the brand found that half of respondents were not confident they could distinguish processed from ultra-processed foods, while nearly half viewed frozen foods as unhealthy as, or worse than, chips and cookies.

The campaign launched in early October at Santa Monica’s Third Street Promenade with a 40-foot installation and the message “End the Era of Ultra-Processed Food” projected onto the Clock Tower Building. Running through November 15, the effort combines Meta ads, programmatic advertising and retail activations. Whole Foods Market activity began October 15, supported by in-store digital ads, freezer and shelf materials, and targeted advertising through Amazon DSP. MikMak retargeting connects interested shoppers directly with retailers through an add-to-cart option, carrying the campaign from a public installation to the grocery purchase.

text:
GenZ-led, the fiercest protest in history, in France 

The wave of protests, which quietly began in late September from working-class school premises in northern Paris, France, has escalated into a massive social upheaval, developing into one of the country's worst days of violence in years. The school gate blockades, initiated by high school students aged between 15 and 18, citing teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, dilapidated buildings unable to withstand extreme temperatures, lack of chairs and equipment, and inadequate facilities, quickly evolved into a broader national crisis concerning the cost of living, inequality, and public services.
Regarding this uprising, which was spearheaded by the slogans 'Neglected schools, sacrificed youth,' a 19-year-old told AFP news agency, 'Generation Z has risen, they want their voices to be heard.'

Thousands were arrested in the initial weeks of this movement, with some reports indicating that 87 percent of them were minors. Dozens of schools were set on fire or looted, and an incident was reported in Lens where a 15-year-old student lost an arm after being hit by a police stun grenade. By early October, particularly by October 6, the number of participants in the protests surged to between 250,000 and 450,000. Trade unions, teachers, and Yellow Vest protesters also lent their support. Paolo Stuppia, a sociologist at Sciences Po, points out that Generation Z is facing a multifaceted crisis comprising educational breakdowns, cost-of-living pressures, climate issues, the rise of the far-right, and uncertainties surrounding artificial intelligence. Similar youth-led cost-of-living protests were also observed during this period in other European countries, including Italy, Portugal, and Belgium.

This movement, sometimes dubbed 'Yellow and Young' by organizers, transformed into a massive day of protests across France on October 17. The Ministry of Interior estimated that approximately 550,000 people participated in over 100 cities, with about 110,000 gathering in Paris. However, the CGT trade union stated that participation was closer to 800,000. While most marches, comprising students, teachers, trade unions, and Yellow Vest supporters, remained peaceful, violence erupted at the fringes of the protests, especially as night fell.

Masked individuals forcibly entered and set fire to the historic city hall building in Limoges, central France, a 19th-century Neo-Renaissance architectural masterpiece opened in 1883. The fire caused significant collapse of its roof, and the iconic clock tower also fell, reminiscent of the 2019 Notre Dame Cathedral fire. Local authorities described it as a 'heritage disaster.' Approximately 2,000 people, including hundreds who anticipated violence, had initially gathered that day and blocked a highway, and regional officials stated that police units were helpless against a mob of hundreds.

The destruction did not stop there. The tourist office in Lyon was set ablaze, and individuals who broke into Marseille City Hall defaced its walls with graffiti. In numerous cities such as Paris, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, and Toulouse, barricades were constructed using trash bins and bicycles and set on fire, and many cars were also torched. Paris's Place de la République became a zone of intense clashes. It is estimated that approximately 1,500 establishments across the country, including supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury shops, clothing stores, and electronics stores, were looted. Officials noted that some of the looting was carried out by youths from poor suburban areas and opportunistic gangs.

Police attempted to control the situation using tear gas, water cannons, and baton charges, while protesters launched projectiles and fireworks. During the clashes in Saint-Étienne, a 17-year-old lost an arm after being hit by a crowd-control grenade. Criticisms of excessive force and accusations against the police force have been raised, with dozens of incidents currently under investigation.

Two deaths have been reported in connection with the protests. One protester died from a heart attack in or near Paris, which authorities have not directly linked to the violence. The other death was that of a 22-year-old police officer who was killed after being hit by a vehicle in Nantes. Over 500 to 1,000 police, gendarmerie, and firefighters were injured, some seriously. Many protesters were also injured. The number of arrests, recorded as 1,200 on the night of October 17, later rose to 1,800, and subsequently to 2,400 as reported. A record 855 people were arrested in Paris alone. Economic damage amounting to hundreds of millions of euros has been reported, and some city streets were described as resembling 'wastelands' during debris removal.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu accused far-left gangs and criminals of hijacking the marches. Mr. Nuñez, who later admitted that police control had been lost in some areas, offered his resignation, but President Emmanuel Macron rejected it.

Addressing the nation from the Élysée Palace on October 18, President Macron expressed his 'anger and shame,' questioning, 'How can the French people do this to France?' He distinguished between legitimate demands and unleashed violence, pledging that those who destroyed, looted, or attempted to undermine the Republic would be brought to justice. Although he did not declare a full state of emergency, he ordered a review of intelligence and preparedness, and empowered local prefects to ban certain gatherings. He also took steps to call for discussions with students, teachers, and trade unions.

Prime Minister Lecornu, who convened crisis management meetings, ordered a partial curfew in Paris's Place de la République and Les Halles areas, effective from 11:00 PM to 6:00 AM, leaving open the possibility of imposing a state of emergency if necessary. Similar restrictions or orders targeting minors were also imposed in cities including Marseille, Lyon, Nice, Lille, and Bordeaux. However, scattered unrest was still reported on October 18 and 19.

The emergence of this unrest approximately six months before the 2027 presidential election, in which Mr. Macron cannot seek re-election, has also become politically sensitive. While criticisms are being leveled against the government's preparedness in the face of weeks of student actions, analysts point out that this situation has elevated the political opportunities for far-right forces, including Marine Le Pen's National Rally, which is leading in opinion polls. Many mayors representing various parties have also criticized the government's actions, and the crisis, which began in school classrooms, has left a deep uncertainty in France's social and political landscape.

text:
Seven Victories in One Day. Then a Poem from the Enemy.

The invading army won seven battles in a single day.
Its enemy commander was letting it win.

It was 612.
Sui forces were advancing toward Pyongyang, the capital of Goguryeo, an ancient Korean kingdom.
Eulji Mundeok saw their hungry soldiers and kept retreating to draw them deeper in.

Earlier, Yuwen Shu, one of the Sui commanders, had urged a withdrawal: their provisions were exhausted.
Yu Zhongwen insisted that pursuing Eulji could still win them glory.

The Samguk Sagi records Yu’s angry reply:
“You command 100,000 men. If you cannot defeat this small enemy, how will you face the emperor?”

Encouraged by their victories, they crossed the Salsu River and camped near Pyongyang.

Then Eulji sent Yu a poem:

神策究天文
妙算窮地理
戰勝功旣高
知足願云止

“Your brilliant strategies have fathomed the heavens.
Your ingenious plans have mastered the earth.
Your victories have already brought you great glory.
I hope you know when enough is enough—and stop.”

The praise was a taunt.
Yu sent back a letter lecturing him.

Eulji then offered a false surrender: if the Sui withdrew, he would bring Goguryeo’s king to pay homage to their emperor.

With their soldiers exhausted and Pyongyang difficult to storm, the Sui commanders withdrew.
Goguryeo troops harried them from all sides.

At the Salsu River, when half the army had crossed, Eulji struck its rear.
The retreat became a rout.

The Samguk Sagi records that of the 305,000 men in the nine Sui armies that had crossed the Liao River, only 2,700 returned to Liaodong fortress.
The Sui emperor later imprisoned Yu.

If Yu had accepted the earlier call to withdraw, could the Sui have avoided disaster at Salsu?

text:
In August 1823, a trapper named Hugh Glass was walking ahead of his party along the Grand River in what is now South Dakota when he stumbled onto a grizzly bear with two cubs.

The bear tore him apart. By the time the other men got there and killed it, Glass had deep gashes all over his body, his scalp was ripped open, and his throat was so badly torn that he could barely breathe. Nobody thought he'd live through the night.

He did. And that became a problem.

The trappers were deep in Arikara country, and the Arikara had already killed a lot of men from this same outfit that summer. Carrying a dying man slowed everybody down. So the leader, Andrew Henry, offered extra pay to two men who would stay behind with Glass, wait for him to die, bury him, and then catch up.

One was an older trapper named John Fitzgerald. The other was a teenager. Tradition says it was a young Jim Bridger, who would later become one of the most famous mountain men in the West, though historians aren't completely sure.

They waited a few days. Glass didn't die. Then, the story goes, they got spooked by signs of Indians nearby. They took his rifle, his knife, and his gear, left him lying there, and rode off. When they caught up with the others, they said Glass was dead.

He wasn't.

When Glass came to, he was alone, unarmed, and so hurt he couldn't stand up. The nearest friendly post was Fort Kiowa on the Missouri River, roughly 200 miles away.

So he started crawling.

He lived on berries and roots. At one point, according to the accounts, he drove some wolves off a buffalo calf they'd killed and ate the raw meat. Little by little he got strong enough to stumble along on his feet. Somewhere along the way he may have gotten help from a band of Sioux. Weeks later, he made it to Fort Kiowa.

Most people would have stopped there. Glass went looking for the men who left him.

He traveled hundreds of miles more, survived another Arikara attack that killed the men he was traveling with, and finally walked into Henry's fort on the Bighorn River. He found the young man first. Glass was furious, but the kid was barely more than a boy, and Glass let him go.

Then he tracked down Fitzgerald, who by then had joined the Army at Fort Atkinson in Nebraska. Killing a U.S. soldier would have gotten Glass hanged. So he settled for getting his rifle back, and he walked away.

If you've seen The Revenant, a lot of that movie is made up. Glass didn't have a son who got murdered, and the real story didn't end in a revenge killing. It ended with a man who crawled back from the dead, found the people who left him, and decided not to kill either of them.

He went right back to trapping. About ten years later, in 1833, he was killed by Arikara warriors on the Yellowstone River.

text:
Tuesday--October 20, 2026—Sorrowful Mysteries
Peace and Justice Kissed—We see only injustice!

Ephesians 2:12-22
Psalm 85
Luke 12:35-38

Today’s reading from Ephesians tells us that Christ is our peace. He broke down the wall that divided people and, through the cross, created one new person in place of the two. That new person is the Church—the household of God. We are no longer strangers. We are built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ himself as the capstone, growing into a living temple where God dwells by the Spirit.

The psalm describes what that household is meant to be like: kindness and truth meet; justice and peace kiss. In ordinary life those things often pull against each other. Telling the truth can seem unkind. Doing justice can disturb the peace. We prefer softer stories that let us avoid the cost. At the cross those opposites are not smoothed over; they meet.

From the outside the cross looks like pure injustice. An innocent man is condemned and executed. No mercy is shown to him. That judgment is true as far as it goes. But the New Testament asks us to see the same event from the side of the Father and the Son. Jesus is not merely a victim overpowered by others. He freely offers himself. As true man he enters the full weight of our rupture—our alienation from God and from one another. As true God he can carry that weight without being destroyed by it, and he offers the whole of it back to the Father in love. Justice is not set aside or ignored; it is met from inside the human story by the one person able to bear it and remain faithful. Mercy is not a later softening of that justice. It is what becomes possible once the cost has been carried: those who were far off are given a way home. The enmity is put to death by the cross itself.

Because we now belong to that household, the Gospel can speak of us as servants who stay ready, lamps lit, waiting for the master’s return. The language is strong, yet the Master who comes does not exploit his servants. He girds himself and serves them. Our readiness is not the posture of slaves under a harsh lord. It is the posture of people who already live in the temple where justice and peace have kissed, and who wait for the one who has already served us at the cost of his life.

Keep the lamps lit—not out of fear, but because we are members of the household whose peace has already been established through the cross, and whose Master still comes to serve.

text:
📖Mark 1:4🕊
"John did baptize in the wilderness, and preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins." 

What does Mark 1:4 mean?
John 1:6–8 describes John the Baptist as the witness to the Light, which is Jesus. Luke 1:5–25 goes into greater detail about John's birth to an elderly priest and his formerly barren wife. Mark simply says, "John appeared." He introduces John as an adult already performing his public ministry—calling people to repent of their sins and baptizing those who did.

Baptism did not originate with John. According to Jewish sources, a stepped bath, called a mikveh, was ordained by the Midrash to purify people before entering the Temple, to cleanse the bride and groom before marriage, and for women after birth (Leviticus 12:1–5) or after menstruation (Leviticus 15:19–30). Its most revered use, however, was for Jewish converts. The mikveh needed to be filled (or mixed) with God-given water, as from rain, a river, or a melted glacier. Although the Jews currently have no temple to enter, the mikveh is still used for the latter purposes. In Jesus' time, it's believed it was also used to convert from one Jewish sect (Essene, Pharisee, etc.) to another.

"John's baptism," then, is a purification rite for those who agreed with his call to repent for the forgiveness of their sins. Rather than asking people to offer a sacrifice in the temple in Jerusalem, John offers a radical alternative for his era: simply repenting and being baptized. This message of repentance would be continued and furthered by Jesus.

text:
My Western Conference Standings predictions (with brief justifications)

1. San Antonio Spurs

I anticipate the Spurs to take their Finals momentum into the regular season. There’s a good chance Wemby is considered the best player in the world by the end of the season. I think Harper will play at an All-Star level, and they’ve upgraded their roster with the addition of Tobias Harris. They typically have a clean bill of health, and 60 wins could be on the cards.

2. Oklahoma City Thunder

The only reason I don’t have the Thunder as the number 1 seed is because I do think losing Lu Dort matters especially during the regular season, and I worry about J-Dub’s hamstrings. I think they’ll manage him during the season, and losing Dort may make them a better offensive team by subtraction, but he brought a ton of value with the defensive reps night in and night out. There’s something to be said about someone who can guard the other team’s best player over the course of a grueling 82-game season. It also complicates the managing of Alex Caruso during the regular season too, and he may have to play more to fill that void. 60 wins is still very likely here.

3. Houston Rockets

I could have some recency bias with spending so much time with the team this offseason, but it’s also reinforced how good I think this team will be this season. They’re elite defensively. They’re deep. The offensive process will be a lot better this season. The additional ball handlers are huge, and Ime Udoka reiterated to me the offense will have a lot more variety. I anticipate a leap from Amen Thompson too, which takes this team to a whole new level.

4. Minnesota Timberwolves

They’ll be incredibly fun, but they’ll also be really good. I pencil them in at fourth place in the conference because the Wolves do have a history of taking their foot off the gas during the regular season, and I think that will creep in at times too. I expect them to be one of the best transition teams in the league, and they’ll just generally be extremely tough to guard. They should still have enough defense and depth to secure a top-four seed.

5. Denver Nuggets

It feels as though the sentiment around the Nuggets hasn’t been this low for quite some time, and losing Peyton Watson hurts, but this is still a very good team when they’re healthy. They know how to stack regular season wins, and they’ll lean on what they’re good at. Always helps having a top-four player in the world, and a star duo that has so much chemistry they bring to the table every night.

6. Los Angeles Lakers

Having Luka Doncic is going to get the Lakers into the top-six because he’s that good. I wasn’t a huge fan of their offseason, but I trust JJ Redick enough to get the most out of this group over the course of 82 games. Their playing style will change and will be a little more fluid offensively, but I do worry about the defense and depth on the wings, and the backup center position will be an issue.

7. Phoenix Suns

The Suns had a quietly solid offseason, and they’ll be very competitive in the West. They’re not going to make any real noise, but they’re well coached, and their starting lineup knows how to win regular season games. They have a lot of guys that are going to put their hands up for playing time, and that healthy competition is going to keep good standards all season long.

8. Portland Trailblazers

There’s every chance that the Blazers finish above the Suns, but there are more question marks. I question the fit, I also think Damian Lillard will be carefully managed throughout the regular season which could hurt them in the standings. If Deni Avdija takes another leap then we are having a different conversation, but I have them in the top-eight.

9. Dallas Mavericks

Dallas may surprise a few teams this season, and walking into matchups with Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving is no joke. I actually like their pieces, and they impressed me during this offseason when spending time with the team, but ultimately the margin for error is low. I think Flagg takes a leap but Kyrie may be managed throughout the regular season too, and there’s also a chance the front office decides to sell high on Kyrie and a few role players before the trade deadline.

10. Utah Jazz

The Jazz are my big movers this season, and I wouldn’t be surprised if they finished higher than this. Youth for a few pieces is mainly the reason I have them here, but there’s a lot of internal growth I see coming out of this roster and they’ll be in most games every night. I do have questions about the lineups, the front court cluster and the size of the role Darryn Peterson will play as a rookie, but I trust Will Hardy to figure it out.

11. L.A. Clippers

The Clippers will be a competitive outfit for large portions of the season with a host of contributors. I trust in the coaching staff, but ultimately, it’s a roster that lacks star power. I think the fanbase will be proud of this team after the controversial offseason they had. Just missing out on the play-in feels on trend currently.

12. Golden State Warriors

The Warriors still have Steph Curry, and that matters when trying to win games, but him alone is also problem. The margin for error is zero with this team, and Yaxel Lendeborg is a critical addition. There are so many holes. Not having Jimmy Butler until later in the season, Draymond Green a year older, and the unreliability of Kristaps Porzingis means another disappointing campaign.

13. Memphis Grizzlies

I’m a fan of Memphis’ upside, and I think Cam Boozer could win Rookie of the Year, but this is a young team and they’ll ultimately lose a lot of games. They’ll be well coached and have good principles, but this is very much a growth year for them. Exciting future ahead.

14. Sacramento Kings

It seemed highly unlikely to say this before preseason, but I think losing Ben Simmons actually hurts this team a lot as someone who brought natural playmaking and connective tissue. I think they can be competitive to start the campaign with a healthy starting 5, but I anticipate them being sellers at the trade deadline, and they’ll dwindle towards the bottom of the standings as a result.

15. New Orleans Pelicans

I don’t think it will be long until the Pelicans start selling up shop. I think we are close to the end of the Zion Williamson experience. It’s only a matter of time before the offers for Herb Jones and Trey Murphy are too tempting to ignore. A strange roster that has pieces that can help other teams, but just so limited together. I think they move forward with Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen as they turn a new chapter towards the trade deadline.

Sidebars: 
- Injuries will ensure this list is completely inaccurate come April 

- There's a gap between the Spurs, OKC and the rest of the pack 

- For the first time in a long time, I think the East is very comfortably better than the West overall this year

🌙 QUIET TONIGHT… BUT COULD A PATTERN CHANGE FINALLY BE SHOWING UP?
A clear and cool night is ahead across Central Arkansas, with most overnight lows falling into the mid to upper 40s. The next several days remain mostly sunny and seasonable, with highs generally in the upper 70s to around 80°.
🔥 In the short term, the drought and fire danger remain the biggest concerns. Wildfire danger is HIGH across all 22 counties in our coverage area, and burn bans remain in effect across all 22. With dry vegetation and very little rain expected through the upcoming week, conditions remain favorable for fires to spread quickly.
🌾 The seasonal drought outlook does offer some longer-range hope, showing drought improvement across much of Central Arkansas and even the potential for drought removal across parts of the north through late January.
🌧️ And this is the part we’ll really be watching: the latest 8–14 day hazards outlook is highlighting the potential for heavy precipitation across Central Arkansas. text:
Today in History 
October 20th
1968
Jacqueline Kennedy Marries Aristotle Onassis

On October 20, 1968, former First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis married Greek shipping magnate Aristotle Onassis in a private ceremony on his island of Skorpios, Greece. The marriage captivated the world, marking a dramatic new chapter in the life of one of America’s most admired and recognizable women.

Five years earlier, Jacqueline had endured the assassination of her husband, President John F. Kennedy, in Dallas, Texas, on November 22, 1963. Her dignity and composure during the national tragedy earned her widespread admiration. However, behind her public image, she struggled with grief, intense media attention, and concerns about the safety of her two children, Caroline and John Jr.

The assassination of her brother-in-law, Senator Robert F. Kennedy, in June 1968 deepened her fears. Jacqueline reportedly became increasingly concerned that the Kennedy family was being targeted. Her relationship with Onassis, a wealthy and powerful international businessman, offered the possibility of greater privacy, security, and independence.

Onassis, who was 62 at the time, had built an enormous fortune through international shipping and was known for his luxurious lifestyle, influential connections, and ownership of the private Greek island where the wedding took place. Jacqueline, then 39, had known him for several years.

The wedding was a small Greek Orthodox ceremony attended by family members and close associates. Jacqueline’s children were present, symbolizing the beginning of a new family arrangement.

The marriage surprised many Americans. Some viewed it as a departure from the romanticized legacy of the Kennedy presidency, often remembered as Camelot. Others understood Jacqueline’s decision as an effort to reclaim control over her life after years of personal tragedy and relentless public scrutiny.

Following the wedding, Jacqueline became internationally known as “Jackie O.” The couple divided their time among Greece, Paris, and New York, frequently traveling aboard Onassis’s luxurious yacht, Christina. Despite their wealth and glamorous surroundings, their marriage reportedly experienced difficulties, including long periods apart and differences in lifestyle.

Their union lasted until Onassis died on March 15, 1975, at age 69. Jacqueline subsequently returned to a more independent life in New York City, eventually establishing a respected career in book publishing.

Historically, the marriage represented more than a union between two famous individuals. It reflected Jacqueline Kennedy’s determination to build a future beyond the tragedies that had defined her public life. Although controversial at the time, her decision demonstrated her willingness to challenge public expectations and pursue personal happiness on her own terms. #OTD

Across ten compositions, centuries of temptation, labor, excess, and consequence are recast as a visual reckoning with the systems we accept simply because someone declared them to be so. [NOTE: The source of inspiration for “Fiat Moria” is “Netherlandish Proverbs” by Bruegel. “Fiat Moria” is a loan word, and it's deliberate. Moria isn't Latin. It's Greek, and it's Erasmus's word. He built “In Praise of Folly” on it in 1509, out of the same Northern humanist world Bruegel was painting a generation later. text:
President Trump Attacks Ethiopia Over Its Grand Dam Ambitions, Renews Offer to Mediate Nile Dispute

CAIRO, Egypt (Somali Report) - US President Donald Trump has renewed his criticism of Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), raising the possibility of renewed American mediation in the dispute between Ethiopia and downstream countries Egypt and Sudan.

Speaking at a rally in Syracuse, New York, on October 9, Trump accused Ethiopia of taking “all the water from the Nile” and described US financing of the project as a mistake.

“They took all the water from the Nile River, and that is not good at all for Egypt. Now the river has no water in it, but I worked that out,” Trump said.

According to Egypt’s Al-Ahram Weekly, published on October 15, Trump’s remarks have revived discussions about restarting negotiations to reach a legally binding agreement governing the dam’s operation and water releases.

Salah Halima, deputy chairman of the Egyptian Council for African Affairs, said renewed US mediation could provide an opportunity to resolve the dispute. However, he warned that progress would depend on Ethiopia’s willingness to negotiate.

Ibrahim Menshawy, a Cairo University professor of international law, said any peaceful settlement must protect Egypt’s Nile water interests and follow international watercourse principles.

The dispute remains unresolved despite previous negotiations involving Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan, including US-hosted talks during Trump’s first presidential term.

Ethiopia maintains that the dam is essential for electricity generation and national development, while Egypt fears that its operation could threaten vital water supplies. Sudan has also raised concerns about dam coordination, information sharing and flooding risks.

Trump previously offered to restart high-level mediation in a January letter to Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi. In August, senior US adviser Massad Boulos also indicated Washington’s willingness to support renewed negotiations.

text:
First, Christa was raised a Christian. She was baptized. As a child, she read the Bible to her grandmother and her friends. She believes in Jesus. She does not reject Jesus. 

Second, you have a fundamental misunderstanding of Buddhism which is common. The Buddha is not a deity. He’s not even the only Buddha. Anyone can become a Buddha. Buddhism doesn’t have a deity. Buddhism isn’t a religion. It’s just a way of life. It’s not really incompatible with Christianity — other than that in Buddhism, one does not have to accept Jesus as the saviour. 

Siddhartha Gautama, who is called the Buddha, was a prince who lived his entire childhood in opulence never seeing anything but the inside of the palace walls. One day, at 29, he ventured outside the palace saw people suffering in abject poverty and disease. He was so affected by what he saw that he left his kingdom behind and went out into the world to find a way to ease suffering. 

He lived an acetic life for 6 years studying various religions and their teachings looking for an answer. He even starved himself until a young girl offered him a bowl of rice and he realized nothing so extreme would bring the answer to suffering. He then sat under a tree for days and was tempted by the devil who he rejected. 

He then began to teach that life is full of suffering but it is caused by lust, craving and ignorance. If one lives a moral life, does good for others and is compassionate above all, one can be freed from the endless cycle of suffering. 

If I sound a bit passionate in describing his story, it’s because Buddhism is what brought me back to Jesus. My childhood was a lot like Christa’s and I turned my back on the Lord when I was 15, at the worst of times because humans I asked for help who were a priest and 2 nuns, deserted me. I thought that was God deserting me. It took me decades to understand they were just flawed humans who chose not to help me for whatever reason. When things got worse after they didn’t step in to help, I stopped believing in the God they represented to me. 

Many decades later, I found Buddhism and it served as the first thing that ever explained my childhood and why I suffered so much. It gave me hope that I’d never had before. 

I already knew that the one thing humans need more than anything is compassion from another human. And that it is the one thing you rarely get, most especially when you are an abused child. Most of my life, I thought I was worthless and I just wanted to die. Buddhism gave me something to strive for while I was alive. 

Many of the teachings of Buddhism are similar to the teachings of Jesus that I already knew and I recognized that from my youth. But the Buddha lived 600 years before Jesus. That struck me. How could a holy man who lived centuries before Jesus in another part of the world that was never even exposed to Judaism have had such similar teachings? 

That’s when I began to explore writers who were Buddhists and became attracted to Christ’s teachings. And writers who were Christians and became interested in the tenets of Buddhism to help them become better Christians. 

And that’s where I began to wonder if perhaps I was really a believer of Christ but not of those who claimed to represent Him. That opened my heart. Then the Lord visited me and called me back to him 3 years ago. And then, Christ’s teachings took on an entirely new meaning for me. 

Perhaps Christa is on a very similar journey. That may be why the Lord showed me her story. I’m still not sure if it was because I needed to see I’m not the only one with such a wretched childhood. Maybe I should write and tell her my story and about how Jesus has changed me. But it seems she has others around her to do that. I’m awaiting more clarity. The Lord always provides. 

I took a few minutes to explain in hopes you would understand that some children feel rejected by the Lord and this is a path back. Buddhism is not evil or a cult. I still love its compassion teachings.

Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. text:
Make images : Guilfoyle–AKTOR–Vertical Gas Corridor: New Disclosures and Political Implications
Intelligence-style evidence assessment | 20 October 2026
The latest reporting establishes a significant intersection between U.S. energy diplomacy, AKTOR's commercial interests and Kimberly Guilfoyle's activities as ambassador to Greece. It does not, however, establish that Kyriakos Mitsotakis or Donald Trump personally participated in misconduct, blackmail or a coordinated political scheme.
The most important development is that the controversy has moved beyond press reporting into formal congressional scrutiny in Washington, while the Greek government has publicly responded to questions about the Vertical Gas Corridor.
1. What has been established?
The White House requested Guilfoyle's resignation on October 13, and she subsequently resigned. The departure followed multiple allegations of improper conduct, which she denies. The resignation is established; the underlying allegations are not judicial findings. 
The Wall Street Journal reported that AKTOR paid lobbyist Christos Marafatsos $160,000 through June 2026 for work establishing U.S. government connections. His presence alongside Guilfoyle in diplomatic meetings raises questions about potential conflicts of interest. 
On October 16, government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis rejected suggestions that the Corridor originated with Guilfoyle and said ministers had denied receiving threats. This is an official denial, not an independent resolution of the allegations. 
2. The AKTOR connection: Why it matters
The September 25 Wall Street Journal investigation reported several consequential details:
Guilfoyle promoted AKTOR-linked energy business during engagements with Balkan governments.
Marafatsos, a registered lobbyist for AKTOR, attended diplomatic meetings, reportedly without all participants knowing his commercial role.
AKTOR and state-backed DEPA established Atlantic-SEE LNG, pursuing agreements for U.S. LNG supplies across southeastern Europe.
AKTOR estimated potential pretax earnings of approximately €1.8 billion over 20 years from signed and prospective LNG arrangements.
AKTOR's lawyers disputed improper promotion, saying the company's participation in the Corridor preceded its relationship with Guilfoyle. Her lawyers also rejected the suggestion that she was exclusively promoting AKTOR. 
Analytical significance: The key issue is not whether AKTOR was entitled to pursue gas contracts. It is whether official U.S. diplomatic access was used to provide an undisclosed commercial advantage to a particular company.
That question requires meeting records, lobbying disclosures, procurement evidence and any applicable ethics findings.
3. Congressional scrutiny has become formal
On October 1, Representative Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio seeking explanations concerning Guilfoyle's conduct.
His letter specifically addressed the promotion of a Greek company, the participation of its lobbyist in official meetings, and reported remarks concerning possible political pressure on Greece. 
This is documented congressional oversight. It is not proof that the reported conduct occurred or that either country's head of government directed it.
4. What the October 19 disclosures add
Kathimerini's October 19 investigation examined Guilfoyle's relationship with the Trump family and her actual influence in Washington.
Sources interviewed by the newspaper offered conflicting accounts: some suggested that her political access was overstated, while others described officials treating her claims of direct access to Trump seriously. These are attributed accounts, not independently established descriptions of Trump's decision-making. 
This distinction matters because claiming access to the President is not evidence that the President authorized a particular commercial transaction.

Multiple independent fact-checkers (Snopes, Reuters, AFP, AAP FactCheck, Boom, and others) have thoroughly debunked it:

CNN never published any such article. A CNN spokesperson confirmed the image is fabricated/doctored.⁠Reuters
There is no University of California study (or any credible study) recommending penile COVID-19 vaccine injections or claiming the penis offers the “fastest release” of the vaccine. UC confirmed the claim is false.⁠Factcheck.afp
The doctor pictured is real (Mohitkumar Ardeshana, an internal medicine physician), but he told fact-checkers the article is “completely fake” and that he never made any such statements.⁠Snopes
The diagram showing a “safe area for injection” was taken from unrelated instructions for penile self-injection used in treating erectile dysfunction—not vaccines.⁠
