text:
PORTLAOISE, 18 MAY 1988 — WHO WAS WATCHING, AND WHO SUMMONED THE CAMERAS?

Thirty-eight years after the events outside Portlaoise Prison, two diplomatic telegrams raise questions that neither London nor Dublin appears to have satisfactorily answered.

There is something rather curious about the events outside Portlaoise Prison on 18 May 1988. Not simply what happened that day, but who was there to witness it—and, perhaps more importantly, how they came to be there in the first place.

For there was, it seems, an ITN television crew present. And its appearance was sufficiently troubling to provoke diplomatic exchanges between Dublin and London at the highest levels.

The British Government denied having anything to do with the crew's presence. Indeed, a diplomatic telegram dated 18 May 1988 records an assurance from the British Secretary of State that the United Kingdom authorities were not responsible for the television crew being there, nor had they supplied information to the media.

But the explanation offered was rather less convincing than the certainty of the denial.

Perhaps the journalists had been tipped off by a family. Perhaps the information had come from Sinn Féin. Nobody, it seems, could say with any confidence.

And therein lies a rather interesting question.

Who, precisely, was outside Portlaoise Prison that day? Who organised the presence of the television crew, and who knew enough about the unfolding events to ensure that cameras would be waiting?

There is, of course, another question—one that deserves to be asked without presuming the answer.

Was MI5, the British Security Service, operating outside Portlaoise Prison on 18 May 1988? And, if so, under whose authority, for what purpose, and under what cover?

Were any British intelligence officers present, either openly or operating under journalistic, diplomatic, police or other cover? Were any individuals acting on behalf of British intelligence agencies, whether directly or through intermediaries?

And were the Irish authorities aware of any such presence?

These are questions, not accusations. The surviving telegrams do not establish that MI5 was present, much less that its officers organised the television coverage.

But they do establish something important: that the presence of the cameras caused concern at the highest levels of government, and that the British authorities were anxious to distance themselves from responsibility.

A further telegram, dated 19 May, records a British Foreign Office minister expressing surprise that information might have originated from official sources. Yet the same correspondence acknowledges that the possibility of a leak from elsewhere could not be entirely excluded.

One might reasonably suppose that, almost four decades later, someone ought to be able to establish precisely what happened.

Who alerted ITN? Who authorised or facilitated access? Were intelligence reports prepared? Were British security or intelligence personnel operating in the area? And did any government department subsequently investigate how the television crew learned of the events?

If MI5 was not present, let that be established by a proper examination of the surviving records.

If it was present, the public is entitled to ask why, in what capacity, and with whose knowledge.

For the question is not whether a television camera happened to be pointed at Portlaoise Prison on a May morning in 1988.

The question is who knew where to point it—and why.

And until the relevant records are examined and the facts established, the denials issued in May 1988 remain just that: official denials, rather than independently verified answers.

THE KILLING ZONE | SEAN O'BRIEN

text:
Why Is Sake Offered to God -Kami- at Shinto Shrines? 🍶

At many Shinto shrines, sake is more than a drink. It is an offering.

Rice has long been sacred in Japanese culture, and sake is made by transforming rice through fermentation. Because of that, sake became closely connected with harvest rituals, festivals and offerings to the kami.

At Ise Jingu, several kinds of sacred sake are still prepared and offered during important ceremonies.

The idea is simple. People receive the gifts of nature. Then they return part of those gifts to the kami in gratitude.

After some ceremonies, sacred sake may also be shared with participants.

So in Shinto, drinking sake can sometimes mean more than celebration.

It can represent gratitude, connection and a shared blessing.

text:
Intel got an upgrade Monday. But JPMorgan still isn't calling it a Buy.

JPMorgan moved $INTC  from Underweight to Neutral and kept its $85 target. The stock rose about 4%.

The bullish case: AI agents need CPUs as well as GPUs, and tight supply of leading-edge silicon could lift Intel's earnings estimates through this season and into 2027. JPMorgan puts its 2028 EPS estimate roughly 15% above consensus.

But better earnings expectations don't automatically mean the business is recovering.

Intel's share of server CPU revenue has fallen from 77% to 53% since JPMorgan's 2022 downgrade. Outside foundry revenue was barely $1B annualized in the first half of 2026.

That is why Monday's upgrade matters less than it might sound. On Sept. 17, multiple higher price targets and an Outperform upgrade helped send the stock as much as 9% higher. This time, JPMorgan improved its stance without changing its target.

And $INTC remains down 20.1% since Oct. 6.including Friday's 5.79% drop.

→ If you're positioning $INTC for CPU pricing power, tighter supply helps the case. But the announced 10% price increase still needs to show up in realized pricing through a quarter.

→ If you're betting on the foundry turnaround or an SK hynix deal in Ohio, Monday offered no new proof. Those discussions remain preliminary.

Oct. 29 is where the earnings thesis meets the numbers. 

→ Will Q3 results and Q4 guidance support the improved outlook, or is the market getting ahead of the business?

text:
🌍 GLOBAL MARKET RECAP — OCTOBER 20, 2026
SpaceX & Netflix Day | Updated around 08:45 CEST

Wall Street's tech rebound did not travel to Asia: the Kospi is falling around 3–4% as foreign investors sell chipmakers again. Treasury yields rose back to 5.15%, France imposed curfews after violent protests, and Brent holds near $110. Tonight: SpaceX's first-ever earnings as a public company, and Netflix.

📜 ON THIS DAY — October 20, 1987
The day after Black Monday, before the opening bell, the Federal Reserve issued a one-sentence statement: it "affirmed today its readiness to serve as a source of liquidity to support the economic and financial system". Newly appointed Chairman Alan Greenspan let the market know that the lender of last resort was there. The Dow rebounded about 5.9% that day, and the crash did not turn into a banking crisis. It was the birth of what traders would later call the "Greenspan put": the belief that the Fed will step in when markets break. In 2026, with inflation at 3.7% and a December hike priced in, the question is whether that put still exists.

1️⃣ GLOBAL EQUITIES — A TECH REBOUND, NOT A BROAD ONE
Wall Street closed Monday mixed. The Nasdaq rose 1.11% to 26,431 and the S&P 500 0.41% to 7,691, while the Dow slipped 0.07% to 51,966 and the Russell 2000 gained 0.25%. Consumer discretionary rose 1.8% and technology 1.4%, with chip and memory stocks ending their long losing streaks as AI credit worries eased; Amazon gained almost 5%. But higher yields hit the rate-sensitive sectors: utilities fell 2%, real estate 1.2% and financials 0.8%. This morning U.S. futures are almost flat, with the S&P 500 near 7,744. [Inference] The rebound was led by the most oversold stocks; for it to become a recovery, it needs this week's earnings.

2️⃣ U.S. MACRO — THE CALENDAR IS EARNINGS
With the Fed in its quiet period and few data releases, the earnings season is driving the market. This morning General Motors, GE Aerospace, RTX, 3M and Northrop Grumman report before the open. After the close come Netflix, Intuitive Surgical, Capital One and above all SpaceX. Tomorrow evening Meta and Tesla follow. In the background, the main macro theme remains unchanged: inflation at 3.7%, producer prices at 6.3% and oil above $100.

3️⃣ BONDS & FED — YIELDS RISE AGAIN
Treasury yields resumed their climb on Monday. The 10-year rose 6 basis points to 5.15%, the 2-year 3 basis points to 4.77% and the 30-year 5 basis points to 5.48%. [Inference] After last week's flight-to-safety rally, the bond market is returning to the inflation theme: with oil near $110, the space for the Fed to remain patient is narrowing. The Fed meets on October 27–28; futures price no change in October and a high probability of a hike by December.

4️⃣ EUROPE & FX — FRANCE IN THE STREETS
Europe fell on Monday. The Stoxx 600 lost 0.8% to 639.56 and the CAC 40 1.1% to 7,868, with banks under pressure: Barclays fell about 2.5%. The reason was in Paris: cost-of-living protests over the weekend turned into riots and looting in Paris, Lyon and Marseille. About 2,400 people were arrested, the Prime Minister ordered localised curfews, including in Lille and parts of Paris, and the Interior Minister admitted that police had "lost control" in some cities. European futures point to a lower open this morning. The euro trades around $1.123, the dollar index near 101.8 and the yen around 158.2.

5️⃣ ASIA — SEOUL SELLS THE AI TRADE AGAIN
The tech rebound in New York did not convince Asia. The Kospi is falling around 3–4%, after Monday's 1.8% gain, as foreign investors and institutions return to selling: SK Hynix is down about 3.6% and Samsung 1.5%. A new AI infrastructure company, Elice Group, debuted almost 30% below its IPO price, a sign that financing for AI is becoming harder. The Nikkei is down about 1%, with SoftBank losing over 3%, Hong Kong around 1% and Australia 0.8%, while Shanghai is flat. [Inference] Asia is still treating the AI sell-off as a financing problem, not a temporary correction.

6️⃣ OIL, GOLD & COMMODITIES — BRENT HOLDS NEAR $110
Oil remains near its highs. Brent trades around $109.6 per barrel and the November WTI contract rose more than 2% on Monday to about $103.7. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites and reduced tanker traffic through Hormuz keep the risk premium high, while Iraq has increased its exports to more than 3.4 million barrels per day. President Trump said he has not made a final decision on the Russian sanctions waiver, which adds uncertainty. Gold trades around $4,145 an ounce, slightly lower as yields rise.

7️⃣ GEOPOLITICS — THE LULL NEARS BREAKING POINT
The situation around Iran is getting tenser. The Revolutionary Guards declared the Strait of Hormuz "closed" and threatened seven undersea internet cables that pass through it, while U.S. Central Command insists the Strait is "open for business". Iran says it has blacklisted 122 vessels. U.S. Defense Secretary Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Benjamin Netanyahu, who reportedly said there is "a job to finish", and reports say the Pentagon has prepared plans for new strikes if ordered. Iran's foreign minister says the seven-day ceasefire proposal is still available. Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov condemned the U.S.-Israeli attacks, and a Houthi attack in Yemen reportedly killed dozens. President Trump also threatened to withdraw U.S. forces from Europe, accusing European leaders of not helping on Iran.

8️⃣ SPACEX & AI — THE BIGGEST IPO FACES ITS FIRST TEST
Tonight SpaceX publishes its first results as a public company. Its June IPO was the largest in U.S. history at $135 per share; the stock peaked at $225.64 but now trades around $119.5, about 11% below the offer price, for a valuation of about $1.4 trillion. Day Two in Doha, Qatar, at the 2026 Global Security Forum #GSF2026 @GSECForum, co-hosted by @QIASSQatar and @TheSoufanCenter. 

“ I think Saudi Arabia is in a very difficult position,” said Ambassador Tom Barrack @USAMBTurkiye, questioning whether military force could resolve the war in Yemen.

“These kinetic reactions have never worked. It doesn’t work. It’s probably not likely that it’s going to work.”

Tom Barrack, President @POTUS Donald Trump’s @realDonaldTrump ambassador to Türkiye and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, who has also been involved in Lebanon [#Yemen coming soon?], is one of the president’s most influential and trusted advisers.

His remarks offered an unusually candid assessment of Saudi Arabia’s military campaign against the Houthis, Washington’s reluctance to become directly involved, and the changing American approach to security in the Middle East.

On Saudi Arabia, Yemen, and the Houthis

Barrack questioned what emerging regional security partnerships would actually mean for the war in Yemen, particularly as Saudi Arabia strengthens its relationships with Pakistan, Türkiye, and potentially Egypt.

“What does it mean if Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, maybe Egypt join in a situation as we have now with Houthis?”

“Does that mean that Turkey’s going to put ground troops with Saudi Arabia against Ansar Allah?”

“Does it mean the United States is going to send fighter jets?”

“Does it mean that Turkey is going to supply T-2 drones at no cost in this modern war?”

“Everybody’s trying to figure it out.”

On American military assistance to Saudi Arabia, Barrack drew a clear distinction between supporting Riyadh and entering another regional war.

“I think the president’s been clear that he supports Saudi Arabia and the backing that they need logistically he will supply.”

“America getting involved in the ground kinetic battle somewhere else seems fruitless.”

Barrack also questioned the long-term purpose of armed nonstate groups across the region, including the Houthis in Yemen, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and militias in Iraq.

“What’s the answer to Yemen with Ansar Allah, or Lebanon with Hezbollah, or Iraq with the militias?”

He argued that the solution must come from governments assuming responsibility for their own security and creating conditions in which armed groups no longer have a role.

“That’s not America’s job.”

Barrack also suggested that direct negotiations between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, facilitated by Oman, offered a more promising path than continued military escalation.

“To have a Qatari majlis and have people sit down and have coffee, or have the Houthis,  Ansar Allah sit down with Saudi, with Oman as an intermediary, or doing what Qatar is trying to do with us. They’ve been endlessly patient trying to mediate with us with Iran. Has to be a better solution.”

On America’s changing role in the Middle East

Barrack argued that the United States is not abandoning the region but changing the terms of its involvement.

“America is the guarantor to the world for the last 80 years. It’s no longer there.”

“What’s happening in this administration is not an abandonment. It’s a message for realignment.”

“The U.S. no longer wants to own, doesn’t need to own.”

He pointed to the failures of previous American interventions, particularly Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, and Syria.

“Iraq, what a disaster. We’re dealing with Iraq now from 2003 on, 23 years of failed policies.”

Barrack argued that Washington should support regional governments rather than attempt to control their political and military decisions.

text:
John Overdeck proposed to his wife in the spring of 2002, a few weeks before his new hedge fund started investing with about $27 million. Today that fund runs $85 billion, and he has offered her $723 million to settle the divorce.

She wants about $2.2 billion. And the bigger fight is with his co-founder.

Here's the backstory. Overdeck won a silver medal for the US at the International Mathematical Olympiad and later worked as Jeff Bezos' technical assistant at Amazon. David Siegel is a computer scientist with a PhD from MIT. The two met at D.E. Shaw in the 1990s and started Two Sigma in 2001.

The roles were clean. Overdeck ran the modeling teams that design the trading strategies. Siegel's engineers built the systems underneath. Their operating agreement required the two of them to agree on most decisions.

That consensus rule is the whole story.

Around 2022, Overdeck and some allies drafted a proposal asking Siegel to step aside. Insiders called it "the manifesto." By 2023 both founders had to sign off on senior executives' pay, and some bonuses sat frozen. Two Sigma's own SEC filing that year listed the founders' relationship as a material risk.

Clients noticed. The State of Wisconsin Investment Board held more than $1 billion with the firm at the end of 2023 and later pulled all of it.

In August 2024 both founders handed the co-CEO jobs to two other executives. Overdeck returned to the management committee in 2025, and one of those CEOs later resigned, citing "ongoing governance challenges since Mr. Overdeck's return."

Now the divorce. Laura Overdeck is asking for cash equal to 35% of his Two Sigma stake. Her side values that stake at $6.2 billion. His side says about $4.5 billion.

His testimony explains why he is fighting so hard: "Maintaining voting parity with Dr. Siegel is a principal concern." If he has to sell shares to raise the cash, control of Two Sigma could tip toward Siegel. A family court in Newark could end up shaping who runs an $85 billion quant fund.

Meanwhile the flagship Absolute Return Enhanced fund is up about 16% through September, per the WSJ.

For founders, the lesson sits in the operating agreement. Equal votes and a consensus clause feel great at $27 million. At $85 billion they turn every disagreement into a standoff, and a personal life event can reshape who controls the company.

Write the tie-breaker into your founding documents while you still like each other.

text:
What on earth is the Viking apocalypse doing on the door of a Christian church in Kent?

At All Saints’ Church in Staplehurst, Kent stands an extraordinary medieval wooden door, traditionally dated to around 1050, whose elaborate ironwork appears to depict Ragnarök, the Norse vision of the end of the world. The great serpent Jörmungandr, which encircles the earth, breaks loose. Nature descends into chaos, the gods battle monstrous forces, and the world is consumed by destruction. Yet from the catastrophe emerge two human survivors, destined to populate a renewed world. But look carefully at the upper part of the door. Above the terrifying imagery of cosmic destruction is a small Christian cross. For me, this is the most fascinating detail of all. It offers a remarkable glimpse into the encounter between Christianity and the ancient pagan imagination. The Norse understood something profound about the fragility of creation, the struggle between good and evil, and humanity's longing for a world restored. Yet their gods themselves were subject to destruction.

Christianity proclaimed something altogether different: a God who enters His creation, submits Himself to death, conquers it, and promises not merely survival after catastrophe but the redemption of creation itself. We cannot know with certainty what the medieval craftsman intended, but it is tempting to see that little cross as an extraordinary statement of Christian hope rising above the ruins of the old world.

Nearly a thousand years later, it remains a wonderful reminder that the conversion of Europe was not simply a matter of replacing one set of beliefs with another. It was a profound transformation of how people understood history, suffering, death and eternity. And sometimes that transformation can be glimpsed in something as humble as an old church door.

RHAPSODY OF REALITIES - Tuesday, October 20th, 2026.

 PASTOR CHRIS

TOPIC: CHRIST JESUS—THE ULTIMATE REDEEMER

_In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace (Ephesians 1:7)._

Redemption is one of the beautiful truths in the Gospel because it reveals not only what Christ accomplished, but also who He is. The Scriptures present the picture of a redeemer as one who has both the legal right and the ability to secure another's freedom. In the Lord Jesus Christ, we find the perfect and ultimate fulfilment of that picture. He is the Redeemer who paid the full price for our salvation and brought us into everlasting freedom. 

In the law of Moses, a kinsman-redeemer could redeem a relative who had fallen into debt or bondage. The redeemer had a legal right to act on behalf of the one in need, but he also had to pay the required price. Freedom wasn't obtained by mere desire or good intentions; a price had to be paid. 

This helps us understand the significance of Christ's sacrifice. Humanity's greatest problem was not merely the devil's oppression; it was the issue of sin. Sin had brought separation from God and placed mankind under judgment. The righteous demands of justice had to be satisfied. A price had to be paid. 

What a blessing to know that the Lord Jesus took our place and paid the full price required for our redemption. The payment wasn't silver or gold; it was His precious blood. The Bible says, “Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold…But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:18-19). 

When He shed His blood, He obtained eternal redemption for us. The debt was settled. The claims against us were satisfied. The penalty of sin was fully addressed. The Lord Jesus paid the price you could never pay. He accomplished what you could never accomplish for yourself. 

Through His sacrifice, you've been brought into righteousness and fellowship with God. He met every demand of divine justice, paid the full price with His own blood, and secured your eternal liberty. Therefore, live with gratitude and confidence, knowing that your salvation is eternally secure in Him.
                 
PRAYER
Dear Father, I thank you for the redemption that is mine through the blood of Jesus Christ. I rejoice in the knowledge that the full price for my salvation has been paid. I walk in righteousness, in fellowship with you, and in grateful acknowledgment of the fulfilment of the full blessings of the Gospel in my life, in Jesus' Name. Amen.

FURTHER STUDY
1 Peter 1:18-19 NIV 
For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life handed down to you from your ancestors, [19] but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or defect.

But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this building; [12] Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us. [13] For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh: [14] How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? text:
There’s a growing consensus that social media is so harmful to young people that governments should enforce age restrictions. 

Some even argue that because kids without social media risk being excluded by their peers, parental choice is insufficient.

I understand the concern, agree that most social media consumption is probably a waste of time, and much of it is genuinely harmful.

But I think there’s a deeper paternalism underlying this argument, and perhaps even a discomfort with freedom itself: 

the idea that because many people exercise a freedom poorly, we should deny it to everyone.

I remember a kid in my high school math class asking why we had to learn all this stuff when we’d probably never use it.

The teacher replied, rather bluntly, that he probably wouldn’t, but a few of the smarter kids would.

Indeed, much of what we teach is never directly useful to most students. 

Yet we don’t organize education around what the median student will eventually use. 

We preserve the opportunity for every child to develop their highest faculties, even if only a minority ultimately pursue them.

Why should we think differently about the internet?

For every thousand teenagers mindlessly scrolling TikTok, 

there might be one discovering a lifelong intellectual obsession, 

finding a mentor halfway across the world, or meeting the people with whom they’ll eventually build something extraordinary.

I personally see this firsthand, high school and college students reach out to me through LinkedIn, Instagram, and Twitter, 

and I’m often happy to offer guidance or answer questions. 

I do believe that sometimes a single conversation with someone outside a child’s immediate environment can change their trajectory.

When I was growing up, the internet introduced me to people who taught me about crypto, coding, trading, and countless other subjects. 

It exposed me to a universe of ideas far beyond the relatively orthodox environments of home and school.

As Patrick Collison observes, the ability to befriend exceptional people anywhere in the world is an extraordinary advantage our generation has over those before.

And crucially, we cannot know in advance which children will take advantage of it.

If anything, I think this freedom becomes more important in the age of AI.

As intelligence and information become increasingly abundant, 

the scarce human qualities will be judgment, taste, intellectual independence, 

and the agency to decide what is worth pursuing in the first place.

AI can teach you almost anything. 

But it cannot substitute for developing your own convictions through encounters with extraordinary people, competing ideas, and communities outside the world you were born into.

Social media, for all its faults, is one of the greatest mechanisms ever invented for precisely those encounters.

Now, there’s a reasonable objection: children don’t have the same capacity for judgment as adults. 

We already restrict their access to alcohol, guns, and voting. Why should social media be different?

While children do not enjoy every liberty on identical terms to adults, 

their freedom to think, speak, and encounter ideas deserves an exceptionally high degree of protection as their brains develop. 

A government may reasonably regulate addictive product design, predatory behavior, or the exploitation of minors. 

But excluding young people wholesale from the modern public square is a much more serious proposition.

Nor does the fact that some children feel socially pressured to participate automatically justify taking the choice away from every family. 

There is something deeply illiberal about evaluating freedom solely by whether the average person makes good use of it.

Freedom has never meant guaranteeing that people make optimal decisions. 

It means preserving their ability to make decisions at all.

7 Days in Costa Rica

Adults-Only All-Inclusive Escape 

Discover the natural beauty of Costa Rica's Guanacaste region while indulging in the luxury of an adults-only, all-inclusive resort overlooking the sparkling Pacific Ocean. This seven-day getaway combines relaxation, adventure, and unforgettable wildlife encounters in the unique tropical dry forest ecosystem. From exhilarating zip line adventures and ATV excursions to horseback rides along pristine beaches and a sunset sailing experience, this journey offers the perfect blend of excitement and tranquility.

Day 1: Welcome to Costa Rica

Upon arrival at Liberia International Airport, you'll be warmly greeted by representatives of Costa Rica Dream Travel and transferred to the beautiful shores of Papagayo Bay. After a seamless check-in at your hotel, enjoy the remainder of the day at leisure. Relax by the infinity pools, stroll along the beach, or toast the beginning of your tropical getaway with a cocktail overlooking the Pacific.

Experience Costa Rica from a thrilling new perspective as you soar through the treetops on an exhilarating zip line canopy tour.

Glide above the tropical dry forest, crossing from platform to platform while enjoying panoramic views of this remarkable ecosystem. Feel the rush of adrenaline as you fly like a bird through the canopy and discover the vibrant biodiversity that makes Guanacaste so unique.

Dry Forest Canopy Zip Line Tour

Safety equipment

Professional guides

Hotel taxes

Set out on an exciting ATV adventure through the rugged landscapes of Guanacaste's dry forest.

The combination of beautiful landscapes and off-road excitement makes this one of the region's most popular excursions.

Included:

English-speaking guide
Safety and riding equipment
All-inclusive accommodations

 Tour Duration: Approximately 3.5 hours

Day 4: Horseback Riding Along Costa Rica's Coast

After breakfast, embark on a memorable horseback riding adventure through some of Guanacaste's most scenic coastal landscapes.

Ride along forest trails and stunning beaches, beginning at Playa Blanca, where soft sands and crystal-clear waters invite you to take a refreshing swim. Continue on toward Playa Matapalo, passing through lush forests filled with native wildlife. Keep an eye out for monkeys, iguanas, exotic birds, and other fascinating creatures that call this region home.

Hotel taxes

Day 6: Sunset Sailing & Snorkeling Adventure

Spend the morning enjoying the resort before setting sail on an unforgettable catamaran cruise along Costa Rica's famed Gold Coast.

Cruise past secluded bays, pristine beaches, and lush tropical forests while searching for dolphins, sea turtles, flying fish, and, depending on the season, even whales. Anchor in a tranquil bay where you can snorkel in crystal-clear waters or relax on a secluded beach.

0–5sThe Seed Bearer
Low wide shot. @Mochi stands alone in the grass, sword pointed up, cape fluttering. A dark army of horned silhouettes fills the foggy horizon. Close insert: the seed in her belt pouch pulses soft green. Slow push-in as she takes a deep breath. Sound: wind, distant war horns, faint magical hum.

5–10sThe Charge

Fast ground-level tracking shot. The army storms forward. @Mochi darts between giant boots, ducks under a swinging axe, slides under a blade, mud and grass spraying, cape snapping. She stays sharp, the army is motion-blurred. Sound: pounding footsteps, clanging steel.

10–15sThe Offer

Low angle. @DarkLord strides out of the fog and plucks @Mochi up in one gauntlet, holding her at eye level. Violet eyes glow. He rumbles: "Give me the seed, little knight." She stares up, then yanks her pouch shut and says: "No." Subtitles on. Sound: heavy armor creaks, deep voice, her small brave voice.

15–20sSmall Is Strong

@Mochi wriggles out of the gauntlet through a gap at his wrist, scrambles up his arm, dashes along his back, jams her sword into the hinge of his knee joint. Quick cuts, close and fast. @DarkLord staggers, his huge leg buckles, and he crashes to the ground like a falling tower, shaking the whole field. The army freezes. Sound: metal screech, earth-shaking thud, silence.

20–25sThe Planting

Close on @Mochi in the churned mud, dusty and breathing hard. She digs a tiny hole with her paws, drops in the glowing seed, pats the soil. text:
I once met a taxi driver who taught me a lesson I'll never forget.

I was waiting at the airport when a shiny, spotless taxi pulled up. The driver stepped out in a neat white shirt, black tie, and perfectly pressed black trousers. He walked around the car, opened the back door for me, and handed me a laminated card.

“Hello, I'm Wasu, your driver,” he said with a smile. “While I put your bags in the trunk, please take a look at my mission statement.”

The card read, “My mission is to take every customer to their destination safely, quickly, and affordably, while making the journey as pleasant as possible.”

I was impressed. The inside of the taxi was just as clean and well-kept as the outside.

Then Wasu asked, “Would you like some coffee? I have regular and decaf.”

I jokingly said, “No, I'd rather have a cold drink.”

“Of course!” he replied. “I have Coke, Diet Coke, lassi, water, and orange juice in the cooler.”

I was surprised. I'd never tried lassi before, so I asked for one.

He handed it to me and then offered me something to read. He had magazines, a Bible, and a few other books in the car.

As we started driving, he showed me a list of radio stations I could choose from. He had already adjusted the temperature and asked if I was comfortable. He even explained which route would be best at that time of day.

Finally, he told me I could chat with him about the local sights or simply enjoy the ride in silence. Whatever I preferred.

I couldn't believe how thoughtful this man was.

“Wasu, have you always treated your customers this way?” I asked.

He smiled at me through the rear-view mirror.

“Not at all. For my first five years as a taxi driver, I complained about everything, just like many other drivers. Then one day, I heard something that changed the way I looked at life.”

He explained that we all have a choice. We can behave like ducks, constantly quacking and complaining, or we can be like eagles, rising above the noise and finding a better way forward.

“That really made me think,” he said. “I realised I was spending too much time complaining. So I decided to change myself instead of blaming everything around me.”

He started looking at other taxi drivers. Many had dirty cars, unfriendly attitudes, and unhappy customers.

“I decided I didn't want to be like that anymore. I started making small changes. I kept my car clean, treated people kindly, and tried to make every ride a good experience. When customers appreciated it, I looked for more ways to improve.”

I asked him if all that effort had made a difference.

He laughed and said, “Absolutely! In my first year after changing my attitude, I doubled my income. This year, I expect to earn four times what I earned before. Now, customers call me directly to book their rides.”

Wasu hadn't waited for the world to change. He had started by changing himself.

And that made all the difference.

Sometimes, we spend so much time complaining about people, situations, and the things we cannot control that we forget to look at what we can change.

We can't always choose what happens to us, but we can choose how we respond.

So, the next time you feel like complaining about everything, remember Wasu.

Don't waste your energy quacking like a duck. Spread your wings and rise like an eagle.

Life can look very different when you change your attitude.

text:
"Suck It Up: Betrayal Is Not Deception" 
Last week’s falling-out between Ukrainian President Zelensky and the American president has left me torn. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel directly, he has also said that Ukraine should change its president. Zelensky said that America now stands on the side of the aggressor, and told Europe’s leaders to their faces that they are the “real leaders.”
Without America’s support, what is Ukraine to do?
Zelensky had to lay his cards on the table for Europe’s “real leaders”: if Ukraine loses, Europe will have to take in twenty million Ukrainian refugees; if the fighting continues, next year’s war will have a funding gap of 70 billion euros.
Faced with his request, the “real leaders” didn’t exactly rise to the occasion. They actually didn’t agree, and said they needed to study it further!
What the hell is there to study? The EU’s GDP in 2025 is nearly 19 trillion euros. What is another 70 billion to resist the Russian aggressor?
Watching the “real leaders” hesitate, wanting to say something but holding back, Zelensky immediately named Canada, Japan and Australia, hoping they too would put up a bit more money.
Faced with Zelensky asking for money yet again, I, as an Australian taxpayer, am torn. I have three worries:
First, if I help him raise another 70 billion, will Ukraine definitely defeat Russia next year? If it doesn’t, how much will be needed the year after?
Second, if the war goes on, could someone blow up a nuclear power plant, or even use nuclear weapons? The recorded history of humankind shows again and again that in war, people have never been sparing with the most advanced weapons: if they have knives, they use knives; if they have guns, they use guns; if they have poison gas, they use poison gas; if they have nuclear bombs, they use nuclear bombs.
Third, Australia’s economy is in poor shape now, and a major reason is the high price of oil. The world’s energy production capacity sits in one single pool. From the very start, this war blew up Europe’s gas pipelines, and now Ukraine has begun bombing Russia’s gas and oil facilities. If the fighting continues, oil in Australia will surely get ever more expensive. If we keep giving money, our economy will get worse. And what are the consequences of a bad economy? Melbourne’s economy is struggling, and this city, billed as the world’s most livable, now has terrible public safety. France’s economy is poor too. Last week there were riots there, and many shopping centres, restaurants, cars and police stations were burned.
I believe these three worries must also be the worries of the “real leaders.” Being torn makes people cautious. So I began to study this war, which has now lasted longer than the First World War, to find out what it is really about.
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, and Ukraine became independent the same year and began to elect its own presidents. At independence, seven regions in Ukraine’s east and south, plus the capital Kyiv, were mainly Russian-speaking. These eight Russian-speaking areas were the engine of Ukraine’s economy, and its seaports and main industries were concentrated there.
For reasons I can’t quite fathom, independent Ukraine suffered from severe corruption and a weak economy. The people were discontented and changed presidents often. In 2010 they elected a pro-Russian president. In 2014, a section of the people, unhappy with his drift toward Russia, drove him from office by force (Ukraine calls it the “Revolution of Dignity”; Russia calls it an “illegal uprising”), and he fled to Russia. This is exactly what Putin keeps repeating: that today’s Ukrainian government is illegitimate because it was founded on violence, not democracy.
Putin’s complaints don’t stop there. After independence, Ukraine gradually restricted the use of Russian. After the 2014 revolution the restrictions grew tighter: soldiers, civil servants, doctors and teachers were required to use Ukrainian, and schools were no longer allowed to teach in Russian.
Among these wealthy Russian-speaking regions, the share of Russian speakers was highest in Crimea, at 97%, and lowest in Mykolaiv Oblast, at 66%. After independence, people in these regions grew increasingly resentful and held referendums that were illegal. Why illegal? Because Ukraine’s constitution says that to become independent, all Ukrainians must vote together; the Russian-speaking regions cannot decide on their own. But the people of Crimea ignored this and voted to join Russia, so Putin, for whom blood is thicker than water, took Crimea back in one stroke.
The other Russian-speaking regions in the east and south saw the example and followed it. They not only held referendums but also raised their own armed forces and seized government buildings. The Ukrainian army used force and suppressed the separatism in most places, but some areas have remained under pro-Russian armed groups.
I believe there must be a Russian hand behind the unrest in these regions. But the hidden hand is not only Russia’s. Some say the hand that drove the legitimate pro-Russian president from power was America’s, and they point as evidence to footage of Americans, after the coup succeeded, training Ukrainian police in how to keep order and teaching Ukrainians how to prevent corruption.
Facing this mess, the comedian Zelensky was elected president in 2019 by a landslide. As soon as he took office, he actively sought to join NATO, hoping for Western military protection.
Putin saw this and lost his temper: if Ukraine joined NATO, NATO troops could march right up to Russia’s border. So in 2022 Putin struck first and launched his “special military operation.”
Yesterday, Zelensky, in front of television audiences around the world, said with great hurt: we have been betrayed by America.
Ukraine has indeed been betrayed by America. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel, he has also throttled the speed of the satellite internet that Ukraine’s military relies on so heavily, and halted other sanctions on Russia.
Zelensky looked miserable on television. How could he not? Ukraine has become what it is today under his leadership. This is not the first time America has betrayed Ukraine. In 1994, Ukraine was the world’s third-largest nuclear power. When it decided to give up its nuclear weapons, it was America and the West that pushed it to do so. The United States, Britain and Russia signed the Budapest Memorandum, pledging that if Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons, they would respect Ukraine’s sovereignty and borders and safeguard its security.
Yet in 2014, Russia seized Crimea with barely a shot fired, and America and the West did not fire a single shot in response! If that isn’t betrayal, what is?!
This puzzles me: why didn’t America and the West support Ukraine in fighting Russia in 2014 the way they do now? And why didn’t Ukraine, equally losing territory, fight Russia to the death in 2014 as it does now?
I suspect there is something unspoken behind this. Perhaps it was this very thing that let Putin taste success, and so we have today’s Ukraine: a population down by 20 million, 20% of its territory lost, its economy largely destroyed, and more than a million dead or wounded.
What is this unspoken thing? I don’t know.
What I do know is this: the American president who promised in 1994 to protect Ukraine’s security was Clinton; the American president when Russia seized Crimea in 2014 was Obama; the American president who gave Ukraine money and weapons in 2022 was Biden; and the American president who now doesn’t support Ukraine fighting on is Trump.
Which of them represents America?
Zelensky’s grievance is ultimately because he is too young. He doesn’t understand America, doesn’t understand the West, doesn’t understand human nature.
When Putin was young, he didn’t understand America and the West either. He was 47 when he took office, and he wanted to join NATO. The Soviet Union had only recently collapsed, and he felt the West was stronger, more advanced and richer than Russia, so he wanted in. His thinking was simple: as a NATO member, Russia would not only gain NATO’s protection but could also concentrate on its economy. He offered a warm face and got a cold shoulder: NATO didn’t want Russia. Putin understood at once that the West saw Russia as an enemy, and so Russia had to maintain strong military power.
Moreover, since the war began, Putin has repeatedly said that Russia was betrayed by America, because when the Soviet Union dissolved, America, on NATO’s behalf, promised Russia verbally that NATO would not expand eastward and would not pose a military threat to Russian territory. Yet in 2019 Ukraine wrote its aim of joining NATO into its constitution, openly courting the alliance. Putin’s view is that Ukraine could never have done this without America’s tacit approval.
I dug further and found a 2013 CNN video in which former U.S. President Bill Clinton is interviewed by Piers Morgan, on Piers Morgan Live, broadcast in September 2013. Morgan asked whether Putin had ever broken a private agreement. Clinton answered: “No, he did not.” And: “He kept his word in all of the deals we made.” Clinton also described their relationship as “brutally blunt.” He was speaking of the period around 2000, when the two men overlapped in office.
Digging further still, I found that in June 2001, at a joint press conference in Slovenia after meeting Putin, the American president at the time, George W. Bush, said something that went down in history: “I looked the man in the eye. I found him very straightforward and trustworthy … I was able to get a sense of his soul.”
Having come this far, I know I cannot possibly get to the bottom of the causes of the Ukraine-Russia war, let alone judge who is right and who is wrong. But I know one thing: if the fighting goes on, more people will die, the economy will get worse, and Sydney’s public safety will end up like France’s. Worst of all, it could lead to nuclear war.
So, as a selfish Australian taxpayer, I no longer want to support Ukraine.
Unfortunately, last month Australia added another A$15 million in aid for Ukraine, and so far Australian taxpayers have thrown A$1.9 billion of firewood onto this Ukraine-Russia fire.
I hear that the Australian prime minister has more than 60 advisers on taxpayer-funded salaries. They can’t possibly be unaware of what I have set out here. If they do know, why do they keep letting the prime minister spend taxpayers’ money pouring oil on the fire?
Could it really be as the conspiracy theory says, that the West wants to use the Ukraine-Russia war to eliminate Russia, the greatest threat to world peace?
If so, Ukraine has truly become the sucker among mercenaries: fighting all these years, losing so much territory, so many lives, without bringing Russia down, while its Western paymasters are starting to lose their nerve!
Who should bear responsibility for the Ukraine-Russia war? Putin, who struck first, is certainly not blameless, but is he the only one responsible? Do the Ukrainians who restricted Russian-language schooling for children whose mother tongue is Russian bear no responsibility? Do the Western voters who keep sending Ukraine money bear none?
Whether in East or West, education, the media, history books, films and literature all cast “betrayal” (breaking promises, treachery, ingratitude, defection…) as immoral, so that when people are accused of “betrayal,” they blush. But anyone who has lived past seventy, East or West, comes to understand that most betrayals in this world are done out of necessity.
Betrayal and deception are not the same thing. Deception is knowing the outcome in advance and deliberately deceiving someone. Betrayal is making a promise without knowing its consequences, and abandoning it when you discover you cannot bear them.
C. S. Lewis made the same point about a wrong road: the person who turns back soonest is the one truly making progress.
To help my two granddaughters and their descendants navigate this conflict-ridden world and stay as safe and wise as possible, I wrote this book recommending fourteen must-read titles, including C.S. Lewis’s Mere Christianity.

His thinking was simple: as a NATO member, Russia would not only gain NATO’s protection but could also concentrate on its economy. He offered a warm face and got a cold shoulder: NATO didn’t want Russia. Putin understood at once that the West saw Russia as an enemy, and so Russia had to maintain strong military power.
Moreover, since the war began, Putin has repeatedly said that Russia was betrayed by America, because when the Soviet Union dissolved, America, on NATO’s behalf, promised Russia verbally that NATO would not expand eastward and would not pose a military threat to Russian territory. Yet in 2019 Ukraine wrote its aim of joining NATO into its constitution, openly courting the alliance. Putin’s view is that Ukraine could never have done this without America’s tacit approval.
I dug further and found a 2013 CNN video in which former U.S. President Bill Clinton is interviewed by Piers Morgan, on Piers Morgan Live, broadcast in September 2013. Morgan asked whether Putin had ever broken a private agreement. Clinton answered: “No, he did not.” And: “He kept his word in all of the deals we made.” Clinton also described their relationship as “brutally blunt.” He was speaking of the period around 2000, when the two men overlapped in office.
Digging further still, I found that in June 2001, at a joint press conference in Slovenia after meeting Putin, the American president at the time, George W. Bush, said something that went down in history: “I looked the man in the eye. I found him very straightforward and trustworthy … I was able to get a sense of his soul.”
Having come this far, I know I cannot possibly get to the bottom of the causes of the Ukraine-Russia war, let alone judge who is right and who is wrong. But I know one thing: if the fighting goes on, more people will die, the economy will get worse, and Sydney’s public safety will end up like France’s. Worst of all, it could lead to nuclear war.
So, as a selfish Australian taxpayer, I no longer want to support Ukraine.
Unfortunately, last month Australia added another A$15 million in aid for Ukraine, and so far Australian taxpayers have thrown A$1.9 billion of firewood onto this Ukraine-Russia fire.
I hear that the Australian prime minister has more than 60 advisers on taxpayer-funded salaries. They can’t possibly be unaware of what I have set out here. If they do know, why do they keep letting the prime minister spend taxpayers’ money pouring oil on the fire?
Could it really be as the conspiracy theory says, that the West wants to use the Ukraine-Russia war to eliminate Russia, the greatest threat to world peace?
If so, Ukraine has truly become the sucker among mercenaries: fighting all these years, losing so much territory, so many lives, without bringing Russia down, while its Western paymasters are starting to lose their nerve!
Who should bear responsibility for the Ukraine-Russia war? Putin, who struck first, is certainly not blameless, but is he the only one responsible? Do the Ukrainians who restricted Russian-language schooling for children whose mother tongue is Russian bear no responsibility? Do the Western voters who keep sending Ukraine money bear none?
Whether in East or West, education, the media, history books, films and literature all cast “betrayal” (breaking promises, treachery, ingratitude, defection…) as immoral, so that when people are accused of “betrayal,” they blush. But anyone who has lived past seventy, East or West, comes to understand that most betrayals in this world are done out of necessity.
Betrayal and deception are not the same thing. Deception is knowing the outcome in advance and deliberately deceiving someone. Betrayal is making a promise without knowing its consequences, and abandoning it when you discover you cannot bear them.
C. S. Lewis made the same point about a wrong road: the person who turns back soonest is the one truly making progress.
To help my two granddaughters and their descendants navigate this conflict-ridden world and stay as safe and wise as possible, I wrote this book recommending fourteen must-read titles, including C.S. Lewis’s Mere Christianity.

text:
China's former revolutionary base areas embrace new chapter of development

Two bridges over the Huajiang River in southwest China's Guizhou province offer a striking glimpse into the remarkable transformation of China's former revolutionary base areas.

The first is the Huajiang Chain Bridge. With its iron chains and wooden-plank deck, it spans a section of the Beipan River. In 1935, as the Right-Flank Column of the Central Red Army advanced into southwestern Guizhou, the 11th Regiment of the Third Red Army Corps held its position here, buying precious time for the main force. This wartime lifeline embodied the determination to overcome every challenge and fight for victory.

The other one, the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge, is pushing the boundaries of bridge construction in mountainous terrain through intelligent construction, innovative materials, advanced wind-resistant designs, and environmentally friendly building techniques.

The old and new bridges now stand within sight of each other, offering a vivid picture of how former revolutionary base areas have changed, and Guizhou is far from the only example. #LongMarch90

Third, Australia’s economy is in poor shape now, and a major reason is the high price of oil. The world’s energy production capacity sits in one single pool. From the very start, this war blew up Europe’s gas pipelines, and now Ukraine has begun bombing Russia’s gas and oil facilities. If the fighting continues, oil in Australia will surely get ever more expensive. If we keep giving money, our economy will get worse. And what are the consequences of a bad economy? Melbourne’s economy is struggling, and this city, billed as the world’s most livable, now has terrible public safety. France’s economy is poor too. At independence, seven regions in Ukraine’s east and south, plus the capital Kyiv, were mainly Russian-speaking. These eight Russian-speaking areas were the engine of Ukraine’s economy, and its seaports and main industries were concentrated there.

In 2010 they elected a pro-Russian president. In 2014, a section of the people, unhappy with his drift toward Russia, drove him from office by force (Ukraine calls it the “Revolution of Dignity”; Russia calls it an “illegal uprising”), and he fled to Russia. After independence, people in these regions grew increasingly resentful and held referendums that were illegal. Why illegal? The other Russian-speaking regions in the east and south saw the example and followed it. They not only held referendums but also raised their own armed forces and seized government buildings. The Ukrainian army used force and suppressed the separatism in most places, but some areas have remained under pro-Russian armed groups.

Some say the hand that drove the legitimate pro-Russian president from power was America’s, and they point as evidence to footage of Americans, after the coup succeeded, training Ukrainian police in how to keep order and teaching Ukrainians how to prevent corruption.

Yesterday, Zelensky, in front of television audiences around the world, said with great hurt: we have been betrayed by America.
Ukraine has indeed been betrayed by America. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel, he has also throttled the speed of the satellite internet that Ukraine’s military relies on so heavily, and halted other sanctions on Russia.

Yet in 2014, Russia seized Crimea with barely a shot fired, and America and the West did not fire a single shot in response! If that isn’t betrayal, what is?!
This puzzles me: why didn’t America and the West support Ukraine in fighting Russia in 2014 the way they do now? And why didn’t Ukraine, equally losing territory, fight Russia to the death in 2014 as it does now?
I suspect there is something unspoken behind this. Perhaps it was this very thing that let Putin taste success, and so we have today’s Ukraine: a population down by 20 million, 20% of its territory lost, its economy largely destroyed, and more than a million dead or wounded.

text:
Before Lanka Was Conquered, Despair Had to Be Overcome

Imagine being prepared for a crown and finding yourself walking into exile.

Then, while living far from home, your wife is abducted. Across the sea stands an adversary with an immensely powerful kingdom, a formidable army, extraordinary knowledge and spiritual powers.

You have no throne from which to command a campaign. An ocean separates you from the person you must rescue.

Where do you begin?

That is where the story of Ram speaks to the struggles of our own lives.

We remember the arrow that brought Ravana down. But consider everything that had to happen before that arrow could be released: grief endured, uncertainty faced, friendships formed, trust earned, strengths discovered and an ocean crossed.

Victory began long before the battlefield. It began in the decision to keep going.

Ram grieved. He felt anguish. His love for Sita made her absence unbearable. His courage becomes more meaningful when we recognise that pain.

We sometimes imagine that strong people remain untouched by suffering. Then, when our own confidence breaks, we assume we lack what it takes.

But courage can begin with a trembling voice. You can be heartbroken and still take responsibility for your next step.

Think of the examination you failed after months of preparation. The promotion that went to someone else. The medical report that changed your plans. The financial pressure you quietly carry. The family difficulty you cannot leave behind when you walk into work.

“Why me?” is a deeply human response.

Yet there comes a moment when another question must find its voice:

“Given where I stand today, what can I do next?”

Ram’s journey offers something practical here. He sought help. He built an alliance with Sugriv. He placed trust in Hanuman. He listened, learned and brought different abilities together around a shared purpose.

Even a cause as personal as rescuing Sita required the strength of others.

How often do we exhaust ourselves trying to prove that we can manage alone? We hesitate to ask a colleague, approach a mentor, admit a gap in our knowledge or tell our family that we are struggling.

Seeking help requires humility. Building a team requires faith in what others can contribute.

And leadership requires us to see potential before it has fully revealed itself.

Who around you is waiting to be trusted with greater responsibility? Whose ability have you overlooked because it arrived without an impressive title?

Then there is the ocean.

Every difficult ambition eventually brings us to one: a shortage of money, experience, support, time or confidence. We stand at its edge and calculate all the reasons we cannot cross.

The bridge to Lanka gives us a powerful image to carry into such moments.

A crossing takes shape through coordinated effort. Someone must begin. Others must contribute. Work must continue while the far shore still looks distant.

Your next step may be an application, a difficult conversation, an hour of study, a request for guidance or a fresh attempt after rejection.

Small enough to do today. Significant enough to move you forward.

And what of Ravana’s ten heads?

In our lives, one difficulty can seem to acquire ten voices:

You are too old. You are too late. You lack influence. You have already failed. What will people say?

Fear becomes overwhelming when every voice speaks at once.

Bring your attention back to the task before you. Learn what you need to learn. Gather the people who can help. Prepare carefully. Act with integrity. Give your effort a direction.

Do not let the size of the challenge decide the size of your response.

This Dussehra, as Ravana’s effigy burns, think of something you have surrendered to too soon.

An ambition. A responsibility. A conversation. Your belief in your own ability to begin again.

Bring it back into the light.....(1/2)

First, if I help him raise another 70 billion, will Ukraine definitely defeat Russia next year? If it doesn’t, how much will be needed the year after?
Second, if the war goes on, could someone blow up a nuclear power plant, or even use nuclear weapons? The recorded history of humankind shows again and again that in war, people have never been sparing with the most advanced weapons: if they have knives, they use knives; if they have guns, they use guns; if they have poison gas, they use poison gas; if they have nuclear bombs, they use nuclear bombs.
Third, Australia’s economy is in poor shape now, and a major reason is the high price of oil. The world’s energy production capacity sits in one single pool. From the very start, this war blew up Europe’s gas pipelines, and now Ukraine has begun bombing Russia’s gas and oil facilities. If the fighting continues, oil in Australia will surely get ever more expensive. If we keep giving money, our economy will get worse. And what are the consequences of a bad economy? Melbourne’s economy is struggling, and this city, billed as the world’s most livable, now has terrible public safety. France’s economy is poor too. Last week there were riots there, and many shopping centres, restaurants, cars and police stations were burned.
I believe these three worries must also be the worries of the “real leaders.” Being torn makes people cautious. So I began to study this war, which has now lasted longer than the First World War, to find out what it is really about.
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, and Ukraine became independent the same year and began to elect its own presidents. At independence, seven regions in Ukraine’s east and south, plus the capital Kyiv, were mainly Russian-speaking. These eight Russian-speaking areas were the engine of Ukraine’s economy, and its seaports and main industries were concentrated there.
For reasons I can’t quite fathom, independent Ukraine suffered from severe corruption and a weak economy. The people were discontented and changed presidents often. In 2010 they elected a pro-Russian president. In 2014, a section of the people, unhappy with his drift toward Russia, drove him from office by force (Ukraine calls it the “Revolution of Dignity”; Russia calls it an “illegal uprising”), and he fled to Russia. This is exactly what Putin keeps repeating: that today’s Ukrainian government is illegitimate because it was founded on violence, not democracy.
Putin’s complaints don’t stop there. After independence, Ukraine gradually restricted the use of Russian. After the 2014 revolution the restrictions grew tighter: soldiers, civil servants, doctors and teachers were required to use Ukrainian, and schools were no longer allowed to teach in Russian.
Among these wealthy Russian-speaking regions, the share of Russian speakers was highest in Crimea, at 97%, and lowest in Mykolaiv Oblast, at 66%. After independence, people in these regions grew increasingly resentful and held referendums that were illegal. Why illegal? Because Ukraine’s constitution says that to become independent, all Ukrainians must vote together; the Russian-speaking regions cannot decide on their own. But the people of Crimea ignored this and voted to join Russia, so Putin, for whom blood is thicker than water, took Crimea back in one stroke.
The other Russian-speaking regions in the east and south saw the example and followed it. They not only held referendums but also raised their own armed forces and seized government buildings. The Ukrainian army used force and suppressed the separatism in most places, but some areas have remained under pro-Russian armed groups.
I believe there must be a Russian hand behind the unrest in these regions. But the hidden hand is not only Russia’s. Some say the hand that drove the legitimate pro-Russian president from power was America’s, and they point as evidence to footage of Americans, after the coup succeeded, training Ukrainian police in how to keep order and teaching Ukrainians how to prevent corruption.
Facing this mess, the comedian Zelensky was elected president in 2019 by a landslide. As soon as he took office, he actively sought to join NATO, hoping for Western military protection.
Putin saw this and lost his temper: if Ukraine joined NATO, NATO troops could march right up to Russia’s border. So in 2022 Putin struck first and launched his “special military operation.”
Yesterday, Zelensky, in front of television audiences around the world, said with great hurt: we have been betrayed by America.
Ukraine has indeed been betrayed by America. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel, he has also throttled the speed of the satellite internet that Ukraine’s military relies on so heavily, and halted other sanctions on Russia.
Zelensky looked miserable on television. How could he not? Ukraine has become what it is today under his leadership. This is not the first time America has betrayed Ukraine. In 1994, Ukraine was the world’s third-largest nuclear power. When it decided to give up its nuclear weapons, it was America and the West that pushed it to do so. The United States, Britain and Russia signed the Budapest Memorandum, pledging that if Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons, they would respect Ukraine’s sovereignty and borders and safeguard its security.
Yet in 2014, Russia seized Crimea with barely a shot fired, and America and the West did not fire a single shot in response! If that isn’t betrayal, what is?!
This puzzles me: why didn’t America and the West support Ukraine in fighting Russia in 2014 the way they do now? And why didn’t Ukraine, equally losing territory, fight Russia to the death in 2014 as it does now?
I suspect there is something unspoken behind this. Perhaps it was this very thing that let Putin taste success, and so we have today’s Ukraine: a population down by 20 million, 20% of its territory lost, its economy largely destroyed, and more than a million dead or wounded.
What is this unspoken thing? I don’t know.
What I do know is this: the American president who promised in 1994 to protect Ukraine’s security was Clinton; the American president when Russia seized Crimea in 2014 was Obama; the American president who gave Ukraine money and weapons in 2022 was Biden; and the American president who now doesn’t support Ukraine fighting on is Trump.
Which of them represents America?
Zelensky’s grievance is ultimately because he is too young. He doesn’t understand America, doesn’t understand the West, doesn’t understand human nature.
When Putin was young, he didn’t understand America and the West either. He was 47 when he took office, and he wanted to join NATO. The Soviet Union had only recently collapsed, and he felt the West was stronger, more advanced and richer than Russia, so he wanted in. His thinking was simple: as a NATO member, Russia would not only gain NATO’s protection but could also concentrate on its economy. He offered a warm face and got a cold shoulder: NATO didn’t want Russia. Putin understood at once that the West saw Russia as an enemy, and so Russia had to maintain strong military power.
Moreover, since the war began, Putin has repeatedly said that Russia was betrayed by America, because when the Soviet Union dissolved, America, on NATO’s behalf, promised Russia verbally that NATO would not expand eastward and would not pose a military threat to Russian territory. Yet in 2019 Ukraine wrote its aim of joining NATO into its constitution, openly courting the alliance. Putin’s view is that Ukraine could never have done this without America’s tacit approval.
I dug further and found a 2013 CNN video in which former U.S. President Bill Clinton is interviewed by Piers Morgan, on Piers Morgan Live, broadcast in September 2013. Morgan asked whether Putin had ever broken a private agreement. Clinton answered: “No, he did not.” And: “He kept his word in all of the deals we made.” Clinton also described their relationship as “brutally blunt.” He was speaking of the period around 2000, when the two men overlapped in office.
Digging further still, I found that in June 2001, at a joint press conference in Slovenia after meeting Putin, the American president at the time, George W. Bush, said something that went down in history: “I looked the man in the eye. I found him very straightforward and trustworthy … I was able to get a sense of his soul.”
Having come this far, I know I cannot possibly get to the bottom of the causes of the Ukraine-Russia war, let alone judge who is right and who is wrong. But I know one thing: if the fighting goes on, more people will die, the economy will get worse, and Sydney’s public safety will end up like France’s. Worst of all, it could lead to nuclear war.
So, as a selfish Australian taxpayer, I no longer want to support Ukraine.
Unfortunately, last month Australia added another A$15 million in aid for Ukraine, and so far Australian taxpayers have thrown A$1.9 billion of firewood onto this Ukraine-Russia fire.
I hear that the Australian prime minister has more than 60 advisers on taxpayer-funded salaries. They can’t possibly be unaware of what I have set out here. If they do know, why do they keep letting the prime minister spend taxpayers’ money pouring oil on the fire?
Could it really be as the conspiracy theory says, that the West wants to use the Ukraine-Russia war to eliminate Russia, the greatest threat to world peace?
If so, Ukraine has truly become the sucker among mercenaries: fighting all these years, losing so much territory, so many lives, without bringing Russia down, while its Western paymasters are starting to lose their nerve!
Who should bear responsibility for the Ukraine-Russia war? Putin, who struck first, is certainly not blameless, but is he the only one responsible? Do the Ukrainians who restricted Russian-language schooling for children whose mother tongue is Russian bear no responsibility? Do the Western voters who keep sending Ukraine money bear none?
Whether in East or West, education, the media, history books, films and literature all cast “betrayal” (breaking promises, treachery, ingratitude, defection…) as immoral, so that when people are accused of “betrayal,” they blush. But anyone who has lived past seventy, East or West, comes to understand that most betrayals in this world are done out of necessity.
Betrayal and deception are not the same thing. Deception is knowing the outcome in advance and deliberately deceiving someone. Betrayal is making a promise without knowing its consequences, and abandoning it when you discover you cannot bear them.
C. S. Lewis made the same point about a wrong road: the person who turns back soonest is the one truly making progress.
To help my two granddaughters and their descendants navigate this conflict-ridden world and stay as safe and wise as possible, I wrote this book recommending fourteen must-read titles, including C.S. Lewis’s Mere Christianity.
