text:
"Suck It Up: Betrayal Is Not Deception"Last week’s falling-out between Ukrainian President Zelensky and the American president has left me torn. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel directly, he has also said that Ukraine should change its president. Zelensky said that America now stands on the side of the aggressor, and told Europe’s leaders to their faces that they are the “real leaders.”
Without America’s support, what is Ukraine to do?
Zelensky had to lay his cards on the table for Europe’s “real leaders”: if Ukraine loses, Europe will have to take in twenty million Ukrainian refugees; if the fighting continues, next year’s war will have a funding gap of 70 billion euros.
Faced with his request, the “real leaders” didn’t exactly rise to the occasion. They actually didn’t agree, and said they needed to study it further!
What the hell is there to study? The EU’s GDP in 2025 is nearly 19 trillion euros. What is another 70 billion to resist the Russian aggressor?
Watching the “real leaders” hesitate, wanting to say something but holding back, Zelensky immediately named Canada, Japan and Australia, hoping they too would put up a bit more money.
Faced with Zelensky asking for money yet again, I, as an Australian taxpayer, am torn. I have three worries:
First, if I help him raise another 70 billion, will Ukraine definitely defeat Russia next year? If it doesn’t, how much will be needed the year after?
Second, if the war goes on, could someone blow up a nuclear power plant, or even use nuclear weapons? The recorded history of humankind shows again and again that in war, people have never been sparing with the most advanced weapons: if they have knives, they use knives; if they have guns, they use guns; if they have poison gas, they use poison gas; if they have nuclear bombs, they use nuclear bombs.
Third, Australia’s economy is in poor shape now, and a major reason is the high price of oil. The world’s energy production capacity sits in one single pool. From the very start, this war blew up Europe’s gas pipelines, and now Ukraine has begun bombing Russia’s gas and oil facilities. If the fighting continues, oil in Australia will surely get ever more expensive. If we keep giving money, our economy will get worse. And what are the consequences of a bad economy? Melbourne’s economy is struggling, and this city, billed as the world’s most livable, now has terrible public safety. France’s economy is poor too. Last week there were riots there, and many shopping centres, restaurants, cars and police stations were burned.
I believe these three worries must also be the worries of the “real leaders.” Being torn makes people cautious. So I began to study this war, which has now lasted longer than the First World War, to find out what it is really about.
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, and Ukraine became independent the same year and began to elect its own presidents. At independence, seven regions in Ukraine’s east and south, plus the capital Kyiv, were mainly Russian-speaking. These eight Russian-speaking areas were the engine of Ukraine’s economy, and its seaports and main industries were concentrated there.
For reasons I can’t quite fathom, independent Ukraine suffered from severe corruption and a weak economy. The people were discontented and changed presidents often. In 2010 they elected a pro-Russian president. In 2014, a section of the people, unhappy with his drift toward Russia, drove him from office by force (Ukraine calls it the “Revolution of Dignity”; Russia calls it an “illegal uprising”), and he fled to Russia. This is exactly what Putin keeps repeating: that today’s Ukrainian government is illegitimate because it was founded on violence, not democracy.
Putin’s complaints don’t stop there. After independence, Ukraine gradually restricted the use of Russian. After the 2014 revolution the restrictions grew tighter: soldiers, civil servants, doctors and teachers were required to use Ukrainian, and schools were no longer allowed to teach in Russian.
Among these wealthy Russian-speaking regions, the share of Russian speakers was highest in Crimea, at 97%, and lowest in Mykolaiv Oblast, at 66%. After independence, people in these regions grew increasingly resentful and held referendums that were illegal. Why illegal? Because Ukraine’s constitution says that to become independent, all Ukrainians must vote together; the Russian-speaking regions cannot decide on their own. But the people of Crimea ignored this and voted to join Russia, so Putin, for whom blood is thicker than water, took Crimea back in one stroke.
The other Russian-speaking regions in the east and south saw the example and followed it. They not only held referendums but also raised their own armed forces and seized government buildings. The Ukrainian army used force and suppressed the separatism in most places, but some areas have remained under pro-Russian armed groups.
I believe there must be a Russian hand behind the unrest in these regions. But the hidden hand is not only Russia’s. Some say the hand that drove the legitimate pro-Russian president from power was America’s, and they point as evidence to footage of Americans, after the coup succeeded, training Ukrainian police in how to keep order and teaching Ukrainians how to prevent corruption.
Facing this mess, the comedian Zelensky was elected president in 2019 by a landslide. As soon as he took office, he actively sought to join NATO, hoping for Western military protection.
Putin saw this and lost his temper: if Ukraine joined NATO, NATO troops could march right up to Russia’s border. So in 2022 Putin struck first and launched his “special military operation.”
Yesterday, Zelensky, in front of television audiences around the world, said with great hurt: we have been betrayed by America.
Ukraine has indeed been betrayed by America. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel, he has also throttled the speed of the satellite internet that Ukraine’s military relies on so heavily, and halted other sanctions on Russia.
Zelensky looked miserable on television. How could he not? Ukraine has become what it is today under his leadership. This is not the first time America has betrayed Ukraine. In 1994, Ukraine was the world’s third-largest nuclear power. When it decided to give up its nuclear weapons, it was America and the West that pushed it to do so. The United States, Britain and Russia signed the Budapest Memorandum, pledging that if Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons, they would respect Ukraine’s sovereignty and borders and safeguard its security.
Yet in 2014, Russia seized Crimea with barely a shot fired, and America and the West did not fire a single shot in response! If that isn’t betrayal, what is?!
This puzzles me: why didn’t America and the West support Ukraine in fighting Russia in 2014 the way they do now? And why didn’t Ukraine, equally losing territory, fight Russia to the death in 2014 as it does now?
I suspect there is something unspoken behind this. Perhaps it was this very thing that let Putin taste success, and so we have today’s Ukraine: a population down by 20 million, 20% of its territory lost, its economy largely destroyed, and more than a million dead or wounded.
What is this unspoken thing? I don’t know.
What I do know is this: the American president who promised in 1994 to protect Ukraine’s security was Clinton; the American president when Russia seized Crimea in 2014 was Obama; the American president who gave Ukraine money and weapons in 2022 was Biden; and the American president who now doesn’t support Ukraine fighting on is Trump.
Which of them represents America?
Zelensky’s grievance is ultimately because he is too young. He doesn’t understand America, doesn’t understand the West, doesn’t understand human nature.
When Putin was young, he didn’t understand America and the West either. He was 47 when he took office, and he wanted to join NATO. The Soviet Union had only recently collapsed, and he felt the West was stronger, more advanced and richer than Russia, so he wanted in. His thinking was simple: as a NATO member, Russia would not only gain NATO’s protection but could also concentrate on its economy. He offered a warm face and got a cold shoulder: NATO didn’t want Russia. Putin understood at once that the West saw Russia as an enemy, and so Russia had to maintain strong military power.
Moreover, since the war began, Putin has repeatedly said that Russia was betrayed by America, because when the Soviet Union dissolved, America, on NATO’s behalf, promised Russia verbally that NATO would not expand eastward and would not pose a military threat to Russian territory. Yet in 2019 Ukraine wrote its aim of joining NATO into its constitution, openly courting the alliance. Putin’s view is that Ukraine could never have done this without America’s tacit approval.
I dug further and found a 2013 CNN video in which former U.S. President Bill Clinton is interviewed by Piers Morgan, on Piers Morgan Live, broadcast in September 2013. Morgan asked whether Putin had ever broken a private agreement. Clinton answered: “No, he did not.” And: “He kept his word in all of the deals we made.” Clinton also described their relationship as “brutally blunt.” He was speaking of the period around 2000, when the two men overlapped in office.
Digging further still, I found that in June 2001, at a joint press conference in Slovenia after meeting Putin, the American president at the time, George W. Bush, said something that went down in history: “I looked the man in the eye. I found him very straightforward and trustworthy … I was able to get a sense of his soul.”
Having come this far, I know I cannot possibly get to the bottom of the causes of the Ukraine-Russia war, let alone judge who is right and who is wrong. But I know one thing: if the fighting goes on, more people will die, the economy will get worse, and Sydney’s public safety will end up like France’s. Worst of all, it could lead to nuclear war.
So, as a selfish Australian taxpayer, I no longer want to support Ukraine.
Unfortunately, last month Australia added another A$15 million in aid for Ukraine, and so far Australian taxpayers have thrown A$1.9 billion of firewood onto this Ukraine-Russia fire.
I hear that the Australian prime minister has more than 60 advisers on taxpayer-funded salaries. They can’t possibly be unaware of what I have set out here. If they do know, why do they keep letting the prime minister spend taxpayers’ money pouring oil on the fire?
Could it really be as the conspiracy theory says, that the West wants to use the Ukraine-Russia war to eliminate Russia, the greatest threat to world peace?
If so, Ukraine has truly become the sucker among mercenaries: fighting all these years, losing so much territory, so many lives, without bringing Russia down, while its Western paymasters are starting to lose their nerve!
Who should bear responsibility for the Ukraine-Russia war? Putin, who struck first, is certainly not blameless, but is he the only one responsible? Do the Ukrainians who restricted Russian-language schooling for children whose mother tongue is Russian bear no responsibility? Do the Western voters who keep sending Ukraine money bear none?
Whether in East or West, education, the media, history books, films and literature all cast “betrayal” (breaking promises, treachery, ingratitude, defection…) as immoral, so that when people are accused of “betrayal,” they blush. But anyone who has lived past seventy, East or West, comes to understand that most betrayals in this world are done out of necessity.
Betrayal and deception are not the same thing. Deception is knowing the outcome in advance and deliberately deceiving someone. Betrayal is making a promise without knowing its consequences, and abandoning it when you discover you cannot bear them.
C. S. Lewis made the same point about a wrong road: the person who turns back soonest is the one truly making progress.
To help my two granddaughters and their descendants navigate this conflict-ridden world and stay as safe and wise as possible, I wrote this book recommending fourteen must-read titles, including C.S. Lewis’s Mere Christianity.

text:
Before Lanka Was Conquered, Despair Had to Be Overcome

Imagine being prepared for a crown and finding yourself walking into exile.

Then, while living far from home, your wife is abducted. Across the sea stands an adversary with an immensely powerful kingdom, a formidable army, extraordinary knowledge and spiritual powers.

You have no throne from which to command a campaign. An ocean separates you from the person you must rescue.

Where do you begin?

That is where the story of Ram speaks to the struggles of our own lives.

We remember the arrow that brought Ravana down. But consider everything that had to happen before that arrow could be released: grief endured, uncertainty faced, friendships formed, trust earned, strengths discovered and an ocean crossed.

Victory began long before the battlefield. It began in the decision to keep going.

Ram grieved. He felt anguish. His love for Sita made her absence unbearable. His courage becomes more meaningful when we recognise that pain.

We sometimes imagine that strong people remain untouched by suffering. Then, when our own confidence breaks, we assume we lack what it takes.

But courage can begin with a trembling voice. You can be heartbroken and still take responsibility for your next step.

Think of the examination you failed after months of preparation. The promotion that went to someone else. The medical report that changed your plans. The financial pressure you quietly carry. The family difficulty you cannot leave behind when you walk into work.

“Why me?” is a deeply human response.

Yet there comes a moment when another question must find its voice:

“Given where I stand today, what can I do next?”

Ram’s journey offers something practical here. He sought help. He built an alliance with Sugriv. He placed trust in Hanuman. He listened, learned and brought different abilities together around a shared purpose.

Even a cause as personal as rescuing Sita required the strength of others.

How often do we exhaust ourselves trying to prove that we can manage alone? We hesitate to ask a colleague, approach a mentor, admit a gap in our knowledge or tell our family that we are struggling.

Seeking help requires humility. Building a team requires faith in what others can contribute.

And leadership requires us to see potential before it has fully revealed itself.

Who around you is waiting to be trusted with greater responsibility? Whose ability have you overlooked because it arrived without an impressive title?

Then there is the ocean.

Every difficult ambition eventually brings us to one: a shortage of money, experience, support, time or confidence. We stand at its edge and calculate all the reasons we cannot cross.

The bridge to Lanka gives us a powerful image to carry into such moments.

A crossing takes shape through coordinated effort. Someone must begin. Others must contribute. Work must continue while the far shore still looks distant.

Your next step may be an application, a difficult conversation, an hour of study, a request for guidance or a fresh attempt after rejection.

Small enough to do today. Significant enough to move you forward.

And what of Ravana’s ten heads?

In our lives, one difficulty can seem to acquire ten voices:

You are too old. You are too late. You lack influence. You have already failed. What will people say?

Fear becomes overwhelming when every voice speaks at once.

Bring your attention back to the task before you. Learn what you need to learn. Gather the people who can help. Prepare carefully. Act with integrity. Give your effort a direction.

Do not let the size of the challenge decide the size of your response.

This Dussehra, as Ravana’s effigy burns, think of something you have surrendered to too soon.

An ambition. A responsibility. A conversation. Your belief in your own ability to begin again.

Bring it back into the light.....(1/2)

Yet in 2014, Russia seized Crimea with barely a shot fired, and America and the West did not fire a single shot in response! If that isn’t betrayal, what is?!
This puzzles me: why didn’t America and the West support Ukraine in fighting Russia in 2014 the way they do now? And why didn’t Ukraine, equally losing territory, fight Russia to the death in 2014 as it does now?
I suspect there is something unspoken behind this. Perhaps it was this very thing that let Putin taste success, and so we have today’s Ukraine: a population down by 20 million, 20% of its territory lost, its economy largely destroyed, and more than a million dead or wounded.
What is this unspoken thing? I don’t know.
What I do know is this: the American president who promised in 1994 to protect Ukraine’s security was Clinton; the American president when Russia seized Crimea in 2014 was Obama; the American president who gave Ukraine money and weapons in 2022 was Biden; and the American president who now doesn’t support Ukraine fighting on is Trump.
Which of them represents America?
Zelensky’s grievance is ultimately because he is too young. He doesn’t understand America, doesn’t understand the West, doesn’t understand human nature.
When Putin was young, he didn’t understand America and the West either. He was 47 when he took office, and he wanted to join NATO. The Soviet Union had only recently collapsed, and he felt the West was stronger, more advanced and richer than Russia, so he wanted in. His thinking was simple: as a NATO member, Russia would not only gain NATO’s protection but could also concentrate on its economy. He offered a warm face and got a cold shoulder: NATO didn’t want Russia. Putin understood at once that the West saw Russia as an enemy, and so Russia had to maintain strong military power.
Moreover, since the war began, Putin has repeatedly said that Russia was betrayed by America, because when the Soviet Union dissolved, America, on NATO’s behalf, promised Russia verbally that NATO would not expand eastward and would not pose a military threat to Russian territory. Yet in 2019 Ukraine wrote its aim of joining NATO into its constitution, openly courting the alliance. Putin’s view is that Ukraine could never have done this without America’s tacit approval.
I dug further and found a 2013 CNN video in which former U.S. President Bill Clinton is interviewed by Piers Morgan, on Piers Morgan Live, broadcast in September 2013. Morgan asked whether Putin had ever broken a private agreement. Clinton answered: “No, he did not.” And: “He kept his word in all of the deals we made.” Clinton also described their relationship as “brutally blunt.” He was speaking of the period around 2000, when the two men overlapped in office.
Digging further still, I found that in June 2001, at a joint press conference in Slovenia after meeting Putin, the American president at the time, George W. Bush, said something that went down in history: “I looked the man in the eye. I found him very straightforward and trustworthy … I was able to get a sense of his soul.”
Having come this far, I know I cannot possibly get to the bottom of the causes of the Ukraine-Russia war, let alone judge who is right and who is wrong. But I know one thing: if the fighting goes on, more people will die, the economy will get worse, and Sydney’s public safety will end up like France’s. Worst of all, it could lead to nuclear war.
So, as a selfish Australian taxpayer, I no longer want to support Ukraine.
Unfortunately, last month Australia added another A$15 million in aid for Ukraine, and so far Australian taxpayers have thrown A$1.9 billion of firewood onto this Ukraine-Russia fire.
I hear that the Australian prime minister has more than 60 advisers on taxpayer-funded salaries. They can’t possibly be unaware of what I have set out here. If they do know, why do they keep letting the prime minister spend taxpayers’ money pouring oil on the fire?
Could it really be as the conspiracy theory says, that the West wants to use the Ukraine-Russia war to eliminate Russia, the greatest threat to world peace?
If so, Ukraine has truly become the sucker among mercenaries: fighting all these years, losing so much territory, so many lives, without bringing Russia down, while its Western paymasters are starting to lose their nerve!
Who should bear responsibility for the Ukraine-Russia war? Putin, who struck first, is certainly not blameless, but is he the only one responsible? Do the Ukrainians who restricted Russian-language schooling for children whose mother tongue is Russian bear no responsibility? Do the Western voters who keep sending Ukraine money bear none?
Whether in East or West, education, the media, history books, films and literature all cast “betrayal” (breaking promises, treachery, ingratitude, defection…) as immoral, so that when people are accused of “betrayal,” they blush. But anyone who has lived past seventy, East or West, comes to understand that most betrayals in this world are done out of necessity.
Betrayal and deception are not the same thing. Deception is knowing the outcome in advance and deliberately deceiving someone. Betrayal is making a promise without knowing its consequences, and abandoning it when you discover you cannot bear them.
C. S. Lewis made the same point about a wrong road: the person who turns back soonest is the one truly making progress.
To help my two granddaughters and their descendants navigate this conflict-ridden world and stay as safe and wise as possible, I wrote this book recommending fourteen must-read titles, including C.S. Lewis’s Mere Christianity.

Are 🇨🇳 Chinese Spies Luring 🇮🇳 Indian Military Veterans?

Chinese spies are targeting Indian military veterans, journalists, and scholars with a new low-profile tactic: offering $300–500 per article to write on geopolitics, defense procurement, military exercises, and combat doctrines.

Recruiters pose as Hong Kong PhD students, think-tank interns, or consulting-firm representatives and contact targets on LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Naukri, and Indeed. Initial tasks appear academic but quickly shift to seeking inside knowledge on troop deployments, weapons performance, and defense deals. 

Rear Admiral Girish Kumar Garg (@girishkgarg) was approached on LinkedIn by two Hong Kong-based “PhD students” who praised his analytical skills and naval experience. 

A former Army colonel and the @THEEURASIATIMES journalist himself received similar offers; when the journalist refused to share non-public information, recruiters offered higher pay.

India’s University Grants Commission issued a January 2026 advisory warning higher-education institutions and defense-linked personnel about foreign entities using job portals to solicit source-based articles on sensitive topics. 

The #IndianNavy has also circulated the warning to veterans.

In the latest development, J&K Police have filed a case and started a probe against a Jammu-based Army officer’s wife for allegedly collecting and sharing sensitive information with foreign intelligence operatives, including those linked to China.

Second, if the war goes on, could someone blow up a nuclear power plant, or even use nuclear weapons? The recorded history of humankind shows again and again that in war, people have never been sparing with the most advanced weapons: if they have knives, they use knives; if they have guns, they use guns; if they have poison gas, they use poison gas; if they have nuclear bombs, they use nuclear bombs.
Third, Australia’s economy is in poor shape now, and a major reason is the high price of oil. The world’s energy production capacity sits in one single pool. From the very start, this war blew up Europe’s gas pipelines, and now Ukraine has begun bombing Russia’s gas and oil facilities. If the fighting continues, oil in Australia will surely get ever more expensive. If we keep giving money, our economy will get worse. And what are the consequences of a bad economy? Melbourne’s economy is struggling, and this city, billed as the world’s most livable, now has terrible public safety. France’s economy is poor too. Last week there were riots there, and many shopping centres, restaurants, cars and police stations were burned.
I believe these three worries must also be the worries of the “real leaders.” Being torn makes people cautious. So I began to study this war, which has now lasted longer than the First World War, to find out what it is really about.
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, and Ukraine became independent the same year and began to elect its own presidents. At independence, seven regions in Ukraine’s east and south, plus the capital Kyiv, were mainly Russian-speaking. These eight Russian-speaking areas were the engine of Ukraine’s economy, and its seaports and main industries were concentrated there.
For reasons I can’t quite fathom, independent Ukraine suffered from severe corruption and a weak economy. The people were discontented and changed presidents often. In 2010 they elected a pro-Russian president. In 2014, a section of the people, unhappy with his drift toward Russia, drove him from office by force (Ukraine calls it the “Revolution of Dignity”; Russia calls it an “illegal uprising”), and he fled to Russia. This is exactly what Putin keeps repeating: that today’s Ukrainian government is illegitimate because it was founded on violence, not democracy.
Putin’s complaints don’t stop there. After independence, Ukraine gradually restricted the use of Russian. After the 2014 revolution the restrictions grew tighter: soldiers, civil servants, doctors and teachers were required to use Ukrainian, and schools were no longer allowed to teach in Russian.
Among these wealthy Russian-speaking regions, the share of Russian speakers was highest in Crimea, at 97%, and lowest in Mykolaiv Oblast, at 66%. After independence, people in these regions grew increasingly resentful and held referendums that were illegal. Why illegal? Because Ukraine’s constitution says that to become independent, all Ukrainians must vote together; the Russian-speaking regions cannot decide on their own. But the people of Crimea ignored this and voted to join Russia, so Putin, for whom blood is thicker than water, took Crimea back in one stroke.
The other Russian-speaking regions in the east and south saw the example and followed it. They not only held referendums but also raised their own armed forces and seized government buildings. The Ukrainian army used force and suppressed the separatism in most places, but some areas have remained under pro-Russian armed groups.
I believe there must be a Russian hand behind the unrest in these regions. But the hidden hand is not only Russia’s. Some say the hand that drove the legitimate pro-Russian president from power was America’s, and they point as evidence to footage of Americans, after the coup succeeded, training Ukrainian police in how to keep order and teaching Ukrainians how to prevent corruption.
Facing this mess, the comedian Zelensky was elected president in 2019 by a landslide. As soon as he took office, he actively sought to join NATO, hoping for Western military protection.
Putin saw this and lost his temper: if Ukraine joined NATO, NATO troops could march right up to Russia’s border. So in 2022 Putin struck first and launched his “special military operation.”
Yesterday, Zelensky, in front of television audiences around the world, said with great hurt: we have been betrayed by America.
Ukraine has indeed been betrayed by America. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel, he has also throttled the speed of the satellite internet that Ukraine’s military relies on so heavily, and halted other sanctions on Russia.
Zelensky looked miserable on television. How could he not? Ukraine has become what it is today under his leadership. This is not the first time America has betrayed Ukraine. In 1994, Ukraine was the world’s third-largest nuclear power. When it decided to give up its nuclear weapons, it was America and the West that pushed it to do so. The United States, Britain and Russia signed the Budapest Memorandum, pledging that if Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons, they would respect Ukraine’s sovereignty and borders and safeguard its security.
Yet in 2014, Russia seized Crimea with barely a shot fired, and America and the West did not fire a single shot in response! If that isn’t betrayal, what is?!
This puzzles me: why didn’t America and the West support Ukraine in fighting Russia in 2014 the way they do now? And why didn’t Ukraine, equally losing territory, fight Russia to the death in 2014 as it does now?
I suspect there is something unspoken behind this. Perhaps it was this very thing that let Putin taste success, and so we have today’s Ukraine: a population down by 20 million, 20% of its territory lost, its economy largely destroyed, and more than a million dead or wounded.
What is this unspoken thing? I don’t know.
What I do know is this: the American president who promised in 1994 to protect Ukraine’s security was Clinton; the American president when Russia seized Crimea in 2014 was Obama; the American president who gave Ukraine money and weapons in 2022 was Biden; and the American president who now doesn’t support Ukraine fighting on is Trump.
Which of them represents America?
Zelensky’s grievance is ultimately because he is too young. He doesn’t understand America, doesn’t understand the West, doesn’t understand human nature.
When Putin was young, he didn’t understand America and the West either. He was 47 when he took office, and he wanted to join NATO. The Soviet Union had only recently collapsed, and he felt the West was stronger, more advanced and richer than Russia, so he wanted in. His thinking was simple: as a NATO member, Russia would not only gain NATO’s protection but could also concentrate on its economy. He offered a warm face and got a cold shoulder: NATO didn’t want Russia. Putin understood at once that the West saw Russia as an enemy, and so Russia had to maintain strong military power.
Moreover, since the war began, Putin has repeatedly said that Russia was betrayed by America, because when the Soviet Union dissolved, America, on NATO’s behalf, promised Russia verbally that NATO would not expand eastward and would not pose a military threat to Russian territory. Yet in 2019 Ukraine wrote its aim of joining NATO into its constitution, openly courting the alliance. Putin’s view is that Ukraine could never have done this without America’s tacit approval.
I dug further and found a 2013 CNN video in which former U.S. President Bill Clinton is interviewed by Piers Morgan, on Piers Morgan Live, broadcast in September 2013. Morgan asked whether Putin had ever broken a private agreement. Clinton answered: “No, he did not.” And: “He kept his word in all of the deals we made.” Clinton also described their relationship as “brutally blunt.” He was speaking of the period around 2000, when the two men overlapped in office.
Digging further still, I found that in June 2001, at a joint press conference in Slovenia after meeting Putin, the American president at the time, George W. Bush, said something that went down in history: “I looked the man in the eye. I found him very straightforward and trustworthy … I was able to get a sense of his soul.”
Having come this far, I know I cannot possibly get to the bottom of the causes of the Ukraine-Russia war, let alone judge who is right and who is wrong. But I know one thing: if the fighting goes on, more people will die, the economy will get worse, and Sydney’s public safety will end up like France’s. Worst of all, it could lead to nuclear war.
So, as a selfish Australian taxpayer, I no longer want to support Ukraine.
Unfortunately, last month Australia added another A$15 million in aid for Ukraine, and so far Australian taxpayers have thrown A$1.9 billion of firewood onto this Ukraine-Russia fire.
I hear that the Australian prime minister has more than 60 advisers on taxpayer-funded salaries. They can’t possibly be unaware of what I have set out here. If they do know, why do they keep letting the prime minister spend taxpayers’ money pouring oil on the fire?
Could it really be as the conspiracy theory says, that the West wants to use the Ukraine-Russia war to eliminate Russia, the greatest threat to world peace?
If so, Ukraine has truly become the sucker among mercenaries: fighting all these years, losing so much territory, so many lives, without bringing Russia down, while its Western paymasters are starting to lose their nerve!
Who should bear responsibility for the Ukraine-Russia war? Putin, who struck first, is certainly not blameless, but is he the only one responsible? Do the Ukrainians who restricted Russian-language schooling for children whose mother tongue is Russian bear no responsibility? Do the Western voters who keep sending Ukraine money bear none?
Whether in East or West, education, the media, history books, films and literature all cast “betrayal” (breaking promises, treachery, ingratitude, defection…) as immoral, so that when people are accused of “betrayal,” they blush. But anyone who has lived past seventy, East or West, comes to understand that most betrayals in this world are done out of necessity.
Betrayal and deception are not the same thing. Deception is knowing the outcome in advance and deliberately deceiving someone. Betrayal is making a promise without knowing its consequences, and abandoning it when you discover you cannot bear them.
C. S. Lewis made the same point about a wrong road: the person who turns back soonest is the one truly making progress.
To help my two granddaughters and their descendants navigate this conflict-ridden world and stay as safe and wise as possible, I wrote this book recommending fourteen must-read titles, including C.S. Lewis’s Mere Christianity.

An ”immune reset” using modified cells could offer a permanent cure for millions living with severe autoimmune diseases.

A groundbreaking medical shift is underway, as researchers have repurposed cancer-fighting technology to tackle chronic autoimmune diseases, potentially offering a functional cure rather than lifelong symptom management.

 By adapting Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, scientists can now genetically reprogram a patient's own T-cells to target and eliminate the rogue B-cells responsible for driving autoimmune destruction. This approach acts as a literal 'immune reset'. 

In clinical trials, patients suffering from debilitating, overlapping conditions like lupus, systemic sclerosis, and myositis have achieved complete, drug-free remission after just a single infusion, experiencing restored mobility and the total disappearance of autoantibodies.

Traditional treatments for autoimmune conditions rely on heavy, lifelong immunosuppressive drugs that broadly dampen the body's defense systems, leaving patients vulnerable to infections and serious side effects. In contrast, this new era of cell-engineering platforms and highly targeted therapies aims to correct the root cause of the illness. 

Emerging trials, including those utilizing mRNA-based CAR T-cell techniques and inverse 'tolerogenic' vaccines, are showing unprecedented success in retraining the immune system to tolerate the body's own tissues. 

While long-term data is still being compiled, the initial results represent a paradigm shift, transforming chronic, life-altering conditions into treatable—and potentially curable—maladies.

source: University of North Carolina School of Medicine. (2026). CAR T Cell Therapy Poised to Transform Autoimmune Disease Treatment.

text:
SAGE-CP: When Marginal Coverage Hides Route-Conditional Failures in Adaptive VLM Ensembles : https://t.co/PHQrD1jUJg

"M. TanveerDepartment of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Technology Indore, Indiamushirakhtar.ml@gmail.commtanveer@iiti.ac.in
Abstract
Adaptive vision-language model (VLM) ensembles save computation by stopping early on easy images and escalating harder ones. Although a single conformal threshold can make the final predictor marginally valid, it can still fail severely along one of its computational routes. We characterize this failure precisely: if a route has prevalence π, marginal 1−α coverage allows its conditional coverage to fall to [1−α/π]+. To repair the mismatch, we learn the router on development data, freeze every routing choice, and calibrate the returned score separately for early exits and escalated inputs. We call this pipeline Sequential Adaptive Group-Conditional Ensemble Conformal Prediction (SAGE-CP). Its calibration step is standard Mondrian split conformal prediction applied to the operational groups created by the router. Under exchangeability, the resulting sets have finite-sample coverage within each route. Across ten benchmarks, four frozen VLMs, and five aligned splits, both global calibration and SAGE-CP achieve 0.900 marginal coverage at a 0.90 target, but their route behavior differs substantially. SAGE-CP raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887 and reduces the mean route gap from 0.324 to 0.025, using the same routed scores and 1.177 source calls per image. The stronger guarantee increases macro mean set size from 1.893 to 2.212; the sets nevertheless remain smaller than those of the full ensemble (2.486) while using 70.6% fewer source calls. Sets grow on six datasets, with the largest change from 1.044 to 2.623 labels on Flowers-102. The route-reliability result persists across six fixed query fractions, while finer exit-depth groups reveal the expected need for more calibration data on rare routes. Finally, across five datasets, SAGE-CP reduces measured batch-one latency by 58.8%–63.4% and gross GPU energy by 55.7%–57.5% relative to full inference. Thus, routing provides the computational savings, while route-stratified calibration attaches coverage to the operational paths created by the router.
1Introduction
Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP support zero-shot image classification by comparing an image representation with text representations of candidate labels (27). Their behavior depends on the visual backbone, pretraining corpus, and scaling strategy (7; 15; 33). Consequently, different frozen VLMs need not make the same errors. Combining their evidence can produce a stronger predictor, but evaluating every source for every image also fixes inference cost at that of the full ensemble.Adaptive acquisition offers a more flexible operating point. A system can evaluate a strong source first, stop when the evidence is sufficiently clear, and acquire additional sources only for ambiguous inputs. Related work uses score aggregation to conformalize multiple predictors (24; 20; 1), while cascades and early-exit methods reduce computation by allocating different amounts of inference to different inputs (13; 18; 9). Combining these ideas creates an adaptive ensemble in which an image’s output and computational path are determined jointly. Some images exit after one source, whereas others are escalated through a longer sequence.Conformal prediction (CP) can wrap a fixed predictor with a label set whose marginal coverage is at least 1−α under exchangeability (34; 3). Work on conformal VLMs has studied the effects of backbone and score choice, transductive adaptation, localized thresholds, score variability, and test-time augmentation (12; 31; 14; 37; 30). These advances improve how a fixed VLM or ensemble is calibrated and how efficiently it represents uncertainty. An adaptive ensemble introduces a different question: does a marginal guarantee remain informative for each population created by its routing policy?The distinction matters because marginal coverage averages over the routing decision. A system can overcover images that stop early while concentrating most errors among escalated images, or it can fail in the opposite direction. Although unrestricted pointwise conditional coverage is unavailable without additional assumptions (5), finite, prespecified groups can receive meaningful conformal guarantees (35; 16; 22; 4). The computational routes of a frozen adaptive predictor provide such groups: they are observable without the test label and correspond directly to the acquisition paths experienced at deployment.Marginal validity can nevertheless hide an extreme route failure. We prove that a route with prevalence at most α may have zero coverage while the complete predictor remains marginally valid. The experiments show that this possibility is practically relevant. At a 0.90 target, global calibration achieves 0.900 mean marginal coverage across ten datasets, yet its mean minimum-route coverage is only 0.623. On Food-101, Oxford Pets, and Caltech-101, the minimum falls to approximately 0.30–0.37.We address this mismatch by aligning calibration with the deployed computation. We learn the complete routing policy on independent development data and freeze all design choices before final calibration. Since route membership under the frozen policy is observable without labels, standard Mondrian split CP can calibrate the returned score separately within each route. We call the resulting pipeline Sequential Adaptive Group-Conditional Ensemble Conformal Prediction (SAGE-CP).This repair changes the calibration boundary rather than the predictor. SAGE-CP does not retrain a VLM, alter the routed probabilities, or require additional inference beyond the adaptive policy. Routing supplies the source, latency, and energy savings, while route-stratified calibration attaches coverage to the operational populations created by that routing. We formalize the necessary separation between development and calibration and prove that a finite routing policy learned on independent development data remains valid after it is frozen.Routes are therefore more than an arbitrary post-hoc taxonomy. A route decides which sources are acquired and which score is returned, coupling group membership to the computation itself. Another fixed partition can validly protect a different declared population, but it need not protect the early-exit and escalated populations. Our target is specifically operational: the guarantee should hold along the acquisition paths that users experience.Our experiments are organized around four research questions (RQs). RQ1 examines whether marginal coverage can conceal route-conditional failures. RQ2 evaluates whether route-specific calibration repairs these failures without requiring full-ensemble inference. RQ3 tests whether the findings remain consistent across datasets, risk levels, calibration sizes, route granularities, and routing policies. Finally, RQ4 determines whether fewer source evaluations translate into measurable reductions in latency and energy consumption.Our contributions are:
1.A sharp prevalence-dependent characterization of what marginal conformal validity can hide. It quantifies the worst attainable coverage within a route and the largest attainable coverage gap between two routes as functions of route prevalence.
2.A calibration-safe adaptive-VLM protocol based on Mondrian split conformal prediction, together with a finite-sample route-conditional coverage theorem. The finite routing policy, conformity score, source order, and route partition may be selected using independent development data and then frozen before calibration.
3.A controlled five-split evaluation across ten datasets and four heterogeneous VLMs. At the same mean marginal coverage (.900), routed scores, and source usage, SAGE-CP increases mean minimum-route coverage from .623 to .887 and reduces the mean route-coverage gap from .324 to .025. Descriptive paired stability intervals exclude zero in favor of SAGE-CP on eight datasets; on the remaining two, they include zero, indicating no consistent difference across splits.
4.A real batch-one sequential deployment study across five datasets. Relative to full-ensemble inference, SAGE-CP reduces measured end-to-end latency by 58.8%–63.4% and sampled gross GPU energy by 55.7%–57.5%. The measurements include image loading and decoding, preprocessing, device transfer, synchronized GPU inference, routing overhead, and peak memory.The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 positions the work within conformal classification and adaptive inference. Sections 3 and 4 formalize the route-coverage failure and present SAGE-CP. Sections 5 and 6 describe the evaluation and findings, followed by the scope of the conclusions in Sections 7 and 8.
2Related Work

Conformal classification and VLMs.
Common conformal classification scores include the least-ambiguous set-valued classifier (LAC) score, adaptive prediction sets (APS), and regularized adaptive prediction sets (RAPS). These scores convert classifier probabilities into finite-sample-valid label sets with different efficiency and adaptivity properties (29; 2). A systematic evaluation of conformal vision and vision-language foundation models shows that the backbone, score, and adaptation strategy all affect coverage and efficiency (12). Conf-OT adapts zero-shot logits through a transductive optimal-transport procedure (31), whereas localized VLM conformal prediction varies thresholds using feature-space similarity around a query (14). Empirical-Bayes r-values incorporate variability across score realizations (37), and test-time augmentation can improve conformal efficiency through a separately learned augmentation policy (30). These methods address set efficiency, transfer, or local adaptation. In contrast, we study coverage within the groups induced by adaptive source acquisition.
Multiple predictors and adaptive computation.
Score averaging and symmetric aggregation exploit multiple predictors while preserving conformal validity (24; 20; 1), but these approaches ordinarily acquire every constituent output. Cascaded conformal inference instead prunes candidates across increasingly expensive models (13), and nested early-exit prediction sets address consistency across intermediate exits (18). Conformal Cascade uses conformal set size to defer large language model (LLM) queries and provides a general 1−K​α accepting-tier guarantee, which becomes tighter under an additional selection-preservation condition (9). Conformal learning-to-defer quantifies uncertainty in a rejector that allocates decisions between a model and a human expert (10). SAGE-CP addresses a complementary target: it returns a label set from the final adaptively aggregated VLM evidence. The selection rule is frozen before calibration, and the induced route groups are protected directly rather than through a per-stage union bound.
Mondrian and conditional coverage.
Unrestricted distribution-free pointwise conditional coverage is impossible without strong assumptions (5). Finite partitions permit meaningful group guarantees, and several methods extend or learn such groups (35; 16; 22; 4). Hierarchical pooling can also stabilize class-conditional conformal prediction when infrequent labels make classwise calibration data scarce (25). Our finite-sample scarcity problem is analogous, but the groups are computational routes rather than semantic classes. Mondrian CP calibrates separately within the categories of a fixed taxonomy (34). Once the router is frozen, its routes form such a taxonomy, and standard split Mondrian calibration produces exactly the same thresholds and sets as SAGE-CP. Proposition 3 formalizes this identity. The conformal quantile itself is standard; the new statistical target is the adaptive route. We characterize why this operational partition matters, how severely marginal coverage can fail within it, and how the routing policy can be learned without contaminating final calibration.Unlike demographic strata or feature clusters, a route is part of the predictor rather than side information about an input: it determines both the acquired models and the returned score. This coupling makes route coverage a direct deployment target when reliability is required along acquisition paths. Routes are not universally superior to other partitions; a different fixed taxonomy can protect a different declared population. In every case, the development/calibration boundary is essential because the route, score, and taxonomy must be fixed before the final conformal quantiles are fitted.

4Method

4.1Intuition
The bound reveals what went wrong: the guarantee averaged over the routes. The repair is to make those routes part of the calibration target. This needs a clean separation of roles. Development data design the routing and aggregation policy. Final calibration data provide coverage. Once the policy is frozen, route membership is observable without the test label. We can then calibrate a threshold for the score distribution on each operational path. In short: develop first, freeze once, and calibrate by route.Routing and calibration solve different problems. Routing decides which evidence is acquired and creates the compute savings. Mondrian calibration is not unique to routes; it protects whichever fixed, covariate-only groups define the reliability target. We use routes because early-exit and escalated inputs are the operational populations created by the deployed predictor.

text:
Israel’s proposed Security Hexagon points to a wider strategic design: extending its military reach across the Red Sea and Horn of Africa to contain Iran and Ansarullah in #Yemen .

Somaliland is central to this calculation. Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025 opened a new diplomatic channel in a region overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical artery for global trade and energy supplies. Reports of a potential Israeli military foothold at Berbera, alongside allegations of #UAE -backed military infrastructure intended for US and Israeli use, raise questions about the emergence of a forward operating network near Yemen.

Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions add another layer. Its January 2024 memorandum with Somaliland proposed coastal access, but Addis Ababa stopped short of recognition. On 19 October, #Ethiopia’s ambassador to #Israel , Tesfaye Yetaye Anteneh, warned that recognition might prompt #Somalia to demand the withdrawal of Ethiopian troops, increasing exposure to Al-Shabaab. Somaliland’s ambassador, Dr Mohamed Hagi, and Somaliland Chronicle editor Saeed Ibrahim rejected that assessment. Meanwhile, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud offered Ethiopia access through joint use of Somali ports, providing an alternative to a recognition deal.

The strategic concern is that commercial access and counterterrorism cooperation might become instruments for building an external military architecture. A foothold at Berbera would improve surveillance and logistical access around the Red Sea, while potentially increasing pressure on Ansarullah and Iran. Somaliland would gain external backing for its recognition campaign, but at the risk of becoming a frontline in a wider regional contest. Ethiopia, meanwhile, faces a choice between diversifying its trade routes and becoming entangled in rival security alignments.

Mohamud’s objections to Israeli military plans and the alleged expansionist vision associated with Greater Israel reflect fears that regional sovereignty is being subordinated to external strategic designs. The decisive question is whether the Security Hexagon develops into a mechanism for collective security or a network for projecting power against regional opponents. If the latter, the Horn of Africa risks becoming an extension of the confrontation involving Israel, the US, Iran and Ansarullah, with consequences for maritime security and the autonomy of African states.

text:
Nobody is arguing about lower congestion, freer roads or whatever. In terms of liveability, other parts of Nigeria generally offer better liveability than Lagos because of its huge population relative to its landmass. That is one. So, it is not even an argument about Abuja alone; we are talking about the entire country.

Abuja has a lower population than many other places in Nigeria, including cities and states in both the South and the North, so it naturally experiences less population pressure. Abuja’s population is around 4 million, while Oyo State has around 7 million people, Ogun State has almost 9 million, and Ibadan alone is home to millions of people. So, there is generally less congestion in many other parts of Nigeria than in Abuja, and especially Lagos. In terms of congestion and road pressure, many Nigerian cities offer better liveability than Lagos. When you travel outside Lagos, the difference hits you.

However, the point is about the video. The guy who posted it was talking about this particular design. Nowhere in Abuja will give you this exact view. I am not saying Abuja is not beautiful or that it is not a purpose-built city. That would be a lie. But in terms of this coastal view and design, Lagos offers a unique combination of skyscrapers surrounded by the Atlantic. That is not news; it is simply what the video was highlighting.

Besides, I hope you understand that the constant congestion and environmental challenges we discuss in Lagos are not necessarily permanent. They are influenced by the current administration, and a change of government is coming in the next six months. You cannot predict the transformation the next government might bring. The fact that the current governor has struggled to manage the city as effectively as some of his predecessors does not mean the next governor will not outperform all of them combined. You never can tell. Different leaders come with different ideas, fresh perspectives and new capacities.

Overall, Lagos has a much larger concentration of economic and commercial infrastructure than Abuja and any other Nigerian city. The fact that Lagos is dirty today does not mean it will still be dirty six months from now. Mind you, the head of LAWMA has been removed. You do not know who will come next or what new ideas they might bring, even under the same administration.

A new government is also on the horizon, so you cannot predict its approach to environmental management or the effort it will put into maintaining the city. Do not be too quick to draw permanent conclusions from temporary circumstances.

In a system like ours, where leadership changes every eight years, you should understand that a city's fortunes and dynamics can change significantly with a new administration.

text:
Durga Puja is a puja first. The name says it. The pandals, lights, food and music all grew around the worship, never the other way round.

Even its timing comes from scripture. 
Our tradition counts the 6 months of Dakshinayana as the night of the devas, and autumn falls inside that night. 
The Devi’s own season was spring, still kept in Bengal as Basanti Puja. 
Rama could not wait for spring. Before facing Ravana he needed her grace, so she had to be woken out of season. 
The Kalika Purana says Brahma awakened her for Rama’s sake, and lays down that she be awakened in a bel tree. 
Bengal’s Krittivasi Ramayana tells how Rama gathered 108 lotuses for her, found one missing, and was ready to offer his own eye in its place. 
This is Akal Bodhan, the untimely awakening. It is why the Puja still begins with Bodhan at a bel tree, and why Sandhi Puja still offers 108 lotuses.

The reason we pray to her is laid out in the Durga Saptashati, the text recited in every pandal. 
When Mahishasura drove the gods out of heaven, none of them could defeat him. 
Their combined radiance took form as one Devi, and each god handed her his own weapon. 
She is the shakti behind the gods themselves. 

Like Krishna in the Gita, she promises to come again whenever asuras torment the world. 

And she names this very season: whoever hears her glory with devotion during the great worship held every autumn is freed from all troubles. The autumn Puja is ordained in the Saptashati itself.

The same text tells of King Suratha, who lost his kingdom, and the merchant Samadhi, thrown out by his own family. 
Both still loved the people who had wronged them, and asked the sage Medhas why. 

He said this is Mahamaya, who drags even the wise into attachment and, when pleased, herself grants liberation. 

The Gita says this Maya is hard to cross, and the Saptashati says the way across is her grace. 

The two made an image of the Devi from river clay and worshipped it for 3 years. 
Suratha got back his kingdom. Samadhi asked for knowledge and was freed. Bengal still shapes her from river clay.

The daughter coming home is devotion, not its absence. 

The Saptashati says she dwells in every being as mother, and the Agamani songs of Ramprasad Sen made her Uma, Bengal’s own daughter. 

Loving the Devi as your own child is bhakti at its most intimate. That same daughter stands in the pandal with 10 weapons, killing Mahishasura.

Yes, most people in the pandals today come for the lights, the food and the photos. 
That is the result of decades of the colonial secular mindset this post comes from, which then calls the result the nature of the festival. 

A temple full of tourists is still a temple. As for the meat, Shakta texts lay down bali to the Devi, its meat was eaten as prasad, and Kalighat still offers meat bhog. Many Bengali homes keep Ashtami vegetarian and fast until Anjali.

Splitting religion from culture is a Western habit. For us, celebration has always sat under worship. Forget the worship, and the celebration loses its reason to exist.

text:
Just to set the records straight…

For all non-Bengalis who confuse Durga Puja (of Bengal) with Navaratri (outside Bengal), there's a simple big difference in the way it's celebrated. While Navaratri could be religious (as people claim it to be), Durga Puja is a cultural festival. There's a remarkable difference between religion and culture.

Why is Durga Puja not religious, but cultural? Here's a Bongs take!

1. For most Bengalis, they have nothing to do with devotion, and everything to do with celebration. Religion (as it has become) is an organized way to deal with devotees, and the Bengalis are far far away from any sort of blind beliefs.

2. God/Goddess is an image that's alienated from family of our own lives and seen as an authority. To Bengalis, Durga is just a part of our family. She could be termed as the Goddess, but never seen with a God-like image. There's way more love than devotion. It's a very human connection. She's the daughter of the house who's come for Autumn break to her parents house with kids and friends 

3. While people outside Bengal may fast as much as they like, Bengalis will continue to feast on Mutton Biriyanis and all sorts of delicious non-veg food (even at Puja premises where organizers often arrange for meals). Had there been any religious angle, things might not have been so simple.

4. Durga Puja as a festival is deeply connected to arts, crafts, music, theater, films ... everything! It's an all-round celebration. Only a very tiny percentage of people would bother to offer prayers. For the rest of us, Durga and the spirit of Durga puja is all in our heart. Even if we offer 'Anjali' (a prayer), our eyeballs hover all over the surrounding beauties in laal-paar-sada-sarees (a beautiful dress that ladies prefer to wear).

5. Durga puja is all-inclusive. Many Muslims in Bengal celebrate it too. Even there are religious Muslims who are the Presidents and Secretaries of Puja committees. No 'religious' festival could ever break these barriers!

6. There are hundreds of government and private awards given for 'Best Puja'. Not a single parameter in judgement relates to the devotion aspect of it. The Best Puja judgement takes into consideration the artistic finesse of the idol-making, the decorations around it, the lights, the sound, the safety measures, the theme, the concept, the social relevance of the theme, etc. It never considers how devotedly people offer prayers. So, devotion doesn't even come in our way of celebrating Durga Puja.

For those who have never witnessed Durga puja in Kolkata but have a lot to comment on it, please do make a visit. Your idea of a festival will change. Our country had no religion, but we thrived on our culture. It's time we pack religions into the sacks and throw them back to the western world (from where it has come) and fall back on our all-inclusive cultural ways of celebrating life once again.

Originally penned by Niilanjanaa Daschakraaborty

text:
This latest article from Thomas Pikkety, the renowned French economist and leading authority on wealth inequality, should be essential reading here in the UK.

His argument is simple.

France has never been wealthier. Yet education funding per student has fallen by 20% since 2017, public services are struggling, and inequality is deeply embedded in the system.

Sound familiar?

The problem isn't that our countries have run out of wealth. It's how that wealth is distributed, who controls it, and the political choices made to protect it.

For decades, we've been told that austerity, declining public services and falling living standards are unavoidable consequences of economic crises, yet those same decades have seen extraordinary concentrations of private wealth.

Socialise the costs. Privatise the gains.

This is the reality we all need to wake up to.

These aren't inevitable economic outcomes. They're the consequences of political choices, made over time, that have prioritised the accumulation of private wealth over the needs of society.

And as public anger grows, we're seeing a deeply concerning response: The rise of the far right, directing that anger towards immigrants, disabled people, those claiming welfare and other vulnerable groups, rather than towards the economic structures responsible for the inequalities people are rightly furious about.

As @NaomiAKlein describes fascism, "it's capitalism's most ferocious threat response. A way of directing public anger downwards at the vulnerable, rather than upwards at the system."

Fascism doesn't challenge the status quo. It protects it by giving people someone else to blame.

The fundamental question isn't whether our societies can afford something better. It's why, when we've never been wealthier, we're repeatedly told we must accept less.

We need to fundamentally rethink an economy built around extraction, exploitation and wealth concentration, and start building one that delivers equitable, sustainable prosperity for everyone.

And with the UK Budget next week, this should be a serious warning to @UKLabour.

If the Budget fails to acknowledge this fundamental reality, and instead offers another round of "difficult decisions" that protect concentrated wealth while asking ordinary people to shoulder the burden, then @andyburnham really hasn't understood what's happening across Europe.

What's unfolding in France isn't an isolated protest. It's a warning of what happens when people stop accepting that a society growing ever wealthier somehow can't afford to give them a better life.

This isn't something politicians can keep kicking down the road.

The warning signs are everywhere. The question now is whether those in power are prepared to confront the causes, or continue defending the very system that's driving the anger.
