text:
France imposes curfews as riots spiral
Weeks of protests over rising living costs and deteriorating public services have descended into violent clashes and widespread destruction
Published 19 Oct, 2026(FULL)
https://t.co/tvaBkZXbmh
France will introduce localized curfews as the unrest over rising living costs and deteriorating public services has escalated into widespread violence and destruction, leaving the authorities struggling to restore order.
The unrest escalated over the weekend, with nearly 2,400 people arrested, hundreds of businesses looted, and buildings set on fire across the country. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police lost control in several major cities.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu announced on Monday that he instructed the regional authorities to introduce curfews following an emergency government meeting.
“They will be partial and may be highly localized,” Lecornu said, adding that declaring a state of emergency cannot be ruled out.
Later on Monday, Paris police imposed an overnight curfew from 11pm to 6am in designated areas around Republic Square and the Les Halles district, restricting access for both adults and minors.
Nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured over the weekend, according to the Interior Ministry. In Limoges, rioters set fire to the city’s historic 19th-century town hall, causing the roof to collapse. Clashes, arson, and looting were also reported in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, and other cities.
Nunez offered his resignation on Sunday, acknowledging failures in anticipating and containing the violence. President Emmanuel Macron refused to accept it, instead ordering a review of security planning and intelligence failures and demanding changes to policing tactics.
More than 2,500 businesses were targeted on Saturday alone, according to Alain Di Crescenzo, the president of the French Chambers of Commerce and Industry.
The Association of Mayors of France called for gatherings outside town halls on Monday, denouncing failures in policing and warning of a “real risk to the entire nation.”
The protests began in September at a high school in Creteil, near Paris, over teacher shortages and deteriorating facilities. The movement has since spread to public sector workers and trade unions demanding higher wages, better services, and relief from rising living costs, while opposing spending cuts in the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
France is grappling with growing public debt (around 119% of GDP) and a substantial budget deficit. The government is seeking to reduce the shortfall through spending cuts and tax measures, while growing political uncertainty has pushed borrowing costs to the highest levels in more than 20 years.
The protests echo the 2018 Yellow Vest movement, which challenged Macron’s economic policies. Yellow Vest activists have joined the demonstrations and called for another round of protests on October 24.
The crisis has intensified pressure on Macron in the final months of his presidency, drawing criticism from across the political spectrum ahead of the 2027 election.
Right-wing politician Marine Le Pen, who leads in first-round presidential polling, called Macron a president “without credibility or authority” who has “lost all touch with reality.”
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) party, blamed “ten disastrous years”of Macron’s policies for the crisis and accused Nunez and police commanders of “complete incompetence.”

CanaryMedia: A new gas line or cash to electrify? California lets households choose,” by Alison F. Takemura.

“Before replacing gas service lines, utilities will need to offer customers a financial incentive to electrify instead, thanks to a new law.”

“When one of the nation’s biggest investor-owned utilities, Pacific Gas and Electric, wanted to replace Merrian Borgeson’s aging gas service line in Berkeley, California, she asked the company not to do it.” She was in the process of fully electrifying her home + would be replacing her stove—the only gas appliance left in the house —with an induction version during an upcoming kitchen remodel.

“The upgrade, which in PG&E’s service area typically costs $20,000 to $30,000, plus interest and operation and maintenance costs, gets paid for by all gas customers over the life of the infrastructure.”

“Now, I have no gas in my house,” Borgeson, “but the customers all around me are paying for that pipeline for the next 50 years.”

“A new law, the Home Energy Choice Act (Assembly Bill 2313), will require utilities to give households scheduled for a service line replacement the option of getting the new line or taking a financial incentive potentially worth several thousand dollars to get off gas instead.” Crucially, “the incentive to switch to all-electric equipment such as a heat pump, induction range, + heat-pump water heater, will be less than the cost to replace the line, resulting in savings that will be shared among all gas customers.”

“Natural Resources Defense Council [NRDC] has calculated that PG&E’s gas customers could save a total of $20 M if the utility gave 1,000 households a $17,500 incentive apiece rather than replacing their service lines.” For context, PG&E replaces about 15,000 service lines annually.

“In California, the next step is for the Public Utilities Commission to create a detailed framework for utilities to follow, including incentive levels, with larger amounts for customers in disadvantaged communities.” Other states are looking to emulate California with bills of their own, Velez said, pointing to Illinois, Maryland, Minnesota, Oregon, + Washington.

The electrostate is coming for the methane gas industry faster + faster. Yeah, + I live in Washington State, so fossil fuel folks can just take it on the chin.

text:
Paxton’s office prosecuted Hoffman and secured a guilty plea with an admission that he sexually touched the child’s genitals with sexual intent. That is not “protecting a pedophile.”
Hoffman was charged with continuous sexual abuse of a young child (a first-degree felony that can carry life). The local DA recused, so the AG’s office handled it. The first trial ended in a hung jury (7–5 for guilty). After that, the child refused to testify again. Without the victim’s testimony, prosecutors said they could not prove the felony elements. They offered a misdemeanor plea (indecent assault + display of harmful materials) that included the sexual-contact admission, some jail time, a lifetime no-contact order, and temporary loss of Hoffman’s law license. 
The initial one-day proposal is what the ads highlight. The judge rejected it, imposed 60 days, and Hoffman served roughly 30. He was not required to register as a sex offender in Texas because of how the plea was written; he does have to register in Nebraska. 
The outcome was light relative to the allegations. The stated reason was practical: a hung jury plus an unwilling key witness left no clear path to a felony conviction without further traumatizing the child. That is a prosecutorial judgment call, not evidence that the AG’s office shielded a pedophile.

text:
The Hallmarked Man Alternative Reread (8)

Mike (@MikeInWales2021) & Mozart – Galbraith’s Deep Dive into The Cuckoo’s Calling (CC) – Part 3, Chapters 1–3

After the difficulties of The Hallmarked Man (THM), and while we all wait impatiently for the publication of STE, Mike and Mozart are delighted to return to following Strike as he investigates the death of Lula Landry.

We have reached Part Three of The Cuckoo’s Calling, introduced by a quotation from Virgil’s Aeneid:

Forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit.

“Maybe one day it will be cheering even to remember these things.”

Mike’s Overview

Hello everyone. First, I apologise for the long wait since our last post. This is entirely my fault, not Mozart Galbraith’s. I hired a building firm to work on some projects, which began in February. Now, in October, the work that should have been finished in a month is still ongoing. The main issue is getting them to show up. To speed things up, I’ve taken on some of the minor tasks myself and spent every day they’ve been here cleaning up their mess. Needless to say, this has taken a huge toll on my time and many other things have fallen behind.

I’m ashamed of how long it’s taken me to write this summary (Mozart’s doing the main writing this time). I’ve retreated to an empty room and told my wife to leave me alone until I return.

So, here we go:

Chapter 1

We begin in Strike’s office. Robin expertly wraps a present for Strike’s nephew, while Strike reciprocates by writing her a pay cheque. However, his memories are in Cornwall and his sister Lucy. Robin also has other matters to consider, like HR interviews later. Strike asks if she wants the job.

Wardle has successfully arrested someone thanks to Strike’s mysterious informant and sends him the Landry police file by courier. There are many documents to sift through and a CCTV DVD to watch, but he doesn’t have a working DVD player in the office. Strike starts going through Tansy’s evidence to verify her version of events. He reads Duffield’s statement and memories of his mother’s death by drug use are triggered. He reflects on his own life, which isn’t great at the moment, and longs for a normal time with friends.

He returns to examining the statements and discovers Lula has made SIXTY-SIX calls to Duffield and Tony Landry. By midnight, he’s been at this for six hours but perseveres until exhaustion. He goes to bed and falls asleep instantly.

Chapter 2

Strike visits Lucy’s Bromley home, avoiding it as much as possible because he dislikes her husband Greg. Upon seeing him, Lucy doesn’t greet him but asks why Charlotte isn’t there. Strike fibs about Charlotte being at her sister’s in Scotland for some imagined crisis.

The party atmosphere is chaotic. There’s noise, over twenty screaming kids, an iPod in a docking station playing music (who had one of those in 2010?), food on a trestle table, kids getting hurt during games, nosy guests and wine in plastic cups. Did Lucy really believe Charlotte would willingly attend this suburban chaos? Lucy’s questions are deflected by her need to be a good hostess.

We learn about a Strike/Charlotte agreement: NO CHILDREN. He’s interrupted by a female guest who asks about his leg and his father Jonny Rokeby. This provokes a strong reaction from Strike, and she leaves, deeply offended.

Greg is more direct with his questions, asking where the gorgeous Charlotte is and if they’re splitting up again. Strike doesn’t bother to answer.

Spotting a lull in the commotion, Strike heads to their living room and uses the TV and DVD player to watch the police evidence DVD. While there, he sees a photo of a former SIB colleague called Tracey. He watches the grainy, blurry DVD repeatedly until he gathers all he can from it. He phones JB and Derrick Wilson but gets answerphone messages.

Jack enters the room, greets his uncle and quickly asks if he bought him a present. Strike hands over the gift to a delighted Jack, who’s extremely pleased with his paratrooper action figure.

Lucy finds them ten minutes later playing “soldiers”. She’s stressed and in a bad mood, telling both of them off in turn. Strike returns to the garden and takes up a defensive position behind a table covered in bowls of jelly and ice cream. (Good choice.)

Chapter 3

Strike is woken by his ringing mobile, charging next to his camp bed – it was JB wanting to make arrangements to meet Strike next day for lunch. Strike asks him for Lula’s laptop, and JB agrees to bring it along.

That chore dealt with, Strike luxuriates in a cigarette…and the peace, quiet and solitude of his bedroom/office. No noise, no children, no Greg, no interfering sister … and no nosy party people. Bliss.

He finally makes contact with Derrick and is told not to come over this week as Freddie Bestigui is at home. Strike asks for mystery girl Rochelle’s surname from the signing-in log. Reluctantly, Derrick looks and comes up with ‘Onifade’.

Strike looks up Guy Somé’s clothing on his computer and sees some very expensive clothes indeed, even the puzzlingly named ‘ready-to-wear’ (aren’t all clothes sold like that? 🤔). He also notes that all of Robin’s attempts to get an appointment for Strike have proven fruitless, despite the belief that Lula was his favourite model.

Mozart’s Detailed Analysis

Chapter 1 – Following the Evidence

We rejoin Strike on a wet Wednesday in London. The rain brings back memories of Cornwall, Aunt Joan and Uncle Ted’s spare room, where he stayed during childhood visits.

By Friday afternoon, the weather has improved little, but Strike and Robin’s working relationship continues to develop. Robin is preparing for another interview, this time in the HR dept. at a media consultancy in the West End. Strike pays her for a week’s work, less Temporary Solutions’ commission.

Their exchange is warm and easy. They speak simultaneously and congratulate each other, before Robin shows Strike the neatly wrapped present he has bought for Jack. I suspect Strike, with his ex-boxer’s hands, would have struggled to wrap it himself! He appreciates Robin’s efforts, asks about her interview and wishes her luck.

There is something rather lovely about this ordinary office conversation. Robin is still technically a temporary employee, and Strike cannot offer financial security, but they are developing a comfortable rhythm. Robin is also beginning to see that the agency offers something more interesting than another temporary office placement or boring full time employment.

Meanwhile, Strike is struggling physically. His walk down Denmark Street to smoke has become increasingly unpleasant in the incessant rain. He knows he needs to give up smoking and recover some fitness, but knowing what he ought to do and actually doing it are two different things!

His mobile rings. Eric Wardle, the police officer dealing with the Landry investigation, has news about a promised office file in connection to Lula’s death. Strike is unimpressed by the delay, but Wardle promises to pass on anything useful. Maintaining this relationship could prove invaluable.

Later that evening, the promised file arrives from Scotland Yard. It contains witness statements, the autopsy report, medical records, details of Lula’s medication, telephone records, security information and material recovered from her laptop. There is also a DVD marked “CCTV 2 Runners”, although Strike’s second-hand computer has a DVD drive that has never worked.

Strike works late, examining discrepancies between witness accounts and the physical evidence. The autopsy confirms that Lula died after falling onto the road, suffering a broken neck and internal bleeding. She was wearing only one shoe, and the clothes on her body differed from those she had worn when entering her building. Such details may seem minor, but the smallest inconsistency can help reconstruct events.

Tansy Bestigui’s changing account remains particularly interesting. Initially, she claimed to have heard Lula going from the bedroom to the bathroom. Later, she added details suggesting she had also heard the sitting-room window opening.

Her husband, Freddie, maintains that he was asleep until his wife’s screams woke him. He says he rushed into the sitting room in time to see Tansy running past in her underwear. He also explains the broken vase of roses he had sent to Macc, intending to introduce himself to the rapper.

Freddie’s account is not entirely convincing, but Strike is careful not to confuse an unpleasant personality with a murderer. Freddie admits to his wife’s cocaine use and acknowledges the strain in their marriage. Nevertheless, the police appear to have accepted much of his explanation.

The crucial question is not whether Freddie is likeable, but whether his account fits the evidence. Strike is particularly interested in the cocaine found beside the bath and the precise moment when Tansy claims to have seen Lula falling past the window. The file does not properly document the flat’s layout, making it difficult to establish where everyone was standing. Yet Tansy repeatedly insists that Freddie was asleep when Lula fell. Why is she so determined to establish that detail?

This is an excellent example of Strike’s investigative method. He does not immediately decide that someone is lying or assume that the police conclusion must be correct. Instead, he records inconsistencies and considers what further information he needs.

The file then takes him to Evan Duffield, Lula’s volatile boyfriend. Duffield admits attempting to prevent Lula from leaving him and confirms that he visited her building on the night of her death. He also describes wearing a wolf’s-head mask to avoid photographers.

His violent temper and heroin use make him an obvious suspect, particularly given the bruising on Lula’s upper arms. But Strike knows that drug addiction does not automatically explain someone’s behaviour. Duffield may be unpleasant and dangerous, but those qualities alone do not prove he killed Lula.

Galbraith refuses to make the solution as simple as choosing the most objectionable suspect. Duffield’s movements are supported by a driver who took him from Kentigern Gardens to d’Arblay Street. Other witnesses claim to have seen a man wearing a wolf mask, although their evidence is inconclusive. Wardle has also questioned the reliability of Whycliff, who might have been motivated by money.

Once again, Strike has evidence that is suggestive rather than decisive.

As the hours pass, his exhaustion becomes increasingly apparent. He smokes, yawns and looks out at the rain-soaked streets, wondering whether he will ever return to an ordinary social life. His injuries, lost military career and failed relationship with Charlotte have left him isolated. The agency and his growing connection with Robin are providing a purpose, but he is not ready to expose himself to other people’s curiosity or pity.

We then meet the two women who saw Lula during her final afternoon: Ciara Porter and Bryony Radford. The make-up artist remembers Lula as cheerful and excited about Deeby Macc’s impending arrival. Porter recalls a different mood: Lula seemed low and anxious, refusing to discuss what troubled her. She also provides a potentially significant detail: Lula had spoken of leaving everything to her brother.

Was this merely a passing remark, or did it reflect something more serious? Strike cannot yet know, but it adds another layer to the mystery.

Lula’s mother, Lady Yvette Bristow, maintains that her daughter was perfectly happy when she visited her. She believes Lula’s death was an accident, suggesting she slipped over the balcony on a cold night. Her account contrasts sharply with the more troubling picture emerging from other witnesses.

Tony Landry, Lula’s uncle, says he saw her the day before her death and that she seemed normal. He had travelled to Oxford for a conference and claims not to have realised she had repeatedly tried to contact him until later that afternoon.

The telephone records tell a different story. After making only a few calls during the morning, Lula repeatedly contacted two numbers shortly after lunchtime: those belonging to Evan Duffield and Tony Landry. The calls came in bursts, with short intervals between them.

What had happened to make Lula so anxious to speak to these two men? Strike cannot answer that yet, but the pattern is worth remembering. The contrast between Lula’s cheerful public image and her urgent attempts to contact people in her private life is becoming harder to ignore.

Strike is also frustrated by the incomplete security records from Kentigern Gardens. The movements of residents are not consistently documented, and the police have copied only the log for the day before Lula’s death. He had hoped to discover the surname of Rochelle, the elusive woman mentioned in the visitors’ records, but the information he needs is missing.

Nearly at midnight, he turns to the police report on Lula’s laptop. The officers have searched for emails suggesting suicidal intentions, but Strike begins reading the correspondence himself.

And here, at last, the case changes.

Lula’s photographs make her seem almost unreal to Strike. Her beauty has been celebrated so often that it has become abstract, an image endlessly reproduced in magazines and online. Her emails reveal a different person: funny, sociable, affectionate and full of plans for the future.

She emerges not simply as the beautiful model whose death attracted so much attention, but as a real person with friendships, private jokes and ordinary anxieties. Strike begins to understand her as someone who was alive and laughing only days before she died.

One message to a designer friend asks for help finding a birthday present for Rochelle. It is an affectionate, playful exchange, ending with Lula’s familiar sign-off, “Love ya. Cuckoo.” That final word offers a glimpse of Lula’s private world and reminds us how little her public image tells us about the person behind it.

Strike also revisits the claim that Lula regarded Guy Somé “like a brother”. Somé says he returned home from Japan on the night of her death and went straight to bed. Yet he lived within walking distance of Lula’s building, and the CCTV camera on Alderbrook Road might have captured anyone approaching from the opposite direction to Charles Street.

The police appear to have accepted Somé’s explanation, but Strike is not ready to do so without question.

Finally, exhausted, Strike closes the file, removes his prosthesis, unfolds his camp bed and falls asleep to the sound of traffic and rain.

Chapter 2 – A Birthday Party, a CCTV Camera and Two Runners

We leave Strike’s gloomy office and follow him to the Bromley home of his sister, Lucy. He arrives carrying the present Robin has wrapped for his nephew Jack. A magnificent magnolia tree stands in the front garden, its white flowers promising a more attractive scene later in the spring.

Strike has never been comfortable visiting Lucy at home. He prefers to meet her elsewhere, partly because she always seems harried by family life and partly because he has little time for his brother-in-law, Greg.

Lucy’s first question is not about Strike’s journey or injured leg, but Charlotte. Where is she? When Strike says Charlotte has gone back to Ayr for the weekend, Lucy immediately assumes another relationship crisis. She remains invested in his private life and seems unable to accept that his choices might differ from hers.

Outside, Strike encounters the domestic chaos he has deliberately avoided. His three nephews are tearing around the lawn with their party guests, while parents drink wine and beer. Greg, a quantity surveyor, has taken charge of the music. Strike finds his combination of forced cheerfulness and occasional aggression irritating.

Greg asks after Charlotte, and the conversation turns to Strike’s leg. A woman at the party recognises him as Lucy’s brother and expresses amazement that he can walk so well. Having apparently followed his progress through Lucy’s updates, she then asks whether he really is Johnny Rokeby’s son.

Strike is typically blunt. He has little patience for strangers prying into his parentage, particularly when they treat his prosthesis as an invitation to ask personal questions. When the woman persists, he tells her to mind her own business.

Strike has spent much of his life dealing with the consequences of being the son of a famous rock star, yet he has no interest in exploiting that connection. His military service, injury and life since leaving the army matter far more to him. Other people, however, continue to see him through the lens of his father’s celebrity.

Eventually, Strike escapes into the house and finds a quieter room in which to examine the DVD Wardle has supplied. The contrast is useful: outside is the noise and chaos of family life; inside, Strike is trying to establish what happened on the night Lula Landry died.

The footage begins with a snowy London street. The camera covers the junction of Bellamy Road and Alderbrook Road, where a lone man enters the frame. Tall and hooded, with his hands in his pockets, he wears a white scarf over his face. His clothing makes identification difficult, although Strike notices a mark on his jacket that might be a logo.

The man approaches the junction, appears to consult something in his pocket, then turns into Bellamy Road and disappears. The clock reads 01:39.

The taller man is recognisable as the individual Strike has just watched, his white scarf still covering his face. He is followed by a smaller, slighter man, also hooded and dressed in dark clothing. The film jumps to 02:12 with two runners in view.

Strike notices the second man’s running style. His fists are clenched, and he seems to struggle to keep up. As they pass beneath a streetlamp, a design on the back of his sweatshirt becomes briefly visible. Strike pauses the recording and examines it carefully.

This is a fine illustration of the patience detective work requires. Strike replays the footage, trying to decipher the logo. He thinks the first word may end in “ck”, while the second appears to begin with a “J”. The image is blurred, and he cannot be certain.

He watches again, concentrating on their movements rather than their clothes. Neither man appears to communicate or look back; they simply run, each absorbed in his own efforts.

The police seem to have regarded the taller man’s companion as evidence against him. Strike recognises that the footage suggests some connection between the two men: they are running through the same streets in heavy snow, in the early hours, dressed in a strikingly similar fashion. But he wants to know where the second man went.

The recording then cuts to the interior of a bus. A girl gets on, her face heavily shadowed but her blonde ponytail distinctive. The man who follows her resembles the taller runner: tall, hooded and wearing a white scarf across his face.

The footage moves to Theobalds Road. If the man walking quickly along the street is the same individual, he has removed the scarf, although his build and manner of walking appear similar. Strike notices that he seems to be making a conscious effort to keep his head bowed.

The DVD ends. Strike has not solved the mystery, but he has found a possible link between the man walking towards Kentigern Gardens and the taller runner on the CCTV footage. The second runner’s sweatshirt logo may also offer a way of identifying him.

Strike telephones John Bristow, leaving a message to say he has watched the footage and read the police file. He wants to ask further questions and hopes to meet Bristow the following week.

He then calls Derrick Wilson, the security guard at Kentigern Gardens, repeating his request to inspect the interior of number 18. Strike is determined to see the building himself rather than rely entirely on written accounts and incomplete security records.

Then Jack arrives, looking for his uncle. He is delighted to discover that Strike has brought him a present and eagerly unwraps the package to find a toy soldier.

Their conversation is one of the chapter’s lighter moments. Jack asks whether Strike had guns when he was a soldier and whether he still has them. Strike explains that he had two but had to give them back. Jack, with the straightforward logic of a seven-year-old, declares that this is a shame.

Strike helps him free the toy from its packaging and fix the gun into the soldier’s hand. Lucy soon finds them. Jack is playing happily, but she is irritated that he has opened his present before the party is over and sends him back outside.

The encounter reveals a softer side to Strike. Despite his impatience with Lucy and Greg, he gives Jack his attention, answers his questions honestly and helps him enjoy his present. His reluctance to have children does not mean that he dislikes them; he simply understands that family responsibilities are not what he wants for himself.

The chapter closes with Strike returning to the party, attempting to avoid curious mothers and their questions by helping to manage the children’s disputes before retreating behind a trestle table covered in jelly and ice cream.

Chapter 3 – Rochelle, a Designer and a Very Interesting Logo

Chapter Three opens early on Sunday morning, with Strike being woken by his mobile. It is John Bristow, sounding strained and anxious. His mother is unwell, and he has been unable to arrange a nurse to stay with her that afternoon. Nevertheless, he is keen to meet Strike the following day and wants to know whether there have been any developments.

Strike asks about Lula’s laptop, which is currently at their mother’s flat. Would Bristow bring it to their meeting? He readily agrees.

Strike has already spent hours examining the police file and begun building a picture of Lula through her emails. Now he wants to examine the laptop itself, rather than rely on what the police have chosen to extract from it.

After the call, Strike enjoys a rare moment of peace, smoking in his quiet office and appreciating the absence of children screaming around him. The contrast with Lucy’s birthday party is amusing. He may be fond of his nephews, but he is equally fond of being able to shut the door on family life!

Later, after several unsuccessful attempts to contact Derrick Wilson, Strike finally gets through to the security guard at Kentigern Gardens. Wilson explains that he cannot arrange a visit that week because Mr Bestigui is causing trouble, but offers to let Strike know when a suitable opportunity arises.

Strike asks about Rochelle, the friend from rehabilitation whom Kieran Kolovas-Jones mentioned in connection with Lula. He wants her surname, which has so far eluded him.

Wilson consults the visitors’ log and identifies her as Rochelle Onifade. She last visited in early November.

It is a small but important breakthrough. Strike now has a full name to investigate, and the timing of Rochelle’s visits may help reconstruct Lula’s movements and relationships. Once again, he is patiently filling gaps in incomplete records.

Having finished the call, Strike returns to the computer and resumes examining Guy Somé’s clothing designs. This brings us back to the CCTV footage, particularly the distinctive logo briefly visible on the second runner’s sweatshirt.

Somé’s website divides his work into two sections. The ready-to-wear collection includes maroon suits, narrow knitted ties and leather accessories, while the other features expensive designer pieces costing thousands of pounds.

Strike is looking for the stylised GS he noticed on the runner’s sweatshirt. It is clearly visible on several items in the menswear section, including a hooded zip-up jacket.

There is, however, a problem. Despite Robin’s efforts, Somé’s organisation has been unwilling to cooperate with requests for an interview about Lula’s death. His company appears determined to maintain a corporate silence, even though Lula was one of its most famous models.

This reluctance is worth noting. Somé was part of Lula’s professional world, and Strike has already discovered that their relationship may have been closer than the police investigation suggests. Yet the fashion house shows little enthusiasm for helping him understand what happened.

Strike now has two useful leads: Rochelle Onifade, whose name he has finally established, and the distinctive GS logo that may connect the CCTV runner to Guy Somé’s clothing.

The connection is not proof. The logo may indicate that the runner was wearing a garment from Somé’s collection, but Strike still needs to establish who the man was and why he was there at that hour. Nevertheless, the CCTV footage and the designer’s website have given him something concrete to investigate.

Today’s commemorated feasts and saints
Greatmartyr Artemius at Antioch (362). Righteous Child Artemius of Verkola. Ven. Gerasimos the New Ascetic, of Cephalonia (1579). Ven. Matrona of Chios (14th c.).

Greatmartyr Artemius at Antioch
Commemorated on October 20
Holy Great Martyr Artemius of Antioch was a prominent military leader during the reigns of the emperor Constantine the Great (May 21), and his son and successor Constantius (337-361). Artemius received many awards for distinguished service and courage. He was appointed viceroy of Egypt. In this official position he did much for the spreading and strengthening Christianity in Egypt.

Saint Artemius was sent by the emperor Constantius to bring the relics of the holy Apostle Andrew from Patras, and the relics of the holy Apostle Luke from Thebes of Boeotia, to Constantinople. The holy relics were placed in the Church of the Holy Apostles beneath the table of oblation. The emperor rewarded him by making him ruler of Egypt.

The emperor Constantius was succeeded on the throne by Julian the Apostate (361-363). Julian in his desire to restore paganism was extremely antagonistic towards Christians, sending hundreds to their death. At Antioch he ordered the torture of two bishops unwilling to forsake the Christian Faith.

During this time, Saint Artemius arrived in Antioch and publicly denounced Julian for his impiety. The enraged Julian subjected the saint to terrible tortures and threw the Great Martyr Artemius into prison. While Artemius was praying, Christ, surrounded by angels, appeared to him and said, “Take courage, Artemius! I am with you and will preserve you from every hurt which is inflicted upon you, and I already have prepared your crown of glory. Since you have confessed Me before the people on earth, so shall I confess you before My Heavenly Father. Therefore, take courage and rejoice, you shall be with Me in My Kingdom.” Hearing this, Artemius rejoiced and offered up glory and thanksgiving to Him.

On the following day, Julian demanded that Saint Artemius honor the pagan gods. Meeting with steadfast refusal, the emperor resorted to further tortures. The saint endured all without a single moan. The saint told Julian that he would be justly recompensed for his persecution of Christians. Julian became furious and resorted to even more savage tortures, but they did not break the will of the saint. Finally the Great Martyr Artemius was beheaded.

His relics were buried by Christians. After the death of Saint Artemius, his prophecy about Julian the Apostate’s impending death came true.

Julian left Antioch for a war with the Persians. Near the Persian city of Ctesiphon, Julian came upon an elderly Persian, who agreed to betray his countrymen and guide Julian’s army. The old man deceived Julian and led his army into the Karmanite wilderness, where there was neither food nor water. Tired from hunger and thirst, Julian’s army battled against fresh Persian forces.

Divine retribution caught up with Julian the Apostate. During the battle he was mortally wounded by an unseen hand and an unseen weapon. Julian groaned deeply said, “You have conquered, Galilean!” After the death of the apostate emperor, the relics of the Great Martyr Artemius were transferred with honor from Antioch to Constantinople.

Saint Artemius is invoked by those suffering from hernias.

text:
Ouch: 

A source check on the links SweetZombieJesus posted. You’ll be stunned to know that not one single one of his arguments is actually supported by them. Shocker I know.

He’s even misattributed at least one. Makes you think what else he’s lying about?

Liza Cowan’s 1970 recording is completely misrepresented.
https://t.co/eN7LbrMM5N

“Gay” describes sexuality; it doesn’t settle gender identity. “Transvestite” was period language. Quoting one label while leaving out the rest of Johnson’s interview gives a misleading picture.
https://t.co/eN7LbrMM5N

Johnson’s 1972 interview in Out of the Closets is another early first-person source. She discusses transvestites’ experiences and discrimination. Read the interview, not just its title.
https://t.co/Hhz7QBrxPK

Steve Watson’s 1979 again, does not support your argument.
https://t.co/0iyfYer5yy

Watson’s he/him narration is the reporter’s wording. It isn’t, by itself, Johnson saying “I am a man.” The same interview has Johnson describing going out in drag full-time.
https://t.co/0iyfYer5yy

Eric Marcus’s 1989 interview gives Johnson’s own account: she got downtown around 2am, when the raid and riot were underway. It challenges the “first brick” story, but places her at Stonewall. Again, it doesn’t support your argument.
https://t.co/LAYZCle4Ci

Randy Wicker is valuable: he was Johnson’s friend and housemate for 12 years. But he was close to her, not a detached observer. Treat his recollections as hearsay and compare them with others.
https://t.co/WX71mx8wqX

Robert Heide’s account is a later eyewitness recollection. It supports his memory of Johnson shouting and throwing rocks. It can’t prove she started the uprising or threw the first brick.
https://t.co/ji6lzf612q

Jim Kepner’s 1988 video does not remotely support any arguments you make.
https://t.co/bcnNqDdYBw

Pay It No Mind includes Johnson’s final interview, recorded in 1992. The documentary was released in 2012. The film’s editing and promotional labels are interpretation.
https://t.co/GKJalfuj8R

Holly Woodlawn’s memoir offers personal recollections of the downtown scene. Useful testimony, but retrospective memoir isn’t a contemporaneous transcript or definitive proof of Stonewall’s exact chronology.
https://t.co/0YmelCaawb

Donn Teal’s The Gay Militants and Arthur Bell’s Dancing the Gay Lib Blues are near-contemporary movement histories. They help with context; but don’t prove anything about Johnson.
https://t.co/vNjWF1nkDe
https://t.co/nqIJ6sGHpc

The Slate article “The Chickens and the Bulls” documents a gay extortion ring. It is background on criminal exploitation—not evidence that Johnson, Rivera or STAR House took part.
https://t.co/reQYk5FDmf

https://t.co/qQW1TLDWUG makes claims about Ed Murphy and Mike Umbers exploiting boys. Those claims concern alleged activity by those men. The article does not show Johnson or Rivera trafficked STAR residents.
https://t.co/S26hoAcCLI

Arthur Bell’s 1971 “After-Hours 28” reports allegations and charges involving Umbers. Charges are not the same as convictions—and the article does not connect those allegations to children at STAR House.
https://t.co/NXa1PTxC7i

The screenshot credits “After-Hours 28” to Allen Young; references I found attribute it to Arthur Bell. Check the original issue’s byline before repeating the attribution.

మంగళవారం విజయదశమి పర్వదినాన్ని పురస్కరించుకుని వరంగల్ పోలీస్ కమిషనరేట్ పరిధిలో ప్రజలు ప్రశాంత వాతావరణంలో, ఆనందోత్సాహాలతో, భక్తిశ్రద్ధలతో పండుగను ఘనంగా జరుపుకోవాలని వరంగల్ పోలీస్ కమిషనర్ ఎన్. శ్వేత, ఐపీఎస్ ఆకాంక్షించారు.

ఉదయం స్థానిక పోలీస్ హెడ్‌క్వార్టర్స్‌లోని ఆయుధ భాండాగార మందిరంలో పోలీస్ కమిషనర్, పోలీసు అధికారులు వేద పండితుల ఆధ్వర్యంలో దుర్గామాత సన్నిధిలో సంప్రదాయబద్ధంగా ప్రత్యేక ఆయుధ పూజలు నిర్వహించారు. చెడుపై మంచి సాధించిన విజయానికి ప్రతీకగా నిలిచే విజయదశమి పర్వదినాన్ని పురస్కరించుకుని ఈ పూజా కార్యక్రమాలు నిర్వహించారు. అనంతరం సాయుధ పోలీసు విభాగం, మోటార్ ట్రాన్స్‌పోర్ట్ విభాగానికి చెందిన సిబ్బందితో కలిసి పోలీసు వాహనాలకు ప్రత్యేక పూజలు నిర్వహించారు.

ఈ సందర్భంగా పోలీస్ కమిషనర్ మాట్లాడుతూ ప్రజలందరికీ విజయదశమి శుభాకాంక్షలు తెలిపారు. ప్రజలు పండుగను ఆనందోత్సాహాలతో ఘనంగా జరుపుకోవాలని ఆకాంక్షించారు. వరంగల్ పోలీస్ కమిషనరేట్ పరిధిలో ప్రశాంత వాతావరణాన్ని నెలకొల్పేందుకు పోలీసు శాఖ అహర్నిశలు కృషి చేస్తోందని తెలిపారు. పోలీసు శాఖలో ఆయుధాలు కీలక పాత్ర పోషిస్తాయని, విజయదశమి రోజున ఆయుధాలకు ప్రత్యేక పూజలు నిర్వహించడం ఆనవాయితీ అని పేర్కొన్నారు. ఈ పర్వదినం ప్రజలందరి జీవితాల్లో విజయాలు, సుఖసంతోషాలు నింపాలని ఆకాంక్షించారు. అనంతరం జమ్మి చెట్టుకు ప్రత్యేక పూజలు నిర్వహించారు.

ఈ కార్యక్రమంలో ఈస్ట్ జోన్ డీసీపీ అంకిత్ కుమార్, సెంట్రల్ జోన్ డీసీపీ ధార కవిత, అడిషనల్ డీసీపీ (అడ్మినిస్ట్రేషన్) రాయల ప్రభాకర్ రావు, అడిషనల్ డీసీపీ (క్రైమ్స్) బాలస్వామి, ఆర్మ్డ్ రిజర్వ్ అడిషనల్ డీసీపీలు సురేష్, శ్రీనివాస్, ఆర్మ్డ్ రిజర్వ్ ఏసీపీలు అంతయ్య, సురేంద్ర, రిజర్వ్ సబ్‌ఇన్‌స్పెక్టర్లు స్పర్జన్ రాజ్, సతీష్, శ్రీధర్, మోటార్ ట్రాన్స్‌పోర్ట్ విభాగం సిబ్బంది తదితరులు పాల్గొన్నారు.

text:
Fired for Refusing COVID Jabs and Blocked From Jobs Without Mandate, Firefighters Seek Jury Trial | Greg Piper, Just The News

Unlike firefighter challenge that Supreme Court just rejected, plaintiffs in Microsoft's home town say they provided "hard facts" that Redmond rejected religious accommodations nowhere near "undue hardship" standard.

Can the government fire public workers for refusing vaccination on religious grounds, when it could easily accommodate them in several ways, then sabotage their ability to get work that doesn't require vaccination?

Those are the questions set before the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in litigation by firefighters against the Seattle suburb of Redmond, the home of Microsoft, two weeks after the Supreme Court declined to review the 9th Circuit's ruling against a similar challenge by firefighters against a regional fire agency in Washington's Snohomish County.

Both sets of challengers accuse lower courts of chronically misapplying a 2023 SCOTUS precedent for Christian postal worker Gerald Groff, which raised the standard for employers to reject religious accommodation requests such as Sundays off for Groff, by reaching speculative conclusions that accommodation would cause employers "undue hardship."

SCOTUS denied review despite a 3-3 circuit split on whether employers must show only a "reasonable concern" that an accommodation would create an undue hardship, or actually "prove" it.

Unlike the Snohomish firefighters, however, the Redmond firefighters provided "hard facts" that the city could have accommodated them without endangering the health of patients when they answer emergency calls, in contrast to the "tenuous chain of improbable events" Redmond officials invoked to deny religious accommodations, their opening brief says.

After all eight plaintiffs received accommodations, the city singled out firefighters for COVID vaccine mandates – police officers were exempt despite the fact that they also "rode in ambulances and provided life-saving care" – which continued into 2022 after Redmond had "relaxed" other COVID-related rules on first responders, the brief says.

Perhaps the most explosive of the plaintiffs' allegations is that the city actively hid no-mandate jobs that didn't "involve contact with medical patients" from unvaccinated firefighters, negotiated by their union to minimize firings, and instead gave them to vaccinated firefighters.

Mayor Angela Birney made plain her animus against the religious firefighters by explicitly citing their requests for religious accommodation in her Sept. 21, 2021, executive order banning religious accommodations, and told plaintiff Joshua Frei days later she would accept nothing less than "zero risk of transmission" from firefighters, the plaintiffs claim.

Birney's executive order, terminated in February 2023, is notable for its false claim that vaccination stops COVID infection and transmission, two months after breakthrough infections from the Delta variant became inescapable and eight months after then-Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Rochelle Walensky acknowledged them.

The "public expectation is that Redmond firefighters will not expose patients to the potential transmission of COVID-19 by being unvaccinated" and will get vaccinated "to protect themselves from the disease," the executive order says.

"The government cannot erase a religious accommodation simply because leaders decide there should be 'consequences for the unvaccinated,'" said Texas-based First Liberty Institute senior counsel Cliff Martin, who represents the firefighters alongside D.C.-based Williams & Connolly and the California-based Church State Council.

He was quoting from the mayor's alleged conversation with Human Resources Director Cathryn Laird, cited in a related appellate brief against individual defendants, in which Birney said the city should be seen "making the unvaccinated uncomfortable" and "treat[ing] [them] differently" for the sake of "public perception."

The opening brief against the city itself says Laird then told plaintiff Matthew Peterson that Redmond had to show a "consequence for being unvaccinated," which was being made uncomfortable and treated differently.

Obvious accommodations ignored by Redmond, Biden judge

U.S. District Judge Jamal Whitehead, nominated by President Biden, gave a superficial reading of the facts of the Redmond challenge when he issued summary judgment to the city last December, finding the situation indistinguishable from the Snohomish challenge the 9th Circuit rejected, the opening brief says.

Redmond had four ways of granting religious accommodations without undue hardship, defined by SCOTUS in Groff as "excessive" or "unjustifiable" costs that employers may refuse to bear without violating Title VII civil rights of employees, the plaintiffs allege.

The city could have asked vaccinated firefighters to "swap" so unvaccinated colleagues get "non-patient-facing roles," reassigned plaintiffs to the Fire Prevention unit – which already had two vacancies – or to jobs with city-identified accommodations, or let them keep masking and testing, the accommodations they were granted before Birney's order.

The Seattle area was among the first to officially experience the novel coronavirus, which showed up in West Coast blood donations in mid-December 2019, and Redmond acknowledged its firefighters showed "exceptional" compliance with personal protective equipment controls, with no known firefighter-to-patient transmissions, the brief says.

Yet just "hours" after Redmond approved the last of the religious accommodation requests, explicitly allowed under the healthcare worker mandate imposed the prior month by then-Democrat Gov. Jay Inslee, the union learned the city had reneged on its agreement to allow "masking and pre-shift testing" in lieu of vaccination and revoked all accommodations.

Six of the eight plaintiffs took leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act, for the "emotional distress of being forced to choose between their faith and their jobs," to delay termination. The seventh used FMLA to care for a family member and retired to avoid firing, and the eighth stayed on and was fired two weeks after the Oct. 18 jab deadline, the brief says.

Four days after the jab deadline, the city for the first time found four jobs with "possible accommodations," one of which plaintiff Brian Robillard already held when he was ordered to get vaccinated or quit, yet it notified only the six plaintiffs on leave for emotional distress and told them to expect an answer by Dec. 17 of that year, the plaintiffs allege.

On the cusp of their return in March 2022, the six stated their interest in accommodations "for the third time," yet three-of-the-four slots had already expired or been filled, and the city falsely claimed the fourth had been filled. Redmond offered no accommodations when the six returned, resulting in their firing, the brief says.

Irrelevant that city 'perhaps' violated federal law

The city's good-faith defense was a joke, the plaintiffs claim: It gave six of them "the chance to apply" for four jobs, never told the other two, "gave some of those jobs to vaccinated firefighters," then completed "an ever-shifting process" without "a real shot at receiving reassignment."

Redmond repeatedly delayed its undue-hardship defense and ended up never providing evidence, the absence of which was "especially obvious" for plaintiff Robillard, who was already in "a non-patient-facing position that did not require vaccination" yet was ripped from him and given to a vaccinated colleague, according to the brief.

Judge Whitehead granted summary judgment for Redmond by not requiring any evidence of good-faith accommodation, refusing to find prejudice in the city's mediocre undue-hardship defense, and making himself his own expert witness in claiming masking and testing would not protect "both the workforce and the public," the brief says.

The Biden nominee ignored the swap and Fire Prevention accommodations, didn't consider whether Redmond could have left Robillard in his job before he went on leave – while conceding the city "perhaps" violated FMLA – and never mentioned evidence of retaliation, including when the mayor "called out" unjabbed firefighters in her executive order, plaintiffs claim.

They have indisputably proven they engaged in a "protected activity under Title VII" and suffered "an adverse employment action" – requesting accommodations and getting fired – and all that remains is for a jury to determine "whether the City retaliated against them because they requested religious accommodations."

The city took only a "hardline stance on vaccination" more than a month after Inslee's order that expressly allowed religious accommodations, just after the city had approved the plaintiffs' requests, suggesting it was "happy to offer accommodations in the abstract" but not when "faced with real requests that it perceived as problematic," the brief says.

text:
1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.
2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”
Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.
3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.
Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.
4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.
This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.
Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle
5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.
Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.
6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.
Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.
7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.
No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.
8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.
9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.
10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.
Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.
11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.
Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again
12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.
Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.
Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.
13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.
In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.
14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.
Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?
15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.
What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”
16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.
He Defended Faith and Family
17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.
Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.
He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.
No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.
18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.
Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.
19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.
That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.
20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First
21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.
Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.
22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.
Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.
23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.
24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.
Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.
25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.
Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.

Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.

text:
THE MAN WHO CHANGED MY LIFE! 🥹

One night in 2008, my friend Oliver called to inform me that I had been offered supplementary admission into the University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN).

The only problem then was that I needed between ₦5,000 and ₦7,000 to pay my acceptance fee by 9a.m the following morning to secure the admission.

My dad and I rushed to the house of an uncle I was learning the provision business from and whose shop I worked in. We pleaded with him to lend us ₦5,000 since my dad hadn't received his salary.

Do you know what this man said?.....He told us he didn't have ₦5,000 to give us.

Omo! I nearly lost it!...Because earlier that day, I and five other boys had been at his shop, and we sold over ₦150,000 worth of provisions. Yet, he couldn't lend me ₦5,000 to secure my admission?

Anyways, my dad and I left his house and headed to the home of one of his friends.

The moment we explained our situation, this man gave me ₦10,000 and gave my dad an additional ₦5,000. Since it was already late, he asked one of his younger brothers to drive us home in his car.

Before we left, he told me to visit his office the following day after paying my acceptance fee.

I did exactly that......When I got to his office, he took me to UBA Bank and opened my very first bank account. Right there, he deposited ₦105,000 as my starting balance!

Then he looked at me and said: “Don't touch this money until you get to UNN. And promise me one thing: Make sure you make your dad and me proud.”

Chaiiiii, I cried like a baby inside that bank. 🥹

From 2008 to 2012, whenever I returned home from school, I would drop my bags at home and head straight to this man's house to tell him I was back and share my school experiences with him.

Between 2016 and 2021, when I started working, I made it a tradition to gift him half a bag of rice and a gallon of groundnut oil every December as a little token of appreciation.

Then, in 2023, when I got married, he called me and said:
“Now that you're married and building your own family, please stop sending me half a bag of rice and groundnut oil every December. My family and I are grateful for everything. It's time to focus on your own family going forward.”

That statement alone told me the kind of man he is!

Till today, whenever I see his children around the neighbourhood, I give them a few thousand naira and tell them: “Tell your daddy that Uncle Chuka says hello.”

He always calls me afterward and says: “Thank you so much, my boy, for your thoughtfulness. But you're beginning to spoil these children oh!” 😂

And I always reply: “Sir, please let me spoil them. They're only enjoying the goodness of their father.”

Sometimes, God answers our prayers through people who choose to show up for us when we need help the most.

My dad's friend didn't just help me secure admission into UNN. He gave me hope, supported my education, and taught me a lesson about kindness and generosity that I will never forget.

Today, whenever I have the opportunity to extend that same kindness to his children, I do it with joy. Because when someone is good to you, don't just remember them. Find ways to keep their goodness alive.

May God bless everyone who has ever helped someone at a critical point in their life. 🙏
