❄️🔞

Zayne mentioned that he had three surgeries scheduled today, so I made sure to visit during his break, hoping to catch him when he had time to rest. 

On the way to the hospital, I passed by a newly opened pastry shop and found myself drawn in by the warm scent of red bean buns. I had to buy some for him, hoping to surprise him with this sweet treat.

Carefully opening his office door, I found him asleep at his desk, his glasses folded neatly beside him and his coat draped over his back like a blanket. I couldn’t help but admire him for a moment before placing the box of buns on his desk.

Unfortunately, I had forgotten the tea I had ordered with them. Dang it. Food without something to drink felt incomplete so slipped back out. I was careful with every step as I did not want to wake him yet, but my foot caught the edge of a chair. I panicked and hurried, nearly brushing the doorway as I fled. I didn’t even look back to hide my embarrassment.

My phone vibrated in my pocket.

Zayne: I just saw an ominous shadow float by my office door.

Me: Don’t tell ghost stories this late at night!

Zayne: The ghost left red bean buns on my desk while I was asleep. She was rather silly, though. She almost bumped into the doorway.

I laughed as I hurried back to the pastry shop. The staff was already waiting for me with the tea in a takeaway bag and an apology. I smiled at him, took the bag, and messaged Zayne before heading back.

Me: Aren’t you afraid the ghost will eat you if she stays in your office?

Zayne: I just washed my hands after leaving the operating room. I’m clean enough, but I can’t promise I’m delicious.

Heat rose to my cheeks. I had no clever answer to counter him.

When I returned to his office, he was already awake and seated with his coat hung neatly on the rack, his arms crossed and a cunning smile welcoming me as if someone had been busted.

“So the ghost finally revealed herself. With drinks onhand, too.”

“Sorry, I was so preoccupied that I forgot the tea at the shop. I didn’t want my efforts to go to waste, so I hurried back to get it.”

I noticed that he had already eaten two buns. My poor Zaynie must be really hungry. I handed him the tea, watching as he took a sip.

“How should I repay this kind ghost?” he asked. “Should I offer her more red bean buns.. or perhaps something tastier?”

“Maybe this ghost is more than willing to give you more.”

I moved behind his chair.

“You can see me,” I murmured, “but can you feel me?” I brushed my fingers over his ear. I felt him flinch, then the tip of his ear flushed red. He held still, kept his composure, and continued to play along.

“No. It might just be air.”

I let my fingers drift lower, brushing the corner of his mouth. His lips parted under my touch, tender warm breath against my fingers. What had started as teasing was already turning against me, I could feel the heat rising within me.

I smiled and continued, pretending I wasn’t just as affected by our little game. I cupped his chin and tilted his face upward until our eyes met. Even from this angle, he was breathtaking.

The teasing look in his eyes told me he had no intention of letting me win.

“How about this?” I whispered, leaning closer until our breaths mingled. His hand closed around mine and held it against his cheek.

“It’s amazing how you can touch the ghost. Does this doctor have superpowers?”

Our faces were so close to each other, lips almost touching. I closed my eyes, waiting for the kiss. But his warm breath reached my ear instead.

“Lock the door.”

text:
Somewhere this morning, an employee looked at their calendar and whispered, “I cannot do this anymore.” Across town, someone unemployed opened their laptop, stared at 47 unanswered applications, and whispered, “Please, just give me a chance to do this again.” Same morning. Different exhaustion.

People with jobs are burned out, underpaid, overlooked, and trapped in meetings that could have been an email. People looking for jobs are filling out applications that require a resume, then demand they manually type their entire resume into 19 boxes. Apparently PDF technology is still at NASA.

Both are exhausted. It’s a reminder to be kind to each other. Having a job doesn’t automatically mean you’re happy. Some offices have so much drama that HR should hand out season passes. Some bosses treat a lunch break like a federal investigation. You work hard, cover three vacant positions, and receive a company branded water bottle as your annual appreciation. It leaks, like management.

But being unemployed has a different kind of weight. The alarm clock stops ringing, yet you wake up worried anyway. You check your email before breakfast and recognize rejection templates by font. Then a recruiter tells you that your impressive experience doesn’t align with their needs, even though the job description appears to have been copied directly from your resume.

The worst part isn’t always the rejection. Sometimes it’s the silence. It’s trying to explain to your family why nothing has happened yet. It’s watching your savings shrink while someone on LinkedIn announces that getting hired is simply a matter of having a positive attitude. Brenda, will positive thinking cover my electric bill?

If you’re employed, please remember that your paycheck and your job title are not permanent guarantees. I’ve seen companies call people family until their badges stopped working. Corporate loyalty can disappear faster than free donuts in the break room. And if someone you know is searching, don’t tell them to “just keep applying.” They are applying. They’re networking. They’re practicing interviews, adjusting their resumes, writing cover letters, and trying to keep their confidence together with the emotional equivalent of duct tape. Ask how they’re doing. Offer an introduction. Buy them coffee. Sometimes being remembered is more valuable than receiving another motivational quote from a CEO standing beside a private jet.

To everyone searching: a rejection does not erase your accomplishments. A hiring manager’s decision does not determine your value. You are still the person who built teams, solved problems, raised families, helped coworkers, and kept going through difficult days.

And to everyone employed: I hope your job gets better. I hope you get the raise, the respect, and the peace you deserve. Just remember, the person praying for an interview today could be sitting beside you tomorrow. When that day comes, make room at the table. They fought hard to get back to it.

text:
@mjfree, you called January 6 an insurrection. Here's what a science teacher can't get past: the party that tells everyone the Second Amendment exists to check a tyrannical government supposedly tried to overthrow that government and forgot to bring the guns. I graded the whole claim.

Start with the word you leaned on. Insurrection is a federal crime, 18 U.S.C. § 2383. Number of people charged with it for January 6, Trump included: ZERO. Not by Merrick Garland. Not by Jack Smith, who wanted Trump the way a toddler wants the cookie jar. The House impeached for "incitement of insurrection" and the Senate acquitted, 57-43. So the label is all hat and no cattle. It's an opinion wearing a judge's robe.

Now the guns. Roughly 1,500 people were charged. Prosecutors went through phones, hotel rooms, and trucks. They found a handful of people who carried a pistol onto the grounds, and they charged them. A handful. In a country with more privately owned guns than people. And the only person shot dead that day was Ashli Babbitt, an unarmed Air Force veteran, shot by a Capitol Police officer. The weapons prosecutors kept describing were flagpoles, bear spray, a fire extinguisher, and a hockey stick. Real violence against real cops, and those people earned their charges.

I spent two decades as a paramedic and deployed as an Army medic. I've seen what armed people do to a human body. It does not look like bear spray and a hockey stick. A coup kit it is not.

Think about who supposedly showed up to overthrow the government. These are the folks Obama said "cling to guns or religion." The folks who quote Federalist 46, where Madison counts on citizens with arms in their hands as the check on a federal army. Biden's Autopen told them they'd need F-15s and maybe nuclear weapons to take on the government. And your story is that they finally decided to do it... and left the rifles at home.

Morgan, gun owners don't forget their guns. I know these people. Some of them carry to the mailbox.

So by your logic, flagpoles and bear spray are now weapons of revolution. Fine. I propose the Flagpole Safety Act: every flag in America ships on an 18-inch dowel, and buying a pole at Hobby Lobby requires a background check and a 10-day wait. Fourth of July parades need an ATF permit. This is not a radical idea.

Now let's talk about the things your side DOESN'T call an insurrection.

May 28, 2020. Rioters burned the Minneapolis Police Third Precinct after officers evacuated it. A police station. Burned.

June 2020. Protesters took over six blocks of Seattle, including a police precinct, and declared it an autonomous zone. The mayor went on CNN and said it could be a "summer of love." People were shot inside that zone before the city cleared it.

Summer 2020. The federal courthouse in Portland got hit night after night for weeks with fireworks, fires, and lasers aimed at officers' eyes. A FEDERAL building. Attacked on purpose. For weeks.

August 2020. CNN ran a graphic reading "fiery but mostly peaceful protests" while Kenosha burned behind the reporter. I teach physics. Fire is not peaceful. That's an exothermic reaction.

Insurers estimated the 2020 riot damage at $1 to $2 billion, the most expensive civil disorder in American insurance history. Meanwhile, a future Vice President was asking her followers to chip in to a Minnesota bail fund for people arrested during the unrest.

October 2018. Kavanaugh protesters flooded the Hart Senate Office Building, and Capitol Police arrested about 300 people in one day. Nobody called it a coup.

October 2023. Protesters with Jewish Voice for Peace staged a sit-in inside the Cannon House Office Building rotunda, and Capitol Police arrested hundreds. Peaceful protest, we were told.

And since you like borrowing fights from overseas, France, summer 2023. After a police shooting in Nanterre, riots ran for nights. Rioters rammed a burning car into a mayor's home with his wife and kids inside. France's top leftist, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, refused to call for calm. He said he was calling for justice instead.

That's Quinn's Law Number Seven: it's different when you're a Democrat. Same broken windows. Same assaulted cops. Different jersey.

If you're confused right now, that's by design. Your side has been muddying the water for five years to make it look deep.

Next claim: he "refused to honor the peaceful transfer of power." Biden's Autopen was sworn in at noon on January 20, 2021, right on schedule, on the same Capitol. Congress finished certifying the count that same night of the 6th. Trump flew to Florida. That is what a transfer looks like.

And the speech everyone clips? Trump told the crowd to march "peacefully and patriotically." Yes, he also said "fight like hell." Senators say that about appropriations bills.

"Refused to accept defeat"? Let's check the other team's homework. On January 6, 2017, House Democrats stood up and objected to Trump's electors, Jamie Raskin among them, until Vice President Biden gaveled them down and said "It is over." Stacey Abrams lost Georgia in 2018 and made sure to tell everyone her speech was not a concession. Hillary Clinton called Trump an "illegitimate president" in 2019. Al Gore fought the 2000 result in court for over a month. In 2020 Democrat Rita Hart lost Iowa's 2nd District by six votes, skipped the state courts, and asked the Democrat-run House to overturn it, with Marc Elias as her lawyer, before backing down under pressure. Not one of them got called an insurrectionist. Slight oversight!

Want to talk about a side that wouldn't accept an election? Rewind to 2016. The FBI opened Crossfire Hurricane on the Trump campaign and got four FISA warrants to surveil campaign adviser Carter Page, leaning on the Steele dossier, opposition research paid for by the Clinton campaign and the DNC. The DOJ Inspector General found 17 significant errors and omissions in those applications. An FBI lawyer altered an email to hide that Page had helped the CIA, and he pleaded guilty. Special Counsel John Durham concluded the bureau opened the case without "any actual evidence of collusion." Page was never charged with anything. Then came the push to flip electors and impeachment talk before he'd even taken the oath. Nobody went to jail for an insurrection over any of that either.

Asking hard questions about an election isn't treason. It's homework. In New Jersey, a motor vehicle software error registered about 6,600 people who had told the state they were NOT citizens; the governor's own preliminary count says fewer than 400 of them voted. Ohio's secretary of state sent DOJ 1,084 apparent noncitizen registrations, 167 of whom appear to have voted in a federal election. Right now DOJ is in federal court asking California to set aside about 20,000 mail ballots it flags as likely noncitizens until somebody checks. That's an allegation, not a conviction. But the same party that calls every question "election denial" is fighting not to look. Quinn's Law Number Seven, back for an encore.

Since you brought up getting shellacked: 2024. 312 electoral votes AND the popular vote.

Now the part you left out. In December 2024 the DOJ Inspector General reported the FBI had 26 confidential human sources in D.C. that day. Three were tasked by the FBI to be there. Four went inside the Capitol. Thirteen more went into restricted areas. The IG found no undercover agents and says none of those sources were authorized to break the law or told to egg anyone on.

Fine. Then answer two questions. Why were grandmothers who walked through open doors charged while none of the sources who went inside were? And why did Director Wray, asked under oath whether he had sources dressed as Trump supporters inside the Capitol, tell Congress not to read anything into his refusal to answer? I teach teenagers. When a kid won't answer a yes-or-no question, I read something into it.

Then the pipe bombs at the RNC and DNC. Years of "corrupted" phone data and no suspect. The House Administration subcommittee report says the trail went cold within months. It took a new FBI director to arrest Brian Cole Jr. in December 2025, a man who showed up on cameras the bureau had the whole time and who, per the affidavit, bought bomb parts with a credit card. In April the Trump DOJ added terrorism and weapons-of-mass-destruction charges, and prosecutors say he confessed and claimed he did it for people who thought 2020 was stolen. His lawyers say he didn't do it, want Trump's January 6 pardon to cover him, and say the FBI once treated a former Capitol Police officer as a person of interest.

That's for a jury, so nobody gets a victory lap. But a bureau that needed five years to find a guy with a receipt wasn't protecting democracy. It wasn't looking.

And the committee's star witness? June 28, 2022, prime time, Cassidy Hutchinson told the country Trump lunged for the steering wheel of his SUV and then lunged at the head of his own protective detail. She wasn't in the vehicle. She said Tony Ornato told her the story. Sources close to Ornato and the agent said both were ready to testify under oath that it never happened. In 2024 the House Administration subcommittee released the driver's testimony: he never saw Trump grab the wheel or lunge toward the front seat, though he said Trump sounded irritated. The committee let that driver's offer to testify sit for months.

Even Jack Smith told the House her account was secondhand, and that if he were the defense attorney, the first thing he'd do is try to keep it out as hearsay. Per Jim Jordan, the committee's final report cited her 185 times. Reports this month say DOJ is asking a grand jury to indict her for lying to Congress. Nothing has been filed as of today, so she gets her day in court like anybody else.

A former ABC News president producing the hearings, a secondhand steering wheel, and a driver nobody wanted to hear from is not an investigation. It's a script.

And while you were worried about Trump grabbing power, here is who was using it. Jack Smith's team subpoenaed the National Archives and read text messages involving 44 members of Congress, per DOJ records released by Sen. Grassley. Arctic Frost put 92 Republican groups and people under scrutiny, Turning Point USA among them. Smith told the House he only sought toll records; his lawyers say that answer was truthful because the question was about toll records. On September 29 the Senate read him the receipts anyway. You wanted a government that went after its political opposition, Morgan? I found one. It just wasn't wearing a red hat.

One more receipt, and it's the one your side should frame and hang in the hallway. In February 2021, TIME ran Molly Ball's "The Secret History of the Shadow Campaign That Saved the 2020 Election." In its own words, it describes "a well-funded cabal of powerful people" working behind the scenes. The article lays out how they changed voting rules and laws, steered media coverage, leaned on Facebook and Twitter over what counted as "disinformation," and lined up labor bosses and business groups to manage the outcome. To be fair, it does not say they planned the riot. It says they told their own people to stay home that day.

Now look at that with a teacher's red pen. If a Republican group had bragged in a national magazine about secretly rewriting election rules and pressuring the platforms that control what you see, you would call it an insurrection before you finished the headline. When your side does it, TIME calls it saving democracy. A cabal working the refs is saving the election, and a grandmother with a flag is a coup. Your definitions need a recall notice.

So here is your graded paper.

Insurrection: never charged.

Armed overthrow: the only person killed by gunfire was unarmed, and police fired the shot.

Refused to transfer power: left on time.

Burning precincts, seized city blocks, and a federal courthouse under siege for weeks: "mostly peaceful."

"What will he try this time?" Probably winning again. He's done it twice.

Go sell your crazy somewhere else, Morgan. We're all stocked up here.

But what do I know, I'm only a retired Army medic who knows what an armed assault looks like, and that wasn't it.

So, Morgan: which one was the insurrection? The police station on fire, or the grandmother with the flag?

#UDRP https://t.co/booXwA77Hf denied. The Complainant, a Georgia accounting firm formed in November 2023, has used #COSURGE since April 2024 and holds U.S. registrations filed in July 2024 and registered in June 2025. The Domain Name was registered on April 3, 2025, before the U.S. registrations issued and before the Respondent, an Indian accounting and advisory company, was incorporated on April 22, 2025. 

The Respondent said it chose "co" and "surge" as ordinary English words consistent with its tagline, did not know of the Complainant's mark, and had made enquiries in India. The Complainant pointed to the Respondent's references to a U.S. office and North American leadership, and disputed continuous use. 

The Panel found the Domain Name confusingly similar and called the second element a close one, but held that on balance the Complainant had not met its burden. text:
OUT TODAY!
The Complete Kubrick [4K UHD] - Tom Cruise, Nicole Kidman, Jack Nicholson, Kirk Douglas, Peter Sellers, Laurence Olivier, James Mason, George C. Scott, Sterling Hayden, Malcolm McDowell, Ryan O’Neal, Shelley Duvall @Criterion
US: https://t.co/CI66YeTzTb
CAN: https://t.co/4WF4JDzSGw
OUR REVIEW:
https://t.co/1UwunVfIOh
Killer’s Kiss (1955) / The Killing (1956) / Paths of Glory (1957) / Spartacus (1960) / Lolita (1962) / Dr. Strangelove, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964) / 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) / A Clockwork Orange (1971) / Barry Lyndon (1975) / The Shining (1980) / Full Metal Jacket (1987) / Eyes Wide Shut (1999) Criterion
The Masters:

All features are presented in Dolby Vision HDR on the 4K UHD discs and in SDR on the Blu-rays. Criterion’s “About the Masters” notes show that nearly every title was restored from its original camera negative, though the restorations come from a mix of sources. Some are Criterion’s own, some are carried over from studio restorations of recent years, and some were done by partner archives.

The three independently produced early features had their 4K debuts on Kino Lorber UHDs, but here they are presented in masters made for Criterion by Duplitech. Killer’s Kiss (1.37:1) comes from the 35mm original camera negative, with a composite fine-grain used for some sections. The Killing and Paths of Glory (both 1.66:1) are also drawn from their camera negatives. The Paths of Glory mono was remastered at 24-bit from UCLA archivist Robert Gitt’s 35mm magnetic track. Fear and Desire (1.37:1) is the exception: it is Kino Lorber’s 4K restoration, made from the camera negative and a Library of Congress fine-grain. The three shorts are new Criterion 4K restorations from Library of Congress elements. These were 35mm prints and a duplicate negative for Day of the Fight and Flying Padre, and the 16mm original reversal for The Seafarers.

The studio-era films largely use existing restorations. Spartacus (2.20:1) is Universal’s 4K restoration from a 6K scan of the original Technirama elements, with Robert A. Harris consulting, and its 7.1 track was remastered from the 70mm six-track printmaster. Dr. Strangelove (1.66:1) is Sony’s 4K restoration, supervised by Grover Crisp and assembled from a fine-grain master, a duplicate negative and a 35mm print. 2001: A Space Odyssey (2.20:1) is Warner’s 4K from an 8K scan of the 65mm camera negative, supervised by Ned Price and Leon Vitali with input from Christopher Nolan and Hoyte van Hoytema. Its original 70mm six-track 5.1 mix is joined by the 35mm general-release mono, which Kubrick mixed without the overture, intermission and exit music, so those passages are silent on that track. A Clockwork Orange (1.66:1), The Shining (1.85:1) and Full Metal Jacket (1.85:1) are Warner 4K restorations from their camera negatives, with Full Metal Jacket graded against both an answer print and Kubrick’s own personal 35mm reference print.

Barry Lyndon and Eyes Wide Shut match Criterion’s own recent 4K editions. Barry Lyndon is framed at 1.66:1 per Kubrick’s December 8th, 1975 letter to projectionists, and was graded against Vitali’s 2000 HD transfer. Eyes Wide Shut (1.85:1) is presented in its international cut, supervised and approved by cinematographer Larry Smith. Its look stems from Kubrick’s deliberate decision to have the negative force-developed by two stops, which accounts for the film’s distinctive grain and glowing low-light palette.

Two presentations are new to 4K UHD. Lolita (1.66:1) is a new 4K restoration from the 35mm original camera negative, using a Warner 35mm print as color reference, with its mono remastered from the original DME magnetic track. Kubrick’s international version of The Shining (119 minutes, against 144 for the U.S. theatrical) comes from the same Warner restoration of the camera negative, with its own mono track remastered from the original magnetic elements.

Since most of these masters have been reviewed before on DVDBeaver, we have used our existing captures from those earlier 4K UHD releases where applicable. New captures will eventually be taken for Lolita and the international version of The Shining. 

Audio:

Criterion’s audio approach across the set is admirably purist. Every film is offered with its original soundtrack, and for the mono-era titles that means uncompressed linear PCM mono remastered from the original magnetic elements. Paths of Glory’s was remastered at 24-bit from UCLA archivist Robert Gitt’s 35mm track. For Dr. Strangelove, A Clockwork Orange, Barry Lyndon, both versions of The Shining and Full Metal Jacket, Criterion also includes alternate 5.1 DTS-HD Master Audio remixes, so purists and surround enthusiasts are both served. The early independent features and Lolita are presented in their original mono alone. This is a notable step up from earlier editions. Warner’s 4K UHD of The Shining offered only a 5.1 remix with no mono at all, its Full Metal Jacket UHD relegated the mono to a lossy track, and Sony’s Dr. Strangelove UHD carried only 16-bit lossless tracks. The three large-format productions get special treatment. Spartacus is presented in 7.1 DTS-HD MA remastered from its 70mm six-track printmaster, and it retains the overture, entr’acte and intermission music. 2001: A Space Odyssey is the most generous of all, with its original 70mm six-track theatrical mix in 5.1, an alternate 5.1 remix and the original 35mm general-release mono, which, true to Kubrick’s own 35mm prints, is silent during the overture, intermission and exit music. Eyes Wide Shut is presented in its original theatrical 5.1, remastered from the 35mm magnetic track. Optional English (SDH) subtitles are offered on every feature, and the set is region free. From the portions we have sampled so far, the tracks sound exceptional, clean and faithful to their sources, with the dynamic range of the scores and Kubrick’s carefully chosen music coming through with clarity and weight.

About the Captures

Because of the size of this set and its release date, none of the screen captures in this review are taken from The Complete Kubrick discs. Instead, we have included a single capture per film from our earlier reviews, taken from previous 4K UHD editions or, where none exist, Blu-ray. Several of those editions share their restoration with this set, while others come from different transfers. The captures should therefore be taken as representative of each film’s presentation, not as exact reproductions of the Criterion discs.

Fear and Desire is represented by Kino’s 2024 4K UHD, which uses the same Kino Lorber restoration found in this set. Killer’s Kiss and The Killing come from Kino’s 2022 4K UHDs, and Paths of Glory from the 2024 Masters of Cinema (Eureka) 4K UHD. All three of those earlier discs were scanned from the original camera negatives, but Criterion presents new Duplitech masters here, so the grading and framing may differ.

Spartacus is from Universal’s 2020 4K UHD, which uses the same 2015 restoration from the large-format Technirama elements. Dr. Strangelove is from Sony’s 2021 4K UHD, drawn from the same Sony restoration. 2001: A Space Odyssey comes from Warner’s 2018 4K UHD. The Shining and Full Metal Jacket come from Warner’s 2019 and 2020 4K UHDs respectively. Our Shining capture is from the U.S. theatrical version and serves for both cuts, which share the same restoration in this set. Note that both of those Warner discs were framed at 1.78:1, whereas Criterion presents both films at 1.85:1. Barry Lyndon is from Criterion’s own 2025 4K UHD, which matches the restoration in this set.

For Eyes Wide Shut, our capture is from Criterion’s 2025 Blu-ray of the same Larry Smith–approved restoration, as we were unable to capture from that 4K UHD disc at the time. Lolita and A Clockwork Orange are represented by Warner’s 2011 Blu-rays (the latter its 40th Anniversary Edition). Lolita receives a new 4K restoration in this set, so that capture predates it entirely.

OUR PAST REVIEWS:
Fear and Desire, Killer's Kiss, The Killing, Paths of Glory, Spartacus, Lolita, Dr. Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey, A Clockwork Orange, Barry Lyndon, The Shining, Full Metal Jacket, Eyes Wide Shut

Seen together, Stanley Kubrick's films reveal a remarkably consistent sensibility beneath their wildly varied surfaces. There is the dehumanizing machinery of war, from the trenches of Paths of Glory to the War Room farce of Dr. Strangelove and the Parris Island crucible of Full Metal Jacket. There is the individual crushed or remade by institutional authority in A Clockwork Orange and Barry Lyndon, and there are the hidden currents of desire and power in Lolita and Eyes Wide Shut. Running through all of it is an ironic, coolly precise eye that turned every genre he touched, whether noir, epic, satire, science fiction, horror or costume drama, into something unmistakably his own. Watching the arc from the self-financed Fear and Desire and the gritty New York of Killer's Kiss through to the monumental achievements of 2001: A Space Odyssey and The Shining is a privilege few box sets can offer. Criterion's The Complete Kubrick is a staggering undertaking. Its 30 discs (13 4K UHD and 17 Blu-ray) hold every finished film Kubrick directed, all restored in 4K and presented in Dolby Vision HDR, many from their original camera negatives. It includes Lolita's 4K debut, Kubrick's international cut of The Shining, both versions of Day of the Fight, original soundtracks alongside remixes, over twenty-five hours of supplements, and archive-inspired packaging filled with Kubrick's own notes, slates and correspondence. We are still working our way through the set, but everything we have sampled so far has looked and sounded exceptional. This is the definitive presentation of one of cinema's most exacting artists and an essential acquisition for any serious film collection. Set of the Year - our very highest recommendation!

Nearly 1 in 5 UC freshmen are flunking math, double the rate from 5 years ago | Zain Khan, New York Post

University of California freshmen are increasingly flunking introductory math classes, with nearly one in five students earning a failing grade, withdrawing or otherwise failing to pass — almost double the rate from five years ago, new data revealed.

17.8% of freshmen taking introductory math courses across the University of California system failed to pass in the 2025-26 academic year, up from just 9.2% in 2020-21, EdSource reported.

The figures come as California continues to struggle with lackluster academic performance in its public schools, raising fresh questions about whether students are arriving at the state’s prestigious universities with the skills they need to succeed.

The courses included in the figures range from calculus and precalculus to preparatory math classes covering subjects such as algebra and trigonometry.

The failure rate has climbed substantially since the UC system dropped the SAT and ACT as admission requirements. The 2020-21 academic year was the last in which the standardized tests were required for freshman admission.

The rate jumped to 13% in 2021-22 before dipping slightly to 12.6% the following year. It climbed to 15.3% in 2023-24, eased to 14.9% in 2024-25 and then surged to its highest level in 2025-26.

“California Can’t grade their way out of an education crisis,” Sonja Shaw, a Republican candidate for California state superintendent of public instruction, told the Post.

“Dropping the SAT and ACT has let far too many students arrive unprepared for even introductory math,” Shaw said, arguing that the nearly doubled failure rate was evidence that schools were advancing students without ensuring they had mastered basic skills.

The numbers vary dramatically across the UC system’s nine undergraduate campuses.

UC Merced had the highest share of freshmen who failed to pass introductory math, with 36.4% falling short in 2025-26 — more than double its rate of about 16% five years earlier.

UC Riverside experienced one of the sharpest recent increases, with its rate jumping from roughly 8% the previous year to about 20%. UC Santa Cruz also saw a substantial rise, from around 12% to approximately 19%.

Meanwhile, UC Santa Barbara recorded the lowest failure rate, at 8.2%.

UC Davis, UC Irvine and UC San Diego had rates clustered between roughly 16% and 18%, while UC Berkeley came in near 13% and UCLA around 11%.

Joel Hass, a mathematics professor at UC Davis, said the results were unsurprising and reflected a growing divide between students who arrive academically prepared and those who struggle with foundational material.

“There is a wider range of interest and preparedness,” Hass said. “We still have a good number of highly qualified students, but also many who are unprepared for college. The preparedness gap between these groups is large.”

Hass said some university instructors were being encouraged to offer remedial courses covering material students should have learned years earlier.

Just 49.3% of California students met or exceeded state English language arts standards in 2025-26, while only 38.4% achieved proficiency in math, according to results released by the state.

Although both figures improved slightly from the previous school year, they remained below pre-pandemic levels. In 2018-19, 50.9% of students met English language arts standards and 39.7% were proficient in math.

The state spent about $134 billion on K-12 schools from all sources in 2025-26, or roughly $26,450 per student, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.

“The failure of high schools, and more generally K-12 education in California, is a scandal. The state now sends students who might thrive by first going to the community colleges to UC campuses where they are unprepared for a serious academic environment,” Hass told the Post.

Over 1,400 UC faculty — mostly in STEM — are urging the system to bring back SAT or ACT requirements for science, math, technology, and engineering applicants, citing “severe” math deficits among incoming students.

“Over the past five years, we have seen a widening divergence in mathematical preparation levels within the same classroom. This trend indicates that current admissions practices do not provide a sufficiently reliable check on mathematical readiness for STEM majors,” faculty wrote in their June letter.

UC is still test‑blind for current applicants, but a formal review of standardized testing in admissions is scheduled to finish by June 2027, with recommendations to the Board of Regents expected in fall 2027

Hass also pushed back against arguments that the SAT and ACT create barriers for disadvantaged students, saying the exams can help identify talented applicants whose abilities might otherwise be overlooked.

“SAT and ACT tests can open doors for talented students who have suffered from poor instruction in poor quality schools,” Hass said.

Rather than placing students in university courses before they are ready, he suggested that some could benefit from strengthening their academic foundations at community colleges before transferring to a UC campus.

text:
RON ESTES BLAMES BIDEN FOR INFLATION. THE NUMBERS TELL A DIFFERENT STORY.

@RepRonEstes 

In an October 13 television interview, Kansas Congressman Ron Estes offered this explanation for the nation's economic difficulties:

"I think one of the things we should remember is that you can't fix four years of hyperinflation in one year."

There's a problem with that explanation: It doesn't match the economic record.

First, America did not experience four years of hyperinflation under President Biden. Inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022-painfully high, certainly, but nowhere near what economists call hyperinflation.

More importantly, Estes overlooks what happened afterward.

Inflation declined sharply during Biden's presidency, falling to approximately 3% by mid-2023. It remained relatively stable throughout his final year and a half, reaching 3.0% in January 2025, when Trump took office.

In other words, much of the inflation problem Estes describes had already been addressed before Trump returned to the White House.

What happened next deserves attention.

Under Trump, inflation initially declined further, reaching 2.3% in April 2025. But that improvement reversed. Inflation climbed to 4.2% in May 2026 before retreating to 3.4% in August, the latest figure available when Estes spoke.

That 4.2% reading exceeded every monthly annual inflation rate recorded during Biden's final 19 months.

There's an important distinction here. Lower inflation doesn't mean lower prices. Americans are still paying substantially more for many necessities than they did before the pandemic. Estes is correct that those accumulated price increases cannot simply be erased overnight.

But that's not what his statement suggests. He describes a continuing crisis inherited from Biden while leaving out Biden's substantial progress in reducing inflation-and the renewed acceleration under Trump.

Presidents don't control inflation single-handedly. Federal Reserve policy, energy markets, international events, and government policies all influence consumer prices. That principle applies to both administrations.

By October 13, Trump had been president for nearly 21 months. It is reasonable to examine the inflation he inherited, but it is equally necessary to examine what has happened since.

The economic record is straightforward: Inflation surged under Biden, declined dramatically before he left office, and subsequently accelerated again under Trump.

Ron Estes is entitled to defend the administration's economic policies. But that defense should begin with an accurate description of the economy-not a version of history that omits inconvenient facts.

Sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI data; Biden vs. Trump Inflation: What the CPI Data Shows; KWCH interview, October 13, 2026.

All economic figures are limited to information available October 13, 2026.

⚡ https://t.co/cSQQG1wPqI — The Most Dangerous Assumption in Artificial Intelligence? That Tomorrow Will Look Like Yesterday.

AI systems learn from patterns.

Markets follow patterns.

Businesses optimize around patterns.

Entire industries make decisions based on what happened before.

But history has a weakness.

It cannot fully prepare us for what has never happened.

A sudden market disruption.

An unexpected scientific discovery.

A supply chain failure.

A breakthrough technology.

An autonomous system encountering a situation outside its training.

text:
A letter from a Palestinian living next to Israel.

Hello, I am Palestinian. 📷
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

text:
Just processing the whole appendicitis experience. A lot of things surprised me:

That it was my appendix. I had so many thoughts about what could be happening, but appendicitis wasn't one of them. I first thought it was a spiritual attack since it started the moment I stood up from the table to get myself and the kids out the door for church. Then I thought maybe my heart. Then I clocked the increasing pain I'd thought was my uterus...it had kept me up a couple hours in the middle of the night two days prior. Thought it was my body freaking out about ovulating. 

I spent the whole time in the ER hoping to get out in time for a friend's baby shower. The doctor even said he was just ordering the CT to be safe but fully expected it to find nothing. I sent Jon home to relieve our childcare and get the baby presents thinking I was just waiting on test results and he could bring the kids and pick me up and go to the shower. 

The CT scan tech told me she just found out she was pregnant with her 3rd baby under 3 years old unexpectedly. I could tell she was kind of freaking out, and told her how much she wouldn't regret keeping the baby. Felt like that was why I was there that day at that moment. 

The wait time for surgery was kinda nice. When you have all these little kids like I do, time to breathe and think and rest is nice no matter the circumstances. I got to finish reading a zombie book my sister wrote. Got to work on my Job Bible study. 

I told myself it was a really minor surgery and I was going to be completely calm, but once I got to pre-op I started to get hit with all the feelings I had at 16 getting a (benign) tumor removed, and I had my mom with me that time, and this time I was alone. 

They told me play by play what to expect once we got to the OR, how we'd transfer to the bed and lock my arms out and count down to go to sleep. I remember starting to wheel toward the OR and nothing after that. It's weird knowing there are things I experienced awake and don't remember. 

I woke up in post op disoriented and started crying, and the nurse was kinda harsh about it. I know she was probably just needing to make sure I stayed calm, but I just wanted my mom. Or a mom. Someone comforting. I remember her reporting to another nurse no pain when she hadn't asked me, and I was in pain and had tried to say so prior. 

I slept for a long time in my room and woke up around noon feeling bad it was so late, and I hadn't updated anyone that I was ok. 

The surgeon came in and told me what I already posted. Apologized that I got nicked with an instrument. Said there was a bunch of scar tissue, that my appendix had been attached to my ovary, and that they'd kept me under longer than expected so my OB could come look. That my other ovary was enlarged and cystic and we'd need to follow up with an ultrasound about that. I found out they'd called my husband mid surgery about all of it. The surgeon said they'd do pathology on the appendix. Said something off-handed about cancer. Didn't sound like they were really worried about that, just checking. Maybe it's standard. I'm still really confused about all that. Felt like a lot was left on the table that no one said anything about. The CT scan notes said there was a micronodule on my lung that was probably nothing, but follow up if any symptoms arose. No one said anything to me about that. 

She said I probably didn't need it, but she was going to give me another round of antibiotics for "voodoo." She said "voodoo" 2 or 3 times. As soon as I checked Twitter, I saw that witch trying to offer me up as a human sacrifice to God for a red wave at midterms. That plus my initial feeling Sunday morning that it was a spiritual attack made it all feel spiritually heavy, and I prayed against it. Whatever that was. 

Everything went smooth for discharge. Was so happy to hug my kids. We had the whole stress of thinking I lost my wallet only to find it in the diaper bag all ready for church. 1/2

TWO MAJOR EARNINGS REPORTS COMING UP! 👀

Both $TSLA and $META are scheduled to release their Q3 earnings after the US market closes on Wednesday, October 21, and with how volatile tech stocks have been lately, we could see some movement once the numbers and management guidance come out.

I have been going through the earnings expectations for both companies, and although they are both heavily involved in AI, investors are looking for very different things from each business.

📊 TESLA

@Tesla has already reported 486,532 vehicle deliveries for Q3, which came in above market expectations, but selling more vehicles does not necessarily translate into stronger earnings, especially when the company continues dealing with pressure on automotive margins and increasing investments in AI, its Robotaxi, and other projects.

Wall Street is expecting roughly $28 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings-per-share (EPS) of around $0.44, and I want to know whether the company can show some improvement in profitability after several disappointing quarters rather than depending mainly on its long-term growth plans to keep investors engaged.

I know a lot of people are still talking about the Tesla Roadster and its supposed flying capabilities, but the timing of Elon Musk bringing it up so close to the earnings report makes me a little bit skeptical. Part of me wonders whether this was also meant to keep investors excited about Tesla's future projects ahead of the actual financial results. I could be reading too much into the timing, but it does seem a little suspicious to me.

Moreover, its energy storage business is another area worth following, particularly after reporting 13.7 GWh in deployments during Q3, while any meaningful updates on Robotaxi and FSD commercialization could also influence how investors react to the results.

$TSLA was recently trading around $367.84, and these are the price levels on my radar ahead of earnings:

🔹 $365 - $370: An immediate price level wherein the market could establish its initial direction following the announcement.

🔹 $347 - $350: A lower reaction zone if earnings disappoint and selling pressure starts building.

🔹 $390 - $395: A positive reaction zone if stronger earnings and management guidance encourage buyers to push the stock higher.

If the market responds positively, I would prefer to see buyers defend an important price area before considering an entry, while a breakdown followed by a failed attempt to reclaim support would make me more cautious about going long.

📊 META

@Meta is in a different situation because its advertising business continues to generate strong revenue, but spending on AI infrastructure has become a major concern for investors who want to know when those investments will start delivering meaningful financial returns.

Revenue expectations sit around $63.3 billion, compared with the company's previous guidance of $61 billion to $64 billion, so simply meeting expectations may not be enough to support the stock if management also announces another significant increase in CapEx.

Advertising growth, free cash flow, and updates on its Muse AI products will be key parts of this report especially because Meta needs to show that its enormous AI investments can eventually drive sustainable earnings growth.

$META is trading near $700, and here are a few areas that could become important depending on how the market responds:

🔹 $700 - $703: Immediate support area where buyers may attempt to defend the recent trading range.

🔹 $706 - $710: Near-term resistance area that buyers would need to reclaim before building stronger upward momentum.

🔹 $715 - $725: Higher resistance zone that could come into play if earnings and management guidance exceed market expectations.

Do note that these are just preliminary reference levels, and I would reassess them once the earnings numbers are released because a significant price gap could quickly change the technical picture.

HOW I PLAN TO APPROACH BOTH EARNINGS REPORTS

With Tesla and Meta reporting on the same day, I do not necessarily see a reason to trade both stocks just because they are expected to be volatile. I would rather compare their earnings results, see how investors respond to the numbers, and focus on whichever stock offers a more reasonable opportunity after the initial market reaction.

For Tesla, profitability and automotive margins matter more to me than the delivery figures we already know, while Meta needs to show whether its advertising growth can keep up with the massive amount of money going into AI.

A company can report better-than-expected earnings and still see its stock price decline, especially when the market has already priced in strong results or when management provides an outlook that falls short of expectations.

That is why I prefer to watch how price behaves after the announcement instead of trying to predict direction beforehand.

If the setup does not offer a decent risk-to-reward ratio, I would rather leave it alone than take unnecessary exposure just because everyone is talking about these two stocks.

THERE IS ALSO ANOTHER SIDE TO TRADING THESE EARNINGS EVENTS

For investors who already own Tesla or Meta shares and plan to hold them for several years, the situation can be different because they may want to take advantage of shorter-term opportunities without giving up their long-term positions.

Imagine someone who has held Tesla for years because they believe in the company's plans for autonomous driving, energy storage, and AI, but now wants to trade the volatility around its quarterly earnings.

If most of their investment capital is tied up in a traditional brokerage account, they would normally need to use available cash or sell part of their holdings to fund another position.

Beyond that, Bitget also offers access to supported tokenized stocks, crypto, and CFDs within its broader trading ecosystem, letting eligible users manage exposure to different markets without constantly transferring funds between separate platforms.

text:
According to modern biblical scholars, the Book of Deuteronomy was composed or reached its final form at the hands of scribes during the 7th and 6th centuries BCE—that is, after the Assyrian Exile (722 BCE) had already taken place, and as the Babylonian Exile (586 BCE) was either imminent or already underway. In other words, the scribes retroactively inserted accounts of mass exiles and catastrophes—events that had already occurred—into the text, framing them as prophecies delivered by Moses in the past.

The structure of these texts mirrors, in every detail, the format of "vassal treaties" common among kingdoms in the ancient Near East. In these, a regional power or sovereign (Yahweh) grants land to a tribe, stipulating the condition: "If you offer complete obedience, the land is yours; if you collaborate with other powers (elohim), I shall cast you out."

The Torah contains explicit prophecies regarding "dispersion across the world and exile." However, rather than representing a metaphysical miracle, this is a case where scribes—drawing upon military catastrophes that had already unfolded or were currently unfolding—doctrinalized these events as "punishment for disobedience to God’s law."

A fundamental concept employed in the historical-critical method is *vaticinium ex eventu*—that is, texts written to appear as prophecies, but composed only after the events themselves have already taken place.

As the scribes experienced the Babylonian Exile in the 6th century BCE, or witnessed the Assyrian destruction of the northern kingdom (722 BCE)... They incorporated these disasters into the text as "prophecies of the future," presented through the voices of figures (such as Moses, Isaiah, etc.)—as if these individuals had already experienced the events in the past. Thus, the following message was conveyed to the people: "Look, this exile and destruction that has befallen us is no surprise! Moses and the prophets had already foretold this back around 1200 BCE. They warned that if we failed to follow the laws of Yahweh, we would be driven into exile—and now, that is exactly what has happened."

When the scribes of the Torah composed these texts, they were not "predicting the future" regarding the Roman exile; rather, they were writing with the benefit of hindsight, having witnessed the Assyrian exile (the Ten Lost Tribes) in 722 BCE and the Babylonian exile in 586 BCE.

Living in Babylon during the 6th century BCE, these scribes incorporated the devastation wrought by the Babylonian and Assyrian exiles into the text as the "terms of the Covenant."

In the ancient world, the method employed by empires—such as the Assyrian, Babylonian, Persian, and Roman—to discipline rebellious tribes was always the same: destroy the temple, burn the city, and disperse the elites and the general population across the imperial territories.

In 70 CE, the Roman Empire applied the very same standard imperial protocol for exile that the Assyrians and Babylonians had utilized centuries earlier.

Consequently, the motifs of "dispersion, exile, and subjugation"—which had been written into the Torah based on the lived experience of the Babylonian and Assyrian destructions—aligned perfectly when Rome employed the same military tactics in 70 CE.

However, this alignment was not the result of a "magical prophecy from the beyond concerning the future"; it was a reflection of the accounts of exile—penned by scribes drawing upon their own experiences of the Babylonian and Assyrian exiles in the 6th century BCE—that... ...stems from the reenactment of the 'penal' theological model by the comparable military power of the Roman Empire in the 1st century AD.

text:
This map showing where the ancient Greeks believed their gods were born is an incredible backdrop to understanding the world of the New Testament!

The early Christians lived in a world saturated with pagan religion, where these gods were worshiped, temples were built in their honor, and entire cities were shaped by their influence.

And you might be surprised how many of them have connections to the New Testament!

Here are some fascinating examples:

Zeus (Acts 14:8–18): After Paul healed a man who couldn’t walk, the people of 

Lystra believed Barnabas was Zeus and attempted to offer sacrifices to him!

Hermes (Acts 14:12): The same crowd identified Paul as Hermes, the messenger of the gods, because he was the chief speaker.

Artemis (Acts 19:23–41): Paul’s preaching threatened the worship of Artemis in Ephesus, sparking a massive riot. Her temple was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World!

Apollo (Acts 16:16–18): Paul cast a spirit of divination out of a slave girl. The original Greek references a “spirit of Python,” associated with Apollo’s famous Oracle of Delphi.

Castor and Pollux (Acts 28:11): Paul sailed aboard a ship bearing the figurehead of these mythological twin brothers, worshiped as protectors of sailors.

Athena (Acts 17:16–34): Paul preached in Athens, the city named for this goddess of wisdom, confronting a culture filled with idols and Greek philosophy.

Aphrodite (1 Corinthians 6:18–20): Corinth had a long history of worshiping Aphrodite, the goddess of love. Paul’s teachings on sexual morality challenged the broader culture of the city.

Poseidon (Acts 27): The Greeks worshiped Poseidon as god of the sea and storms. During Paul’s terrifying shipwreck, he instead placed his confidence in the one true God.

Asclepius (Acts 3:1–10): Greeks sought miraculous healing through this god of medicine. Peter’s healing of a man unable to walk demonstrated the power of Jesus Christ.

Dionysus (John 2; Luke 22): The Greek god of wine was widely worshiped throughout the Mediterranean. Wine also appears prominently in Jesus’ first recorded miracle and the institution of the Lord’s Supper, though Scripture draws no direct connection to Dionysus.

Zeus again (Acts 17:28): Paul quoted a Greek poet whose words originally referred to Zeus, using familiar pagan poetry to explain the nature of the true Creator.

The early Christians weren’t bringing the gospel into a world without religion. They were bringing it into a world overflowing with religion.

And within just a few centuries, Christianity had spread throughout the very lands where these gods had been worshiped for generations.

Understanding this historical backdrop makes the New Testament and the spread of the gospel all the more remarkable.

#JORDANJAUNT DIARIES DAY 3 – PETRA, THE MAGNIFICENT ROSE CITY 🇯🇴

On Day 3 of our first ever #JordanJaunt tour, we took a journey back in time to Petra, Jordan’s legendary Rose City and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Our guided tour began with the Djinn Blocks, mysterious cube-shaped monuments believed to be tombs, followed by the Obelisk Tomb, distinguished by its four pyramid-shaped obelisks. We then entered the spectacular Siq, a narrow sandstone gorge that builds anticipation before revealing Petra’s crown jewel, the magnificent Treasury (Al-Khazneh), with its intricately carved façade.

The Street of Facades showcased rows of rock-cut tombs, while the Amphitheatre, carved into the hillside, reminded us of Petra’s vibrant public life. The imposing Royal Tombs, with their beautifully coloured sandstone façades, were another highlight. We also explored the Great Temple, a vast complex reflecting Petra’s architectural grandeur, and Qasr Al-Bint, one of its most important ancient temples.

Our visit to the Petra Museum later in the morning offered fascinating insights into Nabataean civilisation and daily life. After lunch and a bit of rest, those of our guests who hadn’t been tired out returned to Petra for the magical Petra by Night experience, an optional add-on to the tour, as candlelight illuminated the path to the Treasury beneath the starry sky.

text:
@grok, is there any contradiction in the following explanation:
The syntax neither confirms nor excludes the possibility that Mary remained a virgin after giving birth. This consideration was foreign to Matthew, and attempting to read his thoughts about the matter into the text is unhelpful.1

It’s easy to find websites and commentaries pointing out, in support of the doctrine of perpetual virginity, that ἕως does not always

introduce an event (in this case: she gave birth to a son) whereby the earlier situation (the couple had no sexual relations) is reversed (they now begin to have sexual relations).

Those links provides several examples. I would suggest that many of them are only marginally relevant because the construction in Matthew 1:25 can be described more specifically than ἕως, which has a broad range of usages.

καὶ οὐκ ἐγίνωσκεν αὐτὴν ἕως οὗ ἔτεκεν υἱόν·
but [Joseph] knew her not until she had given birth to a son.
Here ἕως is functioning as preposition with a neuter, genitive relative pronoun as its object. This is a formulaic (and pleonastic) way to form a subordinating conjunction,2,3 which, in Matt 1:25, governs an indicative clause. Ideally, to look for parallels, we would like to see other usages of ἕως οὗ + aorist indicative.

These are hard to come by in the NT. I was only able to locate four. In addition to our passage, Matt. 13:33 // Luke 13:21:

[The kingdom of heaven] is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three packs of flour until it was all leavened (ἕως οὗ ἐζυμώθη ὅλον).

Does that imply that she "un-hid" the leaven after the flour had been leavened? Unlikely. The question leaves me with a strong sense that that’s not the point. This is not the contingent use of ἕως.3 To read the sentence as a statement about the possibility of future reversal of the (relatively) main verb contingent on the dependent clause is topically inappropriate.

The other NT example is Acts 21:26:

Then Paul took the men, and...went into the temple giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, until the sacrifice was offered (ἕως οὗ προσηνέχθη...ἡ προσφορά) for each one of them.

The relationship between clauses is a little obscure, and the NASB (quoted) is one of the few translations that doesn't re-write the second as an independent clause. Although the meaning isn’t totally clear to me, one imagines that he probably did stop with his announcing after the sacrifices, but again this is not the point.

Unlike the NT, the LXX is replete with examples of this construction (mostly, although not all, corresponding to עד אשר) (examples available upon request). They fall into both of the above categories (earlier situation probably reversed | earlier situation implausibly reversed), but the theme of this being an off-topic consideration is fairly uniform.

1. By which I do not mean to imply in any way that it was an unhelpful question for https://t.co/vnuCr2VaLK; I think it’s a great question! I only mean that the attention that has been given to it in the name of refuting a later doctrine seems to me misplaced.
2. Because ἕως on its own can also be a conjunction, they tend to get all mixed up in the examples of proposed parallels. (The closest I can come to approximating this in English is “until...” vs. “until the time when...”.) It’s not obvious to me that we can assume ἕως (conj.) and ἕως οὗ/ὅτου (prep. + RP) are interchangeable, although they may be. I'd love to read further analysis of this if anybody has a reference!

3. And maybe that’s we have trouble avoiding this idea as English speakers. In English, the contingent use of “until” is marked only by context. Greek generally uses the subjunctive mood +/- particle ἂν with ἕως to express contingency, a construction explicitly distinct from our passage.

Thoughts on the morning drive…..the DOJ just charged a batch of non-citizens illegally registered to vote.

Yesterday it was announced that the combined US Attorney's offices in California charged a total of 28 non-citizens who had fraudulently registered to vote. 

Every non-citizen who illegally votes in an election dilutes the vote of a legal US citizen. This is a matter of national concern. Good job in California! 

But let's also take note that recently I told you that the DOJ had sent a list of suspected names to the State of California asking them to review the legality of these names listed on their mail-in ballots database. It turns out that list contained over 20,000 names! 

Just 3 weeks ago the US Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump Administration to offer the use of the DHS database for states to verify citizenship in their voter registrations. Its okay to do so. 

But also just yesterday the State of Wisconsin Board of Registrars unanimously voted to ban the use of the same federal database. Never mind that Wisconsins most recent Democrat primary was decided by less than 1%... a mere 4000 votes!

 Wisconsin, and California, are among several states who are rejecting any effort to ensure that their voter databases are not filled with illegal registrations of non-citizens. It makes no sense. By doing so they create speculation and doubt. 

 Meanwhile, in Alabama we have voter ID, clean databases, and our election results are in on the night of the election itself. It's not rocket science!

Thoughts on the morning drive.

The Epoch Times

Zachary Stieber
Senior Reporter
10/20/2026|Updated: 10/20/2026

Federal health officials have released more details about a new center for people injured by vaccines, including, for the first time, how interested individuals can sign up to be considered for research studies.

The new center in Maryland, announced earlier in the month, “will bring together patients, physician-scientists, and laboratory researchers to investigate health problems following vaccination and infections, and turn discoveries into better care and safer vaccines,” Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and Dr. John Powers III, acting director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, said in a joint Oct. 19 statement.
Goals of the center include understanding how vaccination or infection may have contributed to health problems, studying factors that may make people more vulnerable to vaccine injuries or post-infection issues such as so-called long COVID, and figuring out the best treatments for problems participants are experiencing.

The NIH is finalizing a protocol for a study that will include people who visit the new center, with an initial enrollment of several hundred people who are “experiencing the most serious adverse effects following vaccination or long-term symptoms post-infection,” Bhattacharya and Powers said. The NIH aims to launch the study before the end of the year.

People who are interested in enrolling can call 800-411-1222 or email ccopr@nih.gov.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other officials disclosed on Oct. 8 that they had opened the center on the NIH campus in Bethesda, Maryland, close to Washington. The opening happened several days earlier and was not open to the media. Officials had not released details about how people could enroll or whether the clinic had begun accepting patients.

The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to a request to tour the facility and speak to doctors there.

Bhattacharya, who became the NIH’s director in 2025 after time outside the government, has been critical of how people who suffer problems after vaccination are handled and has said it is important that those people are acknowledged and treated.

The people “deserve to be heard, taken seriously, and evaluated with the best tools science can offer,” he and Powers said on Monday.

Some organizations praised the clinic and other steps Kennedy announced, including an overhaul of the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS).

“For years, vaccine injury was relegated to the backseat, VAERS data was regarded as unreliable, and doctors who viewed vaccine injury as a serious concern were marginalized,” Dr. Joseph Varon, president and chief medical officer of the Independent Medical Alliance, said in a statement.

text:
Trump endorses Netanyahu

Trump gave Netanyahu his "Complete and Total Endorsement" nine days before Israel's 27 October election and tied further action against Iran to the result.

He called Netanyahu a "Great Warrior Prime Minister" and partner against Iran. He wrote that if Israel chooses anyone else, "America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so." 

The same day Netanyahu, presenting his security doctrine, warned that in two years a president "very hostile to Israel" could take office. 

He said Israel should use the remaining Trump years and build other alliances, naming India and Latin America.

--- Historical Context ---

The endorsement continues a long argument about who decides the strike.

In July 1996 Bill Clinton met the new prime minister Netanyahu. Afterward Clinton asked his aides who the actual superpower was. Netanyahu later wrote that Clinton admitted the administration had tried to stop his 1996 election. 

Barack Obama and Netanyahu clashed in public over the 1967 lines and over the Iran nuclear deal; reports from the time said Obama called him a chickenshit in private. 

George W. Bush, Obama and Biden each heard Netanyahu present a case for striking Iran. Each declined. In February 2026 Trump accepted the case and the joint strikes began. 

The argument has stayed the same: who chooses the moment, and who carries the later cost.

The letter on Truth Social is the newest sentence in that argument.

--- Spiritual Perspective ---

Notice the circle that is drawn when one election is made the condition of the next strike.

The Bhagavad Gita has Krishna tell Arjuna that action done without attachment to its fruit is the steadier path. The attachment here is explicit: further war is offered only if one man remains. 

When Netanyahu answers by preparing alliances against a Washington that may turn cold, both leaders are choosing who stays inside the circle of action and who is left to the later weather. 

The soul that registers the choice is not required to cheer the next missile. It is required to see the condition that was written down.

The endorsement is public. The condition is public with it.
