text:
Before 1963, every alley in America woke to the clang of steel garbage cans five or six mornings a month, before anybody had eaten. A Black designer at Sears asked whether plastic could be molded that big, and since nobody had ever done it, there was no one on earth to ask. He drew it rectangular so it sat flat against the wall, and he put wheels under it so a woman or a child could move it alone.

You have never once thought about that bin in your life, and that was exactly the point.

A Chicago company told Charles Harrison to his face that it did not hire Black people, and then asked him to do the work anyway.

He said yes.

He was twenty-four and broke, and the arrangement came with no desk, no title and no place to sit inside the building. He kept a version of that arrangement, in one form or another, for the next thirty-seven years.

By the end he had designed more than seven hundred products. The plastic trash can in your alley is his, and so is the View-Master your mother kept on the closet shelf.

He wrote later that the trash can arrived with the biggest bang you never heard. He meant it as a joke about a quiet product, and it turned out to be the shape of his entire working life.

He had come back from the Army in 1956 with a bachelor's degree from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago and two years of military drafting behind him. The Army had trained him as a cartographer and sent him to West Germany to help redraw the maps of a country that had recently finished tearing itself and half a continent apart.

He was the only Black draftsman in his topographic unit. He spent two years making a wrecked place legible again, and then he came home and could not get hired to draw a toaster.

He got interviews. He said the openings had a way of closing in the second an employer looked up and saw who had walked through the door.

At Sears he got as far as the design department and a manager named Carl Bjorncrantz. Bjorncrantz told him the company had an unwritten policy against hiring Black people.

He did not dress it up and he did not apologize for it. He said it the way a man tells you the office closes at five.

Then he looked at the drawings again.

The work was good and Bjorncrantz wanted it, so instead of a job he offered Harrison freelance assignments. One week's worth at a time.

Harrison took the assignment home and worked it up at his own table. Then he carried the finished sketches and mock-ups back into the building, handed them across a desk, collected the next week's work and left.

He could not sit in the department that was using his drawings. Every other designer in that room had a desk, a coat hook, a lunch hour and a paycheck with the company's name printed across the top of it, and he had a bus fare and a table at home.

This went on for six months.

Then one day he came in to deliver a design and Bjorncrantz told him the freelance budget was finished. There was nothing more, and Harrison walked back out onto the street carrying the same portfolio he had walked in with.

That same day, his telephone rang. It was Henry Glass, who had taught him industrial design at the Art Institute, asking whether he would come down and talk about a job.

Glass was Viennese, and in 1938, after Germany took Austria, somebody denounced him. He was sent to Dachau and then to Buchenwald, where the camp discovered he was trained and put him to work designing a cemetery for German officers.

His wife got him released in 1939, and he was given three weeks to leave the country. What he packed was his portfolio, because drawings were the only thing he owned that could be turned back into a living.

He reached New York in February of that year and Chicago by 1942. In 1946 he talked the School of the Art Institute into starting an industrial design department, and then he taught in it for twenty-two years.

That is the man who gave Charles Harrison his first real job in design.

Glass did not bother with an interview, because he had taught Harrison as an undergraduate and again as a graduate student. He knew exactly what the man could do, so he put him straight on the payroll and set him to work on furniture.

Harrison stayed about a year, and he credited Glass with teaching him detailing, drawing and production. He also learned the parts of the trade nobody teaches in a classroom, like how to handle a client who does not know what he wants.

Two men whose countries had tried to erase them, one handing the other a drafting job.

After Glass came Ed Klein and Associates, where he drew radios for RCA Victor and the Dial-O-Matic food slicer for the Popeil brothers. After Klein came Robert Podall Associates, and at Podall, in 1958, somebody handed him a nineteen-year-old toy and told him to fix it.

The View-Master was not his invention and he never once claimed it was. William Gruber and Harold Graves had introduced it at the 1939 World's Fair as a stereoscope for adults who wanted to look at scenery in three dimensions.

For two decades it stayed a specialty item, sold mainly to photography people, and it was dark and blocky and heavy in the hand. Harrison rebuilt it in injection-molded plastic and took the weight out of it.

The price dropped far enough that a parent could hand one to a five-year-old without thinking twice. The reels filled up with stories instead of canyons, and later the body turned red.

He also made it explain itself. You raised it to your eyes, you pulled the lever, the picture changed, and nowhere in any of that did you have to read a word.

Harrison was dyslexic, and he had spent his school years losing every argument he ever had with a printed page. None of it was a style choice.

So he built objects that told you what they were by their shape. The design he finished in 1958 stayed in production, with little more than color changes, for over forty years.

In 1961 his telephone rang again and Carl Bjorncrantz was on the other end of it. What he said was, "Well, Chuck, we can hire you now."

Sit with the word now.

Nothing about Harrison had changed in five years. The drawings were the same drawings and the man was the same man, and the only thing that had moved in that time was the policy inside the building.

Harrison told him thanks, but that he already had a good job. It was true, and he did not take it back.

Bjorncrantz asked him to at least come out and talk, and he went. Sears put him in a twenty-person product design and testing laboratory, and made him the first African American executive ever hired at its Chicago headquarters.

He said afterward that Black people in America stood outside the culture in those years. He took that as the condition of his working life, and he had decided he would learn to negotiate inside it.

People who worked under him later reached for a comparison and landed on Jackie Robinson. That is the size of what 1961 meant in that building.

The thing he was proudest of, out of everything he ever drew, was a garbage can.

Until the early sixties a household can was round and made of galvanized steel. It dented when you dropped it, it rusted through at the seam, and empty it was heavy enough that hauling it to the curb was a two-handed job for whoever in the house got stuck with the chore.

And it rang. Every alley in America woke to metal on concrete and metal on truck, five or six mornings a month, before anybody in the house had eaten.

Harrison and another Sears man started asking whether polypropylene could be molded at that size. Nothing that large had ever come out of that process, so there was nobody to ask and no example to copy.

He drew it in 1963, rectangular instead of round so it would sit flat against a wall. He put wheels underneath, so a woman or a child could move it without help.

Then he took the noise out.

It went everywhere, into alleys and driveways and behind restaurants and schools, and it is the reason the bin outside your house has the shape it has. Harrison described the achievement without any ceremony at all.

"No more clang-clang of metal before breakfast."

That can was one object among hundreds, and he drew eight to twelve Sears sewing machines a year for twelve straight years. On a working day he could put one or two product ideas on paper every hour.

Blenders and baby cribs, hair dryers and hedge clippers, riding mowers, cordless shavers, barber chairs, transistor radios, the measuring cup you can see through. He made the Kenmore sewing machines lighter by moving them to die-cast aluminum, and by his own account practically every product in the Sears line passed through his hands at one point or another.

He was a salaried designer, which meant the company owned the drawings. They went out into the world wearing the company's brands, and the households reading those catalog pages never learned whose hand was behind the objects arriving at their door.

In 1993 Sears shut the in-house design department down completely. Harrison was the last industrial designer to walk out of the building, after thirty-two years.

He had come in first and he went out last, and then there was no department left to have been first in. Janet, whom he had met at the Art Institute and married while he was a graduate student, died six years later.

In 2008, at seventy-seven, he stood in a room in New York while the Cooper-Hewitt handed him the National Design Award for lifetime achievement. He was the first Black designer to receive it.

Martha Stewart introduced him at the gala and told the room she had learned to sew on a Kenmore machine. He had drawn eight to twelve of those a year for twelve years, so the odds were good that the machine in her story had come off his board.

The citation credited him with improving daily life for millions of Americans. It came forty-seven years after Sears agreed to put him on a payroll, and fifty-two years after it told him it would not.

He was born on September 23, 1931, in Shreveport, Louisiana, in his grandparents' house. His mother, Cora Lee, had travelled back to her own parents to give birth, because the hospitals of that place and that time did not take Black patients.

The first room of his life was a bedroom in a family house, because the buildings with beds in them would not have his mother.

His father taught industrial arts for a living, at Southern University in Louisiana, then at Prairie View A&M in Texas, then in Arizona. Summers, the boy had the run of those campuses, the experimental farms and the chemistry laboratories and the woodshops.

He built things. He built a boat once, carried it down to a pond and climbed in, and it went straight to the bottom with him aboard.

He told that story on himself for the rest of his life, and the ending never changed. "That's how you learn."

The family moved to Phoenix in 1945, and he graduated in 1948, at sixteen, from the all-Black high school where his father taught shop. It had opened as Phoenix Union Colored High School and was later renamed for George Washington Carver.

That school closed when integration became law. The building is a museum now, and there is a room inside it given over to the work of Charles Harrison.

It is one of the few walls in America carrying his name, and it is inside a segregated school that had to be shut down before anybody put it there.

So go count what is in your house tonight. The bin by the fence, the measuring cup, the hair dryer, the mower in the shed, your mother's sewing machine, the toy in the closet with the paper reels still in the box.

He has been in every room you live in for your entire life. More than seven hundred objects went out into the world with somebody else's name printed on the box.

Not one of them carries his, and that is the only part of this anybody can still fix. It costs nothing but the trouble of telling somebody where the things in their own kitchen came from.

Charles Harrison.

Charles Harrison spent decades designing objects that made everyday life quieter, lighter and easier, yet most reached American homes carrying company names instead of his own.His work lived in alleys, kitchens, workshops and children’s bedrooms long before the design world finally placed his name beside it.
I research and share stories like Charles Harrison’s because history belongs not only to famous products and brands, but also to the people whose hands shaped the objects we use every day.
If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/Vm6JEQzdIW
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text:
"Where is the Man to be found, who wishes to remain indebted, for the defence of his own person and property, to the exertions, the bravery, and the blood of others, without making one generous effort to repay the debt of honor and of gratitude? In what part of the Continent shall we find any Man, or body of Men, who would not blush to stand up and propose measures, purposely calculated to rob the Soldier of his Stipend, and the Public Creditor of his due? and were it possible that such a flagrant instance of Injustice could ever happen, would it not excite the general indignation, and tend to bring down, upon the Authors of such measures, the aggravated vengeance of Heaven?" George Washington, Circular Letter Addressed to the Governors of all the States on the Disbanding of the Army, Head Quarters, Newburgh, June 8, 1783

Source: https://t.co/IuGMRccsHZ

What can we learn?

As the Revolutionary War ended and the Continental Army prepared to disband, General George Washington wrote to state governors to urge national unity, a strong central government, and fair treatment for the soldiers. Many revolutionary soldiers and public creditors were not receiving their promised pay, stipends, or financial support from the states. Washington strongly condemned the idea of neglecting veterans and failing to honor the financial and moral debt owed to those who fought for American independence.

The core appeal rests on gratitude as moral obligation. Scripture commands generous treatment of vulnerable people—including debtors—in the principle that those who have received mercy should extend it to others, just as God liberated Israel from oppression[1]. Washington frames soldiers’ sacrifice as creating a debt of honor that citizens cannot ethically ignore. This echoes the biblical conviction that receiving mercy ought to generate grateful response, with mercy received leading to mercy offered[1].

Washington also emphasizes the sanctity of just compensation. Scripture teaches that even an ox deserves reward for labor, and “the worker deserves his wages”[2]. His indignation at depriving soldiers of stipends reflects biblical warnings: God prohibits oppressing one’s neighbor or robbing them, commanding that wages not be withheld overnight (Lev 19:13). Withheld wages cry out against those who retain them fraudulently, reaching the ears of the Lord (James 5:4).

Finally, Washington invokes divine judgment against injustice. His reference to “the aggravated vengeance of Heaven” reflects the biblical principle that commands for generosity and behavior based on gratitude carry divine sanction, backed by God’s threatened judgment of disobedience[1]. God warns of judgment against those who oppress hired workers in their wages (Mal 3:5).

Washington synthesizes these principles into a civic argument: citizens who benefit from soldiers’ sacrifice incur a binding moral debt—one rooted not merely in sentiment but in the biblical conviction that gratitude must manifest in concrete action, and that failing to honor such obligations invites divine displeasure.

1. Christopher J. H. Wright, Knowing Jesus through the Old Testament (Downers Grove, IL: IVP Academic: An Imprint of InterVarsity Press, 2014).
2. Van Johnson et al., Romans & Galatians: The Gospel according to Paul (Student Manual), ed. Quentin McGhee, Faith & Action Series (Chestnutridge, MO: Faith & Action, 2018).

text:
The day an AI system goes live is not necessarily the day its value becomes clear.

Healthcare organizations often evaluate AI through immediate performance:
▫️How much faster is the task?
▫️How much time does the technology save?
▫️How much work can it automate?

But there is another question worth asking:
What happens after the technology becomes part of the actual workflow?

A new JAMIA study offers compelling evidence.

Researchers at Washington University School of Medicine and collaborating institutions examined the longitudinal impact of ambient AI scribes on 220 primary care clinicians across 36 clinics and 314,845 patient encounters.

Using a quasi-experimental design, they compared documentation and productivity measures over 150 days before and after clinicians received access to the technology.

The findings reveal an interesting progression.

→ Note-writing time decreased by 7% initially, reaching 16% by day 150.
→ After-hours documentation time decreased by 19% by day 150.
→ Time spent in the EHR outside scheduled hours decreased by 13%.
→ Work relative value units increased by 2% at day 150.

Importantly, the researchers found no immediate change in after-hours work or productivity when the technology was first introduced.

Those differences emerged over time.

The study was observational rather than randomized, so the findings should not be interpreted as definitive proof of causation.

And it examined AI-assisted documentation, not independent medical review.

But the broader lesson is significant.

AI performance and operational value are two different measurements.

A tool can demonstrate impressive capabilities while delivering limited practical improvement if the workflow around it remains unchanged.

For healthcare decision infrastructure, that distinction matters enormously.

Consider an independent medical review platform.

Its value should not be measured solely by how quickly AI summarizes clinical documents.

We should also ask:
→ Are qualified reviewers spending less time navigating records and more time exercising clinical judgment?
→ Are cases arriving with fewer documentation gaps?
→ Are unnecessary handoffs and repeated administrative tasks being reduced?
→ Are quality and consistency improving alongside throughput?
→ Does the system continue delivering measurable value after the initial implementation?

At RediMinds, we build AI-enabled infrastructure to make complex healthcare decision workflows more efficient, structured, and defensible.

The objective is not simply to introduce more automation.
It is to create lasting improvements in how evidence is prepared, expertise is applied, and decisions are supported.

Because the return on AI is not just what the technology produces.
It is what the workflow no longer demands of the people responsible for the decision.

text:
Markets are facing two expensive problems at once: an energy shock that threatens to keep inflation elevated and an AI investment boom that increasingly depends on cheap financing, reliable electricity and extraordinary returns on capital. Neither is showing much sign of easing.

Brent has climbed above $110 and WTI past $100 as Hormuz shipping risks and Middle East tensions keep supply concerns elevated. Sustained oil strength would push through diesel, freight, food production and inflation expectations, complicating the Fed's rate outlook.

The geopolitical risk is spreading. Britain is deploying RAF Typhoons on defensive missions over Saudi Arabia following repeated Houthi attacks. No offensive operations are planned, but the additional military involvement underscores how difficult protecting regional energy infrastructure has become.

Washington is already trying to contain the economic damage. Trump's $8B farm-fuel relief program offers temporary support as diesel approaches $6.32 a gallon. But government payments can redistribute the cost of expensive energy; they cannot manufacture additional barrels.

Europe is feeling the pressure differently. Milan's cost-of-living protests escalated into clashes and looting, reflecting frustration over wages, housing and public services. Inflation is becoming a political problem as much as a monetary one.

Meanwhile, AI infrastructure spending continues to accelerate. JPMorgan forecasts nearly $800B in data-center investment for 2026, while reported Nvidia GPU orders point to enormous potential demand. But orders aren't delivered chips, and announced capacity isn't operational infrastructure.

Investors are starting to distinguish between the two.

Elice plunged 32.6% on its Korean IPO debut despite nearly 400x retail subscription demand. Enthusiasm for AI infrastructure doesn't guarantee investors will accept any valuation, particularly when electricity and financing remain unresolved.

Record S&P 500 put activity reinforces the cautious positioning ahead of Nvidia's GTC and major technology earnings. Heavy hedging isn't necessarily bearish, but it shows investors are paying attention to downside risk.

The market can absorb high energy prices or expensive capital for a while. Sustaining both while funding an unprecedented AI buildout is a much harder proposition.

text:
Gavin Newsom Signs ‘Anti-Hate Speech’ Training Mandate That Threatens Churches’ Religious Freedom | David Lindfield, Slay News

Democrat Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed a sweeping workplace training mandate that includes churches and religious nonprofits, raising warnings that California could force Christian employers to deliver instruction conflicting with biblical beliefs about sexuality, gender, and marriage.

AB 1803 requires employers with five or more workers to provide “anti-hate speech” training beginning January 1, 2028.

But the legislation leaves the definition of hate speech to California’s Civil Rights Department, the same agency that treats “misgendering” as workplace harassment, according to California Family Council Vice President Greg Burt.

The California Family Council warns that the law contains no express protections for churches’ religious beliefs and fails to distinguish constitutionally protected speech from unlawful conduct.

State Gets to Define What Counts as ‘Hate’

The mandate requires training addressing workplace speech that “vilifies, humiliates, or incites hatred” against people based on protected characteristics, including sex, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation.

Burt argued that those broad terms could be used against Christians expressing basic religious convictions.

“What does it mean to vilify? What speech actually humiliates?” Burt asked during “Washington Watch with Tony Perkins.”

“[M]any times legislators consider many Christian beliefs when they’re expressed — especially regarding sexuality or gender — they accuse us of hating people.

“That’s [the] farthest thing from my mind.

“But we are simply advocating for our view that sex is determined by biology, and God created us both male and female.

“Well, to many people that is humiliating and that incites hatred,” Burt said.

“And so that’s the problem with this legislation.”

The California Family Council also warned that the statute “fails to separate protected expression from unlawful conduct.”

It cited the Supreme Court’s 2017 holding that “the First Amendment has no hate speech exception.”

Mandate Builds on Existing Gender-Identity Training

The new requirement is being folded into California’s existing sexual harassment training framework.

“[Businesses are] already required to go through sexual harassment training, and we found out several years ago they redefined what sexual harassment means to include gender identity,” Burt said.

“… [The] California Civil Rights Department says misgendering is harassment, and so this training is on top of that already egregious training,” Burt added.

Employers can hire outside trainers or develop their own instruction, but Burt noted that California already offers a free curriculum for its existing training requirements.

“Right now, the state puts together a free curriculum—that’s how they do it with sexual harassment training, but you’re not required to use that training,” Burt said.

“You can come up with your own.

“But we don’t know exactly what ‘anti-hate’ is going to include, right?

“[Their] definition of speech that ‘humiliates’—what does that mean?

“It really depends on the person who’s receiving the language.”

That uncertainty leaves religious employers facing a state mandate without knowing precisely which expressions of their beliefs officials could classify as hateful.

‘You’ve Got to Resist’

Burt urged churches and religious organizations to seek accommodations rather than accept state-directed instruction on moral questions.

“What I think the state is doing is it’s trying to intimidate churches into following through with this,” Burt said.

“They should not be receiving any kind of ideological training from the state on any moral issue.

“That’s why what churches need to be doing is asking for religious accommodations,” Burt continued.

“The federal law and the state law already require businesses to accommodate people’s faith if they’re being required to do something that violates their faith. …

“[T]his is one of those points in history here in California where civil disobedience is going to be necessary.”

He warned that compliance could normalize the state’s intrusion into religious convictions.

“I’m sure they’re already thrilled that they get to retrain the entire population to believe what they believe regarding gender identity,” Burt said.

“And so once we get accustomed to this and say, ‘Well, this is just what California requires, I guess we have to do it.’

“No, you don’t. Folks, you’ve got to resist, and that includes individual employees.

“That’s what we are encouraging people to do.

“And we are having success,” Burt said.

“We have some attorneys we’re working with, and when people have been asking for religious accommodations, they have been accommodated.”

text:
Seattle socialist mayor bankrolls deportation defense for illegal aliens through $4 million taxpayer-funded initiative | Ari Hoffman, The Post Millennial

Seattle’s socialist Mayor Katie Wilson is using a $4 million taxpayer-funded initiative to support immigrant services that include helping illegal aliens fight deportation.

In an October 16 statement, Wilson touted continued spending on legal services, rapid response efforts, and assistance for immigrant workers and businesses. Her announcement was circulated in English, with translations advertised in Spanish, Somali, Chinese, and Vietnamese.

“My office is sustaining four million dollars in ongoing support for immigrant and refugee communities, funding legal services, rapid response, and assistance for immigrant workers and small businesses,” Wilson said.

Seattle’s Legal Defense Network funding solicitation announced an additional $1.25 million annually for services including deportation proceedings, challenges to ICE detention, and efforts to obtain relief from final removal orders. Eligible clients include low-income immigrants who live, work, or attend school in Seattle, or who are detained or face removal proceedings in the city. The city’s broader Immigrant Rapid Response Program explicitly offers services regardless of immigration status.

Wilson then instructed: “If you are threatened or in danger, call 911. To report a bias incident, contact the Seattle Office for Civil Rights.”

The announcement sent in Somali follows Wilson’s dismissal of calls to investigate alleged fraud involving Somali-run daycares. Wilson was previously asked whether she had authorized Seattle police or the Office of Immigrant and Refugee Affairs to investigate the allegations. “No,” she replied. “This whole issue is not really about fraud,” Wilson said, adding: “It's about making an immigrant community a target.”

In September, TPM reporter Katie Daviscourt investigated more than 20 Seattle-area daycare locations, raising questions about more than $5 million in public funding. At several locations, no children appeared present or nobody answered the door. Records reviewed in the investigation showed Daisy Family Childcare received nearly $2 million and collected about $70,000 monthly.

SEIU 925 responded by targeting the journalist. In a September 22 email to lawmakers and early-learning leaders, union Political and Legislative Director Erin Haick accused Daviscourt of “harassing Somali child care providers” and participating in a “sustained, racist attack.” Haick disclosed that five programs mentioned in the reporting were union members.

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown had similarly criticized independent journalists who have been investigating providers since December. In an official statement, Brown said Somali providers were being accused of inadequate fact-checking and directed those experiencing threats or harassment to police or his office’s Hate Crimes & Bias Incident Hotline.

Approximately $37 million in questionable childcare payments were identified by auditors, as well as 1,372 subsidy overpayments totaling more than $2 million.

Seattle’s immigrant-support spending extends beyond attorneys. A city announcement designated $280,000 for community grants covering neighborhood alert systems, volunteer recruitment, rights presentations, family safety planning, and assistance with meals, towing fees, and immigration fees.

The City Council appropriated the $4 million in late 2025, before Wilson took office. Her administration subsequently pledged to distribute it alongside restrictions on using city-owned and city-controlled property for civil immigration enforcement and instructions for police to verify and document reported federal enforcement activity.

text:
Oil prices climbed to a five-month high Tuesday after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed a new round of attacks on Saudi Arabia. Brent crude, the global benchmark, rose as high as $111.05 a barrel, its highest since May, and U.S. West Texas Intermediate touched $104.94, its highest since September, according to Reuters. The Houthis said Monday they hit Saudi energy, airport and military targets, including an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claims, and Reuters said it could not independently verify them.

Shipping is the other worry. At least 18 vessels were reportedly attacked over two weeks, ship tracker Kpler said Monday, according to Reuters. The Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of the world’s energy exports before the war, has been largely shut since the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran in late February, https://t.co/SxcViLb0iV and The National reported. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has suggested Gulf crude flows recovered to about 80% of prewar levels, but ANZ analysts warned that rebound is now under threat, https://t.co/SxcViLb0iV reported.

Washington is also weighing Russian supply. An executive order President Trump issued Friday night waived key Russia-related sanctions and tariffs, including penalties for buying Russian oil and gas, CNBC reported, but Trump said Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate it. Traders don’t appear to be counting on it. “While the prospect of additional Russian diesel supply offers some theoretical relief, traders appear far more focused on the ongoing risk of further damage to energy infrastructure across the Gulf region,” said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade.

At the pump, AAA put the national average for regular gas at $4.28 a gallon Tuesday. AAA says the average has stayed above $4 since late July and is more than a dollar higher than a year ago, and that oil market volatility has produced seasonal record highs this fall. The Federal Reserve meets Oct. 27 and 28, and The National reported that high energy costs are feeding inflation worries ahead of that meeting.

This is exactly why American energy matters. A rebel group fires at a Saudi oil field and families here pay for it at the pump. We have the oil right here at home. Produce it, refine it, and stop letting the Middle East set our gas prices. Thoughts?

Sources: Reuters, CNBC, https://t.co/SxcViLb0iV, The National, AAA

Chase Young Is Giving the Saints the Impact Washington Hoped For!

Who Dat Nation, Chase Young is reminding everyone why he was once one of football’s most exciting prospects. Washington selected the Ohio State standout second overall in the 2020 NFL Draft, and he immediately delivered, earning Defensive Rookie of the Year honors with 7.5 sacks. However, a serious knee injury interrupted that promising start, and his time with the organization ended before he could establish sustained success. Washington traded him to San Francisco in October 2023 for a third-round draft pick, eventually opening the door for a fresh opportunity in New Orleans.

The Saints have watched Young turn that opportunity into production. After recording 5.5 sacks in his first season with New Orleans, he reached a career-high 10 sacks in just 12 games in 2025 despite missing the opening five games with a calf injury. His strong finish showed that his resurgence was already underway before this season. Through six games in 2026, Young has added 5.5 sacks and 24 pressures, while he and Carl Granderson have combined for nine sacks—giving the Saints an encouraging presence on the edges even as the defense works through its struggles.

For New Orleans, Young’s progress offers a reason to believe the defensive front has a player worth building around. Washington saw his ability early, but injuries and uneven availability complicated his development there. The Saints are now benefiting from a more productive stretch of his career, with last season’s breakthrough providing a stronger foundation for his current success. Young still needs to maintain that level, and the defense needs better results overall, but he is giving Who Dat Nation something to appreciate: a talented pass rusher turning those early expectations into meaningful production.

text:
A letter from a Palestinian living next to Israel.

Hello, I am Palestinian. 📷
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

A good IPO should start with a fair company valuation, transparent financial disclosures, and a share price justified by the company’s fundamentals.

Investors should understand what they are buying, the risks involved, and how they could potentially earn returns through dividends and capital appreciation.

text:
This is for every time you, me and everyone we know closed our hearts to other human beings, because we didn't want to get hurt again. 
You may think Gary passionately believes Israel has the right to defend itself by blowing up apartment blocks with sleeping children, but that’s not why he does it. He does it because he needs something. It’s hard to get. We’ll soon find out what it is. 
 
You only see an avatar and a mystifying handle. You don’t see Gary’s potbelly. You don’t see how tired Gary is. You can’t tell how detached Gary tries to look. How above it all. How unfazed by it all. Reddish nose from daily night caps. Usually muscatel. Sometimes old whiskey. Not mixed with cola, though he prefers it that way. He knows that’s primitive. 
 
Most of all you can’t see Gary’s pain. 
 
A lot of pain. 
 
Pain that’s been there for so long that Gary himself doesn’t notice it’s there anymore. 
 
His pain has become a certain kind of attitude, a behaviour. 
 
Gary is not evil. 
 
He has two kids that even though they are in their mid twenties he still supports financially. 
 
He has a wife he’s never beaten. He also hasn’t had intercourse with her in the last 6,5 years. And he doesn’t want to remind himself of the last time they tried. When about halfway through she gave him a quick peck on the cheek, giggled to hide her shame and guilt and said: ‘I guess that ship has sailed.’ 
 
By that ship Gary assumes she meant the passion between them. 
 
But there never had been any of that. 
 
The most intense, most satisfying moment of Gary’s life happened in the late nineties. With a Portugese woman named Silvana. When he got to second base with her in dimly lit bar in the barro alto, not too far from the Fernando Pessoa statue. She’d given him a book with Pessoa’s poem. On the title page she had written: ‘His melancholy reminds me of yours. Whatever you carry inside you, you can show to me.’ 
 
He never did. 
 
When the project for which his US company had sent him to Lisbon ended he returned to Michigan. They chatted over ICQ for a bit and email. It petered out. When he found her on Facebook eleven years later she was married to a Brazilian guy who trains horses. It stung. He asked her if she had married the Horse Whisperer. She never replied. 
 
His wife looks nothing like Silvana, but she is practical, dependable, not a spendthrift and never does anything to embarrass him. At least not in public. 
 
Why do we need to know all this? 
 
Why can’t we know why Gary calls people idiot, retard, moron several times a week on a platform formerly known as Twitter? 
 
Why do we need to know some rude guy on social media drinks one or two glasses of muscatel every night? 
 
The muscatel he drinks because at first it made him feel close to Silvana in her absence. Now he drinks it cause he got used to the smell and the taste of it. And because special people consume special drinks. 
 
And Gary feels special. 
 
Secretly. 
 
Gary is almost certain he’s brilliant. 
 
He thinks he should have gone to MIT and not some unknown college. 
 
He blames his parents for not getting into MIT. 
 
That’s a pattern with Gary. 
 
When something doesn’t go like he likes it to go he blames someone else than himself. Always. 
 
If Israel burning children in tents doesn’t fit with what Gary think Israel stands for, then someone else is responsible for burning those children. 
 
Since Gary knows he is brilliant and it’s only the dumb world that has failed to reward his brilliance he feels a glimmer of that brilliance when he can call other people idiots. Anonymously of course. 
 
Gary is hypersensitive to being shamed. 
 
His mum was a mean drunk and at times would make fun of Gary’s father. She would praise sophisticated men, local men and celebrities alike and then laugh haughtily and tell Gary: ‘Your farm raised father is a slob who never takes me anywhere.’ 
 
That’s just one wound that made Gary avoid any situation where someone could shame him. Especially women. 
 
Another factor in Gary labeling people who empathize with Palestinian little girls trapped in cars with dead relatives and being shot at by big ass Israeli tanks is this: 
 
Gary suffers, it’s often the same pain, his brilliance is never recognized. Not in school, not at home, not at his job. Not even by his three poker friends. Since Covid they don’t even meet anymore. 
 
His children treat him like this somewhat adorable chubby block of grumpiness trying to hard to matter. They love him, but don’t respect him. His advice is always made fun of. His son has even said: ‘The only thing I trust you on is if you design a bridge. But now chatgpt can do that faster.’ 
 
Gary knew his son wasn’t even try to hurt him and exactly that hurt the most. 
 
Gary sometimes wondered if when is never fully loved in childhood, love always eludes you. 
 
His dad’s way of showing love to Gary was to build a bird’s house together. Dad would get upset at some point, start yelling and send Gary inside claiming he could focus better alone. Dad would finish the bird’s house and call Gary and his mum to come look at it. Which made Gary feel useless. Worse was when mum said: ‘He makes me live in a dump, but he will build a mansion for the birdies.’ 
 
The closest Gary’s dad ever got was on his death bed. 
 
When he said Gary’s watch looked really good on him. That it showed a bit of class. 
 
Gary beamed and said: ‘It’s a smartwatch.’ 
 
And dad said: ‘Today watches are smart and people are dumb.’ 
 
Gary with the smartwatch feels the irrepressible need to call people dumb online. 
 
Since nobody has ever really empathized with Gary, he experiences it as a personal affront to have to empathize with injured children in Gaza. He hates that everyone now cares about those, but nobody ever cared about little Gary who had to witness the cold war between his parents, was never excellent at anything, except mathematics at times and one science project in school when he was 15 (which went largely unnoticed). 
 
You know how you can tell Gary’s been vitally damaged? 
 
He’s given up on effort. 
 
No effort in Gary ever got him more than a fairly decent job, a respectable wife, a better home than his parents could afford and two kids who are ok, but always feel very far away, especially when they are in the same room as Gary. 
 
So no, Gary is not going to read ten pro-Palestine books and ten pro-Israeli books, examine his own bias, contact people on both sides, try as hard as possible to reach some kind of fair verdict. 
 
But he also can’t resist commenting anyway. 
 
Since effort is suspect in Gary’s life he doesn’t want to spend too much energy on his comments. 
 
He will share some graph he found somewhere showing how there are more Palestinians today than 20 years ago, so Israel can’t have any genocidal intent. 
 
If anyone counters with graphs of their own he types ‘idiot.’ 
 
Gary doesn’t want to know. Gary already knows what counts: 
 
Associating himself with Israel makes him feel connected to the most succesful people in the US. And success is what Gary respects. Palestinians he associates with the same loud people who want everything for free, like cancelling student debt. 
 
Gary’s proof that he is brilliant is that he calls others idiots. 
 
Accepting dead children also makes him feel supremely rational. 
 
What could be more rational than accepting that sometimes to create a better world some children have to be separated from their arms and their legs, and their parents, and their homes. 
 
It’s all for the greater good and it’s not Israel doing it. Hamas members sit in the cockpit of the Israeli F-35s and force the pilot’s hand. Well, you know, symbolically. I mean, they are terrorists after all. 
 
In Gary’s world some guys with guns are terrorists and some guy, and especially pretty girls who look like Gary’s fantasy girls, can never be terrorists. 
 
Gary’s aspirations in life have been defeated, but they are not dead and supporting Israel feels like some of Israel’s dominance, power, cunning intelligence will rub off on Gary. 
 
In Gary’s fantasies he is exactly the kind of guy who could have engineered the pager attack on Hezbollah. 
 
He is the one who could create an Iron Dome. 
 
He is unrecognized success and brilliant goodness, just like, in Gary’s mind, Israel is unrecognized success and brilliant goodness. 
 
In supporting Israel Gary supports little denied Gary. 
 
And so almost every day Gary dumps some comment on a stranger. Sometimes the stranger foolishly takes the bait and reacts. As if anyone could ever change Gary’s mind. 
 
Gary feels good. Finally someone is hit by something Gary did and said, though negatively. Gary has penetrated. And that is enough. He’s no longer interested now, so his off ramp is yelling ‘idiot’. Like dumping the used condom in the bin after the high has been had. 
 
Gary only wants to make people who still love life bad. 
 
Gary has kinda given up on life. 
 
He’s still here. There is some hope left, not much. 
 
And if you ask him why he is angry or annoyed he will say something like all those crazy lefties are turning the whole country upside down and are falling for Hamas propaganda. 
 
He will not mention the 6,5 years dry spell. 
 
Or the school reunions he dreads because he doesn’t shine there. 
 
He will not say how every time the 25 year old colleague, a mesmerizing mix of Syrian-Korean roots and the most dazzling black curls Gary has ever seen walks past at work Gary feels as worthy as a small piece of cheap pizza stuck on the floor of a subway car. 
 
And so Gary throws some cherry picked information online, calls whoever responds a retard and never realizes that this works exactly like the muscatel. 
 
It gives him a vague hint of what he really needs: 
 
intimacy so warm, so real, so safe, so sensual, so embracing of true Gary, his pain would finally go away. 
 
And so the Palestinians come to stand for everything Gary loathes in himself and about the world and Israelis come to stand for everything what Gary knows he could have been, had the world not thwarted him and spit him out. 
 
That Gary can mumble something about the Balfour declaration or can make the sweeping claim that Palestinians have been offered a state many times, but always choose war, doesn’t change any of that. 
 
He doesn’t actually care about this issue. 
 
Gary cares about soothing Gary’s pain. 
 
And for that the pain of Palestinian children needs to be shrugged off, so Gary can piss off some folks Gary loathes and Gary gets to feel for a fleeting second that anything Gary says can have some kind of effect too. 
 
Once you know Gary’s story, and there are so many Garys, you know you don’t owe Gary a senseless discussion because Gary got infinitely less from life than Gary did deserve when he was born. 
 
Now, through his own actions, he deserves those good things less and less. 
 
I dream of all pro-Palestinians holding hands and forming a circle round Gary and reminding him of every good thing Gary did. Gary may want to shrug off orphaned amputee kids online, but we if we’d list every small act of kindness in Gary’s life of 53 years we’d get to a lot. The trouble is that Gary feels a mix of warmth, but also shame whenever he is kind. Gary has learned to associate pain with having an open heart. 
 
That’s why we should use our collective warmth to melt Gary’s frozen heart. 
 
Ubuntu. 
 
Strangely that would be the first time Gary would feel the least bit of an opening to modify his opinions on Palestine-Israel. 
 
A person is a person through other people. 
 
Gary just ran into too few people who could have made Gary see bleeding Palestinian children on a cold hospital floor and feel called to do something to stop the ones throwing the bombs on them.

text:
The Devi’s own temples settle the question before any text is opened. At Kamakhya, goats, pigeons, ducks and buffaloes are offered; a priest said at least twelve to fourteen buffaloes are sacrificed at Durga Puja, and the temple’s Bar Doloi calledsacrifice part of the daily worship. The buffalo is the demon’s own animal; its meat is not cow beef. The cow is not offered, and the tradition draws that line itself. Kamakhya also serves a non-vegetarian bhog alongside the vegetarian one.

At Puri, one of the Char Dham, Jagannath’s kitchen is vegetarian, but his food is not complete until it is also offered to Vimala. Fish from the Markanda tank is cooked for her in a temporary kitchen and carried in before Jagannath wakes, though the goat is disputed. One sacred complex keeps two ritual obligations without making either the enemy of the other. A civilisation that could not tolerate this would have to abolish one kitchen to protect the other.

The Devi does not keep one kitchen either. Ambika, Chandi and Kali accept bali; Vaishno Devi refuses meat and liquor. In her legend, a tantric figure demands both at a feast and the Devi turns him away; pilgrims seek his blessing at aseparate shrine. Each form keeps its own rule, and the devotee follows the form, not a national menu.

text:
The AM Brief, Tuesday October 20, 2026 Part 3

Good morning,

It’s 9am in Miami and here is a recap of events in the Space sector that caught my eye. Part 3

     Wallops Island, Virginia, has rapidly evolved into a pivotal launch hub for both NASA and the Space Force, underscoring its expanding strategic importance. The Space Force has awarded up to $3.2 billion in defense contracts across a dozen aerospace companies to advance space based missile defense systems operating from the facility. This massive capital injection aims to accelerate national security initiatives, enhance orbital surveillance capabilities, and strengthen US defense posture against next generation aerial and space borne threats amid global geopolitical shifts.

     NASA's Perseverance rover achieved a milestone in interplanetary exploration by setting a new Mars driving record of 28.1 total miles traveled, officially surpassing the previous record held by the Opportunity rover. This accomplishment highlights the exceptional durability and autonomous navigation capabilities of modern robotic explorers on the Martian surface, paving the way for continued geological discovery, sample collection, and extended scientific missions across harsh extraterrestrial terrain.

     Japan’s Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) space mission is scheduled to launch today on its journey to Mars' moon Phobos. The ambitious endeavor aims to collect physical surface samples and safely return them to Earth in 2031. Scientists hope the retrieved material will offer crucial insights into the origins of the Martian moons and the broader evolutionary history of the solar system, marking a major milestone for deep space exploration and robotic sample return technology.

     NASA researchers have identified a newly formed lunar impact crater that spans a diameter larger than the Roman Colosseum. Analysis of high resolution satellite imagery indicates the massive feature was created by a heavy space object collision that occurred roughly two years ago. The discovery provides astronomers with valuable real time observational data regarding impact frequency, surface degradation, and structural changes on the moon's outer crust.

      Planet Labs' Tanager-1 satellite detected a major methane plume near Karachi leaking 2,600 pounds per hour using infrared absorption fingerprints analyzed by neural networks. Human activity drives 60% of global methane emissions, which trap up to 86 times more heat than carbon dioxide over a 12 year period. While Tanager 1 has spotted over 14,400 plumes to date and prompted repairs in regions like the Permian Basin, international mitigation efforts continue to lag behind.

🔔 TODAY THE CHURCH CELEBRATES  
St. Paul of the Cross  
October 20

🕊️ WHAT WE REMEMBER  
St. Paul of the Cross was an Italian priest and founder of the Passionists, a religious community devoted to remembering the Passion of Jesus Christ. He encouraged others to discover God's great love through Christ's suffering and sacrifice.

🔥 WHY IT MATTERS  
St. Paul reminds us that the Cross is not simply a symbol of suffering, but the greatest expression of God's love for us. Through Christ's sacrifice, we find hope, mercy and salvation.

👣 HOW WE LIVE IT  
Spend a quiet moment before a Crucifix today. Reflect on Christ's love and offer Him a struggle or burden you are carrying.

➡️SHARE YOUR FAITH
As Catholic disciples of Christ, share this post on your page! You never know who you might reach today - someone who is curious about our Catholic faith and simply waiting for an invitation!

❓ CATHOLIC CURIOUS?  
Why do Catholics display Jesus on the Cross?

A Crucifix reminds us of the sacrifice Jesus made for our salvation. While we celebrate His Resurrection, we also remember the depth of His love revealed on the Cross.

Want to learn more about Catholic beliefs and traditions? Ask a Catholic friend or explore OCIA (Order of Christian Initiation of Adults) at a parish near you! https://t.co/1RwzdPwW08

🙏 TODAY WE PRAY  
St. Paul of the Cross, help us recognize Christ's love in His Passion and trust in Him through life's difficulties. Pray for us. 🙏

text:
Mo Riles’ wrecked pickup became an online joke, until more than 500 strangers raised $22,000 to replace it.
In South Bend, Indiana, people photographed his green Chevrolet Silverado because it barely looked drivable. Its bed was crushed, panels were mangled, and years of mishaps had left it nearly unrecognizable.

But the truck was Riles’ only transportation, not something he could simply abandon. He had worked much of his life, most recently at Dollar Tree, and needed transportation to medical appointments amid health problems. Local auto detailer Colin Crowel wondered what might be happening in the driver's life instead of joining the ridicule.

On November 30, 2025, Crowel launched a fundraiser to buy him a safer vehicle. Within a month, more than 500 people donated over $22,000. On December 30, Riles drove his damaged Silverado to Gates Chevrolet, where he received a 2019 Chevrolet Silverado. The newer truck seemed so advanced that Riles compared driving it to piloting a spaceship.

Local repair shops also offered to help with future maintenance. Even as he celebrated, Riles insisted the greater gift was seeing his community come together for someone who needed help.

text:
MY SON CALLED ME SELFISH FOR REFUSING TO BUY HIM A HOUSE.

I’m 59 and live in Charlotte, North Carolina. After 30 years working as a nurse, I paid for my son Marcus’s college, helped him buy a car, and gave him $15,000 for his wedding.
Then he asked me for $45,000 toward a house down payment. That was most of my retirement savings. When I refused, he accused me of not caring about him
My daughter-in-law posted online about parents who refused to help their children. Relatives called me selfish, but nobody asked whether I could afford it.
When I offered smaller financial assistance, Marcus rejected it. “If you die tomorrow, the money will go to somebody anyway,” he said.
His words broke my heart.
Three months later, I learned they had expensive car payments, credit card debt, and a wedding loan. They could afford a modest home, but wanted something beyond their budget.
When I confronted Marcus, he admitted everything.
“You had your chance to enjoy life. Now it’s my turn,” he said.
I realized he expected me to sacrifice my future for his lifestyle.
I met a financial adviser and protected my retirement savings. I updated my will, not to punish my son, but to protect myself.
Months later, Marcus lost financial stability and asked to move in. I agreed, provided we established clear boundaries.
He called me selfish again.
I still love him, but love doesn’t mean sacrificing everything.

text:
How Theranos Sold Silicon Valley a $9 Billion Dream

In 2014, a startup called Theranos was valued at $9 billion.

Its founder, Elizabeth Holmes, promised to revolutionize healthcare with a machine that could run blood tests using just a few drops from a finger prick.

Investors believed. The media paid attention.

But was the technology really ready to change the world? 🧵

2/12 — The Vision

Holmes founded Theranos in 2003 after dropping out of Stanford.

Her vision was simple but powerful: make blood testing cheaper, faster, and less intimidating.

Instead of drawing multiple vials of blood, patients could supposedly get answers from a tiny sample.

It sounded like the future of medicine.

But could the technology deliver on that promise?

3/12 — The Rise

Theranos attracted wealthy investors and influential figures.

Its valuation climbed to an estimated $9 billion, and Holmes became one of the most talked-about founders in Silicon Valley.

The company wasn't just selling a product. It was selling a vision of the future.

But what happens when a startup's reputation grows faster than the evidence behind its technology?

4/12 — The Big Opportunity

Theranos partnered with Walgreens to bring its blood-testing services closer to everyday Americans.

Imagine walking into a pharmacy, getting a simple finger prick, and receiving important health information without a traditional blood draw.

The commercial opportunity was enormous.

But before a medical breakthrough can scale, one question matters more than the business plan: does it actually work?

5/12 — Behind the Promise

Questions began to emerge about the reliability of Theranos's technology.

The company had made extraordinary claims about what its devices could do, but concerns about testing accuracy and its laboratory practices were growing.

In healthcare, a faulty result isn't just a business problem. It can affect real decisions about people's lives.

So why were so many people still betting on Theranos?

6/12 — The Investigation

In 2015, The Wall Street Journal began publishing investigative reports by journalist John Carreyrou.

His reporting raised serious questions about whether Theranos could perform the wide range of tests it claimed to offer using its own technology.

The company's carefully controlled story was now facing scrutiny.

What would happen if the public discovered that the product didn't live up to the promise?

7/12 — The Pressure Builds

Theranos disputed criticism and defended its technology.

But scrutiny from journalists, regulators, and others intensified.

The story was no longer just about a promising startup. It was becoming a test of transparency, scientific evidence, and investor trust.

Could a company built on secrecy survive when outsiders started asking difficult questions?

8/12 — The Collapse

Theranos's business unraveled.

Its testing operations faced regulatory action, its partnership with Walgreens ended, and the company eventually shut down in 2018.

The $9 billion valuation belonged to a company that no longer existed.

How did a business with such influential supporters fall so far?

9/12 — The Legal Reckoning

In January 2022, a federal jury convicted Holmes on four counts related to defrauding investors.

The verdict was not simply a judgment on a failed product. It concerned specific representations made to investors.

A bold vision is not a crime. But what happens when promises to investors cross the line into fraud?

10/12 — The Real Business Lesson

Theranos is a reminder that a powerful founder story, prestigious investors, and enormous media attention cannot replace proof.

In industries like healthcare, claims must be supported by reliable evidence.

Growth matters. Fundraising matters. Branding matters.

But none of them can substitute for a product that works.

Why do investors sometimes appear to fall in love with a founder before fully testing the business?

11/12 — The Bigger Question

Theranos didn't collapse simply because its ambition was enormous.

Its story exposed the dangers of secrecy, weak verification, and allowing a compelling narrative to overshadow difficult questions.

The lesson for founders: build trust through evidence.

The lesson for investors: verify before you amplify.

But who should carry the greatest responsibility when a startup fails its customers and investors?

12/12 — Let's Debate

Theranos became one of Silicon Valley's most infamous startup scandals.

But the bigger question goes beyond Elizabeth Holmes.

When a startup makes extraordinary promises and those promises turn out to be misleading, who deserves the most blame?

A) The founder
B) The investors who failed to verify the claims
C) The board and leadership
D) The wider ecosystem that rewards hype over evidence
Reply with A, B, C, or D—and explain your reasoning.

What makes a nation genuinely influential?

The frequency with which its leaders meet great powers?

The eloquence of its diplomatic declarations?

The number of international forums it joins?

Or its capacity to offer indispensable economic, technological and strategic capabilities while retaining independent choices?

Isn't the most demanding lesson of Jamnagar that diplomatic ambition must ultimately be supported by productive strength?

A government can negotiate an agreement.

But who builds the capabilities that make the agreement valuable?

A state can declare strategic autonomy.

But what sustains that autonomy when supply chains fracture, sanctions expand or partners change course?

A nation can aspire to global leadership.

But can aspiration substitute for internationally competitive enterprise, technology and institutions?

The defining question for India's rise is therefore not merely: How should Delhi negotiate with the world?

It is: What must India build so that the world has compelling reasons to negotiate with Delhi?

Some very helpful things in here, particularly on the juxtaposition of pastors/influencers. Wholeheartedly agree with taking men to the hidden parts of ministry in order to expose them to the wonderful calling of shepherding. 

There’s some things that remain untouched or glossed over though. The claim that egalitarianism has been/is being fought against is assumed by the author and remains unqualified. It’s also subjective. I attend a reformed PCA church and reformed seminary. I would disagree that it’s being fought against enough and at times, still being willingly embraced - how many time do we need to go through women deacon overtures? 

MDivs are offered to women at WTS and RTS. They shouldn’t be. Biblical counseling degrees are tailored very much toward women which is also problematic - counseling IS shepherding the soul. We are outsourcing this function in an arguably egalitarian direction. 

Women’s ministry’s in churches often offer a far more robust program to disciple women. RE’s often function more as senators casting votes than shepherds leading souls. 

In addition to this, while the article touches on many young men having witnessed the deluge of pastoral failure over the past decade, something that has negatively effected them, it failed to call leadership to radical accountability when they do in fact make mistakes. Elders are so afraid to own their shortcomings and sins specifically. They will claim from the pulpit that they need the atoning blood of Jesus just as much as anyone (yes and amen!) but when faced with the opportunity to repent publicly, own their mistakes and move on, they typically circle the wagons and go on defense. They demand a level of grace unequally measured to their offense. 

So many men, both young and even reaching to age 40 are begging to be led, discipled and rebuked. Most elders just won’t do it - I’ve experienced this in and out of the PCA. 

Other items that deserve attention - the general health of leaders is poor. They’re obese, riddled by constant tiredness, and generally appear sloppy. In essence, they possess no gravitas. They will continue to find it difficult to get young men to follow them because of this. 

Lastly - ecclesial bureaucracy. Do not underestimate how many men are avoidant of the ministry, particularly in PCA circles, because of this. Everything needs a committee. Appeals are endless. Overtures become tedious arguments that amount to childish mental masturbation. When men “just do things” they are scolded. “Respect the process”, they are told. Often many are left in a state of paralysis by analysis. 

I agree men should be discipled better. God knows I need that. I also believe that radical accountability on leadership is a necessary prerequisite for it.

text:
Greatmartyr Artemius at Antioch

Holy Great Martyr Artemius of Antioch was a prominent military leader during the reigns of the emperor Constantine the Great (May 21), and his son and successor Constantius (337-361). Artemius received many awards for distinguished service and courage. He was appointed viceroy of Egypt. In this official position he did much for the spreading and strengthening Christianity in Egypt.

Saint Artemius was sent by the emperor Constantius to bring the relics of the holy Apostle Andrew from Patras, and the relics of the holy Apostle Luke from Thebes of Boeotia, to Constantinople. The holy relics were placed in the Church of the Holy Apostles beneath the table of oblation. The emperor rewarded him by making him ruler of Egypt.

The emperor Constantius was succeeded on the throne by Julian the Apostate (361-363). Julian in his desire to restore paganism was extremely antagonistic towards Christians, sending hundreds to their death. At Antioch he ordered the torture of two bishops unwilling to forsake the Christian Faith.

During this time, Saint Artemius arrived in Antioch and publicly denounced Julian for his impiety. The enraged Julian subjected the saint to terrible tortures and threw the Great Martyr Artemius into prison. While Artemius was praying, Christ, surrounded by angels, appeared to him and said, “Take courage, Artemius! I am with you and will preserve you from every hurt which is inflicted upon you, and I already have prepared your crown of glory. Since you have confessed Me before the people on earth, so shall I confess you before My Heavenly Father. Therefore, take courage and rejoice, you shall be with Me in My Kingdom.” Hearing this, Artemius rejoiced and offered up glory and thanksgiving to Him.

On the following day, Julian demanded that Saint Artemius honor the pagan gods. Meeting with steadfast refusal, the emperor resorted to further tortures. The saint endured all without a single moan. The saint told Julian that he would be justly recompensed for his persecution of Christians. Julian became furious and resorted to even more savage tortures, but they did not break the will of the saint. Finally the Great Martyr Artemius was beheaded.

His relics were buried by Christians. After the death of Saint Artemius, his prophecy about Julian the Apostate’s impending death came true.

Julian left Antioch for a war with the Persians. Near the Persian city of Ctesiphon, Julian came upon an elderly Persian, who agreed to betray his countrymen and guide Julian’s army. The old man deceived Julian and led his army into the Karmanite wilderness, where there was neither food nor water. Tired from hunger and thirst, Julian’s army battled against fresh Persian forces.

Divine retribution caught up with Julian the Apostate. During the battle he was mortally wounded by an unseen hand and an unseen weapon. Julian groaned deeply said, “You have conquered, Galilean!” After the death of the apostate emperor, the relics of the Great Martyr Artemius were transferred with honor from Antioch to Constantinople.

Saint Artemius is invoked by those suffering from hernias.

Over time the organization grew in size to where it managed a bank, ran a newspaper, owned several properties, and at one point in time was the largest Black fraternal society and Black-owned business in the U.S. The bank was the only one in Richmond to maintain full services during the panic of 1893.

𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗛𝗜𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗬 𝗔𝗦 𝗜𝗙 𝗜𝗧 𝗪𝗘𝗥𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗗𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗜𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬.

𝗥𝗘𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗢𝗟𝗗 𝗧𝗘𝗫𝗧𝗦 𝗧𝗢 𝗙𝗜𝗧 𝗡𝗘𝗪 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬.

𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗜𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗢 𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗖𝗛 𝗢𝗟𝗗 𝗦𝗖𝗥𝗜𝗣𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗘𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗢𝗙 𝗢𝗙 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬.

𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗘𝗫𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗔𝗪𝗔𝗬 𝗙𝗔𝗜𝗟𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗗𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗠𝗔𝗞𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗠 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘 𝗧𝗥𝗨𝗘!

𝗔 𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗜𝗠 𝗢𝗙 "𝗙𝗨𝗟𝗙𝗜𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬" 𝗜𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗘 𝗢𝗙 𝗗𝗜𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗘 𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗘𝗞𝗡𝗢𝗪𝗟𝗘𝗗𝗚𝗘 𝗨𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗟 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗜𝗠 𝗜𝗦 𝗜𝗡𝗗𝗘𝗣𝗘𝗡𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗟𝗬 𝗗𝗘𝗠𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗗.
author: robbservations2
authorBio: To me MOST of the world’s problems (besides greed & selfishness) are due to people believing complete B. S. for no good reason or, for bad reasons.

text:
𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘'𝗦 𝗡𝗢 𝗦𝗨𝗖𝗛 𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗔𝗦 "𝗙𝗨𝗟𝗙𝗜𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬" — 𝗕𝗨𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘 𝗔𝗥𝗘 𝗙𝗔𝗞𝗘𝗗 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗙𝗔𝗜𝗟𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗜𝗘𝗦 𝗜𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗕𝗟𝗘!

The Bible contains numerous claims of fulfilled prophecy. But a 𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗜𝗠 𝗢𝗙 𝗙𝗨𝗟𝗙𝗜𝗟𝗟𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧 is 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗘 that anyone actually predicted the future!

Many supposed fulfillments can be explained through 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗼𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝘃𝗮𝗴𝘂𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲, and 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀.

𝗜. 𝗕𝗔𝗖𝗞-𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗡 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗜𝗘𝗦 — 𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗗𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦 𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗡 𝗔𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗦

• A prophecy isn't impressive if the supposed prediction was 𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗡 𝗔𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗡𝗧 occurred.

• This is called vaticinium ex eventu — 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗵𝗲𝗰𝘆 𝗮𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁.

• Ancient authors sometimes presented known history as though it had been predicted centuries earlier.

• 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗢𝗢𝗞 𝗢𝗙 𝗗𝗔𝗡𝗜𝗘𝗟 is one of the clearest scholarly examples.

𝗘𝗫𝗔𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘: 𝗗𝗔𝗡𝗜𝗘𝗟 𝟭𝟭

• Daniel is set during the sixth century BCE.

• Most critical scholars date its final composition to approximately 𝟭𝟲𝟳–𝟭𝟲𝟰 𝗕𝗖𝗘.

• Daniel 11 describes conflicts involving the Ptolemaic and Seleucid kingdoms with striking historical accuracy.

• Its account closely follows events leading up to the persecution under 𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗰𝗵𝘂𝘀 𝗜𝗩 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝗽𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗲𝘀.

• But its predictions about Antiochus's end do 𝗡𝗢𝗧 match what actually happened.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗢𝗜𝗡𝗧: The accuracy largely disappears where the text appears to move from 𝗛𝗜𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗬 𝗗𝗜𝗦𝗚𝗨𝗜𝗦𝗘𝗗 𝗔𝗦 𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗗𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 into genuinely uncertain future events.

𝗜𝗜. 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗢 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬 — 𝗠𝗔𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗧𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗦𝗔𝗬 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗬𝗢𝗨 𝗪𝗔𝗡𝗧

• Believers frequently interpret ancient passages through the lens of later events.

• Vague statements become supposedly specific predictions.

• Symbolic language is reinterpreted to match a desired outcome.

• Unsuccessful interpretations are revised or abandoned.

𝗘𝗫𝗔𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘: 𝗜𝗦𝗔𝗜𝗔𝗛 𝟳:𝟭𝟰

• Matthew 1:22–23 interprets Isaiah 7:14 as predicting Jesus's virgin birth.

• But Isaiah originally addresses a political crisis in eighth-century BCE Judah.

• The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age; it does not specifically require virginity.

• The Greek Septuagint uses parthenos, a word commonly understood as virgin.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗢𝗜𝗡𝗧: A later religious interpretation 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗜𝗦𝗛 that the original author predicted Jesus centuries in advance.

𝗜𝗜𝗜. 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗜𝗘𝗦 𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗡 𝗧𝗢 𝗠𝗔𝗞𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗜𝗘𝗦 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘 𝗧𝗥𝗨𝗘

• Gospel authors knew Jewish scripture.

• They frequently presented Jesus's life through the language and imagery of those scriptures.

• Some accounts may have been 𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗣𝗘𝗗, 𝗘𝗠𝗕𝗘𝗟𝗟𝗜𝗦𝗛𝗘𝗗, 𝗢𝗥 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗘𝗗 to portray Jesus as fulfilling earlier passages.

𝗘𝗫𝗔𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘: 𝗝𝗘𝗦𝗨𝗦 𝗥𝗜𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗢 𝗝𝗘𝗥𝗨𝗦𝗔𝗟𝗘𝗠

• Zechariah 9:9 describes a king arriving on a donkey.

• Matthew 21:1–7 describes Jesus's entry using a donkey and a colt.

• The parallel wording in Zechariah is Hebrew poetic parallelism, ordinarily referring to the same animal.

• Matthew's account appears to treat the parallel expressions as two animals.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗢𝗜𝗡𝗧: This is evidence of 𝗦𝗖𝗥𝗜𝗣𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗔𝗟 𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗣𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗢𝗙 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗡𝗔𝗥𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘, not independent verification of supernatural prediction.

𝗜𝗩. 𝗣𝗔𝗦𝗦𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗪𝗘𝗥𝗘𝗡'𝗧 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗡 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗜𝗘𝗦

Some supposed messianic predictions were originally about entirely different subjects.

𝗘𝗫𝗔𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘: 𝗛𝗢𝗦𝗘𝗔 𝟭𝟭:𝟭

• Hosea says: "𝗢𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗘𝗴𝘆𝗽𝘁 𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝘆 𝘀𝗼𝗻."

• The context explicitly identifies God's son as 𝗜𝗦𝗥𝗔𝗘𝗟.

• It refers backward to Israel's exodus from Egypt.

• Matthew 2:15 applies that passage to Jesus returning from Egypt.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗢𝗜𝗡𝗧: A statement about an event in Israel's past was later reinterpreted as a prediction about Jesus.

That is 𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗢𝗟𝗢𝗚𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗥𝗘𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗧𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 — 𝗡𝗢𝗧 a demonstrated prediction of the future.

𝗩. 𝗙𝗔𝗜𝗟𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗜𝗘𝗦 — 𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗗𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗗𝗜𝗗𝗡'𝗧 𝗛𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗘𝗡 𝗔𝗦 𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗖𝗥𝗜𝗕𝗘𝗗

The Bible also contains predictions whose straightforward readings conflict with subsequent history.

𝗘𝗫𝗔𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘 𝗔: 𝗘𝗭𝗘𝗞𝗜𝗘𝗟 𝟮𝟲 — 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗢𝗙 𝗧𝗬𝗥𝗘

• Ezekiel predicts that Nebuchadnezzar will attack Tyre.

• The chapter describes Tyre's destruction in sweeping terms.

• Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre, but did not completely destroy the island city.

• 𝗧𝗬𝗥𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗨𝗘𝗗 𝗧𝗢 𝗘𝗫𝗜𝗦𝗧.

𝗘𝗫𝗔𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘 𝗕: 𝗘𝗭𝗘𝗞𝗜𝗘𝗟 𝟮𝟵:𝟭𝟳–𝟮𝟬 — 𝗘𝗚𝗬𝗣𝗧

• Ezekiel acknowledges that Nebuchadnezzar's campaign against Tyre brought his army no adequate reward.

• Egypt is then promised as compensation.

• There is 𝗡𝗢 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗖𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗛𝗜𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗘 that Nebuchadnezzar devastated Egypt to the extent described in Ezekiel 29.

𝗘𝗫𝗔𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘 𝗖: 𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗞 𝟭𝟯:𝟯𝟬 — 𝗝𝗘𝗦𝗨𝗦'𝗦 𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡

Jesus declares:

"𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀 𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗹 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲."

• The discourse includes cosmic upheaval and the coming of the Son of Man.

• The generation of Jesus's contemporaries passed away.

• The full sequence did not visibly occur as a straightforward reading would suggest.

• Christian interpreters offer alternative explanations, but those interpretations are contested.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗢𝗜𝗡𝗧: When an apparent prediction fails, believers often 𝗥𝗘𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗧 𝗜𝗧𝗦 𝗠𝗘𝗔𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 instead of accepting that the prediction may have been mistaken.

𝗩𝗜. 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗙𝗨𝗟𝗙𝗜𝗟𝗟𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧 — 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗛𝗜𝗧𝗦, 𝗜𝗚𝗡𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗠𝗜𝗦𝗦𝗘𝗦

• A supposed fulfillment is celebrated.

• An apparent failure is explained away.

• Vague similarities are treated as astonishing accuracy.

• Contradictions are harmonized.

• Failed predictions become metaphors, conditional warnings, or events postponed into the future.

This is 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗙𝗜𝗥𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗕𝗜𝗔𝗦: emphasizing evidence that supports an existing belief while discounting evidence that challenges it.

𝗔 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗖𝗔𝗡 𝗕𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗧𝗢 𝗙𝗜𝗧 𝗔𝗡𝗬 𝗢𝗨𝗧𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘 𝗜𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗔 𝗥𝗘𝗟𝗜𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘 𝗧𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗢𝗙 𝗦𝗨𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗔𝗟 𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗘𝗞𝗡𝗢𝗪𝗟𝗘𝗗𝗚𝗘.

𝗩𝗜𝗜. 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗪𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗬 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗧 𝗔𝗦 𝗚𝗢𝗢𝗗 𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗘 𝗢𝗙 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬?

A genuinely compelling demonstration of supernatural prediction would require:

𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗜𝗙𝗜𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗜𝗢𝗥 𝗗𝗔𝗧𝗘: The prediction demonstrably existed before the event.

𝗦𝗣𝗘𝗖𝗜𝗙𝗜𝗖𝗜𝗧𝗬: It describes an unlikely event in precise, unambiguous terms.

𝗜𝗡𝗗𝗘𝗣𝗘𝗡𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗜𝗙𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡: The fulfillment is established without relying on a story written to match the prediction.

𝗡𝗢 𝗥𝗘𝗧𝗥𝗢𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗧𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡: Its meaning is established before the event, not reconstructed afterward.

𝗡𝗢 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚: Failures are evaluated alongside apparent successes.

𝗡𝗢 𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗥𝗬 𝗘𝗫𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡: Coincidence, reasonable forecasting, deliberate fulfillment, and retrospective writing must be seriously considered.

Even meeting these conditions would establish an 𝗨𝗡𝗨𝗦𝗨𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗬 𝗔𝗖𝗖𝗨𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗗𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡, not automatically prove that a god was responsible.

𝗩𝗜𝗜𝗜. 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗖𝗟𝗨𝗦𝗜𝗢𝗡

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗕𝗟𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗔𝗜𝗡𝗦:

• 𝗕𝗔𝗖𝗞-𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗡 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬 — History presented as though it were predicted beforehand.

• 𝗥𝗘𝗧𝗥𝗢𝗙𝗜𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬 — Earlier writings reinterpreted to match later events.

• 𝗦𝗖𝗥𝗜𝗣𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗬 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗙𝗨𝗟𝗙𝗜𝗟𝗟𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗦 — Narratives shaped to resemble earlier passages.

• 𝗙𝗔𝗜𝗟𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬 — Predictions that did not occur as a straightforward reading suggests.

• 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗧𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 — Apparent successes emphasized while failures are rationalized.

There is 𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗢𝗡𝗚 𝗛𝗜𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗟𝗜𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗥𝗬 𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗘 for these mechanisms. There is 𝗡𝗢 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗬 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗘𝗟𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗚, 𝗜𝗡𝗗𝗘𝗣𝗘𝗡𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗟𝗬 𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗜𝗙𝗜𝗘𝗗 𝗗𝗘𝗠𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 that biblical prophecy required supernatural foreknowledge.

That distinction matters: it is stronger to say 𝗡𝗢 𝗕𝗜𝗕𝗟𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗬 𝗛𝗔𝗦 𝗕𝗘𝗘𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗖𝗜𝗡𝗚𝗟𝗬 𝗗𝗘𝗠𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗧𝗢 𝗥𝗘𝗤𝗨𝗜𝗥𝗘 𝗦𝗨𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗔𝗟 𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗘𝗞𝗡𝗢𝗪𝗟𝗘𝗗𝗚𝗘 than to claim that every purported fulfillment has been conclusively disproved.

text:
As your friend and sister, I am deeply saddened by your comment below. It really pierced my heart that I can love and care for someone who can be this callous about a very painful chapter in our history. 

Samora Machel’s contribution is a matter of historical record. Under his leadership, Mozambique sheltered South African exiles and supported the ANC’s liberation struggle, enduring apartheid military raids and destabilisation. Many died from the cross border incursions of the apartheid army into Mozambique.  But many were saved by the protection Machel offered. Apartheid South Africa aligned with RENAMO, the armed militias fighting Machel's government. 

Machel worked closely with Oliver Tambo and publicly defended the liberation movement. After South African forces attacked ANC safe houses in Matola in January 1981, he continued to affirm solidarity with the oppressed people of South Africa. 17 people were killed.

There is also a global, post and anti colonial element to Machel's place in history. Machel led FRELIMO’s struggle against Portuguese colonial rule and became Mozambique’s first president at independence in 1975. He regarded Mozambique’s freedom as inseparable from the liberation of its neighbours. 

The Nkomati Accord was a tragic and painful moment that even Tambo understood.  Machel was put in a corner by the well resourced apartheid regime- in  exchange for ending support for RENAMO's military operations, apartheid SA demanded Machel restricts ANC presence in Mozambique. Basically, he had to choose between supporting the ANC or continuing the civil war in his country - which killed hundreds of thousands, caused hunger and disease. The Nkomati Accord was blackmail.

Machel and Mozambique paid a heavy price. We honour him. And your post, my friend and brother, is shameful and ignorant.
