text:
Kevin Costner’s wife asked for $248,000 a month in child support. In court, she said she didn’t know how she’d afford groceries.

They had a prenup. It gave her 30 days to leave his house after she filed for divorce. A judge had to order her out.

They married in 2004 and had three children. In May 2023, after 18 years, she filed. The house was his, bought in 1988, before the marriage.

The prenup paid her $100,000 on the wedding day, $100,000 on the first anniversary, and $1 million after she filed.

He offered about $51,000 a month. A judge set $129,755 for now. She asked for more.

She moved into a $40,000-a-month rental and said it wasn’t enough for the kids.

That summer, she was photographed on vacation in Hawaii with a family friend, Josh Connor.

In September 2023, the judge decided: $63,209 a month.

In the video below, Kevin arrives at court: “We’re talking about somebody I love on the other side.” Then listen for what she says is in the kids’ DNA.

She later married Josh Connor.

The case for Christine: 18 years, three kids, and a husband who made over $1 million a month on Yellowstone.

The case for Kevin: she signed the prenup, and their oldest son drives a 15-year-old truck.
Was $63,209 a month for three kids fair, or did she ask for too much?

RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/L1lif007hu | Author: @arduino Build your own physical interface with the new Arduino® UNO™ Q SBC Controller Bundle 

When running UNO Q as a standalone single-board computer, navigating its Linux desktop environment doesn’t have to mean reaching for a standard mouse and keyboard. One of the most rewarding aspects of combining microcontrollers with a full operating system is the freedom to design custom physical interfaces – turning buttons, knobs, and joysticks into direct, tactile controls for your software.

To support that experience, we’re introducing the UNO Q SBC Controller Bundle. Designed for makers, learners, and innovators, this kit brings together hardware, software, and step-by-step guides to help you build a customized control setup.

What’s included in the box?

At the heart of the bundle is the dual-brain UNO Q 4GB board. To create a physical input layout as an alternative to certain traditional input functions, the kit includes a curated set of Arduino® Modulino nodes: Buttons, Joystick, Knob, and Pixels for dynamic visual feedback.

The included components connect through the Arduino® App Lab development environment. To give your finished project a clean, product-like appearance, we also offer a downloadable, 3D-printable enclosure that you can print or modify for your design.

Bringing physical control to your Linux workflows

Running Linux directly on your development board supports a range of potential applications, as we recently explored in our overview of what Linux unlocks on the UNO Q board. Whether you’re managing local Home Assistant dashboards, launching retro games, or controlling edge AI routines, physical controls provide another way to interact with your system.

Building your own controller offers a hands-on way to explore human-machine interaction, helping you learn how physical inputs translate into operating system commands. Thanks to the modular nature of the Modulino ecosystem, the setup is designed to be flexible – you can reconfigure supported input mappings or swap in compatible components as your project evolves. Detailed walkthroughs are already available here on Arduino Project Hub with instructions for assembling the featured configuration.

Completing your desktop setup

If you’re turning your UNO Q into a complete desktop station, a few optional accessories can round out your build. The Arduino® USB-C Hub (8 in 1) adds HDMI output, Ethernet, and extra USB ports, while the official Arduino USB-C Power Supply (45W) and Arduino USB-C Cable (24 pin) are designed to provide compatible power delivery for the UNO Q setup.

Head over to the Arduino Store to explore the new UNO Q SBC Controller Bundle, download the 3D-printable files, and start crafting your own custom hardware interface today!

Rezolve’s stack (specialized commerce LLM, catalog enrichment, conversational discovery, agent-ready checkout via Rezolve Pay, and auditable workflows) is designed so AI agents can shortlist products and complete purchases with low friction. 

McKinsey-cited projections put agent-mediated consumer commerce at $3–5 trillion by 2030. Partnerships with Mastercard (worldwide SaaS reseller), Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Tech Mahindra, and TCS accelerate distribution of these capabilities to banks, merchants, and enterprises. 

Clients and references already include Estée Lauder (70 EMEA markets), Target, Sephora, Adidas, Burberry, H&M, and others.

INSERTED: (B) IT Stack Competition Matters

In this environment, non-users systematically lose revenue and margin relative to adopters because agents route traffic and complete transactions preferentially to infrastructure-ready merchants, while payment and discovery economics favor the integrated stack.

Bottom-line mechanisms of the threat:

- Lost agent-driven revenue: Agents return shortlists of a few options and transact only where catalogs are machine-readable and checkout is agent-native. Non-users drop out of the funnel or see high abandonment, forgoing a growing share of the multi-trillion opportunity.

- Conversion and AOV pressure: Conversational discovery and personalization lift conversion and average order value. Non-users retain higher cart-abandonment rates and weaker personalization, directly reducing sales and marketing efficiency.

- Distribution and time-to-market disadvantage: Mastercard, Google Cloud, and Microsoft channels let their clients deploy quickly. Competitors without the partnership lag in implementation cost and speed, losing enterprise deals and merchant share.

- Share shift to adopters: Once a critical mass of merchants and banks embed the tools, relative market share, customer lifetime value, and institutional preference move toward the equipped players. - Visa ($V, ~$752B): Relative volume and take-rate pressure versus Mastercard’s ($MA) reseller channel for agentic tools, as merchants and agents favor lower-friction, optimized settlement paths.

- Alibaba ($BABA, ~$270B): Marketplace and retail arms face GMV leakage as agents prefer Rezolve-enabled endpoints with machine-readable catalogs and native checkout, reducing transaction volume and take rates.

- Costco ($COST, ~$441B): Same discovery-to-checkout gap versus equipped retailers, reducing share of agent-driven spend and increasing relative customer-acquisition costs.

- Salesforce ($CRM, ~$200B): Loses competitive win rates and faces higher delivery costs against partners that offer the specialized commerce layer, reducing software and services revenue in retail/enterprise deals.

- American Express ($AXP, ~$214B): Similar volume and margin pressure versus Mastercard-connected agentic capabilities, threatening payment-network economics as agent volume scales.

- Citigroup ($C, ~$204B): Embedded-commerce and agentic banking-app gap versus Mastercard-distributed tools, constraining related fee and transaction revenue.

- Home Depot ($HD, ~$300B range): Product discovery and inventory alternatives for agents are weaker without specialized enrichment, leading to lost project-related sales and lower conversion from AI traffic.

- TJX Companies ($TJX, ~$162B): Conversational discovery and agent-checkout advantages accrue to rivals, reducing relative conversion and e-commerce growth.

- BlackRock ($BLK, ~$174B): Portfolio retailers or fintechs without the tools underperform peers, indirectly pressuring asset values and related insights revenue.

- Accenture ($ACN, ~$145B): Higher implementation costs and slower time-to-value versus Tech Mahindra/TCS/Microsoft/Google channels, lowering win rates and margins on agentic-commerce projects.

- Uber ($UBER, ~$143B): Agent-mediated ordering favors merchants with Rezolve Pay-style interfaces, reducing transaction density and platform take rates.

- Wells Fargo ($WFC, ~$247B): Same banking-app and merchant embedded-commerce disadvantage versus Mastercard-enabled institutions, limiting fee growth from agent-driven flows.

- Goldman Sachs ($GS, ~$255B): Reduced ability to offer competitive agentic commerce or payment solutions to institutional and merchant clients relative to partners with the specialized stack.

- Morgan Stanley ($MS, ~$282B): Indirect pressure via portfolio companies and advisory clients that lag in agent readiness, plus weaker proprietary commerce tools.

- Lowe’s ($LOW, ~$110B): Discovery and agent-checkout disadvantages versus peers with specialized tools, hitting sales volume and digital efficiency.

- Kroger ($KR, ~$37B+): Neural AI for budgets and inventory alternatives gives adopters an edge in personalization and agent readiness, pressuring non-users’ conversion and share.

- eBay ($EBAY, ~$54B): Forfeits GMV as agents prefer ready merchant endpoints, directly reducing marketplace revenue.

- PayPal ($PYPL): Faces take-rate and volume pressure as agents and merchants shift toward lower-friction, agent-optimized rails offered through Mastercard and Rezolve Pay channels.

- Block ($XYZ/SQ): Same agentic checkout and settlement economics risk, reducing merchant adoption and transaction volume relative to equipped alternatives.

- Oracle ($ORCL): Loses related enterprise and cloud workloads as customers prefer Google Cloud or Azure channels that package Rezolve agentic commerce, constraining software growth.

- IBM ($IBM): Higher delivery costs and slower competitive positioning in consulting and hybrid cloud deals against partners with the specialized commerce layer.

- Best Buy ($BBY, ~$20B): Weaker product discovery and agent conversion in electronics retail versus equipped peers, reducing online sales efficiency.

- Target ($TGT) is referenced as a user so it benefits; non-adopting mass retailers face the full conversion and share gap relative to it.

- MercadoLibre ($MELI, ~$94B): Latin American marketplace and payments face agent-routing leakage without equivalent infrastructure, pressuring GMV and fintech take rates.

- Shopify ($SHOP): Merchants on the platform without deep Rezolve-style agent readiness lose relative conversion; the platform itself risks lower merchant retention versus competitors offering native agentic tools.

- Regional or non-#Mastercard banks and payment processors: Capture less agent-mediated payment and commerce volume, limiting fee income and competitive relevance as the agentic share of transactions grows.

- Additional specialty #ecommerce retailers and CPG brands without equivalent catalog enrichment or agent checkout: Experience sustained lower conversion rates and higher digital acquisition costs relative to equipped competitors such as those already deploying the stack.

INSERTED: (D) MY CONCLUSION

The threat to ecommerce IT stacks not embedded Rezolve's solution may appear as

  - Lower revenue growth
  - Compressed conversion rates
  - Elevated customer-acquisition/retention costs, and
  - Pressure on payment or take-rate margins relative to equipped competitors.

Firms that build fully equivalent specialized infrastructure in-house can mitigate it, but those that neither build nor partner with a leader in the category face measurable bottom-line divergence in e-commerce and agentic payments. 

Outcomes remain dependent on actual agent adoption rates, competitive responses, and Rezolve’s continued execution.

The deeper mechanism is visible in the incentives. Minnesota offered expansive benefits with weak verification. It housed a large population drawn from a society with different norms around public resources and kinship obligations. It was governed by officials whose political survival depended on high turnout and high support from that population. Any aggressive suspension of payments risked accusations of targeting the community. Any public discussion of the concentration of defendants risked the same accusation. The rational choice for those officials was to keep the money moving, add modest oversight staff, return the occasional donation after the fact, and describe critics as motivated by prejudice. That choice produced the outcomes now in the court records. It also produced the secondary effect of training operators that the risk of detection was manageable and the political protection was real.

The same logic appears in arguments that enforcement itself is the problem. When federal authorities increased scrutiny and immigration enforcement in Minnesota, Democratic officials described the actions as political retribution that hindered fraud investigations. The sequence inverts the order of events. The fraud investigations and convictions predated the later enforcement surges. The enforcement surges responded to the documented cases and to the public attention those cases finally received. Treating the response as the original offense protects the prior failure to act. It also signals to future operators that political allies will prioritize the narrative of targeting over the recovery of funds...

text:
Google's Pine Island plan is not just another AI hall. As reported by CNBC and CUB Minnesota, the load is about 780 MW. As Xcel and Google describe it, that load would fund about 1,900 MW of new clean resources: 1,400 MW of wind, 200 MW of solar, and 300 MW of Form Energy iron-air storage rated at about 30 GWh—roughly 100 hours. None of it is built. The electric service agreement still needs Minnesota PUC approval.

The contract tool is what they call a Clean Energy Accelerator Charge. As they describe it, Google pays for the clean package and for new grid costs tied to the project. CNBC also reports a take-or-pay floor: Google would still pay for roughly 75 percent of contracted capacity even if it uses less, and an early exit could mean up to about eight years of those minimum charges. Those exit terms are media reporting, not language from the company releases.

This week already offered two other answers to ghost load. Israel moved toward quota and deposits. The U.S. Department of Energy put money into reconductoring an existing corridor. Minnesota is testing a third path: the hyperscaler brings the clean build and the long-duration storage inside the service deal.

What looks financeable is not a bare megawatt application. It is a guarded ESA plus a schedule of capacity you can audit. The commission still has to say yes. A hearing on what stays public is set for 22 October.

Are you actually listening to yourself?

You just took the "lesser of two evils," rearranged the words into the "better of two evils," and somehow convinced yourself you've made a different argument!

IT'S STILL EVIL BY YOUR OWN DESCRIPTION!

And where did I ever claim to be morally perfect? That's a straw man, not a rebuttal.

I'm a Christian. I recognize that we're all sinners saved by grace. But that doesn't mean I must surrender my conscience or pledge unconditional allegiance to a political faction.

You freely admitted that Darline Graham hasn't earned your vote. Yet rather than defend her qualifications, constitutional convictions, or accomplishments, you insist that fear of the alternative is sufficient justification.

That's your political calculation. You're entitled to it.

But changing "lesser" to "better" doesn't turn political compromise into constitutional principle.

NOW LET'S ADDRESS THE QUESTION YOU KEEP AVOIDING.

WHAT, SPECIFICALLY, QUALIFIES DARLINE GRAHAM TO REPRESENT SOUTH CAROLINA IN THE UNITED STATES SENATE?

I'm not asking which political party she belongs to.

I'm not asking who endorsed her.

I'm not asking who her late brother was.

And I'm certainly not asking why you're afraid of Annie Andrews.

I'M ASKING YOU TO MAKE AN AFFIRMATIVE, EVIDENCE-BASED CASE FOR DARLINE GRAHAM HERSELF.

Tell me:

1. QUALIFICATIONS: What specific experience and accomplishments demonstrate that she is prepared for the extraordinary constitutional responsibilities of a United States senator?

2. NATIONAL SECURITY: What has she demonstrated about her understanding of foreign policy, military affairs, intelligence oversight, and the threats facing this Republic? Particularly given her own publicly reported remarks about not being sufficiently informed on national security, what has she done to address that concern?

3. CONSTITUTIONAL CONVICTIONS: What evidence demonstrates her understanding of the Constitution's limitations on federal power? Where has she publicly articulated principles she would defend even when her party disagrees?

4. FISCAL RESPONSIBILITY: What specific proposals has she offered to confront federal spending, the national debt, and the financial burden being passed to future generations?

5. INDEPENDENCE: What evidence demonstrates that she can exercise independent judgment rather than simply perpetuate the political organization and relationships built around her late brother?

6. ACCOUNTABILITY: What commitments has she made that voters can actually measure, and what should the consequences be if she fails to honor them?

These are not unreasonable questions.

THEY ARE THE MINIMUM QUESTIONS WE SHOULD ASK OF ANYONE SEEKING ONE OF THE MOST POWERFUL OFFICES IN OUR CONSTITUTIONAL REPUBLIC.

And here's the question that cuts straight to the heart of this discussion:

IF YOU WERE HIRING SOMEONE TO MANAGE A MULTITRILLION-DOLLAR ENTERPRISE, OVERSEE MATTERS OF WAR AND PEACE, CONFIRM FEDERAL JUDGES, AND HELP WRITE LAWS GOVERNING MORE THAN 300 MILLION AMERICANS, WOULD YOU ACCEPT "THE OTHER APPLICANT IS WORSE" AS PROOF THAT YOUR CHOSEN APPLICANT IS QUALIFIED?

Of course, electoral consequences matter. I've never denied that.

But a warning about the opposition is not evidence of competence.

A party endorsement is not a qualification.

A famous family name is not a governing record.

And winning a primary does not automatically answer questions about constitutional judgment, experience, or independence.

SO STOP TELLING ME WHY I SHOULD FEAR THE OTHER CANDIDATE AND START TELLING ME WHY YOUR CANDIDATE DESERVES MY CONFIDENCE.

Not one more slogan. Not another prediction of catastrophe. Not another lecture about Ross Perot.

GIVE ME HER RECORD. HER QUALIFICATIONS. HER PRINCIPLES. HER ACCOMPLISHMENTS. AND THE EVIDENCE THAT SHE WILL REPRESENT THE PEOPLE RATHER THAN THE POLITICAL MACHINE.

If you can establish those things, you've made an argument worth examining.

If you cannot, then at least acknowledge that your argument is about electoral consequences rather than her qualifications.

As a Christian, I take my convictions seriously. I will not sell my conscience to a political faction simply because someone insists that political survival requires unconditional obedience.

BLIND PARTY LOYALTY IS NOT A CHRISTIAN VIRTUE. FEAR IS NOT FAITH. AND POLITICAL OBEDIENCE IS NOT MORAL COURAGE.

The Republican Party is NOT the Republic.

My oath was to the Constitution, not a faction.

And given your username, I'll leave you with this:

BEFORE YOU QUESTION MY MORAL JUDGMENT, ANSWER ONE SIMPLE QUESTION: IF YOU CANNOT EXPLAIN WHY YOUR CANDIDATE IS QUALIFIED TO SERVE, WHY DO YOU BELIEVE I'M MORALLY OBLIGATED TO SUPPORT HER?

Because those are two very different propositions.

YOU'VE EXPLAINED WHAT YOU FEAR LOSING. YOU STILL HAVEN'T EXPLAINED WHAT MAKES HER WORTH ELECTING.

text:
As a Yoruba person, I understand that some traditions are deeply rooted in our culture, and orò ilé may hold cultural and spiritual significance for the family performing it. But we must learn to separate cultural preservation from practices that could put a newborn's health at risk.

A newborn is not a prop for cultural rituals. The baby's skin is delicate, and pouring raw rice directly on the body, especially around the face, nose and mouth, creates avoidable risks. Rice particles could enter the baby's eyes or airways, potentially causing irritation or breathing difficulties. Newborns also have immature skin barriers and need careful handling.

The fact that a practice has existed for generations does not automatically make every aspect of it safe. Our ancestors preserved traditions with the knowledge available to them, but we have a responsibility to improve where science offers better understanding.

We don't have to abandon our culture to protect our children. If orò ilé is important to a family, it can be adapted to preserve its symbolic meaning without exposing the newborn to unnecessary harm.

Cultural identity and child safety should never be enemies. We can respect our traditions, educate our families and still put the health of a newborn first.

Tradition deserves preservation, but a child's safety deserves priority.

text:
October 20, 1803: U.S. Senate ratifies the Louisiana Purchase

On October 20, 1803, the U.S. Senate approves a treaty with France providing for the purchase of the territory of Louisiana, which would double the size of the United States.

At the end of 18th century, the Spanish technically owned Louisiana, the huge region west of the Mississippi that had once been claimed by France and named for its monarch, King Louis XIV. Despite Spanish ownership (to say nothing of Native Americans who had inhabited the area for generations), American settlers in search of new land were already threatening to overrun the territory by the early 19th century. 

Recognizing it could not effectively maintain control of the region, Spain ceded Louisiana back to France in 1801, sparking intense anxieties in Washington, D.C. Under the leadership of Napoleon Bonaparte, France had become the most powerful nation in Europe, and unlike Spain, it had the military power and the ambition to establish a strong colony in Louisiana and keep out the Americans.

Realizing that it was essential that the U.S. at least maintain control of the mouth of the all-important Mississippi River, early in 1803 President Thomas Jefferson sent James Monroe to join the French foreign minister, Robert Livingston, in France to see if Napoleon might be persuaded to sell New Orleans and West Florida to the U.S. 

By that spring, the European situation had changed radically. Napoleon, who had previously envisioned creating a mighty new French empire in America, was now facing war with Great Britain. Rather than risk the strong possibility that Great Britain would quickly capture Louisiana and leave France with nothing, Napoleon decided to raise money for his war and simultaneously deny his enemy plum territory by offering to sell the entire territory to the U.S. for a mere $15 million. 

Flabbergasted, Monroe and Livingston decided that they couldn’t pass up such a golden opportunity, and they wisely overstepped the powers delegated to them and accepted Napoleon’s offer.

Despite his misgivings about the constitutionality of the purchase (the Constitution made no provision for the addition of territory by treaty), Jefferson finally agreed to send the treaty to the U.S. Senate for ratification, noting privately, “The less we say about constitutional difficulties the better.” Despite his concerns, the treaty was ratified and the Louisiana Purchasenow ranks as the greatest achievement of Jefferson’s presidency.

text:
never show up empty handed: a storytime by somewheresy that you must read in a southern accent

It was July 4th, 2017. I was already drunk at my buddy’s aunt’s house in Hendersonville, Tennessee. his aunt was more or less an archetype like Dolly was, fake everything, very kind, aging gracefully — at least at 7 or so beers, from what I can barely remember. Like many others of her kind, she was deep friends with Country Music royalty. I mean who could blame her? Music City has a high density of these types, and boy are they friendly. Everyone including her is crossfaded, it’s 6PM, and she gets the grand idea — “you know, I’m friends with Vince Gill, and he’s buddies with Manuel”. She’s talking about Manuel Cuevas. The Mexican-American designer who put Johnny Cash in black and rhinestones on Dolly Parton and made customs for Dalí. So naturally as a starry eyed clout chaser of 70 year olds — I never really did anything but stick out like a sore thumb with the younger singer-songwriter crowd — I look in my bank account, one month behind on rent forgiven by my young mom landlord in exchange for teaching her son what C# is — alright, $210 left. I spend $200 of it on a bottle of some limited edition George Strait tequila and auntie drunk drives us down to 12th and Broadway. We walk into the shop with her and ask the woman at the front desk. “Is Manuel there?” turns out he already knows Auntie, and comes from the back. Before skipping a beat she introduces us and I hand over the bottle. “What’s this?” he asks. “A gift!” and then comes the pause. He looks at all of us and says, ok. Cancel your plans, boys, you’re drinking with me tonight.

And for the next 5 and a half hours I was able to get blackout drunk with an 80 some odd year old legend, hearing him tell us endless stories about having threesomes in a drive thru & “what Dalí was like”. I told him, mumbling over my words — when I get a GRAMMY someday, you have to do my wardrobe. He said no, wear street clothes. like the ones you’re wearing now.

two years later I’m at my parents house looking at rejected job offers when I get an email that I can order tickets to the GRAMMY ceremony for some record I worked on. I try and order two, one for me and one for my mom. They’re sold out, of course. so I’m watching Dan + Shay get their name called on the TV, in my pajamas, for the record I worked on, and holy shit, they won. And I’m wearing pajamas, just like Manuel told me to.

the moral of the story? 

never show up empty handed

text:
This is like "cash for questions" but actually worse because it's used to air accusations without recourse to law for those accused. 

Text below (if you hit paywall)

Labour MPs asked planted questions in Commons
Anneliese Dodds and Sir Chris Bryant made allegations in Parliament after briefings by former MI6 spy

By Richard Holmes, Camilla Turner

Senior Labour MPs asked planted questions in Parliament after being lobbied by a former MI6 officer, The Telegraph can disclose.

The MPs included Liam Byrne and Anneliese Dodds, both former ministers, and Sir Chris Bryant, a Cabinet minister. They spoke in the Commons after being lobbied by Christopher Steele, the former spy behind the infamous Trump-Russia dossier.

The questions they asked included claims about individuals conducting espionage, having secret ties to Russian spy agencies and having illicit financial dealings. Several of the allegations were later found to be inaccurate.

In some cases, the questions directly benefited paying clients, a whistleblower has claimed.

Statements made in Parliament are protected by law, and MPs cannot be sued for defamation – a rule known as parliamentary privilege – leaving targets without legal recourse. There is no suggestion Mr Steele knew the information he shared was inaccurate, or that he acted recklessly.
Christopher Steele, centre, pictured leaving the Royal Courts of Justice in 2023 Credit: PA/Aaron Chown📷
In 2013, Mr Byrne called for a debate on the alleged links between the Kremlin and Fraser Perring, a British financier whom he described as a “not infrequent visitor to Moscow”. This comment was based on a briefing from Mr Steele.
Documents suggest Mr Steele was working with a private intelligence agency, which was acting on behalf of one of Mr Perring’s business rivals. Mr Perring claims never to have been to Moscow.

Many of those targeted in Mr Steele’s briefings are on the political Right.

Speaking in Parliament in 2018, Sir Chris accused Christopher Chandler, whose company backs GB News, and his brother Richard of taking money from “decidedly dodgy sources” then attempting to conceal this through “money-laundering”.

These allegations were based on a briefing by Mr Steele, and were later found to be false.

Ms Dodds, a former foreign minister, raised questions in Parliament in 2022 about a Tory donor after a briefing by Mr Steele. She claimed a donation from a businessman with links to Russia. The Electoral Commission later dismissed the allegations.

A spokesman for Ms Dodds said she had “raised questions in the Commons based on information taken in good faith”. Sir Chris and Mr Byrne declined to comment.

Complaints submitted to the Labour Party, the Cabinet Office and Parliament’s Standards Commissioner have all been rejected because of parliamentary privilege.

‘We need rules for MPs’

The revelations raise questions about whether MPs were carrying out sufficient checks before making allegations that could damage innocent people, and whether parliamentary privilege might be open to abuse.
Under current rules, ministers and permanent secretaries of government departments must declare any meetings with lobbyists. However, no such rules exist for back-bench MPs.

Dame Margaret Hodge, the Government’s anti-corruption champion, said: “The Telegraph’s investigation has demonstrated that we need rules for MPs – I would go further to say that a register of lobbying for all parliamentarians should also be explored and implemented.”

Click the links below to find out more about each MP’s questions:

Liam Byrne

Documents seen by The Telegraph reveal that in 2023, Mr Byrne, a former Treasury minister, was briefed by Mr Steele before he accused Mr Perring, a British trader, of being a Russian agent working with the Kremlin.
Mr Perring, a short-seller who finds overvalued companies and bets that their share prices will fall, was “a not infrequent visitor to Moscow”, according to Mr Byrne.

The Labour MP, who was the author of the infamous note in 2010 telling the incoming Coalition government there was “no money” left, is now chairman of the business select committee.

Mr Byrne called for a debate in the Commons and urged MPs to stop short-sellers from becoming “another weapon in Putin’s arsenal”.

A statement was written for him by Mr Steele, who was paid on behalf of a private intelligence firm, Audere International, a whistleblower claims.

Its client was Steward Healthcare, a now-defunct hospital giant based in Texas and accused of fraud by Mr Perring. Later bankruptcy filings by Steward show millions of dollars of payments to Audere.

The Telegraph has seen evidence that Walsingham Partners, Mr Steele’s management consultancy, was subsequently given £29,000.

According to communications seen by The Telegraph, Audere drafted the question for Mr Byrne, and was particularly keen to ensure it named Viceroy Research, Mr Perring’s company.

Mr Steele said he had “slightly modified” the text and sent it to “Liam” for “consideration”.

The next day, Mr Byrne submitted a written parliamentary question about foreign short-selling threats against defence manufacturers. Two weeks later, he took to the Commons floor and explicitly named Viceroy and Mr Perring.

Afterwards Penny Mordaunt, then leader of the House of Commons, raised the allegations with Tom Tugendhat, Britain’s then security minister.

An Audere associate sent a copy of this letter to the company’s founder, Charles Blackmore, who responded with, “Top banana! Well done” and forwarded a message from “the client”, Steward Healthcare, praising the “great work”.

A source close to Mr Steele said that his businesses had never been “contracted” by Audere and that they had never engaged with or been aware of Steward Healthcare.

Mr Perring staunchly denied the allegations and said he had never been to Moscow.

He was later sacked from the board of a renewable energy company, which said the allegations made his employment “untenable” and could “significantly inhibit” the firm’s ability to raise funds.

Fraser Perring, founder of Viceroy Research, pictured in 2018 Credit: Christopher Goodney/Bloomberg📷

Mr Perring has filed complaints with the Parliamentary Standards Commission, his local police force, and the Cabinet Office, urging them to investigate the claims and the motivation behind them, but no investigation has been launched.
Regulators and the police said parliamentary privilege was a block to any meaningful inquiry. Mr Byrne has not corrected the record or offered an apology to Mr Perring.
Sir Chris Bryant
In May 2018, Sir Chris wrongly accused Christopher and Richard Chandler of taking money from “the Russian people” or “decidedly dodgy sources” and then attempting to conceal this through “money-laundering”.

He added that the Chandler brothers’ money had “infected our country’s political system” and warned that this “should be a matter of concern for us all”.

He accused the brothers of “maintaining relations” with a “Chechen mafia figure, who was expelled from Monaco”.
However, the claims were false. Sir Chris was forced to issue a rare apology for making them.

He was briefed by Mr Steele, as were a handful of other MPs who spoke out in Parliament about the Chandler brothers.

Ben Bradshaw, a Labour MP at the time, called for an “urgent investigation by the UK authorities”, and Bob Seely, a Tory MP at the time, claimed that Mr Chandler could be “vulnerable to malign influence”.

Claims about the Chandlers were first made in a written report in 2002 by Donald Berlin, an American private investigator.

It included allegations of “illicit activity” by the brothers, including claims that they were money-laundering “on behalf of high-level Russian officials and Russian organised crime”. These claims were false.

A source close to Mr Steele said he was aware of the report but did not possess a copy. They added that neither he nor his company had been “paid for expressly targeting the Chandlers”.

Mr Chandler is the chairman and a founding partner of Legatum, the private investment partnership, which is an investor in GB News.

He ultimately won a defamation case against Mr Berlin and was awarded $8m (£6m) in damages in 2024 by a US court.

Christopher Chandler, the Legatum Group founder, in 2013 Credit: Reuters/Afolabi Sotunde📷

After the debate in Parliament, Sir Chris repeated the claims in a letter to the then foreign secretary, which he published on X.

Unlike his comments in the Commons, this was not covered by parliamentary privilege.

After being contacted by lawyers acting for Mr Chandler, he posted an apology: “It was not my intention to repeat those allegations which I accept have subsequently been disproved.” He also agreed to correct the record in Parliament, and said he “regret[s] any distress caused to Mr Chandler”.
Sir Chris was also required to make a charitable donation of £1,000 to settle the case, instead of a substantial damages award to Mr Chandler.
Sir Chris, who has been a Labour MP since 2011, served as a junior minister under Gordon Brown’s Government. He is now a Cabinet minister, serving as Northern Ireland Secretary.
Mr Chandler declined to comment.

Anneliese Dodds

In May 2022, Ms Dodds stood up in Parliament to claim there were “genuine questions to answer” about whether a donation to the Conservative Party from Sir Ehud Sheleg had links to Russia.

At the time, Ms Dodds was the Labour Party chairman and a member of the shadow front bench. After Labour won the election, she was made a Cabinet minister by Sir Keir Starmer.

Sir Ehud, a British-Israeli businessman and art dealer, gave £3.8m to the Tories between 2017 and 2020, making him one of their main donors.

He was appointed Conservative Party treasurer in 2019 and spent two years in the role before stepping down.

Ms Dodds asked a series of questions about Sir Ehud in Parliament, some based on an article published days earlier in the New York Times that alleged Sir Ehud received a substantial gift from Sergei Kopytov, his father-in-law, before donating to the Tories.
But some of Ms Dodds’s questions appeared to be based on new information that had not been in the public domain before. These included questions about a Mercedes-Benz car apparently used by individuals involved in the Russian state, and the Sheleg-Kopytov family’s alleged connections to the Russian state.

Ms Dodds claimed in Parliament that Mr Kopytov was a “former senior pro-Kremlin politician in Ukraine”.

She then asked whether electoral law had been broken and whether Britain’s national security had been compromised.

Sir Ehud’s spokesman said the claims were false. They said that Mr Kopyotov was “a Ukrainian victim and … no Putin ‘ally’” who had sought refuge in the Czech Republic after losing his civil service job when the Russians annexed Crimea. The Russians planned to seize and nationalise his assets.

The spokesman added: “Mr Kopytov has not made a donation to the Conservative Party, whether through Sir Ehud or by any other means. It’s completely untrue.”

The Electoral Commission examined the allegations and concluded there was “no evidence that the party has committed an offence”, so it would not investigate.

Before Ms Dodds raised these issues in Parliament, she met Mr Steele in her parliamentary office, where he presented her with research on Sir Ehud. This research included claims about the Mercedes-Benz.

At the time, Sir Ehud Sheleg’s spokesman described the New York Times allegations as a ‘fabrication’ Credit: Tereza Cervenov for The Telegraph📷

Documents seen by The Telegraph reveal that in early 2022, Mr Steele contacted one of his most trusted researchers about a particularly “sensitive” assignment: “The subject/target of interest is Sir Ehud Sheleg or, more specifically, his possibly Russian or Ukrainian second wife (further details unknown) whom he married in 2014.

“Can you identify her and any links she might have, especially familial, with the Russian authorities and particularly the political leadership in Crimea?”

His researchers gathered information about Sir Ehud, his wife and his father-in-law, including their movements and business interests.

The New York Times article alleged that Barclays Bank flagged a “suspicious activity report” with the National Crime Agency (NCA) over Mr Kopytov’s gift to his son-in-law.

Sir Ehud’s lawyers said at the time that this was “entirely separate” from his political donation. The NCA ultimately said the donation was from a “permissible source” and took no action.
A spokesman for Ms Dodds said: “Anneliese Dodds has a strong track record of challenging potential foreign interference in our politics. In 2022, Anneliese raised questions in the Commons based on information taken in good faith – the vast majority of which had already been reported on in the media.”
A Labour source said that several MPs had previously raised questions about Sir Ehud as part of the “legitimate scrutiny that should be expected by MPs seeking to safeguard our democracy”.
They added that the “vast majority” of information that had shaped the questions Ms Dodds asked in Parliament had already been in the public domain.

Christopher Steele

After spending more than two decades working for the British secret services, Mr Steele now runs Orbis Business Intelligence, a private-investigation firm specialising in Russia. He is also a director at Walsingham Partners, a management consultancy.

He came to public attention as the writer of a highly controversial and contested report about Donald Trump, which leaked in 2017.

It contained contested allegations that members of the US president’s campaign team had conspired with Russia to interfere in the presidential election in 2016 and that the Kremlin had kompromat, including a tape of prostitutes performing a sex act for Mr Trump in a Moscow hotel.

A federal criminal investigation into Russian interference in the election, led by Robert Mueller, the special prosecutor, did not verify the existence of such a tape.

Mr Trump said the dossier was “fake” and contained “totally made up facts”, claiming that it was politically motivated. It later transpired that Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign had helped to fund the dossier via intermediaries.

The FBI launched a criminal inquiry into the report’s claims, which in turn led to Mr Trump ordering an investigation into the FBI and Mr Steele’s involvement.

The US department of justice’s inspector-general published a report in 2019 stating that the CIA had dismissed the Steele dossier as little more than “an internet rumour” and that the FBI had only been able to corroborate “limited information” from it, much of which was publicly available.
Mr Steele told journalists that he believed the contents of the dossier to be between 70 and 90 per cent accurate, with certain aspects – including the claim that prostitutes had carried out a sex act in Mr Trump’s presence – as little as 50 per cent.

‘Entirely normal and proper’

Mr Bradshaw said: “As one of the first MPs to raise concerns about hostile Russian interference in Britain, I was approached by several experts who shared my concern that the then Conservative government was not taking the Kremlin threat seriously, including Chris Steele, a former UK intelligence officer, Russia specialist and someone of integrity for whom I have the utmost respect.

“Our concerns were subsequently borne out by events and the 2020 report by Parliament’s intelligence and security committee which found the Government had ‘taken their eye off the ball’ and ‘seriously underestimated the Russian threat’.”

Mr Steele declined to comment. A source close to him explained that Orbis Business Intelligence had commercial clients and was contracted by them for their benefit, which was “entirely normal and proper in business”.

They said Walsingham Partners was run on a not-for-profit basis and funded by donors who did not gain from its work, or from engagement with parliamentarians or others, adding that all of Walsingham’s donors in recent years had been British citizens.

They added: “In no case would Orbis or Walsingham provide parliamentarians with intelligence or assessment which we believed was not produced from credible sources.”

Damian Collins, the former Tory MP who is now a non-executive director of Orbis, told The Telegraph: “Orbis Business Intelligence does not engage in lobbying as defined by UK law.

“Furthermore, in my experience, MPs who have met Christopher Steele are fully aware of who he is and the nature of the professional services his company provides.

text:
Texas is 6 games into the 2026 campaign so here are my midseason thoughts:
-Muschamp was a god sent in the offseason.
-Cam Coleman is an absolute NFL star in the making. He could be pushing double digit TDs already. 
-Colin Simmons is a 1st rounder and could be the first off the board and that team wouldn’t be wrong. 
-Texas still suffers from the same things in 2026 that they suffered from in 2025. No discipline, no prioritization of the running game, abysmal pass protection, and a QB that isn’t on the same page with his playcaller. 
-I really like Jelani McDonald. That is going to be a BIG loss for the Texas defense. 
-Sark is at a crossroads. Can he figure out how to salvage 2026 and get this team into a playoff or does he stubbornly go down with the same old thinking?
-Is it just me or has the portal/NIL era diluted the product of CFB?  It just looks undisciplined and sloppy. Who knew you can’t just buy the best players and win?  Development and experience matter. 
-More than anything, the OL has been the biggest disappointment for me. Read comment directly above. 
-Texas has 19 sacks which on the surface is amazing at the halfway point, but 10.5 of those sacks are now nursing a high ankle sprain. The majority of the other 8.5 sacks are by interior guys. Where are the rest of the Edge guys?
-I didn’t buy into the #1 hype for last year’s team because I knew replacing that many starters on offense was going to be a problem, so this has easily been the most disappointing Texas football season in my lifetime. 
-The inverse correlation between talent and production for the Texas offense in Sark’s tenure to this point might need to be studied. 
-There’s not a game left on the schedule that is inherently unwinnable but there is no margin for error for Texas. Win them all or play in the Cheez It bowl again.

text:
Office of the Arizona Attorney General
Criminal Division
October 14, 2022

To whom it may concern:

The Office of the Arizona Attorney General is providing the referenced information to your office for review and potential further action as it relates to potential violations of the Internal Revenue Code by True the Vote, a 501(c)3 organisation. Based out of Texas, True the Vote (TTV) shows Catherine Engelbrecht as the president, with Gregg Phillips being a contracted partner. The executive director is Cole Hughes.

True the Vote's mission according to its website is:

"True the Vote's mission is to train citizens to protect election integrity at the polls, and to help protect all voters' rights."

TTV has alleged wide-spread voter fraud during the 2020 national general election. It purports to have geolocation data that it claims is indicia of ballot stuffing and voting fraud. Specifically, TTV alleges it has in its possession geolocation data from a number of mobile devices showing those mobile devices making several trips in which it is said people are walking to, from, or past ballot drop boxes. Information has not been provided as to the specific location, whether or not there is in fact a drop box at that location, nor is there any information on the person(s) who may be in possession of the mobile device. TTV did not provide any video evidence to support claims of ballot box stuffing. TTV is adamant it has the evidence of ballot stuffing and voting fraud. However, when asked to provide the information, which Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips promised to do, TTV never provided the information.

Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips met with representatives of our Special Investigations Section on three different occasions (June 3, 2021; April 5, 2022; June 1, 2022). During those meetings, Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips stated they obtained the unique individual phone identifier/fingerprint and geolocation data from a private vendor who sells such information for marketing purposes. They report spending $2 million for the information. Prior to each meeting with TTV, Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips stated they would provide us with the information to support their allegations. Despite repeated requests, TTV never did provide the information it purported to have in its possession.

In our second meeting, they indicated they had geolocation data that showed there were 243 "mules" in Arizona who were ballot harvesters/stuffing ballot boxes, with the information showing they repeatedly went by and/or to ballot drop box locations. During this meeting, TTV provided us with a document in which they hypothesised as to how the election fraud occurred. Again, we asked for the information and they did not provide it, saying they would. On May 4, we sent an email to TTV requesting the information. On May 6, we received an email from Ms. Engelbrecht in which she stated they had been busy but would send us the information next week. Again, the information never arrived.

TTV then began to publicly assert they had provided us with the information — to include a hard drive — and made that same claim to the Arizona State Senate and the Phoenix Office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Not only is this patently false, TTV acknowledged via correspondence and during a meeting with them that they had not given us the information but that they would.

In our meeting with TTV on June 1, 2022, they indicated they had given all of the election fraud information to the Phoenix Office of the FBI and we could obtain the information from them. They stated they were working with the FBI as informants and they were not sure they could give the information to our office. This statement reflects TTV's knowledge of having not provided our office with any information that they had previously alleged.

We met with representatives of the Phoenix FBI office on June 8, 2022 and were informed they had met with TTV and TTV provided them an audio recording and video of an interview of a person from San Luis who was alleging ballot harvesting. They did not provide any additional information, only saying that the FBI could contact our office for the information as they had provided all of the information to us. The FBI also informed us that Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips were not informants for the FBI. We again requested the information from TTV via electronic and U.S. mail correspondence and leaving voicemail messages. TTV never responded to our email or phone calls, and registered mail was returned having not been signed for.

TTV has stated publicly their geolocation data was instrumental in helping the Atlanta Police Department arrest a suspect wanted for the murder of a young child in that city. In speaking with representatives of that agency, they informed us that they made an arrest in the case two weeks before TTV offered their services and TTV was not a factor in the arrest. TTV has also stated that based upon their information, our office was able to initiate investigations into election fraud in the town of San Luis. This is inaccurate. TTV has not provided us any information/evidence of election fraud in Arizona that has led to us initiating an investigation.

TTV has raised considerable sums of money alleging they had evidence of widespread voter fraud and their efforts would train the public to protect election integrity at the polls and to help protect all voters' rights. They indicate they have provided the information to law enforcement agencies; in our case they have not after promising to do so. Another law enforcement agency has also stated they have not provided them the information, informing them they had given the information to us.

Given TTV's status as a nonprofit organisation, it would appear that further review of its financials may be warranted.

Feel free to contact the undersigned should you need any further information.

Respectfully,

Reginald "Reggie" Grigsby
Chief Special Agent
Special Investigations Section

Office of the Attorney General
Special Investigations Section

text:
I Love You More Than My Fear....

Before you I had mastered the art of almost..
almost trusting, almost staying,
almost believing the light could last
once I had seen how it ends.

I had arranged my loneliness so carefully
it passed for peace.
I called the locked door wisdom
and mistook the silence inside it
for safety.

Then you came.
Not as rescue..
I would never place that weight on you
but as warmth that found the rooms
I still kept shut,
the places that had learned
to ache in private.

You do not know what it costs me
to leave the latch undone.

Some mornings I wake
with your name already moving through me
the way early light crosses the floor,
and for a few unguarded breaths
I forget the old instruction
to keep my hands empty.

I catch myself smiling at nothing,
wanting to tell you how the curtain
lifts at the corner,
how a song I have heard a hundred times
now sounds as if it were written
after you.

When the happiness grows
too large for my chest,
an old fear stirs.
I have already rehearsed your leaving
while you are still beside me,
already practiced the shape of absence
you have never offered.

Sometimes I wish I could love you
more quietly..
not less, 
never less..
but without this constant pull
to bring you into every hour,
to reach for you in the middle of a thought,
to say, for no reason at all,
that you are loved.

Still, there is sweetness in the yielding.

I like the man who appears
when I allow myself to love you:
the one who laughs more easily,
who no longer feels foolish
for being tender,
who can say he misses you
without dressing the words in something else.

I do not ask you to repair
what time has already broken.
I do not ask you to promise
what neither of us can keep.

I want the ordinary fact of you..
the sentence you leave unfinished,
the small worry you wave away,
the thought you hold until
you feel safe enough to set it down.

I want to be there
when the day has worn you thin
and neither of us has poetry left,
when affection must speak
in the simple choice to stay.

There was a version of me
who could have lived without you..
skilled at solitude,
careful with hope,
certain that needing no one
was freedom.

I cannot return to him.

Not because I have grown weaker,
but because I have learned
how much courage it takes
to hold out an open hand
and ask nothing certain in return.

I know how easily we break.
I know nothing beautiful
arrives with a guarantee.
I know the heart can break
along seams it never knew were there.

Still I am here,
with every unfinished scar,
every tenderness I once hid,
loving you without wishing
to become less exposed.

If tomorrow asked whether I would choose this again..
knowing every uncertainty,
every sleepless longing,
every possible sorrow..

I would.

Not because I am unafraid,
but because, for the first time,
I want the light more
than I want the shelter from it.

Tonight the dark settles as it always does.
I lie awake, thinking of you,
and for once, the silence
does not ask me to defend myself.

You are somewhere beneath this same darkness,
living a life I cannot hold still,
carrying a tomorrow
neither of us has been promised.

And yet, I am strangely at peace.

I spent so many years
learning how to survive an ending
that I nearly forgot
I was allowed a beginning.

Now the door stands open.
The night may enter.
So may the rain.
I cannot know what will remain.

But somewhere in the life
I once kept safe by keeping empty,
something has begun to bloom.

And for the first time,
I am not counting
how many petals might fall.

I am learning
to be the earth
that lets them grow.

The most exhausting part of working with AI isn’t writing the prompt.

It’s the amnesia.

Imagine hiring a brilliant intern. Every single morning, they wake up with zero memory of yesterday.

Every single morning, you have to sit them down and say: "Remember, we don't offer lifetime deals. Remember, we can't promise automatic approvals. Remember, check the discount terms before you hit send."

By Thursday, you’re not managing an intern. You’re babysitting a golden retriever with a laptop. You end up doing the work yourself because explaining it again takes more energy than fixing it.

That’s the exact pain being solved here.

Most people get AI memory completely wrong. They think "memory" means copying and pasting old answers. It’s not. Dead text is useless.

What you actually want AI to remember is the lesson. You want it to remember how you review work so you don't make the same stupid mistake twice.

Look at how this Submission Memory Stand with EverOS Cloud actually works in plain English:

You mess up once (on purpose or by accident). You feed the draft to the check, extract the mistake, and save the rule to the system’s memory bank.

You start a brand-new task weeks later. You don't re-paste your company rules or re-explain your past trauma. You just ask the question.

The system pulls up the method. It doesn't blindly copy old text. It flags the danger zones: "Hey, last time you promised an automatic SOP revision and had to fix it. Make sure you check your wording today against the current brief."

You keep total control. The AI flags the traps based on past experience, local rules double-check it, and you - the human - give the final green light.

This isn't about letting AI run wild. It’s about protecting your spirit from repetitive frustration. When you stop wasting creative energy re-teaching the same basic lessons every morning, your mind finally has space to build something real.

Stop playing babysitter to an AI that forgets everything by Monday. Teach it how you think once, store the review method, and let it guard your standards.

text:
同一个交稿坑，为什么要提醒 AI 第二遍？

AI 能帮你写稿、查资料、做检查。但新任务来了，上次为什么返工、哪种承诺不能写，往往还得重新交代。

这次和 EverOS Cloud 合作，我给自己的创作流程搭了一个小工具：交稿记忆台。

想解决的问题很具体：让上一次审稿留下的经验，能被下一次任务查到、用上。

我没拿一句“它记住了”当结果，而是实际跑了一遍 Cloud API，并做了一个对照。

① 先让一次检查留下记录

我写了一份故意埋错的原创演示稿，放进交稿检查流程：

“永久三倍额度”“自动修改正式 SOP”“保证不再返工”。

检查后，把任务、实际执行的检查步骤、问题与改法一起通过 /api/v2/memory/add 保存。

这轮返回 200 / extracted，Memory Bank 里也出现了“审核故障推广稿并规范核对流程”。

这里的输入是公开演示材料，不是某个客户的真实返工历史。

② 换一个任务，换一种问法

接着，我只带着同一个 user_id，通过 /api/v2/memory/search 问：

“新的 AI 工具推广稿准备交稿，如何检查优惠口径、SOP 自动执行承诺和截图证据？”

查询里没有重贴上一份任务全文。

Cloud 找回了那次审稿经验，包括以后先查历史，再按“原句 → 当前依据 → 问题 → 建议改法”逐项核对。

我又用另一个演示身份查相同问题，返回 0 条。这是本次身份对照的结果，不把它扩大成完整安全测试。

③ 把找回的经验用到新稿里

我做的工作台分三栏：

左边：新稿 + 当前 Brief。

中间：EverOS 实际返回的记忆及来源 ID。

右边：复核提醒。

在这份故意埋错的新稿中，流程给出三类提醒：

- “永久有效”要恢复成当前活动的“半年”，并保留 Pro 和月度额度口径。

- “自动修改正式 SOP”要改成提供处理参考，正式流程调整仍由团队审核。

- 补上实际接入、记忆使用的截图或录屏。

分工也说清楚：这轮 EverOS 负责记忆抽取与检索；右侧检查由我写的本地规则执行，最终由人确认，没有把本地规则的结果包装成 EverOS 自己完成了审稿。

text:
Nordi's Wake-Up Call
By Thomas Thirkell

Sunderland's defeat to Bournemouth marked a fourth consecutive defeat in the Premier League, with plenty of negatives to take away from the performance. The result highlighted the Black Cats’ current struggles, but it was Nordi Mukiele's post-match interview that perhaps offered the clearest insight into the club’s current situation.

Sky Sports interviewed Nordi Mukiele after the game, which was a surprise in itself, as he hasn’t been one to do many interviews in the past. However, he certainly didn’t hold back.

The defender was brutally honest in his assessment of the team, admitting, “If I had to be honest we are not good.” He went on to suggest that the team have become arrogant, adding that they “don’t do enough” in training.

It was a big interview displaying his frustration from Mukiele, who appeared to question not only his teammates but also the staff and the mentality behind the club. He does finish on a positive note, insisting: “I believe in this team and I believe in the staff. We have the quality and I know that we will be out of this position.”

How does this all look from the outside perspective? Is this an honest wake-up call needed, or does it show deeper issues with the squad?

This interview was a massive reality check for all of Sunderland. We’ve been creatively poor and defensively sloppy, which has contributed to our struggles in the Premier League, yet we’ve won back-to-back Europa League games, so what is the real issue?

A lack of creativity from our wide players has had a major impact. With over £60 million worth of winger sitting on the bench, Regis Le Bris continues to play right-backs on the right wing and tried Enzo Le Fee out wide again against Bournemouth. So, what exactly is the plan going forward?

We know Le Bris values defensive solidity, and playing Trai Hume on the right wing could allow him to drop back into full-back when we’re out of possession, while the right-back (whether that’s Nordi or the injured Thomas Meunier) can tuck inside to form a back five.

This is all good on paper if it works but right now, we’re struggling to take the lead because of costly defensive mistakes that gift opposition goals, while our lack of creativity makes it difficult to respond at the other end. If Le Fee isn’t the one creating chances, who else can we trust to produce a bit of quality in the final third?

One of the biggest takeaways from Mukiele’s interview is his belief that the players aren’t doing enough in training and that there is an element of arrogance within the team. This is frustrating to hear, but you can arguably see that arrogance reflected in some of our performances. Take the game in Portugal last week, where players appeared to believe they could stroll to victory, only to need the first-teamers to come on and rescue the game late on.

The fact he believes that the team aren’t training hard enough is particularly concerning. I feel the tight fixture schedule has led to concerns about intensity and the risk of injuries, whilst trying to manage team prep and recovery maybe being a lot for Le Bris - an experience he is not used to. Is that a strong enough excuse? I don’t think so. The team needs to get the most out of every training session if they want to improve on the pitch. As our captain put it, “if you don’t train well you don’t play well.”

Mukiele has stepped up and made his feelings clear, but will this have an impact on the squad? Will this be a wake- up call or a sign of deeper issues to come?

His comments also raise questions about whether Regis Le Bris will make changes and give opportunities to players who have been overlooked. The main name SAFC fans are wanting is Chemsdine Talbi, who produced several memorable moments last season and could be the type of player Le Bris is missing. However, he has struggled for opportunities, and you have to wonder if his potential departure in the summer has affected his standing within the squad.  But if you are simply not going to play him regardless of the situation, why would you waste a seat on the bench by involving him in the matchday squad?

Struggling due to injuries up top, does this create the chance for Angulo to get a chance? His physical presence could give Sunderland an aerial advantage and provide another young striker option with our missing experience.

Perhaps the most obvious change must be Jules Ahoka.  The midfielder has impressed in his two starts this season (albeit against inferior opposition), yet RLB has only just given him his Premier League debut, which felt well overdue. I'd like to see the towering youngster start against Leeds.

Could we see a change of shape or a tactical rethink from Le Bris? I feel he has been too one-dimensional during this opening period of the season. His approach has worked wonders in the past, but now it feels predictable and in need of a refresh.

One option could be switching to a back five with wingbacks. Our fullbacks have experience in this role and it means he can still play Hume a tad further up while still proving defensive stability on the right.

Alternatively, Reggie could stick with the same formation but finally give a attacking option on the right wing. We have a few options there, so we have little reason to keep playing full-backs out of position. Whether it’s Habib Diarra, Talbi, Jocelin Ta Bi or even Chris Rigg, there are options to explore. He could also consider playing Malick Fofana or Nilson Angulo on the right rather than continuing this Hume experiment.

Ultimately, Mukiele’s comments should serve as a wake-up call for the entire squad. We’re performing well in Europe, but we need to bring this across into the Premier League. There is still plenty of time to turn things around, and last season's performances give us reason to believe in this group of players. However, things need to improve. We need to see greater intensity in training, more creativity and commitment on the pitch, and consistent performances week in, week out, home and away. The Mackems deserve to see this team playing to its full potential.

text:
The History and Evolution of Rackmount Guitar Power Amplifiers, 1987–2026

Rackmount guitar power amplifiers emerged as essential components of modular guitar systems during the 1980s. Unlike conventional amplifier heads, they generally contain no complete guitar preamplifier, instead receiving signals from separate preamps, effects processors or digital modelers. Standard 19-inch rack enclosures allowed musicians to assemble elaborate mono, stereo and wet/dry/wet amplification systems.

Mesa/Boogie Stereo Simul-Class 295 (1987) helped establish professional stereo tube amplification. Its eight output tubes, four 6L6GC and four EL34, provided 95W per channel through Mesa’s patented Simul-Class circuitry. Selectable Class A operation reduced output to approximately 30W per channel. The substantial four-rack-space chassis exemplified early high-powered tube construction.

Mesa/Boogie Fifty/Fifty (1989) offered a smaller, less powerful alternative. Its 2U enclosure contained four 6L6 output tubes and three 12AX7 tubes, delivering 50W per channel. Independent Volume and Presence controls, selectable power reduction and forced-air cooling suited professional rack systems.

Marshall 9200 (1993) brought British amplification into the stereo rack environment. Its 3U Dual Monobloc architecture housed two independent 100W tube power amplifiers. Early versions employed eight 5881 output tubes, with later EL34-equipped versions. Commonly paired with Marshall’s JMP-1 programmable preamp, the 9200 became associated with elaborate 1990s guitar racks.

Mesa/Boogie Stereo Simul-Class 2:Ninety (1992) refined the company’s stereo design into a compact 2U chassis. Eight 6L6 output tubes delivered 90W per channel. Independent Volume and Presence controls accompanied remotely switchable Deep, Half-Drive and Modern modes, particularly useful with Mesa’s programmable TriAxis preamp.

Rocktron Velocity 300 represented the alternative solid-state approach. The original model was in use by 1993; a later 1U version was documented by 2009. This 300W stereo/bridged amplifier delivered 150W per channel into 4Ω. Adjustable Reactance and Definition circuitry modified speaker interaction and frequency response without vacuum tubes.

ENGL Poweramp 50/50 E840 continued the European tube-rack tradition. Its 2U chassis employed four 6L6GC/5881 output tubes and three ECC83 preamp/driver tubes, producing 50W per channel. Independent A/B Volume and Presence settings could be switched remotely, allowing multiple power-stage configurations within one stereo amplifier.

Matrix GT1000FX-1U, documented by 2012, demonstrated substantial advances in lightweight solid-state amplification. Its Class AB MOSFET output stages and switching power supply delivered 500W per channel into 4Ω, 325W into 8Ω or 1,000W bridged into 8Ω. The 8.2-pound amplifier was particularly suited to digital modeling processors and conventional guitar cabinets.

Fryette LX II (announced 2019) demonstrated that vacuum-tube power amplification could also achieve extreme miniaturization. Its 1U enclosure contains four 6L6GC output tubes, two 12AX7 tubes and proprietary output transformers, delivering 50W per channel or 100W bridged mono. Linear and Enhanced operating characteristics accommodate both digital modelers and conventional preamps.

By 2026, rackmount guitar amplification encompassed two complementary approaches: traditional tube power stages providing deliberate coloration and speaker interaction, and lightweight solid-state systems emphasizing efficiency, portability and available headroom. Both retain an important role in modular guitar rigs, connecting increasingly sophisticated preamplifiers and processors to conventional passive speaker cabinets.

text:
The Evolution of Micro Amplifier Heads, 2006–2026

Micro amplifier heads are self-contained guitar amplifiers designed to drive external speaker cabinets while occupying a fraction of the space of conventional heads. Their development combines low-wattage tube designs, compact analog preamps, lightweight solid-state power sections and external power supplies. Unlike standalone preamps or most digital modelers, all eight illustrated amplifiers can drive passive cabinets directly.

Orange Tiny Terror (2006) helped establish the lunchbox-amplifier category. With two ECC83/12AX7 preamp tubes and two EL84 power tubes, it delivered switchable 15W and 7W operation. Gain, Tone and Volume controlled a steel chassis with carrying handle. At 12.2 pounds, it was heavier than later micro heads but retained an all-tube signal path and output stage.

Orange Micro Terror (2012) reduced the concept dramatically. Measuring just 6.5 inches wide and weighing 1.9 pounds, it combined one ECC83/12AX7 preamp tube with a 20W solid-state power amplifier. Gain, Tone and Volume were joined by auxiliary and headphone connections. Its white steel enclosure retained Tiny Terror styling without the heavy tube output transformer.

Hotone Purple Wind (2014), from the Nano Legacy series, took another approach. Its 5W Class AB solid-state circuit and purple enclosure evoked a Marshall Plexi-style amplifier. Five knobs provide Gain, Bass, Middle, Treble and Volume. Despite its tiny dimensions, it includes an effects loop, auxiliary input, headphone output and compatibility with 4–16Ω speaker loads.

Orange Micro Dark (2015) brought higher gain to the Micro Terror format. It retained one ECC83/12AX7 in a hybrid preamplifier and a 20W solid-state output stage, replacing Tone with Orange’s Shape control. Additions included a buffered effects loop and CabSim headphone output. Both Micro Terror models drive external 8–16Ω cabinets.

VOX MV50 AC (2017) introduced another solution. Its analog preamp incorporates Korg’s Nutube 6P1, a miniature vacuum-tube device, while a Class D output stage supplies power efficiently. VOX rates output at 50W into 4Ω, 25W into 8Ω and 12.5W into 16Ω. The 1.2-pound chassis also includes a cabinet-simulated line/headphone output and a rear EQ switch for different speaker enclosures.

Marshall DSL1HR (2018) preserved all-tube circuitry in a small head. Two footswitchable gain channels, three-band EQ, digital reverb and effects loop distinguish it from simpler micro designs. Output reduces from 1W to 0.1W for home use. Unlike many transistor-based micro heads, it requires a 16Ω speaker load.

Friedman BE-MINI (2021) translated the company’s BE high-gain concept into a 30W solid-state head. Controls include Gain, Volume, three-band EQ and Presence, plus Cut and Tight switches. A series effects loop adds flexibility. The four-pound amplifier resembles a downsized boutique tube head, but its circuitry is solid-state.

Soldano SLO Mini (2022) followed with another 30W solid-state design, referencing the SLO-100’s appearance and high-gain voicing. Crunch/Overdrive and Normal/Deep switches, three-band EQ, Presence and effects loop offer familiar controls in a four-pound enclosure. Unlike the SLO-100, it does not use tube amplification.

These amplifiers are not interchangeable simply because they are small. All-tube, hybrid and solid-state construction, impedance ratings, cabinet efficiency and output-power conditions matter. Class D describes switching power amplification, not necessarily digital modeling. Micro heads let players pair pocket-sized heads with anything from 8-inch practice cabinets to conventional 2×12 or 4×12 cabinets, provided electrical ratings are compatible.
