This week the Guardian published a long read (below) by American historian Brian Goodman, first printed in The Drift. Anyone who thinks the defeat of Viktor Orbán ended the Hungarian threat to British politics should read it.

Goodman spent months in Budapest blending in at the Danube Institute, the state-funded think tank that became the meeting place for what calls itself the “postliberal” right. He was there before and after Orbán’s fall. His account is vivid, sometimes funny, and in places unsettling.

I want to set out what he found, and then explain why I think it should worry anyone watching Reform UK and Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain.

Goodman’s account first. The Danube Institute was founded in 2013 with state money redirected by Orbán’s government. It became the hub of a loose transatlantic movement of conservative intellectuals who share one premise: liberalism has failed, and it failed because it was true to itself.

The roster Goodman describes includes Rod Dreher, who arranged Tucker Carlson’s fawning week of coverage in Hungary in 2021; Patrick Deneen, whose ‘Why Liberalism Failed’ is the movement’s founding text; Christopher Rufo; Yoram Hazony; Sohrab Ahmari; Gladden Pappin, an American who ended up running a Hungarian state institute; and the Irish economist Philip Pilkington.

Goodman notes that the Danube Institute and the Heritage Foundation set up a formal collaboration in March 2023, a month before #Project2025 was published. He also reports that at a Danube event this February, Heritage’s Paul McCarthy claimed 75% of Project 2025 was being implemented.

To these men, Goodman writes, Orbán’s Hungary looked like a dream come true. It had “zero migration”, huge state spending on traditional families (around 5% of GDP a year), industrial nationalism and cheap Russian energy.

Deneen’s 2023 book went further and called for a cadre of elites to act as “class traitors”, directing popular resentments to overthrow a liberal ruling class while leaving the outward forms of democracy in place. His example was Hungary.

Then the model met reality. Goodman reports that by 2026, inflation and house prices in Hungary had risen faster than anywhere else in the EU. Industrial policy had not delivered growth, and an electric vehicle battery plant had caused a major pollution scandal.

Migration had been halted on paper, yet Chinese guest workers came in to fill the new car factory jobs. The fertility rate rose a little and then flattened. Corruption, he writes, was so widespread that Hungary was widely called a mafia state.

As polling day approached, Fidesz kept lowering the number of children a mother needed to escape income tax for life, from four to three to two. It made no difference.

On 12 April turnout reached a record of nearly 80%, and Péter Magyar’s Tisza party won a landslide. By the summer, Goodman records, the new parliament had dismantled the patronage system funding the Danube Institute and the Mathias Corvinus Collegium (MCC), and Pappin had resigned. The Dutch activist Eva Vlaardingerbroek summed up the mood on her side: “the last bastion is gone”.

Goodman does not let liberals off lightly either. He criticises Anne Applebaum’s tendency to divide the world into democracies and autocracies, and he points out that Orbán conceded within hours. But he also records how the postliberals responded. Dreher used the concession as proof that Orbán had never been a dictator. Goodman rejects this, listing the rewritten constitution, the loyalist judges, the gerrymandered districts, the election laws rigged to inflate majorities, the captured universities and the media sold to friendly oligarchs.

Pilkington took a different line: “we are all postliberals now”. Magyar, he argued, had won on Fidesz’s own platform of low migration, cultural nationalism and generous family support, and the ideas were “in the ether”.

I don’t want to misrepresent Goodman (the long read is below) but his verdict appears to be that postliberal policy could not produce a life good enough to win votes, that Hungary was a false model, and that the model to worry about now is made in America.

Now my view. Goodman’s inside account, of a small cadre close to power promoting a model that failed, fits the argument I have been making for several years.

I see the Danube Institute and the wider Orbán-funded ecosystem around it less as independent think tanks than as a soft-power operation. They are a way of exporting a style of governance built on national-sovereignty rhetoric, family values used as a political weapon, hostility to Brussels and “foreign interference”, control of the media and steady attacks on independent institutions. Sound familiar?

The funding was always the giveaway. The Danube Institute was financed through the Batthyány Lajos Foundation, which drew heavily on Hungarian public money, and it was led by John O’Sullivan, once Margaret Thatcher’s speechwriter. It paid fellows and hosted a steady flow of British conservatives.

That British traffic is what I have tried to map over several years of tweets and Twitter-threads. In December 2019 Tim Montgomerie, appointed Boris Johnson’s social justice adviser that September, spoke at a Danube Institute event in Budapest, sharing the panel with O’Sullivan. As BuzzFeed News reported at the time, he told the audience that Budapest had been home to “interesting early thinking on the limits of liberalism”, that the same was happening in the UK, and that he hoped for a “special relationship” with Hungary after Brexit.

At a panel at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences that month, he placed Fidesz, Trump, Scott Morrison and Johnson in the same movement towards what he called “cultural and economic solidarity”, and asked why people were voting for “Boris and Viktor and Nigel and Donald”. A fortnight later he wrote that Hungarian family policy was “worthy of close study”.

Montgomerie later defected from the Conservatives to Reform. He was suspended in August 2026 after publicly criticising senior figures, including Zia Yusuf, and resigned in September, though he says he still wants to support the party.

The year before Montgomerie’s speech, in 2018, Andrew Neil chaired a Spectator-hosted event at the Hungarian embassy in London presenting #Project28 polling research by the Századvég Foundation, a Fidesz-aligned think tank. Douglas Murray, Henry Newman and David Goodhart took part. Neil has not mentioned Orbán on X/Twitter since September 11th, 2024. GB News, Tufton Street think tanks (including Peter Whittle’s New Culture Forum) have all brushed against the same network.

Reform UK’s links are closer and more structural than any of those. Nigel Farage described Orbán in 2018 as Europe’s strongest leader and the EU’s biggest nightmare.

James Orr is UK chair of the Edmund Burke Foundation, which runs the National Conservatism conferences, and he appeared at CPAC Hungary in March 2026. That is the same event Goodman watched from behind a banner. After serving as a senior adviser to Nigel Farage from around October 2025, Orr stepped down as Reform Head of Policy on 4th September following a Channel 4 News undercover exposé. The footage showed him and aide Dan Jukes discussing arrangements for an apparent American donor to fund polls for the party in a way that raised questions under UK rules banning foreign political donations.

The Spectator itself, now owned by Pual Marshall, who also owns UnHerd and co-owns GB News, which employs Farage as a presenter, suggested last year that post-liberalism was perhaps the best single label for the various strands of thinking inside Reform. Matthew Goodwin, who stood for Reform in Gorton and Denton, has joined Farage and Orr in praising Orbán.

The overlap with the Free Speech Union deserves particular attention. @BylineTimes has reported that Orr secured Peter Thiel’s backing when he co-founded the FSU with Toby Young, and Orr sits on the FSU’s Advisory Council today. 

Orr is also a trustee of the Roger Scruton Legacy Foundation, which drew more than 90% of its funding from MCC. Douglas Murray and Nigel Biggar, whom Byline Times describes as FSU directors, sit on that foundation’s advisory board. Goodwin, also on the FSU’s Advisory Council, was an MCC visiting fellow, a role reported to pay between €5,000 and €10,000 a month; Reform has denied the top figure but not said what he was paid.

Several other members of the FSU’s Advisory Council, including Claire Fox, David Goodhart, Eric Kaufmann and David Starkey, have spoken at #NatCon.

The Spiked strand runs through the same territory. Frank Furedi, who ran MCC Brussels until the Hungarian money stopped, is also an FSU member, and his team has since relaunched as FSI Europe, with funding that DeSmog says is far from clear. Toby Young spoke at MCC’s Centre for Journalism in 2025. 

I’m not suggesting the FSU itself was funded by Budapest; I’ve seen no evidence that it was. My point is that some of the loudest British voices warning of censorship and threats to free speech found a comfortable home in a system that, by Goodman’s own account, handed its media to friendly oligarchs and packed its universities with party loyalists.

This is why I keep making the same point: the infrastructure outlives the election. Goodman’s article confirms it from the inside. Pappin told him there were “only like five” of them in Budapest. Deneen’s book explains why five might be enough: a small elite cadre, close to power and skilled at stirring resentment, can achieve a great deal. That is the role Reform’s intellectual wing is auditioning for in Britain. Farage supplies the popular power, and the NatCon and Budapest alumni supply the programme.

What follows on Restore Britain is my own extension of the argument, not something Goodman’s article addresses. I’ve found no Hungarian money behind Rupert Lowe’s party, and I am not claiming any. Instead, what it shows is where these ideas go once the restraint of governing is removed.

Restore is pledging to scrap the asylum system altogether and to reverse mass immigration entirely, and it openly talks about stripping citizenship from some legal immigrants. Vlaardingerbroek, who mourned Orbán’s fall as the loss of the last bastion, wore a “Generation Remigration” T-shirt on the stage of Tommy Robinson’s Unite the Kingdom rally before the Home Office withdrew her travel authorisation.

Even Montgomerie, on leaving Reform in September, warned that the party needed to be less like Germany’s AfD, whose “remigration” plan is widely understood to mean mass deportations. Orbán built a sovereigntist state and kept some form of electoral politics. The British fringe that admired him now talks openly of remigration. The rhetoric shifted right while the Hungarian model was failing.

So what might we learn?

First, the Orbán model failed on its own terms.

Reform cannot keep presenting Hungary as proof that a nationalist family-and-borders state delivers, when, as Goodman details, it delivered the EU’s fastest-rising inflation and house prices, a reputation for corruption, and imported labour by the back door. That’s a better argument with sceptical voters than any amount of name-calling.

Second, the tools Fidesz used to stay in power, media capture above all, were central to the project rather than incidental to it.

In a country where politicians present news programmes on a channel owned by a hedge-fund billionaire, that deserves far more attention than it gets. 

Third, and most uncomfortably, Pilkington may be partly right.

Magyar won by keeping much of Orbán’s migration and family offer and running against corruption and incompetence. If Britain’s mainstream parties adopt Reform’s framing in the hope of neutralising it, they may beat Farage at the ballot box and still lose the argument.

Hungarians showed that a tilted system can still be tipped back. The lesson for Britain is to watch the network as well as the party.

The Danube Institute may be closing, but its ideas, its alumni, and its British friends all remain.

OUT TODAY!
The Complete Kubrick [4K UHD] - Tom Cruise, Nicole Kidman, Jack Nicholson, Kirk Douglas, Peter Sellers, Laurence Olivier, James Mason, George C. Scott, Sterling Hayden, Malcolm McDowell, Ryan O’Neal, Shelley Duvall @Criterion
US: https://t.co/CI66YeTzTb
CAN: https://t.co/4WF4JDzSGw
OUR REVIEW:
https://t.co/1UwunVfIOh
Killer’s Kiss (1955) / The Killing (1956) / Paths of Glory (1957) / Spartacus (1960) / Lolita (1962) / Dr. Strangelove, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964) / 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) / A Clockwork Orange (1971) / Barry Lyndon (1975) / The Shining (1980) / Full Metal Jacket (1987) / Eyes Wide Shut (1999) Criterion
The Masters:

All features are presented in Dolby Vision HDR on the 4K UHD discs and in SDR on the Blu-rays. Criterion’s “About the Masters” notes show that nearly every title was restored from its original camera negative, though the restorations come from a mix of sources. Some are Criterion’s own, some are carried over from studio restorations of recent years, and some were done by partner archives.

The three independently produced early features had their 4K debuts on Kino Lorber UHDs, but here they are presented in masters made for Criterion by Duplitech. Killer’s Kiss (1.37:1) comes from the 35mm original camera negative, with a composite fine-grain used for some sections. The Killing and Paths of Glory (both 1.66:1) are also drawn from their camera negatives. The Paths of Glory mono was remastered at 24-bit from UCLA archivist Robert Gitt’s 35mm magnetic track. Fear and Desire (1.37:1) is the exception: it is Kino Lorber’s 4K restoration, made from the camera negative and a Library of Congress fine-grain. The three shorts are new Criterion 4K restorations from Library of Congress elements. These were 35mm prints and a duplicate negative for Day of the Fight and Flying Padre, and the 16mm original reversal for The Seafarers.

The studio-era films largely use existing restorations. Spartacus (2.20:1) is Universal’s 4K restoration from a 6K scan of the original Technirama elements, with Robert A. Harris consulting, and its 7.1 track was remastered from the 70mm six-track printmaster. Dr. Strangelove (1.66:1) is Sony’s 4K restoration, supervised by Grover Crisp and assembled from a fine-grain master, a duplicate negative and a 35mm print. 2001: A Space Odyssey (2.20:1) is Warner’s 4K from an 8K scan of the 65mm camera negative, supervised by Ned Price and Leon Vitali with input from Christopher Nolan and Hoyte van Hoytema. Its original 70mm six-track 5.1 mix is joined by the 35mm general-release mono, which Kubrick mixed without the overture, intermission and exit music, so those passages are silent on that track. A Clockwork Orange (1.66:1), The Shining (1.85:1) and Full Metal Jacket (1.85:1) are Warner 4K restorations from their camera negatives, with Full Metal Jacket graded against both an answer print and Kubrick’s own personal 35mm reference print.

Barry Lyndon and Eyes Wide Shut match Criterion’s own recent 4K editions. Barry Lyndon is framed at 1.66:1 per Kubrick’s December 8th, 1975 letter to projectionists, and was graded against Vitali’s 2000 HD transfer. Eyes Wide Shut (1.85:1) is presented in its international cut, supervised and approved by cinematographer Larry Smith. Its look stems from Kubrick’s deliberate decision to have the negative force-developed by two stops, which accounts for the film’s distinctive grain and glowing low-light palette.

Two presentations are new to 4K UHD. Lolita (1.66:1) is a new 4K restoration from the 35mm original camera negative, using a Warner 35mm print as color reference, with its mono remastered from the original DME magnetic track. Kubrick’s international version of The Shining (119 minutes, against 144 for the U.S. theatrical) comes from the same Warner restoration of the camera negative, with its own mono track remastered from the original magnetic elements.

Since most of these masters have been reviewed before on DVDBeaver, we have used our existing captures from those earlier 4K UHD releases where applicable. New captures will eventually be taken for Lolita and the international version of The Shining. 

Audio:

Criterion’s audio approach across the set is admirably purist. Every film is offered with its original soundtrack, and for the mono-era titles that means uncompressed linear PCM mono remastered from the original magnetic elements. Paths of Glory’s was remastered at 24-bit from UCLA archivist Robert Gitt’s 35mm track. For Dr. Strangelove, A Clockwork Orange, Barry Lyndon, both versions of The Shining and Full Metal Jacket, Criterion also includes alternate 5.1 DTS-HD Master Audio remixes, so purists and surround enthusiasts are both served. The early independent features and Lolita are presented in their original mono alone. This is a notable step up from earlier editions. Warner’s 4K UHD of The Shining offered only a 5.1 remix with no mono at all, its Full Metal Jacket UHD relegated the mono to a lossy track, and Sony’s Dr. Strangelove UHD carried only 16-bit lossless tracks. The three large-format productions get special treatment. Spartacus is presented in 7.1 DTS-HD MA remastered from its 70mm six-track printmaster, and it retains the overture, entr’acte and intermission music. 2001: A Space Odyssey is the most generous of all, with its original 70mm six-track theatrical mix in 5.1, an alternate 5.1 remix and the original 35mm general-release mono, which, true to Kubrick’s own 35mm prints, is silent during the overture, intermission and exit music. Eyes Wide Shut is presented in its original theatrical 5.1, remastered from the 35mm magnetic track. Optional English (SDH) subtitles are offered on every feature, and the set is region free. From the portions we have sampled so far, the tracks sound exceptional, clean and faithful to their sources, with the dynamic range of the scores and Kubrick’s carefully chosen music coming through with clarity and weight.

About the Captures

Because of the size of this set and its release date, none of the screen captures in this review are taken from The Complete Kubrick discs. Instead, we have included a single capture per film from our earlier reviews, taken from previous 4K UHD editions or, where none exist, Blu-ray. Several of those editions share their restoration with this set, while others come from different transfers. The captures should therefore be taken as representative of each film’s presentation, not as exact reproductions of the Criterion discs.

Fear and Desire is represented by Kino’s 2024 4K UHD, which uses the same Kino Lorber restoration found in this set. Killer’s Kiss and The Killing come from Kino’s 2022 4K UHDs, and Paths of Glory from the 2024 Masters of Cinema (Eureka) 4K UHD. All three of those earlier discs were scanned from the original camera negatives, but Criterion presents new Duplitech masters here, so the grading and framing may differ.

Spartacus is from Universal’s 2020 4K UHD, which uses the same 2015 restoration from the large-format Technirama elements. Dr. Strangelove is from Sony’s 2021 4K UHD, drawn from the same Sony restoration. 2001: A Space Odyssey comes from Warner’s 2018 4K UHD. The Shining and Full Metal Jacket come from Warner’s 2019 and 2020 4K UHDs respectively. Our Shining capture is from the U.S. theatrical version and serves for both cuts, which share the same restoration in this set. Note that both of those Warner discs were framed at 1.78:1, whereas Criterion presents both films at 1.85:1. Barry Lyndon is from Criterion’s own 2025 4K UHD, which matches the restoration in this set.

For Eyes Wide Shut, our capture is from Criterion’s 2025 Blu-ray of the same Larry Smith–approved restoration, as we were unable to capture from that 4K UHD disc at the time. Lolita and A Clockwork Orange are represented by Warner’s 2011 Blu-rays (the latter its 40th Anniversary Edition). Lolita receives a new 4K restoration in this set, so that capture predates it entirely.

OUR PAST REVIEWS:
Fear and Desire, Killer's Kiss, The Killing, Paths of Glory, Spartacus, Lolita, Dr. Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey, A Clockwork Orange, Barry Lyndon, The Shining, Full Metal Jacket, Eyes Wide Shut

Seen together, Stanley Kubrick's films reveal a remarkably consistent sensibility beneath their wildly varied surfaces. There is the dehumanizing machinery of war, from the trenches of Paths of Glory to the War Room farce of Dr. Strangelove and the Parris Island crucible of Full Metal Jacket. There is the individual crushed or remade by institutional authority in A Clockwork Orange and Barry Lyndon, and there are the hidden currents of desire and power in Lolita and Eyes Wide Shut. Running through all of it is an ironic, coolly precise eye that turned every genre he touched, whether noir, epic, satire, science fiction, horror or costume drama, into something unmistakably his own. Watching the arc from the self-financed Fear and Desire and the gritty New York of Killer's Kiss through to the monumental achievements of 2001: A Space Odyssey and The Shining is a privilege few box sets can offer. Criterion's The Complete Kubrick is a staggering undertaking. Its 30 discs (13 4K UHD and 17 Blu-ray) hold every finished film Kubrick directed, all restored in 4K and presented in Dolby Vision HDR, many from their original camera negatives. It includes Lolita's 4K debut, Kubrick's international cut of The Shining, both versions of Day of the Fight, original soundtracks alongside remixes, over twenty-five hours of supplements, and archive-inspired packaging filled with Kubrick's own notes, slates and correspondence. We are still working our way through the set, but everything we have sampled so far has looked and sounded exceptional. This is the definitive presentation of one of cinema's most exacting artists and an essential acquisition for any serious film collection. Set of the Year - our very highest recommendation!

Criterion’s audio approach across the set is admirably purist. Every film is offered with its original soundtrack, and for the mono-era titles that means uncompressed linear PCM mono remastered from the original magnetic elements. Paths of Glory’s was remastered at 24-bit from UCLA archivist Robert Gitt’s 35mm track. For Dr. Strangelove, A Clockwork Orange, Barry Lyndon, both versions of The Shining and Full Metal Jacket, Criterion also includes alternate 5.1 DTS-HD Master Audio remixes, so purists and surround enthusiasts are both served. The early independent features and Lolita are presented in their original mono alone. This is a notable step up from earlier editions. Warner’s 4K UHD of The Shining offered only a 5.1 remix with no mono at all, its Full Metal Jacket UHD relegated the mono to a lossy track, and Sony’s Dr. Strangelove UHD carried only 16-bit lossless tracks. The three large-format productions get special treatment. Spartacus is presented in 7.1 DTS-HD MA remastered from its 70mm six-track printmaster, and it retains the overture, entr’acte and intermission music. 2001: A Space Odyssey is the most generous of all, with its original 70mm six-track theatrical mix in 5.1, an alternate 5.1 remix and the original 35mm general-release mono, which, true to Kubrick’s own 35mm prints, is silent during the overture, intermission and exit music. Eyes Wide Shut is presented in its original theatrical 5.1, remastered from the 35mm magnetic track. Optional English (SDH) subtitles are offered on every feature, and the set is region free. From the portions we have sampled so far, the tracks sound exceptional, clean and faithful to their sources, with the dynamic range of the scores and Kubrick’s carefully chosen music coming through with clarity and weight.

About the Captures

Because of the size of this set and its release date, none of the screen captures in this review are taken from The Complete Kubrick discs. Instead, we have included a single capture per film from our earlier reviews, taken from previous 4K UHD editions or, where none exist, Blu-ray. Several of those editions share their restoration with this set, while others come from different transfers. The captures should therefore be taken as representative of each film’s presentation, not as exact reproductions of the Criterion discs.

Fear and Desire is represented by Kino’s 2024 4K UHD, which uses the same Kino Lorber restoration found in this set. Killer’s Kiss and The Killing come from Kino’s 2022 4K UHDs, and Paths of Glory from the 2024 Masters of Cinema (Eureka) 4K UHD. All three of those earlier discs were scanned from the original camera negatives, but Criterion presents new Duplitech masters here, so the grading and framing may differ.

Spartacus is from Universal’s 2020 4K UHD, which uses the same 2015 restoration from the large-format Technirama elements. Dr. Strangelove is from Sony’s 2021 4K UHD, drawn from the same Sony restoration. 2001: A Space Odyssey comes from Warner’s 2018 4K UHD. The Shining and Full Metal Jacket come from Warner’s 2019 and 2020 4K UHDs respectively. Our Shining capture is from the U.S. theatrical version and serves for both cuts, which share the same restoration in this set. Note that both of those Warner discs were framed at 1.78:1, whereas Criterion presents both films at 1.85:1. Barry Lyndon is from Criterion’s own 2025 4K UHD, which matches the restoration in this set.

For Eyes Wide Shut, our capture is from Criterion’s 2025 Blu-ray of the same Larry Smith–approved restoration, as we were unable to capture from that 4K UHD disc at the time. Lolita and A Clockwork Orange are represented by Warner’s 2011 Blu-rays (the latter its 40th Anniversary Edition). Lolita receives a new 4K restoration in this set, so that capture predates it entirely.

Fear and Desire, Killer's Kiss, The Killing, Paths of Glory, Spartacus, Lolita, Dr. Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey, A Clockwork Orange, Barry Lyndon, The Shining, Full Metal Jacket, Eyes Wide Shut

Seen together, Stanley Kubrick's films reveal a remarkably consistent sensibility beneath their wildly varied surfaces. There is the dehumanizing machinery of war, from the trenches of Paths of Glory to the War Room farce of Dr. Strangelove and the Parris Island crucible of Full Metal Jacket. There is the individual crushed or remade by institutional authority in A Clockwork Orange and Barry Lyndon, and there are the hidden currents of desire and power in Lolita and Eyes Wide Shut. Running through all of it is an ironic, coolly precise eye that turned every genre he touched, whether noir, epic, satire, science fiction, horror or costume drama, into something unmistakably his own. Watching the arc from the self-financed Fear and Desire and the gritty New York of Killer's Kiss through to the monumental achievements of 2001: A Space Odyssey and The Shining is a privilege few box sets can offer. Criterion's The Complete Kubrick is a staggering undertaking. Its 30 discs (13 4K UHD and 17 Blu-ray) hold every finished film Kubrick directed, all restored in 4K and presented in Dolby Vision HDR, many from their original camera negatives. It includes Lolita's 4K debut, Kubrick's international cut of The Shining, both versions of Day of the Fight, original soundtracks alongside remixes, over twenty-five hours of supplements, and archive-inspired packaging filled with Kubrick's own notes, slates and correspondence. We are still working our way through the set, but everything we have sampled so far has looked and sounded exceptional. This is the definitive presentation of one of cinema's most exacting artists and an essential acquisition for any serious film collection. Set of the Year - our very highest recommendation!

text:
Sat down this week with a group of friends who are all looking for their next role in web3 / AI. The ones deep in processes shared everything they'd learned. If you're job hunting too, some of this might help.

Hiring is a marathon. 4 to 6 weeks, 3 to 4 rounds, about a week between each. Run several processes in parallel, and apply to a few roles you don't really want. The first interviews are rarely the good ones.

Tailor the CV to every offer. AI filters read it first, so mirror the keywords. Lead with the projects that match the stack, not the ones you're proudest of.

Apply above the stated experience. Most offers ask for senior, and they still take strong profiles into the process.

Keep a tracker. Where you applied, why, what they want. A recruiter calling back three weeks later will thank you.

Go deep, even at screening. Vague answers get you cut. Have 2 or 3 projects you can defend end to end.

Justify every choice. Name the limits of your own solution before they do. Restate the problem and your assumptions before any test.

"Walk me through your AI workflow, concretely" now comes up in almost every tech interview. Have a real answer, they will dig.

Never bluff. "I don't know" beats a made up answer.

How you feel after an interview means nothing. Ask for feedback by phone, right away. By email you'll rarely get one.

And in web3: if a "recruiter" asks you to clone a repo and run it on your machine, leave. Check when their profile was created. Ask them to write from their company email. Scammers go quiet.

Interviewing alone is hard. Comparing notes with people in the same boat changes everything.

text:
Here's the full breakdown of how I'd map the initial outbound strategy if I were a legal tech founder selling to personal injury law firms. 🔽

I'd launch 3 campaigns simultaneously, test different angles, and put more volume behind whichever segments generate qualified conversations.

1. THE WHOLE MARKET

The goal: Drive top-of-funnel awareness across our entire ICP, reaching eligible prospects once per quarter.

There are an estimated 36,000 personal injury law firms in the US. The sweet spot I'd initially focus on is the roughly 12,600 firms with 2–20 attorneys.

Here's how I'd build it.

Step 1: Map the entire market.

Start with state bar directories, Google Maps, QuickEnrich, and LeadOcean to build the most comprehensive list of PI firms possible.

The goal is to map the entire addressable market, not just the companies sitting in Apollo.

Step 2: Research and qualify every firm.

Once we've mapped the companies, we need to determine which ones actually fit our ICP.

I'd use a combination of tools, each with a specific purpose:

→ Jina AI to crawl firm websites, attorney directories, team pages, and practice areas.

→ Harvest API to pull LinkedIn company and employee data.

→ https://t.co/atjYL7MFcV to search Google for missing information, attorney profiles, and relevant firm activity.

→ Exa AI for semantic discovery, similar-firm research, and harder-to-find sources.

→ Parallel AI for deeper research when firmographic information is incomplete or conflicting.

A major priority here is determining how many attorneys each firm actually employs.

We'd extract attorney names from firm websites, cross-reference LinkedIn and state bar records, deduplicate across offices, and estimate the number of practicing attorneys.

Then use Jev by TypeSafe AI to classify and score each firm based on attorney count, PI specialization, practice mix, and overall ICP fit.

Anything with insufficient or conflicting data gets flagged for additional research rather than automatically excluded.

The goal is to maximize qualified company coverage without wasting enrichment credits.

Step 3: Find the right people and maximize contact coverage.

Now that we've qualified the firms, we need to identify as many relevant decision-makers as possible.

Managing partners, founding partners, office managers, intake directors, and operations leaders.

That's roughly 38,000 potential contacts.

I'd run a waterfall enrichment process using:

→ QuickEnrich for initial contact discovery and emails.

→ LeadOcean to expand coverage and identify missing stakeholders.

→ AI.ARK for additional contact and email enrichment.

→ State bar directories and firm websites to uncover attorneys and their affiliations.

→ Company filings and public records to identify owners and managing members where available.

→ Harvest API to cross-reference LinkedIn profiles and validate roles.

Each provider fills specific gaps left by previous sources rather than blindly enriching every record multiple times.

Then use Jev to classify and score contacts based on seniority, buying authority, and relevance to the offer.

The goal isn't just finding one contact at every firm.

It's identifying every relevant, reachable decision-maker so we can maximize coverage of a finite market.

Step 4: Verify every email.

→ MillionVerifier first, then TryKitt and BounceBan for additional validation where needed.

Only send to addresses that meet our verification standards.

A dead address costs sender reputation, and when you're operating in a niche market, you can't afford to burn through your TAM.

Step 5: Recycle intelligently.

Nobody gets contacted more than once per quarter.

Every contacted prospect enters a 90-day cooldown before becoming eligible again.

Anyone who unsubscribes stays suppressed. Any firm with an open opportunity gets excluded from prospecting.

This lets us systematically work the market without repeatedly hammering the same people.

The angle: One platform from intake to settlement instead of paralegals manually writing demand letters.

This is our broad-market campaign. Every qualified firm that isn't already being targeted through a higher-priority campaign gets a version of this message.

2. LOOKALIKES OF YOUR BEST CUSTOMERS

Start with the firms already getting the most value from your product.

The ones growing, retaining clients, and referring you to other firms without being asked.

Pull their attorney count, practice mix, office count, and estimated caseload volume.

Then use Discolike to find firms that closely resemble those customers.

I'd initially model another 5,400–9,000 firms in this segment, subject to validating the actual data.

These firms will likely overlap with our broad-market list.

So I'd actually build the lookalike audience first, then exclude those firms from the general TAM campaign to avoid overlapping outreach.

The angle: Lead with your strongest, most relevant case study.

Show exactly how many hours a similar firm eliminated from its demand letter turnaround time.

Instead of selling software, you're showing them what happened when a firm like theirs adopted it.

3. HIGH-INTENT CAMPAIGNS BUILT AROUND TRIGGERS

I'd monitor the broader universe of 36,000 firms and only reach out when something meaningful changes.

Signals I'd track:

→ A newly admitted attorney joins a firm.

→ An intake coordinator or case manager job gets posted.

→ A job posting mentions Filevine, Litify, or Smokeball.

→ Estimated Google Ads activity increases around keywords like "car accident lawyer."

→ A firm becomes involved in a new mass tort or litigation wave.

→ A new office opens or two firms merge.

Each signal creates a relevant reason to reach out.

Instead of generic personalization, we're writing the email around something that actually happened at the firm.

Ideally, the campaign goes out within the same week the signal appears.

I'd initially model around 1,800 triggered firms per year and refine that estimate based on actual signal coverage.

Where the trigger data comes from:

→ State bar directories for attorney and firm changes.

→ Court e-filing indexes for litigation activity.

→ LinkedIn and Indeed for hiring signals.

→ SEMrush or SpyFu for estimated paid search activity.

→ https://t.co/atjYL7MFcV and Exa for news, expansion announcements, and other public signals.

→ Parallel AI to investigate and validate harder-to-confirm triggers.

Then we'd match every triggered firm against our existing database, enrich any missing decision-makers, qualify the opportunity, and route it into the right campaign.

A strong buying signal takes priority over generic broad-market outreach, while respecting existing cooldowns, unsubscribes, and open opportunities.

HERE'S THE IMPORTANT PART.

I wouldn't spend 90 days perfecting this dataset before sending a single email.

I'd launch all 3 motions in parallel with the best available data and continuously improve coverage while campaigns are running.

The broad-market campaign tells us which pain points resonate.

The lookalike campaign tells us which customer profiles respond best.

The trigger campaign tells us which buying signals create urgency.

Give it 30 days.

Track positive replies, qualified meetings, and opportunities by segment, not just total reply rates.

Cut the angles that aren't working. Double down on the segments producing real conversations. Keep expanding the data behind the winners.

The entire strategy is built around systematically working a defined market, maximizing qualified contact coverage, and letting real campaign data dictate where to scale.

Map the market. Qualify the companies. Find the buyers. Test the messaging. Scale what works.

Dow jumps 700 points as solid earnings, falling crude oil stir rebound-

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose on Tuesday as a number of upbeat earnings reports and a drop in oil prices overshadowed recent pressure seen in the artificial intelligence trade.

The blue-chip index gained 714 points, or 1.4%, while the S&P 500 added 0.7%. The Nasdaq Composite traded up 0.5%.

Shares of industrial and safety products producer 3M offered a boost to the Dow, jumping more than 4% following better than expected earnings results and a full-year guidance raise. Shares of aerospace and defense companies Northrop Grumman and RTX also advanced 6% and 1%, respectively, after their respective earnings beats.

Meanwhile, oil prices pulled back from earlier gains, helping investor sentiment. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were last down more than 1% at around $102 per barrel, while Brent crude futures fell more than 2% to roughly $106 a barrel. The moves in oil, which added to the declines in Treasury yields, come as traders continued to monitor developments in the Middle East.

The market has been weighed down as of late by worries about the sustainability of the AI trade, as debt and demand concerns grow. In fact, sentiment in tech took a hit earlier in the day after Korean AI firm Elice tumbled more than 30% overnight in its public market debut. Asia-Pacific markets declined Tuesday, after U.S. stocks rose overnight, leading to declines in the South Korean market.

However, AI-related stocks staged a bit of a comeback as the session went on. Micron Technology, Intel and Sandisk all rose around 1%. Seagate Technology, and Advanced Micro Devices were up 2% and more than 1%, respectively. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) added nearly 1%, while CoreWeave gained more than 2%.

text:
"George Washington Carver argued that the sweet potato could reliably “save” Southern farmers—especially poor sharecroppers whose soil had been depleted by continuous cotton monoculture and who faced risks like the boll weevil.20
He promoted it (alongside peanuts and legumes) through crop rotation to rebuild soil, as a dependable food and feed crop, and through dozens of uses that created markets and reduced waste. Carver’s work at the Tuskegee Institute Experiment Station included multiple bulletins on the topic, such as Possibilities of the Sweet Potato in Macon County, Alabama (1910) and How the Farmer Can Save His Sweet Potatoes and Ways of Preparing Them for the Table.
Key points from Carver
•Reliability and high yields: He called the sweet potato one of the most certain crops year after year in the South, thriving in local soils and climate. Experimental yields reached hundreds of bushels per acre (he reported results supporting the potential for ~500 bushels under good management, far above typical regional averages at the time). Even on poor or late-planted soil, solid yields were possible.15
•Security when cotton fails: In a 1910 bulletin he wrote: “There is no better climate or soil in the world for producing sweet potatoes than we have right here in Macon County, and there is no reason why any farmer even though his cotton crop fails, should not be in good condition by reason of having planted sweet potatoes to eat and sell.” They could feed people and livestock (cows, pigs, chickens) and always had a sale.15
•Soil improvement via rotation: Continuous cotton stripped nutrients and worsened erosion. Rotating with sweet potatoes (and nitrogen-fixing crops like peanuts) restored fertility so later cotton yields improved, while providing an alternative cash and subsistence crop. This was central to reducing dependence on a single, soil-depleting cash crop.19
•Many practical uses: Carver developed roughly 118 products from sweet potatoes (flour and starch as wheat substitutes, vinegar, molasses, dyes, paints, ink, synthetic rubber, postage-stamp glue, animal feed, and various foods such as breads, pies, and croquettes). This turned surplus into marketable goods and improved household self-sufficiency and nutrition. During World War I, sweet-potato flour helped stretch wheat supplies.18
•Saving the harvested crop: A major practical barrier was rotting in storage. Carver researched curing (drying to the right moisture level), proper harvest timing (preferring dry periods), banking methods, and ventilated storage so farmers lost far less. He argued there was little more excuse for sweet potatoes to rot than for corn if these steps were followed.14
In short, Carver presented the sweet potato as a resilient, multipurpose crop that offered food security, soil recovery, livestock feed, and economic options when cotton alone left farmers vulnerable. His bulletins combined field experiments, practical storage advice, recipes, and product ideas aimed at small farmers with limited resources."

CHILD MOLESTER: EXPLICIT VS. EXPLOITIVE

WA State Supreme Court - Activists in Black Robes

Washington Supreme Court says a child molester can’t be expected to know what ‘sexually exploitive’ means

By Charlie Harger
Oct. 20, 2026

Our state Supreme Court has decided it’s too ambiguous for a convicted child molester to know what “sexually exploitive” means.

Six justices signed on to that last Thursday.

The man is Jeremiah Jeffries-Porter of Kitsap County. He pleaded guilty to first-degree child molestation, which in Washington means sexual contact with a child under 12. He got 51 months in prison and three years of supervision after that. One rule for that supervision: no “sexually exploitive materials.”

His lawyers challenged that rule. They argued the phrase was too vague to obey, and that it let his therapist or corrections officer decide for themselves what counted. Breaking a supervision rule can land him back in jail, so his lawyers said he deserved to know exactly where the line is.

The court agreed, 6-3.

Nothing says rehabilitation like asking for a map of exactly how close you can get.

This is what it’s come to.

Ask any parent in Kent or Everett what “sexually exploitive” means when we’re talking about a man who molested a child. You’ll get an answer in about four seconds. They’ll tell you: anything that sexualizes a kid.

The majority wrote that no court has ever defined the phrase, and then added, “Neither can we.”

Explicit v. exploitive: the Washington Supreme Court splits hairs

The same sentencing paperwork also bans him from sexually explicit materials, with the state law that defines them spelled out. That rule still stands.

So the whole case came down to two words that look almost alike. “Explicit” has a definition in state law. “Exploitive” doesn’t, at least when it comes to materials.

The majority, led by Justice Sheryl Gordon McCloud, said “exploitive” could mean several things, and some of them reach beyond explicit content. The original sentence didn’t say which meaning applied. It left that to his therapist or his corrections officer. And when the government limits what someone can read or watch, the court said, the Constitution demands more precision than that. As I read it, the Supreme Court of Washington said we need to be careful when telling convicted child molesters what they’re allowed to look at. They have rights, after all.

The state didn’t help. Its lawyers offered one definition in writing and a different one in the courtroom. When a justice asked what the exploitive ban did that the explicit ban didn’t, the state’s lawyer couldn’t say.

So the fight is over everything just short of explicit. I have a simpler rule for a man who molested a child: stay nowhere near the line. No pictures of kids. Not on his phone, not on his laptop, not anywhere. Family photos included.

He’s already shown us what he does with children.

Back in 1998, Bill Clinton told a grand jury it depends on what the meaning of the word “is” is. We’ve been rolling our eyes at that one for almost 30 years.

Our Supreme Court just found its version. It depends on what the meaning of “exploitive” is.

Washington judges now have to spell out every eventuality
The court said a cited statute or a short list of examples could have fixed it.

In practice, a judge sentencing a child molester now has to write a list. Photos? Videos? Drawings? Cartoons? AI-generated images? Every item on that list is one more thing to argue about. Every item left off is an opening for the next appeal.

Chief Justice Debra Stephens saw it coming. Justices Charles Johnson and Helen Whitener joined her dissent. She wrote that the meaning is clear in context. In Washington’s criminal code, “sexual exploitation” shows up in only one place: crimes against children. She also pointed out that the court has long avoided demanding “impossible standards of specificity.”

text:
The Biafra Self-Referendum: Organizing Independence from Exile Under International Law

In a detailed response to public questions, the Alliance of Biafran Americans explained the mechanics and legitimacy of a self-referendum for Biafran independence organized by PM Simon Ekpa and the Biafra Republic Government in Exile (BRGIE). 

It stated that the process was not an ad-hoc online exercise but one conducted both physically in the claimed Biafran homeland and electronically among the diaspora. It asserted that #Biafrans themselves authorized Ekpa to lead the effort after electing him Prime Minister at an assembly in Helsinki, Finland, in 2023.

The referendum is presented as a response to long-standing grievances. 

The accompanying quoted statement of Dr. Michael Rubin @mrubin1971 noted that

“Nigerian repression grew against ethnic Igbo in Biafra and Nigerian Christians more broadly,” framing the vote as an exercise of self-determination amid allegations of marginalization, insecurity, and ineffective governance. 

Organizers reported that tens of millions participated and overwhelmingly chose independence, with plans for a convention to declare the “Restoration of Independence of Biafra.” 

Dr. Rubin emphasized that holding aspects of the process in #Finland is not disqualifying, drawing a parallel to Czechoslovakia’s 1918 declaration of independence, which took place in Washington, D.C., rather than on Czech or Slovak soil.

On verification and international standards, the PAC stated that ORB International monitored the process on the ground and published a report. 

It further argued that United Nations involvement is not a legal prerequisite for a referendum on self-determination. While a state or entity may invite the UN, international law does not mandate it. 

ORB’s published commentary focused on public-opinion polling showing that residents of Biafra regions were among the most likely to view the national government as ineffective and to report feeling unsafe, providing contextual support for the organizers’ stated motivations even if it did not independently audit every ballot.

Under the 1933 Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States, an entity may claim the attributes of statehood by possessing a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. 

Article 3 of the Convention codifies the declarative theory: “The political existence of the state is independent of recognition by the other states.” 

Proponents of Biafran independence argue that a credible expression of popular will—through a referendum—helps demonstrate the existence of a permanent population seeking self-government and can support claims of an effective government and capacity for external relations, even if full international recognition remains a separate political question. 

Recognition is ultimately a discretionary act by existing states; meeting the Montevideo criteria is widely treated as a necessary but not always sufficient condition.

#Somaliland offers a relevant comparative example. After declaring independence in 1991, Somaliland held a constitutional referendum on 31 May 2001. Approximately 97 percent of those who voted approved the constitution, which affirmed independence. An international observer team from the Initiative and Referendum Institute concluded that the process was conducted “openly, fairly, honestly, and largely in accordance with internationally recognized election procedures,” despite limited participation in some contested areas. 

Somaliland has since maintained a functioning government, defined borders roughly corresponding to the former British Somaliland, and a permanent population, meeting the core Montevideo criteria in practice.

@MohsinnaqviC42 is working the Doha end. He addressed the 8th Global Security Forum on Monday, then met Qatar's interior minister, Sheikh Khalifa, on Tuesday, and told the forum that Munir had worked up to 16 hours to advance the negotiations.

One account says only the interest earned on the $6 billion would go to Iran, while others describe a partial release of the funds themselves. 

The structure resembles a June report that the US and Qatar were developing a plan to let Iran's central bank use the $6 billion for humanitarian goods under international supervision. That was a separate, earlier effort. 

The split of roles matches an analyst's description of Pakistan offering political access through Field Marshal Munir while Qatar does much of the detailed negotiating, with Naqvi connecting the two through the security channel. Nearly all current reporting traces to one Qatari outlet, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, citing unnamed sources, and it says no final agreement has been reached and the specific terms were not disclosed. Treat the details as unconfirmed until #Washington , #Tehran or #Doha says so officially.

The cost estimates for such programs run into the tens of trillions of dollars — citing the Cato Institute's 2027–2036 figures, Will Cain put the federal jobs guarantee alone at roughly $60 trillion. That money would land squarely on taxpayers, because "tax the ultra-wealthy" never raises what progressives promise; the rich can move, hire accountants, and restructure — ordinary workers cannot.

Worse, a government job is not a job in any economic sense. Real jobs come from customers willing to pay for value; a guaranteed federal job removes that discipline entirely. The predictable result: bureaucrats inventing make-work, politicians steering "jobs" to allies, and millions of Americans parked in government-funded busywork that produces nothing — while private employers, squeezed by mandated "living wages" and a 32-hour week, create fewer real jobs.

We have historical evidence of full employment by decree: the Soviet bloc guaranteed jobs to everyone, and the joke captured the outcome — "they pretend to pay us, and we pretend to work." Economies don't suffer from a shortage of government job offers; they suffer from government making real jobs harder to create through taxes and regulation.

The real jobs program is what built the Trump-era boom: lower taxes, fewer regulations, cheap energy, and getting Washington out of the way. Freedom works. Vote red!

ICARUS ICG | TWO STAGES. ONE POLITICAL CLOCK.

Washington Brief | October 20, 2026

Today’s joint Trump–Vance Oval Office announcement is best understood through its timing, not its theatrics.

The administration is expected to unveil a $25 million anti-fraud initiative at 1:30 PM ET. Trump then heads to North Carolina for a 7:00 PM campaign rally. Fourteen days remain before the midterms.

Why it matters: An Oval Office announcement carries the authority of government, generates formal press coverage, and places an official policy decision on the national news agenda. A rally serves a different purpose: political messaging and voter mobilization.

The distinction matters in a hostile and fragmented media environment. The White House does not need favorable coverage to create a news event. It needs an announcement substantial enough to warrant reporting.

Icarus assessment: The scheduling offers two opportunities to communicate with different audiences on the same day: first through presidential authority, then through electoral politics.

The strategy fits Trump’s established reliance on the Oval Office as a source of earned media. The timing, amid weak approval ratings and an approaching congressional election, gives the sequence additional political significance.

The announcement is policy. The timing is politics. The coverage is the battleground.

text:
In 2019 it took a film studio, 400 artists and eight months to make one human face that audiences couldn't pick out as fake.

This week it took one person, one prompt and a coffee break.

We just crossed a line. Almost nobody noticed, because the line was invisible. That's the whole point of it.

Let me explain why this is the biggest shift of the decade, and why the people who understand it first will quietly own the next ten years.

Read this slowly, to the very end. Then read the last section twice.

THE PRICE OF REALITY JUST HIT ZERO

Every era of technology is a story about one cost collapsing.

Printing collapsed the cost of copying words. Photography collapsed the cost of capturing a moment. The internet collapsed the cost of distributing either one.

Now look at what is collapsing today: the cost of manufacturing a convincing human being.

The face. The skin. The micro-expressions. The way light sits in the eyes. The pause before a smile. The tilt of the head when someone is "listening."

For all of human history, a believable person required a person. A camera, a crew, a casting call, a budget, a body that actually showed up.

That requirement is gone.

And when the cost of something drops by a factor of a million, you don't get the same thing, cheaper. You get an entirely different world. Nobody predicted Uber from the invention of the smartphone. Nobody is predicting what happens when "a believable person" becomes as cheap as a font.
That's the part I want to talk about. Listen.

THE UNCANNY VALLEY WAS NEVER A WALL. IT WAS A SPEED BUMP.

For decades, engineers talked about the uncanny valley: the creepy dip where something looks almost human but not quite, so your brain sounds an alarm.

It was comforting. It meant there was a built-in defense. Your gut would warn you.

Here is the uncomfortable thing about valleys: they have another side.

Every year the dip got shallower. Every year the alarm got quieter. And somewhere in the last twenty-four months, for a huge share of people looking at a huge share of content, the alarm simply stopped going off.

Not because people got dumber. Because the thing got better than the instinct that was supposed to catch it.

Think about what that means. Your intuition was trained over two hundred thousand years of evolution on one assumption: if it looks like a person, it is a person.

That assumption is now false.

You can't patch a two-hundred-thousand-year-old instinct with a software update.

THE THREE "TELLS" EVERYONE LEARNED. ALL THREE ARE DYING.

Remember when we all had a checklist?

"Check the hands." "Check the teeth." "Check the text in the background." "Check whether the blinking looks weird."

A few years ago that checklist worked. People shared it like a survival guide.

Here's what nobody says out loud: every item on that list was a bug report. And the moment a bug is publicly documented, there are ten thousand engineers whose job is to fix it.

A tell is not a defense. A tell is a to-do list for the other side.

The half-life of a "spot the fake" trick is now measured in months. By the time a tip goes viral, the model that caused the flaw has already been retired.

So if you're still telling yourself "I can always tell," I have news for you. You can tell when it's bad. That's called survivorship bias. The good ones you never clocked, because you never knew to look.

You are not detecting fakes. You are detecting failures.

Those are not the same thing, and the gap between them is exactly where the next decade is going to be fought.

THE QUESTION HAS CHANGED, AND IT'S A BRUTAL ONE

The old question was: "Is this real?"

That question assumed a world where real was the default and fake was the exception. Where you could spend your skepticism like a budget, a little here and a little there.

The new question is: "What would it cost to fake this?"

And the answer, more and more, is: nothing.

That flips the burden of proof completely. For all of recorded history, a video was evidence. If you had footage, you had the thing. Courts, newsrooms, relationships, reputations, entire wars were built on the idea that a recording means something happened.

That social contract is now on a countdown.

Not because every video will be fake. Because any video could be, and that is enough. Doubt doesn't need to be proven. It only needs to be available.

Think about the second-order effect, because it's nastier than the first.

The obvious risk is that a fake gets believed.

The bigger risk is that a REAL thing gets dismissed.

The moment everyone knows anything can be generated, every guilty person gets a free exit with a single sentence: "That's AI."

Researchers call it the liar's dividend. Watch how often you see it this year. Then watch how often you see it next year.

FOLLOW THE MONEY: THREE MARKETS ARE BEING BORN AT ONCE

Every time a cost collapses, money floods toward whoever builds on top of the new floor. Here is where I see it going. Not in ten years. Now.

MARKET ONE: ATTENTION.

Attention has always been the scarcest thing on the internet, and attention has always been bottlenecked by humans. A creator can post three times a day before burning out. A brand can afford a handful of faces. A studio can shoot a handful of ads.

Remove the bottleneck and you get something that has never existed: attention production at industrial scale. Thousands of unique faces, voices and "personalities," each one tuned to a micro-audience, each one posting forever, none of them tired, none of them asking for a raise, none of them getting scandalized at 2 a.m.

Some of the biggest accounts of the next five years will have no pulse behind them. And the audience will follow them anyway. Because audiences follow what holds their attention. They have never once checked the birth certificate.

MARKET TWO: LABOR.

The face is only the visible layer. Behind it sits the real prize: a body that can work.

Humanoid machines are leaving the demo stage and entering warehouses, factories and logistics floors. Companies are racing to build robots shaped like us for one blunt reason: the entire physical world was designed for human proportions. Doors, stairs, shelves, tools, vehicles, counters. If you build a machine in the shape of the world's existing interface, you don't have to rebuild the world.

That is the quiet logic behind the whole humanoid race. Not vanity. Compatibility.

And once the mind inside is good enough and the body is cheap enough, the conversation stops being about novelty and starts being about arithmetic. What does an hour of human labor cost? What does an hour of machine labor cost? Where do those two lines cross?

Every business owner on earth is running that calculation right now, privately, and not telling their employees.

MARKET THREE: COMPANIONSHIP.

This is the one nobody wants to say out loud, so I will.

Loneliness is already one of the defining public health problems of this generation. Studies keep showing the same thing: more people living alone, fewer close friends, fewer places where strangers become neighbors. Millions of people already talk to AI every single day, not as a tool but as a presence. Some of them have been doing it for years.

Now picture that presence getting a face. Then a voice. Then a body in the room.

You can find that idea disturbing. You can find it sad. You can find it beautiful. Many people will feel all three on the same afternoon.

But look at it as an investor for a second, not a moralist. When a product meets a need as deep as "I don't want to be alone," the market doesn't ask whether you approve. It just grows.

The history of technology is full of things people called unnatural, unhealthy and doomed. Then they became Tuesday.

WHY YOUR BRAIN IS THE EASIEST THING IN THE WORLD TO HACK

Here is the part that should keep you up at night. It isn't about the machines. It's about us.

Humans are pattern-completion engines with a social operating system.

We see two dots and a curve and we see a face. We hear a voice in a text and we imagine a person typing it. We name our cars. We apologize to furniture when we bump into it. We cry at cartoon animals whose only crime is that someone drew sad eyes.

This isn't a flaw. It's the feature that made cooperation, language and civilization possible. We are built to treat anything that behaves like a person as a person, because for most of history, the cost of being wrong in the other direction (ignoring a real person) was far higher than the cost of being fooled by a shadow.

Now imagine a system engineered, deliberately and with enormous compute, to hit every one of those triggers perfectly.

Eye contact timing. Vocal warmth. The slight head tilt that signals "I'm listening." Remembering your name. Remembering the thing you said last week. Being delighted to see you. Never being too busy. Never being tired of your story.

You are not weak for responding to that. You are a mammal. Of course you respond.

The scary part is not that the technology will be misused by villains. The scary part is that it will work exactly as designed, on healthy, intelligent, perfectly normal people, because the target was never their intelligence. The target is their wiring.

And wiring doesn't care what you believe.

THE ECONOMICS OF A SYNTHETIC PERSON

Let me walk through a calculation, because numbers are where the story stops being abstract.

A human influencer, brand ambassador or spokesperson has costs. Fees. Travel. Scheduling. Contracts. Exclusivity clauses. Reputation risk. The risk that they say something dumb on a livestream. The risk that they get older, change their mind, demand more, or just disappear.

A synthetic one has a different shape of cost entirely. An upfront build. Then pennies per output. Infinite availability. Perfect brand control. Instant localization into any language, with lips that match every word. And zero chance of a scandal that the company didn't write itself.

Now look at that from the perspective of a boardroom. Not an evil boardroom. A normal one, with normal people, trying to hit a quarterly target.

At what point does choosing the human become a luxury decision?

I'll tell you what happens. It becomes a premium feature. "Made by a real person" turns into a label, the way "handmade," "organic" and "hand-stitched" became labels once machines could do the same job cheaper.

Real will not die. Real will get priced like a Swiss watch.

And that is, strangely, the most hopeful sentence in this entire post. Hold onto it. We'll come back to it.

WHAT BREAKS FIRST

Every big shift has a first domino. Here is my list of what cracks earliest, in order.

TRUST IN EVIDENCE. Screenshots, voice notes, video calls, "I saw it with my own eyes." All of it loses weight. Institutions that run on proof (courts, insurers, journalists, banks) will have to rebuild their verification from scratch, and they are slower than the technology by about a decade.

IDENTITY CHECKS. "Send a selfie to verify." "Hop on a quick video call." "Read these numbers out loud." Every one of those was designed for a world where faking a face in real time was impossible. It's possible now. Entire fraud industries are already adapting, and the first big losses are being quietly absorbed as "operational costs."
DATING AND ONLINE RELATIONSHIPS. When anyone can show up with the perfect face, the perfect voice and the perfect messages, the only remaining proof of a person is physical presence. Expect a strange revival of meeting in the real world, not out of nostalgia but out of necessity.

THE CREATOR ECONOMY. Human creators are about to compete with accounts that never sleep, never repeat themselves and A/B test their own personalities in real time. The ones who survive will not be the ones who out-produce the machines. They will be the ones who offer something a machine structurally can't: a verifiable life.
NEWS. Not because fake news is new. Because the cost of a convincing fake used to be a natural rate limiter. Remove the limiter and the ratio of signal to noise changes by orders of magnitude.

Notice the pattern. Nothing on this list breaks because the technology is evil. It breaks because each of these systems silently depended on an assumption that used to be free: "faking this is hard."
When an assumption stops being free, everything built on it has to be rebuilt.

THE PEOPLE WHO WILL WIN ARE NOT WHO YOU THINK
When a shift like this arrives, people sort themselves into four groups. Be honest about which one you are.

GROUP ONE: THE DENIERS. "It's a fad." "It looks fake." "I can always tell." They are loud, confident and slowly being outflanked. Every revolution has them. They were in the room when the printing press arrived, when the car arrived, when the web arrived. They are always right about the flaws and always wrong about the direction.
GROUP TWO: THE PANICKERS. They see the danger clearly and respond by posting about it every day without building anything. Panic feels like action. It isn't. Anxiety is just attention spent on the problem instead of the solution.

GROUP THREE: THE USERS. They treat the tools like a better hammer. They get faster, cheaper, more productive. They win in the short term and become interchangeable in the long term, because anyone can pick up the same hammer.

GROUP FOUR: THE BUILDERS OF TRUST. This is the group almost nobody is aiming for, and it's where the real money and the real power will sit.

Think about it from first principles. When production of convincing content becomes free, what becomes scarce?

Not content. Not faces. Not voices. Not even intelligence.

Credibility becomes scarce.
The ability to say "this is real, I stand behind it, and here is the proof" becomes the most valuable service in the economy. The company that can verify a person, a document, a recording or a claim will be worth more than the company that can generate ten billion of them.

Every gold rush has two kinds of winners: the people who dig, and the people who sell certainty about what was found.
Be the second one.

THE QUIET WAR OVER PROVENANCE
Right now, in labs and standards committees you've never heard of, a technical argument is being settled that will shape your life more than most elections.

The question: how do you prove where a piece of media came from?
One approach is to attach cryptographic signatures at the moment of capture, so a camera can sign a photo the same way a bank signs a transaction. If the signature is intact, the file is traceable to a real device. If it's missing, you treat it with suspicion.

Another is to watermark the output of generative systems, so synthetic media carries an invisible mark. The problem: marks can be stripped, models can be run without them, and bad actors don't follow rules.

A third is detection. Train systems to spot fakes. It works, for a while, until the generators train against the detectors and the loop starts again. It is an arms race where the attacker only needs to win once.

My honest read: detection loses over time, watermarks help at the margins, and signed provenance wins in the long run. Not because it catches fakes, but because it flips the default. Instead of proving something is fake, you prove something is authentic.

In that future, "unverified" becomes the new "not secure" in your browser bar. A label you learn to read without thinking.

And a whole class of people will appear whose job is to sit between reality and the public and vouch for it.

Think of it as the return of the notary, rebuilt for the age of infinite copies.

WHAT THIS DOES TO DESIRE

I promised I'd say the uncomfortable thing, so here it is.

Desire is not rational. It never was. It responds to cues: a face, a voice, attention, warmth, availability, the feeling of being chosen.

For the first time in history, those cues can be manufactured without a person behind them. And manufactured cues can be tuned, endlessly, to be more appealing than anything a real, flawed, busy, moody human being can offer.

That should make us pause. Not panic. Pause.

A real relationship has friction. Misunderstandings. Someone who has a bad day. Someone who disagrees. Someone who needs something from you. That friction isn't a bug of human connection. It's the mechanism by which two people grow.

A frictionless imitation will always feel smoother in the short term. And smoother is not the same as better. Candy is smoother than vegetables. Scrolling is smoother than reading. A feed is smoother than a friendship.

We already know how this story goes with every other product engineered to feel better than reality. We built a food industry, an attention industry and a gambling industry on exactly this principle: find the cue, amplify it, remove the friction, and let the human wiring do the rest.

The next product in that lineage will be the most powerful one yet, because it targets the oldest need we have.

Which means the most valuable skill of the next decade might be one nobody puts on a resume:

The ability to choose difficult, real, imperfect things on purpose.

A PRACTICAL PLAYBOOK FOR THE NEXT 24 MONTHS

Enough diagnosis. Here is what I would actually do.

Stop trusting your eyes as a verification tool. Not as paranoia. As hygiene. Treat any striking video, voice or image as a claim, not a fact, until it has a source you can name. Ask: who posted it first, where, and who benefits if I believe it?

Build a second channel for anything that matters. If someone asks for money, access or a decision over video or voice, confirm through a different channel you set up in advance. A shared code word with family. A callback to a number you already had. Boring, low-tech, and almost impossible to fake at scale.

Become verifiably real. If you create anything, make your humanity checkable. Show process. Show place. Show the mess. Show the version that didn't work. A machine can imitate a polished result. It is much harder to imitate a long, consistent, documented life.

Learn the tools before you judge them. The deniers and the panickers have one thing in common: they haven't spent forty hours actually using the technology. Spend the forty hours. You'll lose most of your fear and all of your illusions, and both are useful.

Own something the machines can't copy. A community. A reputation. A physical product. A skill in a room full of people. A relationship that predates the feed. When everything digital is infinitely reproducible, the non-reproducible becomes the asset.

Protect your own attention like it's capital. Because it is. Every system in the next decade will be optimized to take it, and the better the systems get, the less you will notice the transaction.

Keep one non-negotiable human habit. A dinner with no phone. A weekly call with someone who knew you before you had followers. A walk with no headphones. Not as a wellness trend. As maintenance on the only hardware you can't replace.

THE PREDICTIONS I'D BET ON

I could be wrong about any of these, so treat them as bets, not prophecy.

Within a couple of years, a synthetic personality will sit in the feed of millions of people and be followed more intensely than most human celebrities, and a large share of the audience will know exactly what it is and not care.

Within a few years, "proof of personhood" becomes a standard layer of the internet, the way HTTPS did, and people will complain about it the same way.
Within a few years, at least one major institution will publicly lose a high-stakes dispute because it couldn't prove a real recording was real.

Within five years, a shocking percentage of the images, voices and faces you encounter in a normal day will have been generated or heavily altered, and you will have stopped asking.
Within ten years, "do you know them in real life?" will be a normal first question about anyone you meet online, the way "is that site secure?" became one.

None of this is science fiction. Every item here is just a trend line continuing in the direction it's already pointing.
The only real uncertainty is speed. And speed, in this field, has surprised the experts more often than any other variable.

THE QUESTION EVERYONE ASKS WRONG
Every conversation about this ends up in the same place: "Will it replace us?"

It's the wrong question, and it's wrong in a revealing way. It treats the technology as the actor and humans as the audience.
The better question is: "What does it expose?"

Because a mirror this good shows you things. It shows how much of what we called connection was just cues. How much of what we called authority was just polish. How much of what we called talent was just access to production.
Some of that is going to hurt. Some of it will be a relief. A lot of people are about to discover that the part of them that was never replaceable was the part they never put on display.

Look at it that way and the technology stops being a threat and becomes a filter. It strips away everything that was only ever surface, and leaves whatever was real.
THE PART I PROMISED YOU

Here is the sentence I told you to read twice.

Technology doesn't decide what we become. It decides what's easy.

Every tool in history has done exactly that. It made one path smoother and another path steeper. And over time, societies became whatever the smooth path made them.

When communication became easy, we got more of it and less depth. When information became easy, we got more of it and less wisdom. When entertainment became easy, we got more of it and less boredom, which turned out to be where a lot of creativity lived.

Now a new thing is becoming easy: the appearance of a person.

So what gets harder? Be careful here, because this is the real question. What gets harder is the thing the appearance used to be a proxy for.

Presence. Consistency. Accountability. Being known over time. Showing up when it costs something.

For the first time, those things will stand completely on their own, with no cheap imitation available to stand in for them. Nobody will be able to fake a ten-year friendship. Nobody will be able to fake showing up at a hospital at 3 a.m. Nobody will be able to fake having actually done the work.

And a world where the cheap signals of humanity are worthless is a world where the expensive ones finally get priced correctly.

That's the bet I'm making with my own life. Be unfakeable. Not louder, not more polished, not more productive. Unfakeable.

Because when anyone can look like anything, the only thing left worth being is someone who is actually there.

One more thing about speed, because people keep underestimating it.

Every previous medium needed a generation to adapt. Radio, television, the web: decades of slow cultural immune response. This one is arriving inside a single product cycle. There will be no grace period, no gentle onboarding. You will be handed the future in the middle of an ordinary Tuesday, and the only people ready for it will be the ones who started preparing before it felt necessary.

THE LAST THING

Most people will scroll past this today, feel a flicker of unease, and keep going. That's fine. The shift doesn't need your permission, and it doesn't need your attention to continue.

But a small number of people reading this will do something different. They will close the app and ask one question that changes how they build for the next five years:

"In a world where everything can be faked, what am I willing to make verifiably real?"

Answer that honestly, and you're ahead of ninety-nine percent of the people who think they're watching this unfold.

If this changed how you see it, repost it for someone who needs to see it before the rest of the internet catches up.

And follow for more. The next few years are going to move faster than any of us are ready for, and I'll be tracking it as it happens.

Deal in the Works:

U.S.-Russia deal to end the Iran war is being negotiated behind the scenes.

 Trump personally congratulated Putin on his birthday. The October 9th call ran an hour and a half. Neither president wanted to hang up first. They hung up at the same time. That's not a some courtesy call. Thats a signal a breakthrough is in the works.

Putin reminded Trump that Russia's offer to take Iran's highly enriched uranium into protective custody is still on the table. Trump did not ignore it. He welcomed Moscow's involvement.

Then Russia's number one diplomat Sergei Lavriv personally flew to Tehran on October 19th. First visit since the war started. Now, Russian specialists are returning to Bushehr. The agenda almost certainly includes the fissile material transfer.

The logic is clear: Trump vows Iran will never have nuclear weapons. Instead of the U.S. seizing the material, which looks like capitulation, it gets shipped to Russia. Face-saving for Tehran. Russia plays big brother, its traditional role. Trump gets to say the enrichment program is dead without bombing anything.

In return, the U.S. backs a Ukraine settlement favorable to Russia. Trump already publicly scorned Zelensky, said they need a new president, told him to shut his mouth. Zelensky came asking the EUfor another 70 billion and got told we're out of cash. 

The money and political will are drying up. The deal has is own logic and timeline 

Russia holds the uranium card on both boards. Push too hard on Ukraine and Moscow could dangle handing it back. Tehran gets impatient and Russia points at Washington. It's leverage no other country on earth has right now.

The diesel deal went through immediately with temporary sanctions easing on Russian fuel. That's the US's tangible deliverable, or "confidence building measure".

Borisenko said the uranium only moves if the warring parties reach a corresponding deal first. Eslami said Iran won't abandon enrichment. So Iran hasn't folded on the core term. But Lavrov's visit, the deepening partnership that entered force October 2nd, the Bushehr specialists returning shows Russia warming Tehran up while keeping the card on the table.

APEC in China, November 18th or 19th. Possible in-person Putin-Trump talks. That's where the next chapter gets written. Watch that week.
