text:
#TonboImaging 

Tonbo Imaging: The Silicon Valley of Indian Defence Tech?

The Indian defence sector is experiencing an unprecedented boom. While established giants build heavy tanks, massive warships, and complex radar systems, a Bengaluru-based company named Tonbo Imaging is quietly acting as the high-tech "eyes" for modern military equipment.

If you are looking to understand this recent IPO, this comprehensive deep dive breaks down Tonbo’s business model, product strategy, competitive moats, valuation, and long-term risks in simple layman terms.

1. The Business Model: Brains over Brawn

Unlike traditional defence companies that build massive, expensive factories to manufacture heavy steel and hardware, Tonbo uses an asset-light business model. Think of them less like a traditional industrial factory and more like Apple.

In-House Innovation: Tonbo keeps the most valuable, high-margin work inside its own labs. They focus entirely on Research & Development (R&D), proprietary product design, artificial intelligence (AI) software, and prototyping

Outsourced Manufacturing: Once a high-tech design is perfected, they don't build it themselves. Instead, they outsource the heavy, high-volume manufacturing to specialized Indian contract electronics partners like Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology. This keeps Tonbo’s fixed costs remarkably low and allows them to scale up production rapidly without owning giant, cash-burning factories.

2. Product Matrix & The Strategic TAM Shift

Tonbo designs advanced thermal imaging systems, night-vision cameras, and smart AI targeting systems that allow soldiers, drones, and missiles to spot targets clearly through pitch darkness, heavy smoke, battlefield fog, or camouflage.

Historically, their revenue was split across two primary product lines:

Tactical Systems (~58% of revenue): Gear built directly for individual soldiers, such as thermal weapon sights, helmet cameras, and handheld night-vision binoculars.

Platform Systems (~40% of revenue): Highly complex imaging systems integrated into larger military machinery, including missile guidance sensors, drone-tracking tech, and digital fire-control systems for armored vehicles.

The Product Mix Shift: Expanding a Once-Limited Market

Management has signaled an aggressive pivot away from individual Tactical Systems and heavily toward advanced Platform Systems and Unmanned Warfare (Anti-Drone systems). This shift is highly beneficial because it directly addresses the company's biggest structural constraint: its historical Total Addressable Market (TAM).

When Tonbo focused purely on individual soldier gear—like supplying the Indian government’s aggregate requirement for roughly 30,000 thermal sights (of which Tonbo has already captured a dominant 51% share)—the domestic market was simply too small to sustain long-term hyper-growth. By pivoting to complex Platform Systems, Tonbo is breaking out of this niche sandbox. Engineering the "seeker head" for a cruise missile or building autonomous tracking software for anti-drone microwave weapons commands substantially higher profit margins.

More importantly, these next-generation applications exponentially expand their TAM. For instance, management is aggressively backing anti-drone warfare under its WaveStrike brand, eyeing a newly unlocked domestic addressable opportunity worth ₹2,500 crore for high-power microwave systems alone. This shift blows the ceiling off their growth limitations and creates deep technological lock-in. Once Tonbo's proprietary tracking software is engineered directly into a multi-million dollar missile system, the government cannot easily swap them out for a competitor, securing multi-decade revenue streams.

3. Narrative vs. Reality: Are the Green Shoots Real?

At an 80x P/E multiple alongside falling current profits, a cynical investor might ask: Is this massive TAM expansion just a glossy PowerPoint narrative designed to sell the IPO, or are there real green shoots?

Fortunately for Tonbo, the green shoots are tangible, validated by hard commercial milestones rather than pure speculation

The BDL Seeker Validation: The company has already transitioned from the testing phase to becoming the sole-source supplier to Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) for a critical uncooled missile seeker program. In defence electronics, graduating to sole-source status on a major domestic missile program is the ultimate "green shoot." It proves the technology has passed rigorous live military trials and is locked into the national procurement pipeline.

Tangible Order Book Pivot: While FY26 backward-looking revenues dropped due to temporary West Asia shipping delays, Tonbo’s forward-looking order book tells a different story. As of mid-2026, their order book stood at ₹314.24 crore, heavily weighted toward high-margin platform electronics. Crucially, they secured an additional ₹118.15 crore in fresh orders in the subsequent months. This surge in order inflows confirms that the transition away from standalone soldier sights and into integrated platform systems is actively generating revenue backlog.

These milestones indicate that the premium valuation isn't built on a hollow narrative; it is an early price tag on a high-margin product pivot that is already underway.

4. The Economic Moat & Long-Term Longevity

An economic moat is a company's structural ability to maintain a competitive advantage over its rivals to protect its long-term profits. Tonbo possesses powerful moats that apply to both its current product lineup and its upcoming mix:

• 100% Proprietary IP & "ITAR-Free" Status: Many global defence products rely heavily on US components, subjecting them to strict US export control laws (ITAR) and geopolitical restrictions. Because Tonbo owns its entire tech stack independently, it can smoothly export its systems globally to neutral countries without needing US government approval. This freedom has already allowed them to deploy systems across 24 countries, effectively bypassing domestic TAM constraints by opening up the vast global defence market.

High-Fidelity AI Software (The New Product Moat): Competitors can buy generic optical lenses, but Tonbo writes the proprietary machine-learning algorithms that sit inside the camera to auto-detect, track, and neutralize targets on the edge. In their new missile seeker program, this technical moat is structurally locked in, making it incredibly difficult for rivals to displace them.

Longevity of the Moat vs. Product-Specific Competitors

This moat can comfortably defend Tonbo’s growth for the next 5 to 7 years, largely due to the long gestation cycles of defence procurement. However, as Tonbo expands its TAM into these lucrative new segments, it is entering territories heavily guarded by capable rivals. The longevity of its moat faces significant threats from key competitive vectors:

The Battle for the Anti-Drone TAM: In the ₹2,500 crore anti-drone space, Tonbo is not alone. They face aggressive competition from established players like Zen Technologies (which dominates anti-drone training and soft-kill simulators) and specialized deep-tech firms like Big Bang Boom Solutions. While Tonbo's high-power microwave technology is unique, these rivals have strong existing relationships with the Indian Armed Forces and are rushing to deploy competing kinetic and electronic counter-drone systems.

Encroachment in Missile Seekers: While Tonbo holds a sole-source contract with BDL today, heavyweights like Astra Microwave Products and Adani Defence are heavily investing in electronic warfare, radio-frequency (RF) seekers, and advanced radar payloads. If these massive conglomerates build or license competing electro-optical seeker technology, Tonbo's absolute dominance in the platform segment could be challenged.

The Microbolometer Trap (Hardware Commoditization): Tonbo designs brilliant software, but the core infrared sensor chips (microbolometers) are imported from a highly concentrated global semiconductor supply chain. If these chips become completely modular and cheap, domestic component manufacturers could purchase them, layer open-source AI tracking software over them, and underbid Tonbo on price.

State-Backed PSU Dominance: Giants like Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) hold immense political capital and distribution power in India. If BEL expands its internal electro-optics divisions via foreign tie-ups, the Indian government may structurally favor the state-owned PSU over a private player for massive prime contracts.

5. Short-Term Volatility: The Immediate Headwinds

While the 3-to-5-year outlook remains promising as their expanded addressable market begins to materialize, investors should expect intense short-term stock price volatility due to concrete financial stresses visible today:

Severe Working Capital Crunch: Tonbo’s working capital cycle has ballooned heavily, meaning its cash is severely trapped in unpaid invoices and rising inventory while waiting for government payouts.

Negative Operating Cash Flows: Despite showing profits on paper, the company has logged negative operating cash flows for consecutive years.

100% Offer For Sale (OFS): The entire public issue consists of existing shareholders cashing out. No fresh capital is coming into the company to clear the inventory buildup or optimize these strained cash flows.

A Cyclical, "Lumpy" Pipeline: Defence revenues are notoriously back-heavy and volatile. Recent geopolitical conflicts in West Asia delayed international shipments, causing an immediate 22.7% drop in their recent annual revenue.

6. Valuation Insight & Critical Triggers for Investors

At its upper price band, Tonbo trades at a premium valuation of ~79x–80x P/E. While this looks incredibly expensive relative to its recent dip in earnings, it aligns with a highly valued Indian defence sector where peers like Paras Defence (~117x P/E) and Data Patterns (~87x P/E) command immense premiums due to pure scarcity of high-tech engineering equity.

This premium valuation leaves no margin for error and assumes that Tonbo will successfully scale its newly validated green shoots to capture the expanded anti-drone and platform TAM. To evaluate the stock post-listing, investors must rigorously track specific structural triggers:

⚠️ Negative Triggers (Leading to Multiple Compression)

TAM Stagnation & Delayed Orders: If the multi-billion-dollar domestic anti-drone or missile seeker market encounters extreme bureaucratic delays, stalling the momentum of current green shoots.

Moat Erosion via Competitor Advances: If Zen Technologies, BEL, or Astra Microwave successfully deploy cheaper, comparable electro-optical and tracking hardware that matches Tonbo's capabilities, neutralizing their technical edge.

Persistent Cash Flow Strain: If working capital days continue to expand beyond current levels, it indicates structural inefficiency in collecting government dues, which will force a de-rating.

Loss of Sole-Source Supplier Status: If BDL or other defense agencies introduce a secondary supplier for programs where Tonbo currently enjoys a monopoly.

✅ Positive Triggers (Validating the Premium Valuation)

Signing of Mega Platform Contracts: If soft orders from organizations like BDL translate into multi-year signed purchase orders for missile seekers, revenue visibility explodes.

Anti-Drone Commercialization: Rapid domestic scale-up and execution of their high-power microwave counter-drone systems, proving that the ₹2,500 crore market opportunity is translating into hard revenue.

International Export Rebound: A normalization of geopolitical trade routes allowing delayed international orders to execute, immediately expanding margins through their high-value ITAR-free advantage.

text:
Dearest Florida friends 

Sharing what JUST HAPPENED

 I stopped by my early voting location in a very red part of Sarasota County today, just to get a feel for things/get some reconnaissance before my volunteer shifts later this week.

I left feeling more encouraged than I have in quite some time. It was a completely different experience from 2024

Across the driveway, Republicans had two canopies and ~ eight volunteers. We had one small canopy and two volunteers.

But here’s what caught my attention.

In less than an hour, at least a dozen people approached our table simply to thank us for being there, offer encouragement, to give us “fingers crossed” or a “flexed muscle sign” or share their thoughts about what’s happening in our country.

Several had just voted. Others were bringing in their completed mail ballots. There were A-LOT of people with their mail in ballot already 

I watched some voters turn down Republican campaign literature and walk over to talk with us instead. 

One woman was particularly irritated after being approached twice by the same volunteer and snapped “you should remember who’s face you shoved your papers in”

One conversation I’ll remember was with a Navy veteran who had served aboard the USS John C. Calhoun. He spoke passionately about military standards, accountability, and his concerns about what’s happening within today’s military leadership and the general direction of the country ( he was a transplant from Atlanta .. LOVES OSSOFF!).

Others came out of the polling place and deliberately veered to our tent to avoid going by the R tent

There were other conversations, too. Unsolicited, thoughtful, and heartfelt.

Whenever I do volunteer, I make it a point to thank people for voting . Bc it’s important . No matter who you vote for , you MUST vote as my Albanian /Greek dad drilled into me .. “ otherwise honey, what happened in my country will happen here”

Now, I’m not going to pretend that one hour at one polling location tells us how an election will turn out. It doesn’t.

But I’ve lived in Sarasota County long enough to recognize when something **feels different.

What struck me wasn’t the number of volunteers or the size of the tents. It was the number of people who made a point of coming over to talk to us and their palpable enthusiasm 

People were engaged. They were grateful. And they wanted us to know it.

I went there expecting to observe.

I came home with a little more hope.🇺🇸

And in this very red corner of Florida, I’ll take that.

🚨 BTC PUBLIC SERVICE ANNOUNCEMENT 🚨

Sometimes it pays to ZOOM OUT and look at the bigger map. 🗺️

Bitcoin is an extremely volatile asset, and too many traders get caught up in the daily chop, which, let's face it, is where BTC spends much of its time. The trick is identifying the levels that actually matter and recognizing when the REAL moves are setting up.

Here are the key levels I'm watching. 👇

📉 BEARISH SCENARIO

text:
“Freedom Beat $100K: The MiG-15 That Money Couldn’t Buy”

In 1953 the U.S. military was desperate. Soviet MiG-15s ruled “MiG Alley,” outclimbing and outgunning UN jets. Communist pilots were ordered never to fly over UN territory so none could be captured.

Operation Moolah offered $100,000 (roughly $1.2 million today) plus asylum to the first pilot who delivered an intact MiG-15. Leaflets and broadcasts flooded the region. No one came during the war.

Two months after the armistice, 21-year-old North Korean Lt. No Kum-sok took off near Pyongyang, pointed south, and flew 17 minutes to Kimpo Air Base near Seoul. U.S. radar was down for routine maintenance. He landed the wrong way on an active runway. Ground crews thought it was an F-86 Sabre until they saw the red stars.

He had never heard of the reward. 

North Korean pilots were banned from foreign radio, and the leaflets missed their bases. He simply wanted freedom.
Eisenhower opposed paying defectors, but the U.S. honored the deal. In 1954 No received the $100,000, put it in trust, and used the interest for college and his family. Chuck Yeager flew the captured MiG in Okinawa. The U.S. publicly offered to return it; no communist country claimed it.

No became Kenneth Rowe, earned engineering degrees from the University of Delaware, became a U.S. citizen, and worked as an aeronautical engineer for Boeing and Lockheed. He taught for 17 years at Embry-Riddle before dying in 2022 at 90. His MiG-15 sits today at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio.

America offered a fortune for a jet. What it got was a man who risked everything for liberty—and proved money cannot buy what freedom inspires.

Have you seen the MiG-15 in Dayton or heard of Operation Moolah?

text:
Yes context is important, but I’d make one correction: 1 Timothy 5:23 itself does not connect Timothy’s wine use with his crying, anxiety over Paul, or Paul facing execution. That part seems to combine passages from 1 Timothy and 2 Timothy.

In the KJV, Paul says:
1 Timothy 5:23 — “Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities.”

The stated reason is very specific: “for thy stomach’s sake and thine often infirmities.” So Paul is recommending a little wine medicinally, apparently because Timothy had recurring physical problems. That actually makes the meme’s point somewhat weaker than it appears: this verse certainly shows that Paul did not regard all consumption of wine as inherently sinful, but it is not simply a general command saying, “Christians should drink wine recreationally in moderation.”

The part about Timothy’s tears comes from 2 Timothy 1:4:
“Greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy;”

And 2 Timothy is indeed written in the setting of Paul’s final imprisonment, when he clearly understands that death is approaching:
2 Timothy 4:6–7 — “For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.”

So Timothy certainly had reason to be deeply distressed about Paul. But Scripture doesn't explicitly say Timothy’s stomach ailments were caused by grief or that Paul prescribed wine because Timothy was crying over Paul's imprisonment. That's a possible reconstruction, but it goes beyond what the text actually tells us.

There’s another interesting contextual detail in 1 Timothy 5. Immediately before verse 23 Paul says:
1 Timothy 5:22 — “…keep thyself pure.”

Then almost as an aside:
“Drink no longer water, but use a little wine…”

That wording suggests Timothy may actually have been abstaining from wine altogether, perhaps out of personal discipline. Paul essentially tells him: don't take abstinence so far that you neglect your health.

So I’d summarize the biblical argument like this:

1 Timothy 5:23 proves that wine itself is not inherently sinful. Otherwise Paul could hardly instruct Timothy to use it. But the verse’s primary subject is Timothy’s health, not Christian liberty to drink socially. For the broader doctrine concerning alcohol, you'd want to combine it with passages such as Psalm 104:15, John 2, Ephesians 5:18, Proverbs 20:1 and Proverbs 23:20–21.

And the distinction Scripture repeatedly makes is rather clear: wine is not universally forbidden; drunkenness absolutely is.

So your instinct about the meme is right: its overall conclusion can be defended, but using 1 Timothy 5:23 as though it were simply a “moderate drinking is allowed” proof-text strips away an important piece of its immediate context.

text:
Bimal Rathnayaka once publicly claimed that wild elephants never damage the property of the wealthy, only that of the poor. He went on to ask the audience, “Have you ever seen a two-story house attacked by a wild elephant?”

This speech by  Bimal Rathnayaka arrives dressed as solidarity with the rural poor, and it leaves having done none of solidarity's actual work. It is a sentence engineered for applause: not for a fence, not for a farmer, and not for an elephant. And that is exactly the political product the JVP has learned to manufacture at the lowest possible cost: a grievance so neatly packaged that it can be forwarded on WhatsApp before anyone asks what, concretely, the party intends to do about it on Monday morning.

Sri Lanka loses more than four hundred elephants and over a hundred and fifty human beings every single year to the human-elephant conflict, the worst such toll anywhere on the planet. Behind every one of those numbers is a specific family on a specific forest edge in Dehiattakandiya, Wasgamuwa, Galgamuwa, Hambantota, Ampara, or Monaragala, where a father sleeps in a tree hut above his chena, burning kerosene and lighting firecrackers through the night so that a single herd does not flatten the season's rice before dawn. His wife counts the explosions. His children learn, before they learn arithmetic, the sound of a bull elephant breaking a jak tree. This is not an abstraction, and it is not a metaphor for class. It is the actual geography of Sri Lankan poverty, drawn in dung and broken fences.

The honest sentence a serious political party would speak is longer and harder to chant. It would acknowledge that successive governments, over seventy years, pushed the landless poor into elephant country through Mahaweli resettlement, dry-zone colonisation schemes, chena regularisation, and quiet tolerance of encroachment; and that no administration since independence has had the courage to redraw those boundaries, fund the Department of Wildlife Conservation at the level the crisis demands, or maintain the electric fences already built. It would admit that the JVP itself, in opposition and now in power, has produced no serious wildlife corridor plan, no credible compensation reform, no managed elephant reserve proposal with a budget attached, and no answer at all to the farmers of Galgamuwa whose claim files have been sitting in district secretariats for longer than some of their children have been alive.

The cheap sentence, the one Bimal Rathnayaka chose, does none of this. It implies, with a wink, that elephants somehow read property deeds and selectively spare the wealthy. It is factually silly, because elephants trample whatever lies in their migratory path, and the wealthy simply do not live in that path, having bought themselves out of the forest edge two generations ago using the very unequal economy the JVP claims to oppose. But the sentence is not meant to be true; it is meant to be shareable. It converts a complicated policy failure, in which the JVP is now a participant rather than a critic, into a simple moral tableau in which the rich are villains, the poor are victims, and the speaker stands on the right side of a line he had no hand in drawing.

This is the deeper trick, and it is worth naming plainly. The JVP's current political economy is not socialism, not reform, and not even administrative competence. It is the industrial-scale manufacture of grievance at the lowest possible unit cost. The method is always the same: take a real wound (and Sri Lanka has no shortage of them, whether it is the IMF programme, fuel queues, fertilizer, the cost of living, the Easter attacks, or now the elephant). Strip out every inconvenient fact, especially those that implicate the speaker's own party or its coalition. Compress what remains into a sentence a village uncle will forward without reading twice. Deliver it in the register of indignation. Harvest the anger. Return to Colombo. Govern, if that is still the word, with whatever political capital the resentment has deposited into the account.

The cost of this method to the party is almost nothing. A tweet is free. A soundbite at a rally is free. A press conference quote is free. The cost is paid elsewhere, and it is paid by the very people the sentence pretends to defend. It is paid by the farmer in Wasgamuwa who hears, from the ruling party, that his misery is a parable about the rich rather than a line item in next year's wildlife budget. It is paid by the elephant that is shot, poisoned, or electrocuted along an illegal fence while the national conversation performs sympathy for the poor without funding either the fence or the forest. It is paid, ultimately, by the idea that politics in this country might one day be about building things rather than naming enemies.

Anger is cheap to cultivate and cheaper still to harvest. Fences, corridors, compensation systems that pay out within a season, veterinary teams, DWC rangers with fuel in their jeeps, and resettlement plans drawn with respect for the dignity of the people being moved: all of these are expensive, slow, unglamorous, and almost impossible to compress into a single quotable line. You can tell which of the two a political party is actually serious about by looking at what it has built, repaired, funded, or staffed in the districts where the elephants walk, not by what its spokesmen say into a microphone in Colombo. By that honest measure, the sentence Bimal Rathnayaka offered this week is not an act of solidarity with the rural poor. It is an invoice sent to them, in their own name, for a political service they never asked to receive.

text:
Think about that for a moment. The woman who had stood beside him through years of uncertainty was apologising for asking a reasonable question.

A few weeks later, she travelled across town to surprise him on his birthday. She had saved money for weeks to buy him a wristwatch he once admired in a shop window.

When she arrived, she discovered he was having dinner with Vanessa and some friends.

Daniel was embarrassed.

Not because he'd hurt Amara, but because she had shown up in a simple dress while he was surrounded by people he wanted to impress.

He took her aside and said, "You should have called before coming."

She looked at him, holding the gift bag.

"I wanted to surprise you."

"I know, but this isn't the right time."

She nodded, handed him the gift, and left.

He didn't follow her.

That night, Amara cried until she fell asleep. The next morning, she sent him a message apologising for making things awkward.

He replied, "It's fine."

Two words.

After everything they had shared, two words were all he could offer her.

By early 2023, Daniel had started pulling away completely. He no longer spoke about marriage. Every conversation about their future became an argument.

One Sunday afternoon, Amara asked him a question she'd been afraid to ask for months.

"Daniel, do you still see a future with me?"

He sighed.

"Why do you always have to make everything so serious?"

"Because I don't know where I stand in your life anymore."

He stared at his phone before replying.

"Amara, I think we've outgrown each other."

She didn't cry immediately. She just looked at him, as if she was waiting for him to laugh and tell her he didn't mean it.

"Outgrown each other?" she repeated.

"Things are different now."

She swallowed hard.

"Daniel, when you had nothing, I never thought you were beneath me. When you failed, I never thought you were a failure. When everybody else doubted you, I stayed. I didn't do those things because I expected you to pay me back. I did them because I loved you."

He looked away.

"I appreciate everything you've done for me."

She shook her head.

"Please don't say you appreciate me. I'm not a favour you received. I'm the woman you said you wanted to marry."

He had no answer.

They broke up that evening.

Three months later, Daniel and Vanessa were officially together.

When Amara found out, she didn't call him. She didn't insult him online or try to ruin his new relationship. She simply deleted their pictures and stopped checking his social media.

But healing wasn't as easy as deleting pictures.

She still remembered his mother's birthday. She still knew how he liked his rice cooked. Sometimes, she'd see something funny and instinctively reach for her phone to send it to him.

Then she'd remember.

They were strangers now, carrying memories that one of them seemed perfectly comfortable leaving behind.

In 2024, Daniel got engaged to Vanessa.

The pictures were beautiful. Expensive outfits, a lovely venue, smiling families, and a caption about finding the woman who understood his vision.

Amara saw the pictures while scrolling through Instagram at work.

She locked her phone, excused herself, and cried in the restroom.

Not because she wanted Daniel back.

But because somewhere inside her, a younger version of herself was still waiting for the promise he made in 2018 to come true.

She had imagined that engagement ring. She had imagined meeting his family in traditional wedding clothes. She had imagined the house they'd furnish together, the children they'd raise, and the ordinary evenings they'd spend arguing over what to eat.

She wasn't mourning just a man.

She was mourning an entire future she'd spent years believing in.

Almost a year later, Daniel reached out to her.

His relationship with Vanessa had ended. They'd had their own problems, and the life he imagined hadn't turned out the way he expected.

His message was simple.

text:
OUT TODAY!
The Complete Kubrick [4K UHD] - Tom Cruise, Nicole Kidman, Jack Nicholson, Kirk Douglas, Peter Sellers, Laurence Olivier, James Mason, George C. Scott, Sterling Hayden, Malcolm McDowell, Ryan O’Neal, Shelley Duvall @Criterion
US: https://t.co/CI66YeTzTb
CAN: https://t.co/4WF4JDzSGw
OUR REVIEW:
https://t.co/1UwunVfIOh
Killer’s Kiss (1955) / The Killing (1956) / Paths of Glory (1957) / Spartacus (1960) / Lolita (1962) / Dr. Strangelove, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964) / 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) / A Clockwork Orange (1971) / Barry Lyndon (1975) / The Shining (1980) / Full Metal Jacket (1987) / Eyes Wide Shut (1999) Criterion
The Masters:

All features are presented in Dolby Vision HDR on the 4K UHD discs and in SDR on the Blu-rays. Criterion’s “About the Masters” notes show that nearly every title was restored from its original camera negative, though the restorations come from a mix of sources. Some are Criterion’s own, some are carried over from studio restorations of recent years, and some were done by partner archives.

The three independently produced early features had their 4K debuts on Kino Lorber UHDs, but here they are presented in masters made for Criterion by Duplitech. Killer’s Kiss (1.37:1) comes from the 35mm original camera negative, with a composite fine-grain used for some sections. The Killing and Paths of Glory (both 1.66:1) are also drawn from their camera negatives. The Paths of Glory mono was remastered at 24-bit from UCLA archivist Robert Gitt’s 35mm magnetic track. Fear and Desire (1.37:1) is the exception: it is Kino Lorber’s 4K restoration, made from the camera negative and a Library of Congress fine-grain. The three shorts are new Criterion 4K restorations from Library of Congress elements. These were 35mm prints and a duplicate negative for Day of the Fight and Flying Padre, and the 16mm original reversal for The Seafarers.

The studio-era films largely use existing restorations. Spartacus (2.20:1) is Universal’s 4K restoration from a 6K scan of the original Technirama elements, with Robert A. Harris consulting, and its 7.1 track was remastered from the 70mm six-track printmaster. Dr. Strangelove (1.66:1) is Sony’s 4K restoration, supervised by Grover Crisp and assembled from a fine-grain master, a duplicate negative and a 35mm print. 2001: A Space Odyssey (2.20:1) is Warner’s 4K from an 8K scan of the 65mm camera negative, supervised by Ned Price and Leon Vitali with input from Christopher Nolan and Hoyte van Hoytema. Its original 70mm six-track 5.1 mix is joined by the 35mm general-release mono, which Kubrick mixed without the overture, intermission and exit music, so those passages are silent on that track. A Clockwork Orange (1.66:1), The Shining (1.85:1) and Full Metal Jacket (1.85:1) are Warner 4K restorations from their camera negatives, with Full Metal Jacket graded against both an answer print and Kubrick’s own personal 35mm reference print.

Barry Lyndon and Eyes Wide Shut match Criterion’s own recent 4K editions. Barry Lyndon is framed at 1.66:1 per Kubrick’s December 8th, 1975 letter to projectionists, and was graded against Vitali’s 2000 HD transfer. Eyes Wide Shut (1.85:1) is presented in its international cut, supervised and approved by cinematographer Larry Smith. Its look stems from Kubrick’s deliberate decision to have the negative force-developed by two stops, which accounts for the film’s distinctive grain and glowing low-light palette.

Two presentations are new to 4K UHD. Lolita (1.66:1) is a new 4K restoration from the 35mm original camera negative, using a Warner 35mm print as color reference, with its mono remastered from the original DME magnetic track. Kubrick’s international version of The Shining (119 minutes, against 144 for the U.S. theatrical) comes from the same Warner restoration of the camera negative, with its own mono track remastered from the original magnetic elements.

Since most of these masters have been reviewed before on DVDBeaver, we have used our existing captures from those earlier 4K UHD releases where applicable. New captures will eventually be taken for Lolita and the international version of The Shining. 

Audio:

Criterion’s audio approach across the set is admirably purist. Every film is offered with its original soundtrack, and for the mono-era titles that means uncompressed linear PCM mono remastered from the original magnetic elements. Paths of Glory’s was remastered at 24-bit from UCLA archivist Robert Gitt’s 35mm track. For Dr. Strangelove, A Clockwork Orange, Barry Lyndon, both versions of The Shining and Full Metal Jacket, Criterion also includes alternate 5.1 DTS-HD Master Audio remixes, so purists and surround enthusiasts are both served. The early independent features and Lolita are presented in their original mono alone. This is a notable step up from earlier editions. Warner’s 4K UHD of The Shining offered only a 5.1 remix with no mono at all, its Full Metal Jacket UHD relegated the mono to a lossy track, and Sony’s Dr. Strangelove UHD carried only 16-bit lossless tracks. The three large-format productions get special treatment. Spartacus is presented in 7.1 DTS-HD MA remastered from its 70mm six-track printmaster, and it retains the overture, entr’acte and intermission music. 2001: A Space Odyssey is the most generous of all, with its original 70mm six-track theatrical mix in 5.1, an alternate 5.1 remix and the original 35mm general-release mono, which, true to Kubrick’s own 35mm prints, is silent during the overture, intermission and exit music. Eyes Wide Shut is presented in its original theatrical 5.1, remastered from the 35mm magnetic track. Optional English (SDH) subtitles are offered on every feature, and the set is region free. From the portions we have sampled so far, the tracks sound exceptional, clean and faithful to their sources, with the dynamic range of the scores and Kubrick’s carefully chosen music coming through with clarity and weight.

About the Captures

Because of the size of this set and its release date, none of the screen captures in this review are taken from The Complete Kubrick discs. Instead, we have included a single capture per film from our earlier reviews, taken from previous 4K UHD editions or, where none exist, Blu-ray. Several of those editions share their restoration with this set, while others come from different transfers. The captures should therefore be taken as representative of each film’s presentation, not as exact reproductions of the Criterion discs.

Fear and Desire is represented by Kino’s 2024 4K UHD, which uses the same Kino Lorber restoration found in this set. Killer’s Kiss and The Killing come from Kino’s 2022 4K UHDs, and Paths of Glory from the 2024 Masters of Cinema (Eureka) 4K UHD. All three of those earlier discs were scanned from the original camera negatives, but Criterion presents new Duplitech masters here, so the grading and framing may differ.

Spartacus is from Universal’s 2020 4K UHD, which uses the same 2015 restoration from the large-format Technirama elements. Dr. Strangelove is from Sony’s 2021 4K UHD, drawn from the same Sony restoration. 2001: A Space Odyssey comes from Warner’s 2018 4K UHD. The Shining and Full Metal Jacket come from Warner’s 2019 and 2020 4K UHDs respectively. Our Shining capture is from the U.S. theatrical version and serves for both cuts, which share the same restoration in this set. Note that both of those Warner discs were framed at 1.78:1, whereas Criterion presents both films at 1.85:1. Barry Lyndon is from Criterion’s own 2025 4K UHD, which matches the restoration in this set.

For Eyes Wide Shut, our capture is from Criterion’s 2025 Blu-ray of the same Larry Smith–approved restoration, as we were unable to capture from that 4K UHD disc at the time. Lolita and A Clockwork Orange are represented by Warner’s 2011 Blu-rays (the latter its 40th Anniversary Edition). Lolita receives a new 4K restoration in this set, so that capture predates it entirely.

OUR PAST REVIEWS:
Fear and Desire, Killer's Kiss, The Killing, Paths of Glory, Spartacus, Lolita, Dr. Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey, A Clockwork Orange, Barry Lyndon, The Shining, Full Metal Jacket, Eyes Wide Shut

Seen together, Stanley Kubrick's films reveal a remarkably consistent sensibility beneath their wildly varied surfaces. There is the dehumanizing machinery of war, from the trenches of Paths of Glory to the War Room farce of Dr. Strangelove and the Parris Island crucible of Full Metal Jacket. There is the individual crushed or remade by institutional authority in A Clockwork Orange and Barry Lyndon, and there are the hidden currents of desire and power in Lolita and Eyes Wide Shut. Running through all of it is an ironic, coolly precise eye that turned every genre he touched, whether noir, epic, satire, science fiction, horror or costume drama, into something unmistakably his own. Watching the arc from the self-financed Fear and Desire and the gritty New York of Killer's Kiss through to the monumental achievements of 2001: A Space Odyssey and The Shining is a privilege few box sets can offer. Criterion's The Complete Kubrick is a staggering undertaking. Its 30 discs (13 4K UHD and 17 Blu-ray) hold every finished film Kubrick directed, all restored in 4K and presented in Dolby Vision HDR, many from their original camera negatives. It includes Lolita's 4K debut, Kubrick's international cut of The Shining, both versions of Day of the Fight, original soundtracks alongside remixes, over twenty-five hours of supplements, and archive-inspired packaging filled with Kubrick's own notes, slates and correspondence. We are still working our way through the set, but everything we have sampled so far has looked and sounded exceptional. This is the definitive presentation of one of cinema's most exacting artists and an essential acquisition for any serious film collection. Set of the Year - our very highest recommendation!

It includes Lolita's 4K debut, Kubrick's international cut of The Shining, both versions of Day of the Fight, original soundtracks alongside remixes, over twenty-five hours of supplements, and archive-inspired packaging filled with Kubrick's own notes, slates and correspondence. We are still working our way through the set, but everything we have sampled so far has looked and sounded exceptional. This is the definitive presentation of one of cinema's most exacting artists and an essential acquisition for any serious film collection. Set of the Year - our very highest recommendation!

text:
Look at the post below.

Yesterday, we reported that Europe’s four biggest mobile operators 🇩🇪🇫🇷🇪🇸🇬🇧are exploring a joint bid to take on Starlink: phones connected straight to satellites, no tower needed.

The replies came on cue: “Europe can’t launch. Europe has no satellites. Europe has no money. SpaceX has no competition. Period.”

We hear this every time Europe talks about tech independence. But are they right? 👇

❌ “Europe can’t launch.”

✅ True, SpaceX launches far more: 165 Falcon 9 flights in 2025. That gap is real.

But even Amazon booked 24 launches on Europe’s Ariane 6 for its own Starlink rival. 
Ariane 6 has already put 100 of its satellites in orbit.

In September, @isaraerospace, a German 🇩🇪 startup, reached orbit. At the same time, Europe’s first reusable rocket prototype is on its pad in Sweden 🇸🇪.

And the @esa has put €900M+ behind a new generation of rockets. That’s more than twice the ~$400M NASA gave SpaceX to develop Falcon 9 and its Dragon capsule.

What will happen to American launchers once these are operational?

❌ “Europe doesn’t build satellites.”

✅ Galileo, Europe’s GPS, is the most precise satellite navigation system in the world. Over 4.5 billion devices use it. Probably yours too.

Finland’s 🇫🇮 @iceye_global runs the world’s largest fleet of radar satellites, which see through clouds and at night.

@Thales_Alenia_S, in Turin, Italy 🇮🇹, built over half of the International Space Station’s living space. It also built the current satellites of Iridium, the American satellite-phone network.

@AirbusSpace, @ThalesAerospace and @LDO_Space  are merging their space businesses into one 25,000-strong champion. And IRIS², the EU’s own 348-satellite network, is moving to full deployment of its governments and defence infrastructure.

If Europe has “nothing”, why are NASA’s astronauts living in it and your phone navigating with it?

❌ “Europe doesn’t have the money.”

✅ EU households keep €12 trillion in cash and bank deposits. That’s more than Nvidia and Apple, the world’s two most valuable companies, combined. Enough to buy SpaceX five times over.

On top of that, Europeans hold $8 trillion in US stocks and bonds. For now.

Because something has changed. Every year, €300bn of European savings leaves the EU. Europe is done watching it go: it has started building a single market for savings and investment, so that European money grows European companies.

Some, like Danish 🇩🇰 pension funds,  have already started dumping US government bonds.

What will happen the day Europe offers a real alternative to American financial markets?

❌ “Europe is years behind on innovation.”

✅ 3 of the last 4 Nobel laureates in physics were born in Europe 🇬🇧🇫🇷🇧🇪. All three did their prize-winning work at American universities.

The world’s first microprocessor, the chip that became the brain of every computer, was designed at Intel by an Italian 🇮🇹: Federico Faggin. Google’s AI lab, DeepMind, was born in London 🇬🇧. OpenAI was co-founded by scientists born in Poland 🇵🇱 and Slovakia 🇸🇰.

Now Washington is cutting research funding, and applications from US-based scientists to the European Research Council have more than doubled. The EU has proposed doubling its budget too.

Europe’s red tape can be cut with a vote. 

Can America win back the trust it has destroyed by threatening, humiliating and insulting its allies?

❌ “Europe needs America more than America needs Europe.”

✅ Look closer.

In April, NASA flew astronauts around the Moon for the first time in over 50 years.

The module that powered their spacecraft, pushed it to the Moon and kept them alive was European, assembled in Bremen, Germany 🇩🇪.

NASA’s Webb telescope launched on a European Ariane 5, so precisely that its fuel should last about 20 years instead of 10.

And the world’s most advanced AI chips can only be made with machines from one company: ASML, in the Netherlands 🇳🇱.

We’ve seen this film before. 

In 1970, American planemakers ruled the skies. Europeans pooled their strengths and built Airbus. Airbus has out-delivered Boeing every year since 2019.

The US just turned 250.

The University of Bologna, in Italy, was founded in 1088, 938 years ago. Europe has been written off many times. 

Those trying to convince Europeans we can’t stand on our own forget who gave the world the Renaissance, the scientific revolution, the welfare state and the World Wide Web, born at CERN in Geneva 🇨🇭.

Betting against Europe isn’t analysis - it’s hubris. 
And that arrogance is pushing European public opinion towards one conclusion: we’re done with America.

One day, those repeating “weak, dependent Europe” will wake up to a Europe running on its own rockets, satellites, capital and talent.

That day is closer than they think. 🇪🇺

text:
The bra makers who secretly built the Apollo spacesuits
In a former girdle factory in Dover, Delaware, women who had spent years sewing Playtex bras and girdles found themselves building the suit that would keep Neil Armstrong alive on the Moon.
NASA had tried stiff, engineered suits from aerospace contractors first, but nothing offered the mobility required for a human body. The International Latex Corporation, the company behind Playtex, won the contract instead, and its seamstresses stitched together 21 layers of nylon, Teflon-coated fabric, and rubber by hand, working to a tolerance of one 64th of an inch on ordinary Singer machines. No automated equipment could be trusted with a mistake that meant the difference between life and death in a vacuum, so the same hands that once sewed Cross Your Heart bras sewed history instead.

text:
A groundbreaking study has demonstrated that bamboo can be successfully processed into a liquid biocrude capable of being refined into usable transportation fuel. Conducted by researchers at Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) in Massachusetts alongside global collaborators, the study indicates that this plant-based alternative could prove highly competitive within the expanding renewable energy sector. 

According to the team's techno-economic modeling, bamboo-derived fuel could cost as little as $2.75 per gasoline-gallon equivalent (GGE) once production reaches a mature commercial scale. This projection accounts for the estimated capital and operational expenditures required to construct and run a specialized refinery. However, researchers emphasize that this figure represents an idealized economic forecast rather than a guaranteed retail price at the commercial pump.

The transformation process relies entirely on hydrothermal liquefaction, an eco-friendly method that uses only heat, water, and pressure without requiring chemical catalysts. In laboratory experiments, the researchers heated bamboo to 572°F (300°C) for a duration of 10 minutes. This thermal treatment successfully converted approximately 35.6% of the bamboo's dry mass into an oil-like biocrude, which can then undergo traditional refining to produce low-carbon diesel or gasoline.

Bamboo offers unique agricultural and environmental advantages over traditional biofuel feedstocks like corn or sugarcane. As a fast-growing perennial grass, it yields massive quantities of biomass annually without needing to be replanted after harvest, drastically minimizing agricultural inputs. Furthermore, the tested bamboo species contained less than 1% ash by dry weight, which significantly reduces solid waste accumulation and operational fouling during refining. 

The study's life-cycle assessment further highlights bamboo's efficiency, estimating that it could match the total energy output of current U.S. corn ethanol production while utilizing a mere 13% of the cultivated land. Additionally, the modeling projects that bamboo fuel produces greenhouse gas emissions roughly 26 times lower than conventional petroleum diesel. This dramatic reduction is largely attributed to the plant's extensive underground rhizome networks, which naturally capture and store substantial amounts of carbon in the soil.

Despite these promising laboratory findings, researchers caution that these benefits must still be validated outside of theoretical models. Transitioning to a viable commercial market will require establishing a highly dependable regional supply chain for raw bamboo, building large-scale processing infrastructure, and ensuring the final refined product consistently meets strict commercial fuel standards. The initial lab work confirms that bamboo can be converted into biocrude; the next crucial step is proving that it can scale into an affordable, low-emission fuel on a global level.

[Woodard, T. M., & Cai, C. M. (2026). Bamboo as a cost-effective feedstock for production of low carbon transportation fuels. *Sustainable Energy & Fuels*, 10(11)]

text:
In the 1975 film “Moonrunners,” audiences were introduced to a Southern family that was known for its quick wit, long drawls and, of course, moonshine. Director Gy Waldron loved Country Music Hall of Famer Waylon Jennings’ narration as The Balladeer so much that he kept the Country crooner in the same role for an inspired television series he was working on called “The Dukes of Hazzard.” Jennings’ voice became integral to the show, including the “Good Ol’ Boys” theme song. text:
That's to say, endorsement from friends don't mean shit.
Israel’s foes have more influence on its elections than its friends
By Jonathan S. Tobin
President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for re-election broke precedent. Or at least, it did in one sense.
Never before had an American president so explicitly and openly stated his preference among candidates for office in the Jewish state. But for all of the huffing and puffing this is provoking among Netanyahu’s political opponents, as well as those Americans in the Democratic Party and the foreign-policy establishment who despise the prime minister, Trump’s statement is far from the first time that an American president has tried to intervene in Israeli politics.

His recent predecessors in the White House did as much, if not more, to try to influence elections in Israel as Trump has now done. Presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden were all very clear about their desire to defeat Netanyahu in past elections. Going back to the distant past before Netanyahu led the Likud Party, President George H.W. Bush also worked hard to defeat then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir in 1992. He succeeded, and the election of Yitzhak Rabin and the Labor-led coalition that year resulted in Israel traveling down the disastrous path to the Oslo Accords.

The Palestinians also have a vote

It remains to be seen whether Trump’s gesture will have the intended effect on the Israeli electorate. But whether or not the boost among voters grateful to Trump for his pro-Israel policies helps Netanyahu win, it’s important to acknowledge that a foreign entity other than the United States has played a far greater role in determining the outcome of Israeli elections. The Palestinian Arabs and their leaders, along with the Islamist regime in Iran and others elsewhere that encourage their intransigence and terrorism, have done more to influence Israeli voters than any American administration, whether it is as friendly as Trump’s or as hostile as that of the elder Bush or Obama.

It’s as simple as this. Had the Palestinians treated the Oslo peace process as an opportunity to create their own state next to Israel, rather than a chance to intensify their efforts to erase the Jewish state, the shift in Israeli politics that enabled Netanyahu’s record run as prime minister is unimaginable.

Netanyahu’s supporters can point to the enormous role that he has played in helping transform the Israeli economy from the socialist model imposed by the founders of the state, who were Labor Zionists. The Jewish state could not have become the Start-Up Nation with a prosperous, free-market First World financial system without the prime minister’s efforts. But his electoral success—he has headed six different governments that ruled for 19 years overall, 15-and-a-half of the last 17 years—is because the Palestinians have always had a decisive say in Israeli politics, especially since Oslo.

Opposing magical thinking

Netanyahu’s place in history is—contrary to the tsunami of criticism that has rained down on him from abroad—the result of the fact that whatever else you can say about him, he has been the main opponent of “land for peace” schemes that have consistently failed.

He has always been different from his opponents on the political left, as well as those who came from Likud, like Prime Ministers Ariel Sharon and Ehud Olmert, in one major respect. Sharon and Olmert blew up the Likud in 2005 to facilitate the withdrawal from the Gaza Strip that led to the formation of the Hamas state there in 2007 and ultimately the tragedy of Oct. 7, 2023. But unlike them or Rabin, Shimon Peres, Ehud Barak, Tzipi Livni or Yair Lapid, who also competed against Netanyahu in elections, he never succumbed to that sort of magical thinking about peace and the Palestinians and their Iranian allies.

Had the Palestinians been capable of paying the price for statehood—living in peace alongside Israel—that they were repeatedly offered by American presidents who opposed Netanyahu, the political history of Israel would have played out very differently in the last 30 years since he won his first term in 1996.

Americans tend to view Israeli politics through the lens of their own expectations and desires for how the State of Israel should behave. But Israelis, like the citizens of any other democratic nation, vote their interests. The majority welcomed Oslo and the hope it brought for peace. Americans and others who blame Netanyahu for the lack thereof and longed for more pliable Israeli leaders, like the opponents he bested in various elections, have acted as if everything the Palestinians have done since then never happened.

Washington versus Bibi

The efforts of the first President Bush to topple Shamir hinged on his insistence on supporting settlement building in Judea, Samaria and eastern Jerusalem. In 1996, Clinton did everything but canvass door to door in Tel Aviv to get Peres elected after the assassination of Rabin on Nov. 4, 1995. Despite Clinton’s great popularity among Israelis, he failed to stop Netanyahu. That was because of a wave of Palestinian terror attacks, coupled with the intransigence of Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, in whom the Americans and many Israelis had invested so much faith in his willingness to make peace.

Clinton had better luck in 1999. His preference for then-Labor Party leader Ehud Barak in the 1999 election was enabled by the perception of Netanyahu’s failures in office and the fact that most Israelis were still willing to give Oslo a chance.

But again, the Palestinians proved to have far more influence over Israeli voters than the Americans. If Barak lasted only a little more than a year-and-a-half in office, it was because at Camp David in July 2000, Arafat turned down an offer of an independent Palestinian state in almost all of Judea and Samaria, a share of Jerusalem as well as the Gaza Strip. Instead, that blood-soaked murderer answered with the terrorist war of attrition known as the Second Intifada, which lasted until 2005, and cost the lives of more than 1,000 Israelis and many more Palestinians. That brought Sharon (who had replaced Netanyahu as leader of the Likud Party) back to power and essentially ended the Labor Party as a major force in Israeli politics.

After Sharon’s withdrawal from Gaza in the summer of 2005 proved as disastrous as Oslo, Netanyahu led Likud, which Sharon had abandoned for the centrist Kadima Party he had formed with some former Labor leaders, back to office in 2009. That and his subsequent victories were again largely the result of issues relating to security and Netanyahu’s opposition to a Palestinian state.

President Barack Obama and his foreign-policy advisers despised Netanyahu and rooted openly for his defeat in 2013 and 2015, even indirectly funneling money via U.S. State Department grants to his opponents. But these efforts failed. And they did so because not even Obama’s tilting of the diplomatic playing field in favor of the Palestinians could persuade them to accept the legitimacy of a Jewish state.

Israelis remain divided on a host of issues, such as forcing Haredi Jews to serve in the army and to support themselves financially, as well as the need to rein in the Jewish state’s out-of-control and all-powerful Supreme Court. Many also blame the prime minister for Oct. 7 since it happened on his watch.

However, Netanyahu’s opponents no longer advocate for a Palestinian state and “land for peace,” even if some of them actually want to return to those failed policies. The anyone-but-Bibi coalition, currently headed by former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces Gen. Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar Party, hopes that Trump’s support notwithstanding, those issues and weariness with Netanyahu’s long tenure in office might lead to his defeat on Oct. 27.

But as long as the Palestinians conceive of their national identity as inextricably tied to a century-old war against Zionism—something made clear by the massacre of 1,200 people in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023—the Israeli right will remain a dominant force. And most of their political opponents will continue to try to appear as if they agree with Netanyahu on the basic questions of war and peace with the Palestinians and other Iranian terror proxies.

Still, the consensus against a Palestinian state and territorial surrenders cannot be broken by American pressure or persuasion. It can only end when the Palestinians and their enablers elsewhere give up the anti-Zionist project, which means nothing is going to change on that issue for the foreseeable future.

An ally, not a vassal state

To acknowledge this is not to say that American preferences have no impact on Israeli voters.

Israelis don’t like being treated as a vassal state, and Netanyahu has capitalized on that time and again, especially when presidents like Obama and Biden sought to force their country into suicidal concessions to the Palestinians or to restrict their ability to defend themselves and to defeat enemies like Hamas and Iran, as Biden tried to do after Oct. 7.

Yet among the top priorities of any premier is maintaining the relationship with Israel’s sole superpower ally, whose security assistance and help on the diplomatic front simply can’t be replaced elsewhere. Manifest incompetence at that task is an electoral liability. Netanyahu’s skill in rallying support at home against American pressure to do things most Israelis oppose is rooted in decisions made by the Palestinians and Iran to stay committed to a war for the destruction of Israel and genocide of the Jews.

If Trump has earned some credit in the view of many Israelis, it is because, by and large, he has acted as if he understood that. And it’s possible to argue that the president’s signal to them will persuade some, especially on the Israeli right, that maintaining the prime minister in office is vital to securing U.S. assistance in finishing the war against Hamas and Iran in the next two years.

That said, nothing Trump says about Netanyahu or the avalanche of opprobrium aimed at him by most Democrats calling for his toppling counts as much with Israeli voters as their understanding that the enduring hatred by Palestinians and Islamists in the Arab and Muslim worlds requires them to keep casting their votes on security issues, rather than domestic concerns.

text:
Some of you sports bettors have absolutely NO IDEA what you’re looking at when you see betting percentages. And it’s costing you money.

Let me teach you something that took me years in this industry to fully understand.

PUBLIC MONEY AND SHARP MONEY ARE NOT THE SAME THING.

TICKETS = The percentage of individual bets placed on a particular side.

HANDLE = The percentage of actual dollars wagered on that side.

Now PAY ATTENTION.

Let’s say 80% of the tickets are on the Cowboys -7, but only 40% of the money is on Dallas.

That means the other 20% of tickets account for 60% of the money. The average wager on the other side is MUCH larger.

But does that automatically mean the professionals are betting against Dallas? NO.

A large wager doesn’t automatically mean a SMART wager.

Sportsbooks pay attention to WHO is betting, WHEN they’re betting, and how consistently certain bettors identify valuable lines.

A respected bettor wagering $5,000 can sometimes influence a line more than an inexperienced customer wagering $50,000.

Now let’s talk about LINE MOVEMENT.

Imagine 75% of reported tickets are on the Chiefs -6.5, but the line moves to Chiefs -4.5.

Most people see Patrick Mahomes and assume Kansas City is the obvious play.

I’m asking WHY the line moved against the popular side.

Was there respected action on the underdog? Did new information affect the market? Was the original line too high?

THAT’S WHAT YOU NEED TO BE STUDYING.

And understand something else. Those betting percentages you see online aren’t necessarily the entire market. They may represent one sportsbook, a group of sportsbooks, or a specific reporting period.

Reverse line movement is a CLUE, not a guarantee. High handle doesn’t automatically mean sharp money.

The goal isn’t to blindly follow the public or fade them. It’s to understand WHY the market moves and whether the odds offer value.

I’ve spent 21 YEARS in this industry, and I’m giving you information that took me decades of experience to learn.

Yet some of you would rather argue, leave negative comments, and dismiss everything I’m explaining instead of actually LISTENING.

It’s amazing how many people who don’t understand the difference between tickets and handle are the first ones trying to tell someone else how this industry works.

I’m sharing this information for FREE because I see people losing money every single day making the same mistakes.

You don’t have to agree with everything I say, but at least take the time to understand what I’m teaching before criticizing it. A little appreciation for someone trying to help wouldn’t hurt either.

STOP WORRYING SO MUCH ABOUT WHO’S WEARING THE JERSEY AND START PAYING ATTENTION TO THE NUMBERS.

You can pick the right team and STILL make a terrible bet because you accepted a terrible number.

21 YEARS OF EXPERIENCE TALKING TO YOU.

This is FREE GAME. Learn something from it.

Retail buyers looking at headline numbers are missing the trap in Note 3 and Note 10 of Cerebras's Form 10-Q. 

To secure OpenAI as a marquee client, Cerebras granted Sam Altman/OpenAI 33.4 million share warrants pre-IPO. Under GAAP (ASC 606), equity granted to a commercial customer is classified as a commercial discount.

It is NOT an R&D or SG&A expense. It is deducted directly off the top line as "contra-revenue":

The hidden risk? There is still $1.13 BILLION in unamortized customer warrant assets sitting on the balance sheet, amortizing through October 2031. Because warrants vest as OpenAI uses compute, the more OpenAI uses Cerebras clusters, the larger the top-line GAAP haircut becomes. Cerebras literally subsidizes OpenAI's compute with its own equity.

Total insider selling has topped $355 million with ZERO open-market purchases since the May IPO. Early venture funds like Benchmark Capital have converted Class B shares to Class A and distributed ~1 million shares directly to Limited Partners, who routinely dump them.

It can and has worked for individual patients and even up to several dozen. The barrier is the pharma companies, not FDA regulations.   

Pharma companies often assert these issues:

1.  "Arranging payment" raises complex ethical and equity issues as Pharma may refuse to offer to only the wealthy who can afford to pay for drug.

2.  Cost reimbursement statutes only cover cost to manufacture, not cost to administer therapy.  Plus "break-even" is not a prosperous biz model such that many shareholders won't endorse and thus many BOD won't sign off on

3.  Some investors only agree to help fund a trial not RTT or EAP

4.  Tech transfer for complex biologics can take months and millions and this tech transfer is not a reimburseable expense under the law.

5.  Personalized biologics exacerbate the cost and manufacturing barriers as they are custom-made for each person.

6.  Big Pharma can "donate" the investigational drug to their patient assistance programs (non-profits) and take the tax-write off, but start up biotechs most often in the rare disease space don't have revenue and no need for tax write off.

7.   Some pharma companies won't allow access as they think adverse events outside a controlled trial population can hurt chances of approval or will increase chances of a hold being placed on a trial.

8.   Some won't allow accesis while a double-blind trial  is going on as they think it's unfair to those on placebo.

9.  If FDA continues to refuse to use real-world evidence from EAPs and RTT to support approval, there is even less incentive for drug manufacturers to allow access.

text:
Ancient wisdom
I was stationed in Germany in the 80s. I was in my early 20s, and I had many German and European friends. Veronica and Ramond, an Irish woman married to a German man, were both politically liberal; Veronica was a stay-at-home mother. Ramond, an English language teacher at the high school. Both were fine with a Mosque in Frankfurt and Islamic centers in their town (Gelnhausen).
Annika = French girl, 24 years old, Home health care worker, Pink and green hair, completely liberal ideology, upset that US forces were in Europe, had Muslim friends, and spoke highly of them.
Fionia= English girl, 23-ish, neon green/blond hair, lesbian, man-hater, trouble-making drunk. Avid leftist ideologies; left England because of warrants over criminal acts while protesting.           Stephan=25, electronics tech, one of the few conservative German Gen Xers I met in Germany. Would only speak against German immigration policy in like-minded company; refused to offend the opposition.
Annette, 23, Stefan's fiancée. A political science major with a full-ride scholarship, an absolute conservative powerhouse. She didn't GAF who she offended; talked publicly and loudly about immigration from 3rd world countries in bars and restaurants like it was a cancer. Called me "Tank" and, on many occasions, thanked other soldiers and me for helping defend Europe. Had plans to immigrate to the US, and boldly said she would leave Sthepan if he didn't like the plan. She told me one night, while drinking beer and Apfelkorn, that Europe was doomed to be invaded, and the government would be the cause. I made the mistake of laughing and told her the US would always be in Europe. She just stared at me like I was retarded.
I still think about what she said and how she defended the premise. The entirety of Europe was a feudal continent from its start; wars filled its entire history. The wars came and went; maps changed and rechanged, invaders came in, were driven out, and other invaders showed up. Europe had a long history of forgetting the bad times when times got good. Annette pointed out that Europe was living one of the longest stretches of peace and prosperity in Europe's entire history. And that peace and prosperity would bring the wolves, as it always had before.
40 years later, European leaders are acting like neutered simps, appeasing and welcoming in some of the same types of invaders their ancestors drove out throughout Europe's history. France, Sweden, Holland, Italy, GB, and Germany's leaders are hollowed-out sock puppets preaching tolerance and unity while the wolves are doing what wolves do.
I left Germany in 1987; Annette and Stephan were still there. I truly hope Annette convinced Stephan to move to the US; I’d even be happy to know Annette left him and moved on her own. Because what's coming in Europe will pale in comparison to the Nazis. The people who cheered on the invasion voted for insanity, assimilation of a barbaric 14th-century theocratic death cult; they should be the ones who live and die by their choices. They used their democracy like a cudgel, beating down opposition in their hubris. “We can change 1400 years of barbarism by giving them a cup of soup and a civil society!”
Wolves thrive in Chaos; they don’t want your civility, they don’t want your cup of soup. Wolves will eat you when you offer them civility, then they will eat your families, and make your territories theirs. And they will mark that territory by pissing on your bones.

text:
🏀 NBA OPENING NIGHT IS HERE.

Here are 10 player prop angles I'm tracking across tonight's Celtics/Pistons, 76ers/Knicks, and Thunder/Spurs matchups.

Opening night is always tricky because the market has to account for new rotations, changing offensive responsibilities, and projected minutes. Historical averages only tell part of the story, and some of the best opportunities come from understanding how a player's role will change this season.

1. Paul George should have significantly more playmaking responsibility in Boston than his historical numbers might suggest. He's expected to operate as a connector and take on point-forward duties when Jayson Tatum rests, while the Celtics incorporate more pick-and-roll actions. George averaged around 10.5 rebounds and assists per 30 minutes during preseason and cleared 8.5 in 16 of 21 games last season with Embiid and Maxey available. Even against Detroit's excellent defense, the rebounds and assists over 8.5 looks appealing.

2. Joel Embiid enters the season with encouraging reports about his health, and his points line at 22.5 looks low if he's playing normal minutes. He averaged approximately 27 points last season when receiving a substantial workload, and he's historically been effective against Karl-Anthony Towns, averaging around 27 points over their last 10 matchups. Even with Philadelphia's additional scoring options, Embiid should remain the primary offensive threat, making his points over one of the stronger looks tonight.

3. Ausar Thompson could see a meaningful increase in offensive responsibility after averaging only around 26 minutes last season. Detroit has emphasized his development as an on-ball creator, and in games where he played at least 30 minutes, he cleared 3.5 assists in 12 of 19 appearances. He also averaged more potential assists against Boston than his season average, suggesting the opportunities were there even when teammates didn't convert. With a projected workload around 30–34 minutes, his assists over 3.5 is worth considering.

4. Duncan Robinson has an interesting three-point matchup against a Boston defense that ranked last in limiting above-the-break attempts last season. That area accounts for a significant portion of his scoring, and against defenses vulnerable to those shots, he averaged roughly three made threes while clearing 2.5 in 16 of 25 games. Boston's added interior depth could change how aggressively it protects the paint, but if the Celtics continue conceding those perimeter looks, Robinson's over 2.5 threes near even money has some value.

5. VJ Edgecombe offers two different angles against New York because his offensive opportunities and defensive responsibilities may move in opposite directions. His points line at 11.5 looks slightly low for someone projected to play around 34 minutes, particularly after averaging approximately 14 points in comparable stretches last season. However, guarding Jalen Brunson should pull him away from the basket and reduce his rebounding opportunities. His rebound chances dropped from 10.2 per game overall to 6.3 against the Knicks, making the under on 4.5 rebounds especially interesting.

6. Karl-Anthony Towns became a major facilitator during New York's playoff run, but his assists line may be relying too heavily on a short stretch of exceptional production. Across the postseason, he averaged approximately 5.8 potential assists while recording 4.9 actual assists, an unusually high conversion rate. Philadelphia should also be better equipped to defend cutters with Embiid available, making the assists under appealing if the market continues pricing Towns based on his postseason peak.

7. Jalen Williams is one of the more interesting opportunities in the Thunder/Spurs game because his recent averages don't fully reflect his production when healthy. In games where he played 30–34 minutes last season, he generated approximately 17 combined rebound and assist chances. Two seasons ago, that number was closer to 19, translating into around 10 rebounds and assists per game. If he's back to a normal workload, the over on 8.5 rebounds and assists remains attractive around -140.

8. Jalen Williams also has an interesting first-quarter scoring line at 3.5 points. He's historically played around seven to eight minutes in the opening quarter, and Oklahoma City could look to establish his offensive involvement early. He doesn't need a big scoring performance to clear the number, making this a reasonable alternative to his full-game points.

9. Isaiah Hartenstein could have an important role defending Victor Wembanyama, which may support a workload around 25 minutes. He collected at least nine rebounds in all three regular-season meetings highlighted in the analysis, and his double-double production improved when he received meaningful playing time. His rebounding props are interesting, but the double-double around +360 could also offer value if he gets the expected minutes.

10. Victor Wembanyama faces a demanding combined points, rebounds, and assists line against Oklahoma City. He averaged approximately 38.9 PRA in 30 minutes last season, while his historical production against the Thunder was around 36.4 in 32.5 minutes. Clearing a line of 40.5–41.5 could require closer to 36 or 37 minutes, depending on his efficiency. That's a substantial opening-night workload against a strong defensive opponent, making the under particularly appealing at 41.5.

The biggest opportunities tonight come from identifying where expected roles and minutes don't match the current market. George and Embiid have strong cases based on their projected responsibilities, while Thompson and Williams could benefit from expanded workloads. On the other side, Towns and Wembanyama have lines that may be asking too much based on historical production and the matchups ahead. With only three games, there's no reason to force action everywhere. The available number matters just as much as the player.

text:
In June 1940, 22-year-old Ben Johnson loaded a dozen horses into a boxcar in Oklahoma. He was working on the Chapman-Barnard Ranch for thirty dollars a month when an unexpected call came from Hollywood. Howard Hughes had bought horses for a film called *The Outlaw* and needed someone to deliver them. Johnson volunteered. Hughes offered him three hundred dollars, more money than he had ever seen at once. After that, Johnson later said, “you couldn’t have driven me back to Oklahoma with a club.”

Hollywood became his new range. He moved horses between sets and doubled for stars including Gary Cooper, Joel McCrea, Gene Autry, Roy Rogers, John Wayne, and James Stewart. His big break came on *Fort Apache*. He was doubling for Henry Fonda when a wagon bolted. Johnson chased it on horseback, caught the lead horse, and brought it under control. John Ford had seen the whole thing and offered him a contract the next day. When Johnson saw he would be paid five thousand dollars a week, he stopped reading, signed, and handed it back.

Over the next years he appeared in several Ford films. He bought a ranch and began building security. Still, at 35 he felt a stronger pull toward rodeo. He took a year away to compete full-time in team roping, honoring his late father who had been a three-time world champion. By the end of 1953 he had won the world championship. He joked that he came home with a championship and didn’t have three dollars.

In 1971 he nearly turned down *The Last Picture Show* because he disliked the language. Ford asked him to take the role. Johnson agreed on one condition: he wanted to rewrite his part and remove the profanity. He played Sam the Lion and critics called it the finest performance of his career. At the 1972 Academy Awards he won Best Supporting Actor. Instead of the speech he had prepared, he told the audience that rodeo cowboys worked harder than anyone in show business and that the championship belt he had won in 1953 meant more to him than the golden statue. The audience rose to its feet.

Johnson remained humble. He appeared in more than 300 films and television shows. Away from the screen he organized celebrity rodeos that raised millions for children’s hospitals. By the 1990s his wealth was estimated at one hundred million dollars. He was inducted into the ProRodeo Hall of Fame and the Western Performers Hall of Fame and received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

On April 8, 1996, he collapsed from a heart attack while visiting his 96-year-old mother. He was 77. Ben Johnson remains the only person in history to have won both a world rodeo championship and an Academy Award. As he once put it, “I’m just a cowboy who got lucky.”
