text:
"Hello, I am Palestinian. 📷

And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." 

Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. 

They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three no's. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. 

Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.

I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

text:
Rudraige and the wider mythological history of Ireland

The Fir Bolg belong to the sequence of legendary peoples who inhabit Ireland before the Milesians, the ancestors of the Gaels in medieval Irish origin literature.

The later arrival of the Tuatha Dé Danann brings a new challenge to the Fir Bolg order, culminating in the Battle of Mag Tuired in the broader mythological tradition.

Rudraige's own story is much less dramatic than that conflict. He is not chiefly remembered for a famous duel or supernatural power. His role is part of the political framework that precedes the later battles.

Rudraige mac Dela is best understood as a regional founder and transitional king in the legendary history of Ireland. His association with Ulster gives him a place in the mythological geography of the island, while his succession after Sláine helps establish the continuity of Fir Bolg kingship.

One especially interesting question is why Irish tradition preserves several legendary figures named Rudraige, with more than one associated with Ulster. That recurring name may reflect older traditions about the Ulaid, but the precise relationship between those figures remains uncertain.

Rudraige offers a useful contrast with Sláine: Sláine inaugurates the kingship; Rudraige demonstrates its continuation through succession and regional authority.

text:
Watch the water. 

The gargoyles are about to be unleashed. Paris has them to protect it. 

People often use "gargoyles" as a catch-all term for all the stone monsters on Paris cathedrals, but architecturally, there is a strict distinction between true gargoyles and chimeras (or grotesques).
1. True Gargoyles (Functional Drains)
What they are: Carved stone water spouts. Their sole medieval engineering purpose was to channel rainwater away from the walls and foundations, preventing moisture from eroding the mortar and stone.
Design: They project outward horizontally, featuring an open mouth and an internal trough that feeds rainwater away from the building.
Where to find them: Integrated into the flying buttresses and upper rooflines (such as along the sides and rear chevet of Notre-Dame).
2. Chimeras and Grotesques (Decorative)
What they are: Purely ornamental statues of mythical beasts, demons, and human-animal hybrids. They do not drain water.
The Notre-Dame Misconception: The famous brooding figures most people photograph—like Le Stryge (the horned, pensive demon resting its chin on its hands)—are actually chimeras, not medieval gargoyles.
History: While medieval churches featured various grotesques, the iconic lineup of chimeras staring out over Paris from the towers of Notre-Dame is largely a 19th-century invention. They were added between 1844 and 1864 by architect Eugène-Emmanuel Viollet-le-Duc during a major Gothic Revival restoration, heavily inspired by the romantic spirit of Victor Hugo's The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Where to See Them in Paris
Notre-Dame de Paris:
Up Close: Climbing the cathedral's towers takes you directly along the Gallery of Chimeras for a face-to-face view with the demons and monsters overlooking the city.
From the Ground: Walking around to Square Jean-XXIII (behind the cathedral on the southeast side) offers the best ground-level view of the flying buttresses and functional gargoyles using binoculars or a telephoto lens.
Other Paris Churches: Look upward at older Gothic and medieval-style structures across the city, such as Sainte-Chapelle or the exterior of Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois, which also feature historical stone spouts and grotesques.

text:
Sergio, I think you're presenting a very selective picture of California and drawing conclusions that extend well beyond the evidence

Let's look at the whole system

California is the largest state economy in the United States, generating approximately $4.25 trillion in economic output in 2025

In that same fiscal year, California accounted for approximately $766.5 billion in federal tax collections, more than any other state

Those federal revenues help finance programs, infrastructure and services across the nation

California is not separate from America's economic success. It is one of its largest contributors

Now, regarding homelessness

There are serious problems with California's administration of homelessness programs. I have no interest in defending waste, corruption or incompetence

The California State Auditor identified inadequate tracking and evaluation of spending. That deserves accountability

But the same audit also identified programs that appeared cost-effective

That distinction matters

Homelessness is a national problem. HUD counted approximately 746,000 people experiencing homelessness across the United States in 2025

California has a particularly severe problem, but housing affordability, inadequate healthcare access, poverty and gaps in behavioral health services are not confined to one state

These are interconnected national challenges

Regarding high-speed rail, the project has experienced substantial delays and deserves serious scrutiny over its costs and management

But claiming the money went toward a train that goes nowhere ignores infrastructure already constructed and the distinction between an unfinished project and a nonexistent one

Accountability requires examining both failures and actual progress

Now consider your central premise

You suggest that distributing private shares bypasses an incompetent government and offers a superior alternative to public assistance

But private wealth transfers and public institutions serve different purposes

One SpaceX share may provide a child with a modest financial asset. That is not inherently bad

It does not provide immediate housing, healthcare, education, food security or the infrastructure upon which economic opportunity depends

Nor does it replace the institutions responsible for protecting those rights and services

I support individuals building assets and financial independence

I also support responsible public institutions, transparency, effective oversight and holding those who misuse public resources accountable

These are not contradictory positions

We can recognize the potential value of private generosity without pretending it replaces functioning public institutions

And we can criticize California's government without dismissing the enormous economic contribution of its people

The same standards of scrutiny should apply to public officials, nonprofit organizations and billionaires alike

What concerns me most is the tendency to turn Americans against other Americans, and states against other states, as though we were competing nations

We are one republic

California's successes contribute to America. Its failures deserve examination, just as failures in every other state do

The objective should be improving the systems we share, not turning their weaknesses into weapons against one another

That requires evidence, cooperation and accountability

Not another division between Americans

The good news? The current roster is entirely capable of pulling them off.

2.  Against Charleston Southern, the tight ends combined for 7 catches and 109 yards. That production should be the baseline. Targeting the tight ends vertically offers high-percentage, rhythm-building throws that can get the ball out of Tate's hands quickly.

3.  Clemson must minimize the penalties and sacks that destroy their down-and-distance sequencing. Right now, this unit is simply not efficient enough to consistently overcome 2nd- or 3rd-and-long.

Every single one of these flaws is correctable with current players and coaches. If Clemson dials them in, we can win this Saturday and every regular remaining regular season game.

-Livestream: https://t.co/ekzwLhhbNa

MANUSCRIPT:
Series:  “1 Cor: Holiness from Messes” #38 
Text:  1 Corinthians 10:25–30
By:  Shaun Marksbury  
Date:  Oct. 17, 2026
Venue:  Living Water Baptist Church 
Occasion:  AM Service

Introduction
If there’s one thing Baptists are known for, it’s food! From potlucks to in-home fellowship times, we typically know how to prepare a meal. Now, this is a skill that’s more important than you might think at first, for even in the ancient world, true fellowship and community formed around the breaking of bread. This could even lead to opportunities to share the gospel with those who don’t know it.

The good news of the gospel transformed how these meals could be enjoyed. For instance, believing Jews could now eat with Gentiles because God tore down the dividing wall. This is one reason why the Apostle Peter was worthy of blame in when he stopped eating with the Gentiles when other Jews came around — Paul said this was “not straightforward about the truth of the gospel” (Gal. 2:14) and hypocrisy (v. 13). The gospel changes both the things we can eat and the people we can eat with, granting a freedom for the glory of God that we shouldn’t ignore. While the concern in this text isn’t primarily Jewish dietary laws, the same freedom in eating connects these issues.

Last time, we began talking about that freedom. Here in 1 Corinthians 10:23–24, we noted that though all things are lawful. Yet, we also noted that we should seek the good of others. That includes the weaker brother who doesn’t quite understand our freedom in the gospel yet, and it also includes the unbeliever we’re trying to reach. And, as we noted last time, our understanding about our freedom should lead us to v. 31, how we might glorify God.

How does that look in the passage before us? Well, there are two sets of commands — one set to eat freely in vv. 25–27, and a negative command to stop eating in vv. 28–30. Because the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord, Christians have a blessed freedom in the Lord to enjoy marketplace food or even food served in an unbeliever’s home.  Nothing placed before us should prompt spiritual anxiety, whether it’s shellfish or a slab of pork that might have been used prior to our arrival in a religious ceremony. It is to the glory of God that we eat, trusting Him when He said He made all foods clean (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15; 11:9) and trusting Him with the what-ifs of the past of food.

The text here says that our freedom is only limited when someone explicitly identifies the food as having an idolatrous history. At that point, we stop. Love for the other person’s conscience and for the gospel’s credibility requires our abstention from food that would have ordinarily been available to us. The same gospel that grants us our freedom should be the cause for which we willingly limit ourselves.

We may face situations like this, so instead of using our freedom as a license to get whatever we want, we must primarily be focused on what glorifies God in the moment. So, we’ll note two ways in which we can do that this morning. First, we will see that we should believe the gospel grants freedom in ordinary settings (vv. 25–27). Second, we will see that we should limit our freedom for the sake of the gospel (vv. 28–30). Let’s consider our freedom and the gospel with the first point:

First, Believe the Gospel Grants Freedom in Ordinary Settings (vv. 25–27)
Eat anything that is sold in the meat market without asking questions for conscience’ sake. For the earth is the Lord’s, as well as its fullness. If one of the unbelievers invites you and you want to go, eat anything that is set before you without asking questions for conscience’ sake.

I’m taking a slight liberty with the text by bringing up the gospel, but the ability to eat here is a gospel result in New Testament theology. Again, we can see Galatians 2 as a parallel to this passage, illustrating that Christians (Jew or Gentile) have a freedom to eat as a result of the finished work of Christ. We might understand on a human level why Peter might have been a bit ashamed to openly eat with the Gentiles when a delegation from James in Jerusalem was investigating this very question, but Paul was correct to call him out publicly.

This conflict was part of the reason the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 was needed. Paul came to Jerusalem with the report of the work they were doing among the Gentiles, and everyone was happy until some Pharisees spoke to the assembly. In v. 5, we read that they said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to command them to keep the Law of Moses.” Of course, the elders and apostles came to a different conclusion in that chapter, but Paul undoubtedly had the seeming Pharisee converts in mind when he said, “false brothers secretly brought in, who had sneaked in to spy out our freedom which we have in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us” (Gal. 2:4). The freedom won by the gospel was at stake.

The Corinthian Christians seemed to have escaped much of the Judaizing ways. The more mature among them understood the freedom they had, though some of the weaker brethren did not yet understand it. Paul might put up some guardrails for the application of this freedom, but he never denies it. In fact, he gives to applications in these verses:

First, Christians Have Gospel Freedom in the Marketplace (vv. 25–26)
This returns us back to what Paul was talking about in 1 Cor 8:7. This is also where the Judaizing Pharisees would have had an issue. They knew a history we might miss: “After sacrificing animals to their idols, pagans would eat some of the remaining meat in the idols’ temples and sell the rest to vendors, who would then sell it in the meat market.”[1] This would have been a violation of the law in their minds.

Yet, Paul delivers a clear command, one that opens the door for freedom: “Eat.” A Christian can go to the marketplace and enjoy it as a bounty that the Lord has given. There is no need for any to be anxious of heart, for it is a blessing from the Lord.

Now, he gives a stipulation here: “Eat… without asking questions for conscience’ sake.” A Christian might be tempted to interrogate the street vendor, asking for information on the spiritual history of the meat, a self-serving question that may come across as hostile to unbelievers.[2] My wife was telling me about a woman who was pounding on the door to the meat department her store at five minutes before closing, demanding they bring out more choices for her; Christians don’t want to come across as such “Karens” for Christ in creating unnecessarily religious tension.

Moreover, this stipulation will help your anxiety more than you know. Sometimes, we ask questions because we want to be “sure.” We want to say we’ve done our due diligence, because we don’t want to be “fooled” into doing something that others can bring against us later. Maybe we’re the weaker brethren, unsure of conscience, so we want to do the “safe” thing by asking questions. Beloved, this is relying on ourselves and not trusting in what God has said.

You might wonder if there is an equivalent application of this today. I read once that someone thought items we buy from the thrift store might carry demons into our homes! You may laugh at that, but there may be similar questions you have. We can’t know everything, and while it’s true that we sometimes fall into preventable errors because we don’t think enough ahead of time, there are questions we don’t need answered. If Scripture says an idol is nothing, and that all food is clean, then why would a Christian needlessly trouble himself with wondering if the food has been sacrificed to an idol? You will be tempted by various “what-if” questions in your spiritual walk, but trust that the word of the Lord above all by not seeking the answers to questions you shouldn’t even be asking.

Look at where the confidence is in v. 26. We read, “For the earth is the Lord’s, and all its fullness” (Ps 24:1). Paul quotes from Psalm 24:1 here, which was what Jews traditionally prayed before eating.[3] To ask about the meat and then try to filter all purchases through a grid of “potentially idolatrous” and “potentially allowable” was to return to the Jewish scruples about “clean” and “unclean” meat and to exercise a lack of faith in what the Lord provides. The Lord owns the whole earth, including the food used in idolatry, and we should eat with thanksgiving rather than worry.

God is sovereign, and the market separates the meat from the temple ritual. The pork or fish is just ordinary food, as its previous religious history doesn’t contaminate it. Asking questions would shrink the available food unnecessarily and risk denying God’s ownership of creation and His good gifts.  Christians need not live with constant suspicion, then, about the religious or cultural history of ordinary goods when that history is not made an issue.

Second, Christians Have Gospel Freedom at an Unbeliever’s Home (v. 27)
Now, I think we have the groundwork for understanding v. 27. This extends the same principle. If it’s okay to buy meat at the market for personal use, then it’s okay to eat meat at someone else’s home, even if it’s the home of an unbeliever. Moreover, if asking questions unnecessarily muddies the waters at the marker, it will at an unbeliever’s home, as well.

This was important for the Corinthian Christians. They still needed to live, and that society valued dinner invitations; a lack invitations meant social ostracization and marginalization.[4] Moreover, Paul had already said he does not want Christians to withdraw from ordinary social contact with unbelievers (5:9–10), and Christians are required to be civil even to pagans.[5] So, ignoring these invitations on the basis of some religious scruple would have been foolish for the Corinthians.

Again, this is a place where the Judaizers would have objected to Paul. The Pharisees cited Exodus 34:15, which warned against cutting a covenant “with the inhabitants of the land,” because they may “play the harlot with their gods and sacrifice to their gods, and one of them invite you to eat of his sacrifice.” They interpreted that to mean it was always wrong to eat with Gentiles because their food might be contaminated by idolatry.[6] Paul isn’t contradicting the Law, because he also forbade idolatry in this chapter; however, clearly, a simple dinner invitation did not necessitate idolatry.[7]

Paul’s advice isn’t different that what our Lord instructed His disciples (Luke 10:8). This would include food that might be considered “unclean” by the circumcision party, and it might also include food sacrificed to idols. Yet, as one writer notes, following liberty over legalism is “using Christian liberty to the Lord’s glory.”[8] Accepting hospitality and sharing a meal is an opportunity for relationship, not an occasion for scrupulous interrogation.

As such, this gospel freedom might even afford gospel opportunities. Yet, those gospel opportunities might impact the choices we make at dinner. That brings us to the next point:

Second, Limit Our Freedom for the Sake of the Gospel (vv. 28–30)
But if anyone says to you, “This is meat consecrated to idols,” do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for conscience’ sake. I do not mean your own conscience, but the other person’s. For why is my freedom judged by another’s conscience? If I partake with gratefulness, why am I slandered concerning that for which I give thanks?

This is where we come to the exception — v. 28 begins with “but,” and Paul issues a negative command in relation to eating. It’s best to read this as a kind of parenthesis in his discussion on freedom, but that doesn’t make it unrelated or unimportant. We’ll note the caution in this text, and then we’ll see how it may affect the cause of the gospel.

First, a Caution that Should Catch our Care (vv. 28–29a)
The identity of the speaker is a big question here. We could assume from the previous discussion in 8:7–13 that this is a weaker brother from your church that has been invited to the same meal.[9] I thought that was what it meant when I first read this, and perhaps that is still the case; this text would then imply that we should value the feelings of the fellow Christian over those of unbelieving host.[10] It is worth potentially offending those outside the church if it means we have the opportunity to love people inside the church. That implication is true, and many commentators hold this to be the proper reading of the text, but there is another interpretation to consider.

The person speaking up to the Christian might be the host himself or even another unbelieving guest.[11] As one commentator notes, “Paul seems to depict the informant as a pagan since they do not use the pejorative term for ‘idol food’ used elsewhere by Paul and other early Jews and Christians, but the neutral or positive term for ‘food offered to a god/divinity.’ ”[12] We might speculate here that this would be someone who may know a Christian is in attendance and is curious about how the Christian will respond to the knowledge that this food being offered to an idol, but it does seem to be an unbeliever.

Now, the Corinthian Christian might be tempted to respond with the same flippancy and self-serving focus that he would to the weaker brother. He might say something like, “It makes no difference to me, as long as the food tastes good!” The unbeliever would walk away with the wrong idea, then, like Christians are not people of conviction or that Christians have no real problem with pagan religion.[13]

Paul requires a different response. He says not to eat it. Often times in these settings, there would be much more food to choose from, so this was not necessarily an offensive gesture to the host.[14] As the Lord provides much bounty, there is no need for the Christian to demand the one disputed food item.

Consider how Paul explains it. This is “for the sake of the one who informed you, and for conscience’ sake.” The “and” is explanatory here;[15] the NLT renders this verse, “out of consideration for the conscience of the one who told you.” This is a moment of service for the good of another, and Christians should be willing to experience a little hunger if it means the advancement of the gospel.

(Some of you are thinking about lunch right now and have an opportunity for direct application!)

In case we thought Paul meant this is to make our own consciences feel better, Paul clarifies in the next verse that it is not about us. We might feel like we’re doing nothing wrong, but once the idolatrous association has been named, the act is no longer neutral.  Eating can appear to the unbeliever like hypocrisy, and that is enough cause for our concern.

This is about protecting the gospel’s credibility, bringing us to the last point:

Second, the Cause of the Gospel Limits Our Freedom (vv. 29b–30)
Paul asks a couple of rhetorical questions here. He asks, “Why is my freedom judged by another’s conscience?  If I partake with thankfulness, why am I slandered concerning that for which I give thanks?” He doesn’t explain what he means, making this a confusing section.

Some think Paul is giving voice to some Corinthian objection, a valid understanding, but it is ultimately a guess that doesn’t quite fit the context. Rather, these questions explain the purpose for his exception to our freedom.  Freedom and thankfulness are good Christian truths, but they must never become excuses to invite an outsider to judge the Christian as inconsistent or hypocritical.

The Christian can alter his behavior without altering his core convictions.[16] As we’ve noted before, he may enjoy a freedom in some contexts and abstain in those which may prove to be a stumbling block to others. Here, Paul is saying it’s far better to avoid causing others to judge and condemn us. And, when the soul of another is at stake, then the Christian should be willing to forgo the steak.

Conclusion
Our freedom in Christ is real and biblical.  Because the earth is the Lord’s, we may receive ordinary food (and ordinary cultural goods) with thanksgiving. And that is glorifying to Him, so we don’t need to walk around with troubled consciences.

Even so, we should gladly limit that freedom when exercising it would give an unbeliever grounds to question the integrity of the Christian or the gospel. Consider Christ Himself as our model: He exercised perfect freedom yet became a servant so that many might be saved. We should not be demanding service; we should seek to serve.

Do all for the glory of God, trusting the good news of the gospel of Christ while seeking to see it spread to those who don’t believe.
------------------------------

[1] Andrew David Naselli, Romans–Galatians, 2020, X, 307.

[2] F. Alan Tomlinson, CSB Study Bible: Notes, 2017, 1826.

[3] Naselli.

[4] Roy E. Ciampa and Brian S. Rosner, The First Letter to the Corinthians, The Pillar New Testament Commentary, (Grand Rapids, MI; Cambridge, U.K.: William B. Eerdmans Publishing Company, 2010), 491.

[5] Matthew Henry, Matthew Henry’s Commentary on the Whole Bible: Complete and Unabridged in One Volume, (Peabody: Hendrickson, 1994), 2263.

[6] Ciampa and Rosner, 490.

[7] Ibid.

[8] John F. MacArthur Jr., 1 Corinthians, MacArthur New Testament Commentary, (Chicago: Moody Press, 1984), 246.

[9] J. I. Packer, Wayne Grudem, and Ajith Fernando, Eds., ESV Global Study Bible, (Wheaton, IL: Crossway, 2012), 1618.

[10] John MacArthur Jr., Ed., The MacArthur Study Bible, electronic ed., (Nashville, TN: Word Pub., 1997), 1744.

[11] John D. Barry, Douglas Mangum, Derek R. Brown, Michael S. Heiser, Miles Custis, Elliot Ritzema, Matthew M. Whitehead, Michael R. Grigoni, and David Bomar, Faithlife Study Bible, (Bellingham, WA: Lexham Press, 2012, 2016), 1 Co 10:28.

Telangana CM Revanth Reddy Offers Prayers at Anjaneya Swamy Temple in Kondareddipalle on Vijaya Dasami

Kondareddipalle, Telangana: Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy, accompanied by his family members, visited the Sri Anjaneya Swamy Temple in his native village of Kondareddipalle on the occasion of Vijaya Dasami and performed special pujas to the deity.

Following the prayers, the Chief Minister received the blessings of the temple priests.

Upon his arrival in Kondareddipalle, located in Vanguru mandal of Nagarkurnool district, Revanth Reddy was accorded a warm welcome by public representatives, senior officials, and a large number of villagers. A rally was also organised through the village as he proceeded towards the Sri Anjaneya Swamy Temple.

MP Mallu Ravi, along with MLCs, MLAs from the erstwhile combined district, and local public representatives, participated in the programme.

The Chief Minister’s visit to his native village on the auspicious occasion of Vijaya Dasami reflected the traditional significance of the festival and his participation in local religious celebrations.

text:
What if barriers between peoples and God proved impossible to cross?

Those once far off draw near through Christs blood as he breaks the dividing wall of hostility.

Strangers become fellow citizens in one household built on the cornerstone of peace.

Discover the unity in Ephesians 2:12-22

Ephesians 2:12: Discovering Our True Home as Fellow Citizens in Gods Household

In the New Revised Standard Version Catholic Edition the passage from Ephesians 2:12 begins with a reminder of past separation and moves toward a vision of profound unity. This text speaks directly to anyone who has felt disconnected or unworthy. It offers a clear path from isolation to belonging within the household of God. The central phrase about fellow citizens with the holy ones highlights how Christ bridges every divide.

How Does Ephesians 2:12 Describe Our Former Separation from God?

The reading opens by recalling a time of alienation. It states remember that you were at that time without Christ being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise having no hope and without God in the world. These words paint a picture of people living outside the promises made to Israel. The text emphasizes that this distance created a sense of hopelessness and exclusion. Yet the verse does not leave readers in that state but sets the stage for transformation through Christ. This section invites reflection on personal experiences of feeling far from spiritual roots. It shows how such separation affects identity and community ties. The analysis reveals a deliberate contrast that prepares the heart for the good news of reconciliation.

What Role Does Christ Play in Breaking Down Dividing Walls According to Ephesians 2:14?

Moving forward the passage describes Christ as the one who creates peace. It reads for he is our peace in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall that is the hostility. Here the focus shifts to active reconciliation that unites former strangers. The image of a broken wall suggests barriers that once seemed permanent now lie in ruins. This part of the text explains that the law with its commandments and ordinances has been abolished to create one new humanity. The result is peace that replaces hostility with shared life. Readers see how this action restores relationships both with God and with one another. The explanation underscores that unity comes not from human effort but from the work of Christ.

How Does Ephesians 2:17 Lead Us into Access Through the Spirit?

The next verses continue the theme of proclamation and access. They note that Christ came and proclaimed peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. Through him both groups have access in one Spirit to the Father. This section highlights the inclusive reach of the message that extends to all people regardless of background. The Spirit becomes the means by which believers draw close to God. The text presents this access as a shared gift that eliminates old distinctions. It encourages a sense of equality among those who enter the presence of the Father. Such teaching deepens appreciation for communal prayer and worship within the Church. The analysis shows a progression from peace to direct relationship with God.

In What Ways Does Ephesians 2:19 Affirm Our Identity as Members of Gods Household?

The passage reaches its peak with the declaration so then you are no longer strangers and aliens but you are fellow citizens with the holy ones and members of the household of God. This statement transforms the earlier description of separation into a new reality of belonging. The household imagery suggests a family structure where every member has a place and purpose. It connects believers to the saints who have gone before and to the living community of faith. The text builds on this by describing the foundation laid by apostles and prophets with Christ as the cornerstone. The entire structure grows into a holy temple in the Lord. This vision offers stability and dignity to all who accept the invitation. It calls for living in ways that honor this shared citizenship and household membership.

The reflection on these verses from Ephesians 2:12 reveals a journey from exclusion to inclusion that remains relevant today. Each section builds upon the last to show the depth of Christs unifying work. The result is an invitation to embrace this identity fully in daily life.

The Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program (WHIP) — a $25 million Department of Justice initiative that offers cash rewards for tips leading to fraud convictions or significant federal enforcement actions.
President Trump and Vice President JD Vance are announcing it today (October 20, 2026) in the Oval Office. Under the program, anyone who submits a tip via https://t.co/GDyPwS4eu7 that results in a fraud conviction or major federal enforcement action can receive up to $30,000. The Justice Department administers it.
The first award is a $10,000 check to conservative influencer/YouTuber Nick Shirley. His viral late-2025 video alleged fraud at Minnesota childcare centers (many linked to the Somali-American community), claiming some appeared inactive while receiving federal subsidies. One woman featured in the video, Fahima Mahamud, later pleaded guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy charges related to inflated meal reimbursement claims. The case drew federal attention, raids, and further investigations amid broader Minnesota fraud scandals (including Feeding Our Future).
This is part of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, established by executive order in March 2026 and led by Vance. The administration has highlighted large-scale fraud, waste, and abuse in federal programs such as Medicaid, SNAP, childcare subsidies, home health/hospice, and pandemic relief, with the White House’s public “Fraud Ledger” claiming hundreds of billions uncovered, stopped, or enforced since early 2025. Tips go through https://t.co/GDyPwS4eu7, which also tracks enforcement actions.
Note that longstanding mechanisms already exist, such as the False Claims Act, which can award a percentage of recoveries in successful qui tam (whistleblower) lawsuits. The new program is a fixed-reward incentive specifically tied to tips that produce convictions or enforcement.

text:
On May 24, 1998, nearly 27,000 feet above sea level, two climbers discovered a woman lying motionless against the frozen slopes of Mount Everest. Her face was pale, her hands severely frostbitten, and her body barely responded to the bitter cold. At first, they thought she was dead.

Then she moved.

As British climber Ian Woodall approached, the woman opened her eyes and whispered words he would never forget.

“Please, don’t leave me.”

Her name was Francys Arsentiev.

She was forty years old.

And just two days earlier, she had achieved one of mountaineering’s most extraordinary accomplishments.

She had become the first American woman to summit Everest without supplemental oxygen.

But now, she was dying on the mountain she had dreamed of conquering.

Francys was born in Hawaii in 1958 and grew up in Colorado.

Her father introduced her to mountaineering when she was young, inspiring a fascination that would shape her life.

She studied business, earned a master’s degree, and worked as an accountant.

Then she met Sergei Arsentiev.

Sergei was an accomplished Russian mountaineer known as the Snow Leopard, a title earned by climbing the highest peaks of the former Soviet Union.

They shared an intense love of mountains.

In 1992, they married.

Together, they climbed challenging peaks, including Denali and Mount Elbrus.

Francys became the first American woman to ski down Elbrus.

But one ambition remained.

Everest.

She wanted to reach its summit without bottled oxygen.

It was an extraordinarily dangerous goal.

Above 26,000 feet lies the region climbers call the death zone.

There, the atmosphere contains so little oxygen that the human body begins deteriorating.

Thinking becomes difficult.

Movement becomes exhausting.

And even simple decisions can become fatal.

In May 1998, Francys and Sergei began their final ascent from Everest’s northern side.

They traveled without Sherpa assistance, a support team, or supplemental oxygen.

After two unsuccessful summit attempts, they tried again on May 22.

This time, they succeeded.

Francys stood on the world’s highest mountain.

Her dream had become reality.

But reaching the summit was only half the journey.

And they had arrived dangerously late.

As darkness approached, the exhausted couple struggled to descend.

They were forced to spend another night high on the mountain, exposed to temperatures around minus thirty degrees Celsius.

Somewhere in the darkness, they became separated.

Sergei eventually reached their high camp.

Francys did not.

He waited.

But when she failed to appear, he made a desperate decision.

He gathered oxygen and medicine and climbed back toward the summit to find his wife.

He knew the danger.

He went anyway.

It was the last time anyone saw him alive.

Meanwhile, an Uzbek climbing team discovered Francys struggling near 27,000 feet.

She was barely able to stand.

Her face and hands were frozen.

She was exhausted, confused, and dangerously weak.

The climbers tried to help.

They gave her oxygen.

Attempted to warm her limbs.

And struggled to move her downhill.

But carrying another person at that altitude requires strength the human body can barely produce.

Their oxygen supplies were running low.

Eventually, they faced an unbearable decision.

Remain and risk dying beside her.

Or descend while they still could.

They left Francys secured to the climbing rope.

On their descent, they encountered Sergei heading upward.

He was searching for his wife.

The following morning, Ian Woodall and Cathy O’Dowd found Francys still alive.

Sergei’s equipment lay nearby.

He had apparently reached her, but something had gone terribly wrong.

Woodall and O’Dowd abandoned their summit attempt immediately.

For more than an hour, they tried to save her.

They offered oxygen.

Spoke reassuringly.

And attempted to lift her from the snow.

But Francys was almost completely helpless.

Her body seemed frozen into the mountain itself.

She begged them not to leave.

“Please, don’t leave me alone.”

Those words pierced through the cold.

They wanted desperately to rescue her.

But their own oxygen was disappearing.

They could not carry her.

And remaining much longer would likely kill them too.

Eventually, they had to walk away.

Francys Arsentiev died on Everest, alone in the snow.

She had reached the summit without oxygen.

But she never returned home.

In 1999, climber Jake Norton discovered Sergei’s body lower on the mountain.

He had fallen while attempting to rescue his wife.

Their eleven-year-old son, Paul, was left without either parent.

For nine years, Francys remained visible beside Everest’s climbing route.

The freezing temperatures preserved her body.

Climbers passing through began calling her Sleeping Beauty.

She became a haunting landmark.

A reminder that reaching the summit means nothing if you cannot survive the descent.

But Ian Woodall never forgot the woman who had begged him to stay.

In 2007, he returned to Everest for a different mission.

Not to reach the summit.

But to restore her dignity.

He located Francys’s remains, wrapped her in an American flag, and moved her away from the main climbing route.

At last, she could rest beyond the gaze of passing climbers.

Everest has claimed hundreds of lives.

Many remain frozen where they fell.

But Francys Arsentiev’s story carries a particularly heartbreaking lesson.

She achieved her greatest dream.

Her husband sacrificed his life trying to bring her home.

And strangers risked their own survival attempting to save her.

Yet none of it could overcome the brutal conditions of the death zone.

The mountain offered no mercy.

Not for ambition.

Not for courage.

Not even for love.

And nearly three decades later, four simple words still capture the tragedy of the woman remembered as Sleeping Beauty.

“Please, don’t leave me.”

text:
My name is Daniel Reed. I’m 35, a mechanic from Ohio, and I’d never been arrested in my life.

But the photograph showed a teenage boy standing outside a burned-down building.

He had my face, my eyes, even the small scar beneath my left eyebrow.

The officer introduced himself as Sheriff Collins. He said the boy had disappeared after a fire at an old children’s home called Pine Hollow.

Twelve people had died that night.

The boy had been the only missing resident.

I told the sheriff my childhood records could prove I grew up in Ohio. I even offered to call my mother.

He shook his head.

“Your mother died six years ago, Daniel. We already checked.”

My stomach tightened.

My mother had told me very little about my early childhood. She always said she’d adopted me as a baby and that the paperwork had been lost in a house fire.

I’d never questioned her.

The sheriff asked me to come to the station voluntarily.

I agreed because I wanted answers.

Inside his office, he showed me an old newspaper clipping. The headline read:

LOCAL CHILD SUSPECTED OF STARTING DEADLY FIRE

Beneath it was the same photograph.

I looked at the date.

October 18.

My birthday.

Then the sheriff opened a second file.

“This case was reopened last week,” he said. “Someone mailed us a letter claiming the missing boy was still alive.”

He turned the letter toward me.

There were only seven words written inside.

“Daniel Reed is not the boy’s real name.”

- Macro: +1.3% for September PPI (producer price index), the biggest rise since March 2022; 89% odds of a rate hike by 9 December; Brent crude at $109.86 a barrel on 16 October, after a missile hit Aramco
- US spot ETF net flows: net outflows across all cryptos, notably ETH (-$320M), BTC (-$237M) and SOL (-$28M).
- Stocks: -4.5% for the Nasdaq over the week to 16 October, its worst week since June; chip stocks slid after Broadcom's CEO compared AI investors to casino gamblers.
- Sectors: 0 out of 8 sectors finished green, only 24 of 298 tokens were up; universe median at -12.7% versus -2.0% for Bitcoin; blockchain tokens held up best with a median of -10.9% (-3.1% cap-weighted). Bitcoin dominance: 60.1%, up 0.5 points. Not a single DePIN or RWA token rose; the largest coins lost the least, while the smaller ones took most of the damage.
- Top performers: ICNT led with +84.0% ($47M market cap, volume up 17.3x), followed by PUFFER, ALEO, UMBRA and ELSA; on the downside, NEON dropped 67.3% (fourth straight losing week) and STRK 50.9% after its announced token unlock, followed by BLUR, BOME and W
- Calendar: Wednesday, Lagarde speaks in Wiesbaden, eight days before the ECB's 29 October decision; Wednesday, Tesla and Meta report after the US close, in a market shaken by the selloff; Friday, US services PMI, the week's main event (forecast 57.9 after 58.8); Friday, euro area composite PMI (forecast 50.6 after 53.1, above 50 still means growth)

🟢 Why is gold back?
- Debasement, dedollarisation, diversification, and what does sound money look like today?
- Sound money: money that politicians can't print at will; in 1871, Menger explains that money comes from markets, not decrees; in 1944, Bretton Woods pegs the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce; in 1971, the US ends that link and the fiat era begins; in 2025, Texas recognises gold and silver as legal tender; an ounce of gold went from $35 in 1971 to $4'177 on 1 October 2026: gold didn't change, the dollar did.
- Purchasing power: the dollar has lost 87% of its value since its convertibility to gold ended in 1971; a 1971 dollar is now worth only about 13 cents ($0.49 around 1980, $0.24 around 2000, $0.13 in 2024).
- The debasement trade: record government debt, deficits funded by new money, rates held below inflation, savers quietly losing value, and capital moving to what can't be printed; US debt passed $39 trillion in March 2026; it stands at around 125% of GDP in 2025, up from under 60% in 2000; the dollar has lost more than 20% of its purchasing power since January 2020.
- Gold in your currency: even the Swiss franc has lost 95% against gold; since 1971, gold is up 207x in pounds (10.2% a year), 117x in dollars (9.0% a year), 53x in euros (7.5% a year) and 21x in Swiss francs (5.7% a year); in 2025 alone, gold gained +67% in dollars, +56% in pounds, +48% in euros and +46% in francs.
- The practical question: you can't spend a gold bar; two modern answers, Bitcoin, with supply fixed by code, and tokenised gold, physical gold that moves on-chain; unlike bullion (dealer hours, settlement in days, delivery in hand) and gold ETFs (market hours, T+2 settlement, no delivery for retail), tokenised gold trades 24/7/365, settles in seconds and can be delivered from 1 gram.
- DGLD, now available on SwissBorg: tokenised Swiss gold right in the app; on-chain co-ownership of allocated Swiss gold, issued by Gold Token SA, part of MKS PAMP; 1 token corresponds to 1 fine troy ounce; every bar can be verified one by one on the Gold Mapper; physical delivery from 1 gram; native on Solana.

🟢 Product update: Top Borgers Bundle
- New community-chosen allocation for the Top Borgers Bundle: BTC 16% (+2 pts), ETH 14% (+1 pt), BORG 13% (unchanged), JitoSOL 11% (unchanged), HYPE 10% (+1 pt), AAVE 8% (-1 pt), LINK 8% (unchanged), BNB 7% (-2 pts), XRP 7% (-1 pt), SUI 6% (unchanged).

🟢 Product update: New listings
- Three new tokens now available:
- CT (Concrete, Ethereum, DeFi): "Institutional grade on-chain infrastructure. Generate yield for any asset. On any chain."; the governance token of Concrete, an on-chain yield vault platform built by Blueprint Finance.
- GTC (Gitcoin, Ethereum, Infrastructure): "Fund What Matters"; the governance token of Gitcoin, which funds open-source and public-goods projects through community grants.
- XDP (Doppler Finance, Base, DeFi): "Rebuilding Capital Markets for the Tokenized Era"; the utility and governance token of Doppler Finance, a yield protocol originally built for XRP holders.

🟢 Guardians App
- Guardians App stats: 960 Guardians, 1'014 quests completed over the last 7 days, 25'233 BORG awarded in total.
- Coming in November: meetup enhancements and an XP rank boost on chests, and possibly a "learn and earn", a merch drop with Nomu and a Founder's Bundle dashboard?

🟢 Crypto custody
- Custody explained: who holds your crypto? How custody works at SwissBorg and how it protects your assets.
- Two valid ways to hold crypto: recent hardware wallet news has many people asking whether their crypto is where it should be, and the answer depends on which responsibilities you want to keep; with self-custody, you hold the keys and look after the device, its origin and the recovery phrase; with regulated custody, a licensed custodian holds them, and you look after your login and phone while setting your own withdrawal controls.
- With a hardware wallet, the maintenance is on you: buy only genuine hardware from official channels; set it up yourself and reject any pre-set recovery phrase; install firmware updates only from the official app and site; check every transaction on the device screen; store the recovery phrase offline, safe from fire and loss; spot phishing that impersonates the manufacturer; plan how someone could inherit it.
- With SwissBorg custody, running the systems is their job: BlockNodes operates the MPC infrastructure, keeps keys inside approved systems and reconciles balances, under AMF supervision; your part is to update the app from the official store, choose a strong passcode and set your withdrawal delay.
- Side by side: with self-custody, you hold the keys via a device and recovery phrase, while at SwissBorg BlockNodes SAS holds them using MPC; you look after the device, its origin, its firmware and the phrase, versus just your phone, passcode and app updates; if you lose the phrase or device, funds may be unrecoverable, while at SwissBorg there is no seed phrase and a checked recovery restores access; anyone with the phrase can move funds at once, versus the device key plus your passcode, then your chosen delay; self-custody isn't a regulated service, while SwissBorg holds MiCA authorisation A2026-011 from the AMF; finally, you rely on yourself and your supplier, versus BlockNodes, its systems and partners.
- SwissBorg: four layers between your crypto and anyone else: your device, only your authorised phone can act and a new one goes through a checked recovery; your SwissBorg passcode, separate from your phone's, needed to sign in and withdraw; your delay, Withdrawal Protection holds crypto withdrawals for 1 to 180 days and no one can override it; their custody, MPC key management, segregated assets and a MiCA-authorised custodian.

text:
There is a reason buyers pay on close, not on intro.

Labs only pay data vendors for data that passes their own quality review, and that review takes 30 to 60 days after delivery. The risk sits on the data company during that window.

Pewter passes that structure to owners in the form it was designed for. We get paid when the deal closes. Owners pay nothing out of pocket. If the deal doesn't close, no one owes anyone anything.

This is not the standard structure in most industries where someone helps you sell something. It is the structure the AI data market created out of necessity, and it happens to be the right structure for owners who want to understand their options without taking on exposure.

One conversation, one estimate, one written offer if the numbers work. No retainer, no upfront cost, no commitment until the paperwork is signed.

text:
Book Review: Where the Crawdads Sing by Delia Owens

★★★★★ – 5/5

What an absolutely wonderful book! Where the Crawdads Sing is one of those rare novels that completely draws you in from the very first pages and stays with you long after you’ve finished reading it.

Set in the breathtaking marshlands of North Carolina, Delia Owens tells the extraordinary story of Kya Clark, a young girl abandoned by her family and left to survive on her own. Known to the locals as the “Marsh Girl”, Kya grows up surrounded by nature, finding friendship, comfort and wisdom in the world around her.

I absolutely loved Kya! What a remarkable character. Her courage, independence, intelligence and determination are truly inspiring. Despite everything life throws at her, she never loses her connection with the natural world or her ability to love and hope. You cannot help but admire her and wish her happiness.

Delia Owens’ writing is simply beautiful. Her descriptions of the marshes, wildlife and changing seasons are so vivid that you feel as though you are right there beside Kya. The landscape almost becomes a character in its own right. There is something wonderfully peaceful and magical about the way Owens brings nature to life.

But this book offers so much more than beautiful scenery. It is a captivating mixture of love story, coming-of-age novel and murder mystery, all woven together brilliantly. There are moments of great tenderness, heartbreak, happiness and suspense. I found myself completely emotionally invested in Kya’s journey.

What I particularly loved was the underlying message about prejudice, acceptance and the importance of looking beyond appearances. Kya may have been rejected by society, but she possesses a wisdom, sensitivity and strength of character that many of those judging her could only dream of.

And what an ending! Absolutely brilliant! I certainly didn’t see everything coming, and it made an already wonderful story even more memorable.

Where the Crawdads Sing is a beautifully crafted, deeply touching and thoroughly enjoyable novel. It made me smile, feel sad, hope for the best and, above all, appreciate the extraordinary resilience of the human spirit.

I loved every minute of this book! A wonderful combination of beautiful storytelling, unforgettable characters, romance, mystery and the magic of nature.

One of the most enjoyable and memorable books I’ve read in quite some time. I cannot recommend it highly enough!

An absolute gem of a novel!

text:
Pittsboro Planning Board Meeting Summary — October 19, 2026

### Key Highlights and Decisions

- 🏛️ **Meeting called to order:** The Pittsboro Planning Board held its regular meeting on Monday, October 19, 2026. Members confirmed a quorum and unanimously approved the agenda and previous meeting minutes.

- 👤 **New planning director introduced:** Kevin Lewis officially introduced himself as Pittsboro's new planning director. Lewis previously worked for the Town of Knightdale for seven years and expressed enthusiasm about improving planning procedures, communication and development reviews.

- 📋 **Major overhaul of development regulations planned:** Pittsboro has issued a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) for a comprehensive update of its Unified Development Ordinance (UDO). Work is expected to begin in early 2027, with extensive Planning Board involvement and public workshops.

- 🌳 **Conservation subdivision ordinance coming in November:** The Planning Board expects to review proposed changes to the conservation subdivision ordinance at its November meeting. A draft is already available on the town's website.

- 👥 **Planning Department staffing vacancies:** Two positions are vacant, both replacements rather than new positions. Lewis indicated the town hopes to receive an accepted offer for a Planner I position soon.

### Development Review and Public Participation

- 🏘️ **Moving away from piecemeal zoning changes:** Lewis explained that previously discussed individual UDO amendments have been paused so their recommendations can be incorporated into the broader ordinance overhaul.

- 🔎 **Greater transparency for development proposals:** Lewis wants the town's interactive development map to include pending development applications, not just approved projects. This would allow residents to learn about proposals earlier.

- 📢 **Concerns about insufficient public notice:** Board members questioned whether residents have enough time to review development proposals when detailed information becomes available only shortly before Planning Board meetings. Lewis acknowledged the concern and supported earlier disclosure.

- 🏗️ **Development review can take six months to a year:** Lewis explained that applications typically undergo multiple rounds of technical review and revision before reaching the Planning Board. He wants proposals to be substantially complete before they are presented.

- ⚠️ **Reducing conditional approvals:** Board members expressed frustration with development recommendations containing numerous unresolved conditions. Lewis agreed that lengthy lists of conditions can create confusion, complicate enforcement and allow important requirements to fall through the cracks.

- 🤝 **Developers must agree to additional conditions:** Lewis clarified that Planning Board members can propose conditions intended to protect public health, safety and welfare, but applicants must agree to those conditions for them to become enforceable.

- 🚗 **Traffic safety must receive attention:** Members cited a previous rezoning proposal along U.S. 15-501 near Powell Place, questioning whether developers should provide preliminary traffic circulation information before receiving favorable recommendations.

- 📊 **Better documentation expected:** Lewis emphasized that staff should provide clearer recommendations, explain unresolved issues and ensure Planning Board members have sufficient information to evaluate projects.

### Planning Board Authority and Responsibilities

- ⚖️ **Planning Board serves an advisory role:** Lewis reviewed North Carolina General Statutes Chapter 160D, explaining that the Planning Board makes recommendations while the Pittsboro Board of Commissioners retains final decision-making authority.

- 📚 **Recommendations must connect to adopted plans:** Board members were encouraged to base their findings on the town's Future Land Use Plan, transportation policies, infrastructure priorities and other adopted planning documents.

- 📝 **More detailed advisory statements encouraged:** Lewis provided examples showing how zoning recommendations should explain consistency or inconsistency with adopted plans, rather than relying on vague conclusions or unsupported objections.

- 🗣️ **Planning Board should not simply rubber-stamp staff recommendations:** Lewis encouraged members to question staff conclusions, develop independent recommendations and propose alternative advisory statements when appropriate.

- ⏳ **Board can postpone decisions:** Members confirmed they can table proposals when additional information is necessary. However, state-law procedures can allow applications to advance to commissioners without a Planning Board recommendation after the applicable review period. Lewis cited a possible 60- or 90-day period but did not confirm the precise deadline.

- 📞 **Staff available for individual consultations:** Lewis offered to meet with board members to answer questions before meetings. He encouraged members to raise important questions again during public meetings so everyone receives the same information.

### Upcoming Planning Initiatives

- 🏙️ **Downtown master plan beginning:** Pittsboro is launching a downtown master planning initiative, with Theresa Thompson leading the effort. The Planning Board will receive updates and participate in reviewing the resulting plan.

- 🚦 **Transportation plan needs modernization:** Lewis identified updating Pittsboro's Comprehensive Transportation Plan as a priority, noting that the existing document is more than 10 years old.

- 🌱 **Planning emphasizes responsible growth:** Lewis described the town's planning priorities as protecting public health and safety, preserving community character, safeguarding natural resources and coordinating development with infrastructure investments.

- 🏡 **Housing variety and infrastructure capacity:** The presentation emphasized evaluating development proposals based on housing diversity, neighborhood compatibility and whether water, sewer and transportation systems can accommodate future growth.

- 📅 **Earlier agenda communication promised:** Lewis wants Planning Board members to receive advance notice of upcoming agenda items, more complete supporting documents and opportunities to request additional information or training.

### Meeting-Specific Developments

- 🚫 **Development application withdrawn from the agenda:** Lewis explained that an applicant requested removal of a development proposal after staff initially recommended denial. The applicant wanted additional time to revise the proposal and potentially obtain a favorable recommendation with fewer conditions.

- 🪑 **Possible Planning Board membership changes:** One member's term expires in December and may be renewed. Another extraterritorial jurisdiction (ETJ) representative appointment requires action by the Chatham County Board of Commissioners. A new member could potentially join in December.

- 🎓 **Training focused on better decision-making:** Much of the meeting consisted of a presentation explaining planning laws, staff responsibilities, development review procedures, legally supportable recommendations and ways board members can participate more effectively.

- 🗺️ **More follow-up on commissioner decisions:** Lewis wants to inform Planning Board members about final actions taken by the Board of Commissioners, including when recommendations are accepted, modified or rejected.

- 🗳️ **No development approvals:** The meeting included no action items, and the board did not vote on any rezoning or development applications.

- 🎤 **No public comments:** No residents signed up to speak during the public comment period.

- 👻 **Downtown Spirit Tour mentioned:** During board comments, members discussed the upcoming downtown Spirit Tour, scheduled for October 23–25. Participants indicated tickets might be sold out, although a waiting list and possible last-minute openings were mentioned.

- ✅ **Meeting adjourned:** Following the training presentation and brief board comments, members voted to adjourn.

### 🔍 Overall Takeaway

- 🏛️ A new direction for Pittsboro's Planning Department: The October 19 meeting signaled Kevin Lewis' intention to improve development review procedures, strengthen communication between staff and the Planning Board, and provide residents with earlier access to development information.

- 🚧 Significant planning changes lie ahead: The comprehensive UDO overhaul, conservation subdivision revisions, downtown master plan and transportation plan update could influence Pittsboro's development patterns, infrastructure investments and neighborhood character for years to come.

- 📣 The central issue is transparency and accountability: Board members repeatedly emphasized the importance of receiving complete development proposals, understanding traffic and safety implications, minimizing unresolved conditions and giving residents meaningful opportunities to participate before recommendations are forwarded to elected commissioners.

- ⭐ Most important item: Pittsboro's new planning director is promising a more transparent, thorough and predictable development review process at a time when the town is preparing major revisions to the regulations governing future growth.

text:
"I'm talking about brand loyalty and the influence that comes from giving millions of families a financial stake in one company."

Yet brand loyalty among 30+ million families does nothing to make them reject other entrepreneurs. It simply keeps them less accepting of the "damn the rich" agrarian culture fallacies that hold back the continuing industrial revolution. If there are problems with it causing exclusion of others than SpaceX, then the obvious solution would be to have *many*companies* CEOs doing what Musk is doing, and as soon as possible.

"Lockheed Martin was developing reusable spacecraft technology with NASA back in the 1990s."

Yes, and the X-33 contract was handed to them within a week of Lock/Mart becoming the largest corporate donor to the 1996 Clinton/Gore campaign. It was handed to them over the objections of the 2 guys sitting in NASA HQ's basement, doing the tradeoffs between Lock/Mart and the Boeing/McDonnel Douglas proposals. I talked to them at the 2000 Space & Robotics Conference. A "Young Lady" from OSTP (run under Al Gore's resposibility) visited them. She made it plain that it was *not* to be the Delta Clipper X-33 proposal, because it had a military development heritage. Of course, at that stage in the competition, that left exactly one alternative.

I suppose no one had told her where the development took place for the engines of the airliner she had flown into her job in the Beltway on, from Stanford.

"I appreciate innovation and philanthropy, but shouldn't we also question how this affects competition and opportunities for the next great American entrepreneur?"

Why yes, we should, in both good and bad. In the good side, this policy can allow entrepreneurs to get a starting nest egg. In the bad, if government demands more corporate vassals, like Lock/Mart and Boeing, whose large employments can provide many dependent voters to political hierarchs, then entrepreneurs' chances will be diminished. One of the advantages of the share dispersal stratagem is that Musk has followed a policy of development keeping ahead of Congress' funding offers, and will need them less.

It is quite possible this will be a major shift forward in the continuing industrial revolution, in that SI will be making it cheaper to design and develop technology, at the same time that more people have assets to invest in doing that development. The competent definition of the continuing industrial revolution describes the process:

“When a society moves from allocating resources by custom and tradition  to allocating   resources by markets, they may be said to have undergone an industrial revolution”  Arnold Toynbee-1884-
Note: In Toynbees’ lifetime the term “custom and tradition” was still a polite euphemism for agrarian culture local Politics.

In moving farther into the continuing industrial revolution, all participants in market networks will become richer, and more able to invest. The down sides all have to do with political hierarchies regaining their growth that became visible during the waves of reaction against market networks during the 20th century. It is long past time to let the old cultures die out, and continue inventing the industrializing cultures of the future, without the "custom and tradition" of political hierarchies so typical of the agricultural revolution.

We have a great deal of invention and trial ahead of us, likely over the next several centuries

text: “Transparency” by Oliver R: an apparition at the threshold of the visibleWith Transparency, Oliver R extends and deepens one of his most fertile intuitions: the kaleidoscope as a mental space rather than a mere backdrop. After Doll K, in which a figure from the Dolls collection already conversed with a floral and chromatic explosion, the artist tightens the motif. The kaleidoscope is no longer a scattered field of colors; it contracts, deepens, and becomes a tunnel.The background is now bichrome: deep blue and burning orange. Perspective turns it into a hypnotic corridor, a succession of petals or scales receding toward a central point. We are no longer facing a decorative pattern, but inside an optical device. The gaze is drawn in. The kaleidoscope ceases to be an object one turns in one’s hands; it becomes a passage. At the center of this vortex appears a creature immediately recognizable as one of Oliver R’s Dolls — those hybrid beings, halfway between a luxury collectible doll, a Parisian department-store mannequin, and an animated character. Yet she is not sharp. She is an apparition. Her presence hovers at the edge of transparency, as if the tunnel both revealed and dissolved her. She does not fully occupy the space: she haunts it.Seated cross-legged, in a pose at once meditative and ceremonial, she wears a jumpsuit with dense blue and red patterns, almost like tapestry. On her head, a red headdress hesitates between turban and veil. Earrings, a necklace of red beads, red slippers: red returns as a connecting thread, both ornamental and ritual. On her right hand, a tattoo remains hard to decipher — a discreet, almost private sign that anchors the figure in a story the viewer will never be able to read completely.The eyes are closed. The nose and mouth are fine. The face does not express absence, but concentrated inwardness. Unlike many previous Dolls, often frozen in a wide, slightly uneasy gaze, this one has withdrawn. She does not look at us. She is elsewhere, or more deeply here.The title Transparency is not incidental. It resonates with the theme of a contemporary exhibition devoted to the interplay of light, layers, and perception. Oliver R does not treat transparency as a merely optical quality. He makes it an existential condition of his Dolls. These figures have always oscillated between object and living being, between artificial perfection and a nearly human emotion. Here, that oscillation becomes literal: the creature is both fully present and already fading into the pattern that surrounds her.The blue-and-orange kaleidoscope is no longer a background. It is the very medium in which the figure exists. Its repetitive, concentric forms evoke at once a mandala, an optical machine, and an organism. The tunnel-like perspective suggests an inner journey as much as a visual trap. One cannot tell whether the Doll appeared at the bottom of the kaleidoscope or whether the kaleidoscope was born from her. In Oliver R’s work, the Dolls are never mere mannequins. They carry a memory, a slight unease, an elegance a little too perfect to be reassuring. Transparency pushes this ambiguity further. By making the figure less sharp, more spectral, the artist does not weaken her presence: he makes it more insistent. What is not entirely visible demands more attention. Here one finds the artist’s signature: a cocktail of Pop Art, Surrealism, and digital Art Brut, obtained by assembling artificial intelligences and digital tools, then fixed in a unique work also intended for physical existence — fine-art paper, dibond, framing, anti-reflective plexiglass. But beyond technique, Transparency marks a shift. The kaleidoscope no longer illustrates a state of mind. It is the theater of that state.The creature with closed eyes, crowned in red, seated at the center of a tunnel of blue and orange, does not offer a single interpretation. She may be meditating, sleeping, absent, or simply dissolving into the pattern that brought her forth. Faithful to his method, Oliver R imposes nothing. He installs an atmosphere, a color, a tension between the sharp and the blurred, and leaves the gaze to do the rest.Transparency is not merely a new piece in the Dolls collection. It is the moment when the kaleidoscope stops surrounding the figure and begins to pass through her.

text:
Evaluating high-value resort promotions, such as complimentary seaplane transfers for extended stays, requires looking far beyond the immediate financial savings. 🌴

Extended resort reservations demand a significant commitment of continuous personal time, which is inherently the most valuable asset any individual possesses. Chasing a massive discount by forcing an unnaturally long vacation schedule simply disrupts the peaceful flow of daily life and introduces unnecessary friction into your routine.

The true essence of luxury is never defined by simply receiving an expensive service for free, but rather by possessing the complete freedom to choose exactly how long you wish to stay without any external pressure. Adapting your personal calendar just to meet the requirements of a hotel campaign instantly places you in a reactive position rather than a state of total control.

Strategic travelers understand that hospitality promotions should naturally align with their existing lifestyle goals instead of dictating their future plans. Securing ultimate flexibility allows you to effortlessly leverage these appealing offers only when they perfectly match your preferred pace of travel. 🥂

Reaching a state of complete financial and professional independence entirely transforms how these travel opportunities are perceived and utilized. Awaiting the day when my wife fully steps away from her corporate commitments is less about unlocking specific hotel deals and entirely about securing our unlimited freedom to explore the world together at any moment. ✈️

Our shared vision for the future remains focused on building a life where we can easily embrace a month-long tropical getaway simply because we feel like it. True wealth is ultimately measured by the ability to let go of external timelines and navigate the globe entirely on your own terms. ✨

text:
Yeah, the poor little autoworkers are mere slaves... oh, wait..
U.S. automobile manufacturing production workers (primarily assembly and parts) currently average roughly $33–$41 per hour, with yearly earnings often in the $70,000–$100,000+ range once overtime is included. 

Benefits are a major part of total compensation, especially at unionized Big Three plants.⁠Bls

Average Hourly and Yearly Wages

Data come primarily from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Current Employment Statistics for production and nonsupervisory workers (not seasonally adjusted), which cover the bulk of factory-floor roles.

Many reports and worker accounts note that substantial overtime can push experienced production workers well into the $80,000–$110,000+ range in a good year.
These are industry averages. Unionized UAW workers at GM, Ford, and Stellantis (the “Detroit Three”) generally earn at the higher end of the scale. 

Under the 2023 contracts (running roughly through 2028), top production rates have progressed from the mid-$30s toward $40–$42/hour (including cost-of-living adjustments/COLA), with skilled trades higher (often mid-$40s). 

Non-union plants (Toyota, Honda, BMW, Hyundai, Tesla, etc.) typically pay less than top UAW rates but remain competitive, often in the mid-$20s to mid-$30s for production roles, with some post-2023 raises to stay attractive. 

Tesla production associate rates commonly fall in the $19–$25/hour range depending on location and experience (higher in high-cost areas), plus performance bonuses or equity in some cases.

Significant Benefits  (The  hidden  compensation)

Benefits add substantial value—often 30–40%+ of total compensation in manufacturing, and more at legacy union plants. 

BLS data show manufacturing workers have high access rates to health insurance (~91%) and retirement benefits (~96%). Total employer compensation costs in manufacturing average around $45–$46+ per hour worked (wages plus benefits).

Key benefits, especially for UAW-represented workers at the Detroit Three:
Health insurance: Often highly favorable for active workers—low or no monthly premiums, low deductibles/co-pays for in-network care in many plans. This is a longstanding strength of UAW contracts.

Retirement: Traditional defined-benefit pensions for workers hired before roughly 2007–2008. Newer hires typically receive strong 401(k) plans with automatic employer contributions around 10% of base pay (up from lower rates pre-2023 contract; no employee contribution required in many cases). Profit-sharing can further boost retirement savings.

Profit-sharing bonuses: Formula-based and can be large in profitable years. Recent examples include GM workers receiving up to ~$10,500 and Ford ~$6,780 for 2025 results (Stellantis paid $0 due to North American losses). Historical payouts have sometimes exceeded $10,000–$14,000.

Paid time off: Generous vacation (scaling with seniority, often 100–200+ hours/year), holidays, and sick/personal time. Supplemental Unemployment Benefits (SUB) help during layoffs.

Other: Cost-of-living adjustments (COLA, restored in the 2023 deals), signing/ratification bonuses in contracts, tuition assistance, and various job security or transition provisions. Skilled trades and longer-tenured workers often have stronger packages.

Non-union manufacturers generally offer solid health and 401(k) benefits (sometimes with matching), paid time off, and bonuses, but typically less generous overall than top UAW packages—particularly on retirement guarantees and profit-sharing formulas. Tesla and similar firms emphasize equity/stock incentives and performance bonuses for some roles.

So,  yeah,  those  poor,  poor,  suffering  autoworkers...
