🇺🇲 The United States can no longer guarantee the security of its Gulf allies as it has for the past eight decades, Trump's envoy Tom Barrack declared Tuesday, signaling a reassessment of the American security architecture that has underpinned Washington's influence across the Middle East.

“America as the guarantor to the world, for the last 80 years, it is no longer there,” Barrack told the Global Security Forum in Doha.

Barrack described the shift as a realignment rather than an abandonment, arguing that the postwar arrangement under which Washington provided military protection in exchange for stable access to Gulf energy no longer serves American interests in its traditional form. He encouraged regional governments to develop their own security arrangements, pointing to the emerging defense partnership between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey as an example of the direction they should pursue.

The message comes at an important moment for Washington's Gulf allies. Iranian attacks have exposed vulnerabilities in regional defenses, commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains under threat, and Saudi Arabia is struggling to protect critical infrastructure against repeated Houthi missile and drone strikes.

For decades, American military power was the foundation of Gulf security calculations. U.S. bases, advanced weapons systems, intelligence cooperation and naval deployments helped sustain a regional order in which Washington exercised influence far beyond its formal treaty commitments.

The vulnerability of America's military infrastructure has become a serious part of that reassessment. A WaPo satellite investigation identified at least 228 U.S. military structures or pieces of equipment damaged or destroyed by Iranian strikes across the Middle East, while the CSIS estimated that repairing damaged bases and fixed infrastructure could cost between $4 billion and $9.4 billion. 

The contrast with China's military infrastructure: A 2025 Hudson Institute study found that Beijing had expanded its network to more than 800 hardened aircraft shelters and over 3,100 aircraft shelters overall, while American construction of comparable protections in the Western Pacific has lagged. 

The comparison concerns the Indo-Pacific rather than the Gulf, but the underlying vulnerability is now visible in the Middle East: expensive aircraft, radars and command facilities concentrated at exposed installations can become targets for comparatively inexpensive missiles and drones. For Gulf governments, the question of who will provide security is  inseparable from whether the existing American military infrastructure can withstand another sustained regional war.

That arrangement is now being openly reconsidered by a senior representative of the Trump administration, even as the Pentagon continues reinforcing its military presence around Iran.

Barrack insisted that the United States is not leaving the Middle East. Yet the distinction may offer limited reassurance to governments whose security planning has long depended on the expectation of American protection.

The implications extend beyond the Gulf. Regional powers seeking alternative defense partnerships could gradually reduce their dependence on Washington, creating opportunities for other states to acquire influence in an area central to global energy markets and international trade.

The strategic consequences will depend on how far the administration translates Barrack's remarks into policy. No comprehensive American military withdrawal or termination of Gulf security arrangements has been announced.

For Washington's allies, however, the uncertainty is already consequential. A security guarantee derives much of its value from the confidence that it will be honored when tested. Barrack's remarks leave Gulf governments with a more difficult calculation about how much protection they can expect from the United States in the next regional crisis.

text:
THE IRAN QUESTION: WINNING THE WAR, LOSING THE PEACE?

Washington is preparing. Jerusalem is watching the clock. Tehran is calculating. Moscow and Beijing are observing.

And everyone seems to be asking the same question:

When will America strike Iran again?

Perhaps we’re asking the wrong question.

American and Israeli military capabilities are hardly in doubt. But military superiority and strategic success are two very different things.

Does Washington seek to destroy military capabilities, compel a political settlement, or fundamentally reshape the regional order?

And does Jerusalem share precisely the same definition of victory?

Consider the calendars.

Israel’s October 27 elections. America’s November 3 midterms. Tehran’s calculations. Moscow’s interests. Beijing’s energy security.

Five different strategic clocks. Not necessarily synchronized.

A military operation may last days. Its geopolitical consequences may last decades.

And what happens the morning after?

Who guarantees Gulf stability? Who secures Hormuz and the Red Sea? Who manages the political vacuum if deterrence collapses?

More importantly, who defines the new equilibrium?

History offers an uncomfortable reminder: Winning a war and winning the peace are rarely the same achievement.

Washington certainly knows how to conduct military operations.

But does it have a political endgame?

Or are we once again attempting to resolve a geopolitical equation through military arithmetic?

One final question.

What if Washington’s greatest risk is not failing to defeat Iran, but succeeding militarily without knowing what to do with the victory?

After all, Noah didn’t start building the Ark when it began raining.

The question is whether anyone in Washington is already building one.

— MFD

text:
When Light Horse Harry was 21 years old, he turned a tavern into a fortress and fended off a British unit with just seven men.

It was January 20, 1778. Lee had been raiding British supply lines so effectively  that the enemy sent a large body of cavalry to grab him. They managed to trap him and seven others inside the Spread Eagle Tavern.

Lee would not surrender. The tiny group barricaded the doors, manned every window they could cover and unleashed fire on the attackers. 

When the British tried to take the horses from a nearby stable, Lee had his men cheer and shout that American infantry was charging to the rescue.

The bluff worked. The British pulled back and rode off. The story raced through the Continental Army. 

Washington was so impressed he offered Lee a coveted spot as an aide-de-camp. Lee turned it down, telling the general he was “wedded to my sword.”

The stand at the tavern added to his growing legend that made him one of the most feared light cavalry leaders of the war.

And his son, Robert E. Lee was born almost exactly 29 years later. January 19, 1807.

authorBio: Podcast Host 🎙️ 10-15 minute stories of forgotten American Heroes

text:
In November, 1780, Henry “Light Horse” Lee, father of Robert E. Lee, was promoted to lieutenant colonel of dragoons during the Revolutionary War.

He commanded the 2nd Partisan Corps, also know as “Lee’s Legion,” an elite unit of light cavalry specialized in hit-and-run tactics, becoming one of the most effective group of chargers in the Continental Army. 

Serving under Lee was a 16 year old  lieutenant named Peter Johnston, the father of Joseph E. Johnston. He rode with distinction, both men earned renown as daring cavalry officers. 

After the war ended, they raised families in different parts of Virginia, never crossing paths, but their names eventually echoed in American history.

Curiously, their sons, Robert and Joseph, were classmates at West Point, graduated, and famously served together in the Mexican War and the Civil War, riding together just as their fathers had done.

More importantly, who defines the new equilibrium?

History offers an uncomfortable reminder: Winning a war and winning the peace are rarely the same achievement.

Washington certainly knows how to conduct military operations.

But does it have a political endgame?

Or are we once again attempting to resolve a geopolitical equation through military arithmetic?

One final question.

What if Washington’s greatest risk is not failing to defeat Iran, but succeeding militarily without knowing what to do with the victory?

After all, Noah didn’t start building the Ark when it began raining.

The question is whether anyone in Washington is already building one.

— MFD

text:
Jeannie Leavitt finished Air Force pilot training first in her class. That gave her first pick of the planes on offer. On the assignment call, she chose the F-15E Strike Eagle fighter jet. A man’s voice came back: “Current policy does not allow women to fly combat aircraft. Would you please make another choice?”
She picked a tanker plane instead, and the Air Force made her an instructor in the T-38, teaching student pilots. Most of her instructors warned her that pushing for a fighter would mark her as a troublemaker. “I might win it, but I might also give myself a miserable career,” she said.
3 months later, the Pentagon lifted the ban. The Air Force’s top general, Gen. Merrill McPeak, announced that she would be its first female fighter pilot. When a reporter suggested she was jumping ahead of qualified men, he answered: “She’s not leapfrogging anyone.”
She trained on the F-15E as the only woman in the program. Not everyone wanted her there. “Some men were subtle with their lack of support, while a couple were outwardly hostile toward me,” she said. She made it through anyway, and her squadron gave her the call sign “Tally.”
She flew more than 300 hours in combat and became the first woman to graduate from the Air Force Weapons School, the Air Force’s version of Top Gun. 18 years after arriving at her first fighter base in North Carolina, she came back to command the whole wing there, the first woman ever to command an Air Force combat fighter wing.
When Hollywood made Captain Marvel, about a female Air Force pilot, Brie Larson came to learn from her. Leavitt helped on set, and in the movie, the hero even drives the same kind of car and wears the same kind of leather jacket she did.
She retired a 2-star general after 31 years. Today, she is the dean of aviation at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in Prescott, Arizona, training the next generation of pilots.
“Honestly, I did not want to be the first female fighter pilot,” she said. “I just wanted to be the best fighter pilot.”

text:
Oct 20, 1803: The Senate ratified the Louisiana Purchase. The president who made the deal wasn't sure it was constitutional.

Napoleon had offered to sell all of Louisiana, about 828,000 square miles, for $15 million. It doubled the size of the United States overnight. Thomas Jefferson was thrilled, and also uneasy. He had always argued the federal government could only do what the Constitution specifically allowed, and it said nothing about buying land from foreign countries.

He drafted a constitutional amendment to make the purchase legal. Then his diplomats warned him that Napoleon was unpredictable and might change his mind if the US took too long. Jefferson dropped the amendment and sent the treaty to the Senate.

Federalists in New England hated the deal. They feared new western states would shrink their power, and a few even talked about breaking away from the Union. It didn't matter. The Senate approved it 24 to 7.

The US didn't have $15 million on hand. It paid largely with bonds sold through British and Dutch banks. That meant British bankers were helping finance a deal that put money in the pocket of Napoleon, Britain's worst enemy.

Two months later the American flag went up in New Orleans. The next spring, Lewis and Clark set out to see what the country had bought.

text:
Whatever happened to "it's not about the tool, it's about understanding the problem?" I feel like I never hear that anymore.

As I've pointed out time and time again, I've always thought this was a pretty silly false dichotomy. Of course you need to understand the problem, but the tools you use shape how you think about it, what you consider possible, and even which problems you bother trying to solve in the first place.

And now, with AI, suddenly everyone seems to understand that tools really do matter.

I think Marshall McLuhan's ideas, famously summarized by John Culkin as "we shape our tools and thereafter they shape us," offer a much more useful way to think about all this.

While I'm as interested as anyone in what AI can do, I do wonder if we've lost sight of what we're actually trying to accomplish. 

I find it especially strange that so much of the tech world, which used to celebrate originality and thinking differently, now seems perfectly happy to clap like seals whenever somebody uses AI to recreate software that already existed 30 years ago.

Maybe it's worth revisiting some of those ideas about digital minimalism, deep work, and thinking differently that were so fashionable just a few years ago. 

They weren't all wrong, and if anything, they might be more relevant now than ever.

text:
When Hannah Collins checked out an old economics textbook from the public library in Boston, Massachusetts, she was simply trying to save money.

Her college bookstore wanted $186 for the same book.

The library offered it for free.

Hannah was a sophomore at a local university, working twenty hours a week at a grocery store to cover rent and school expenses. She had become skilled at finding cheaper alternatives to almost everything.

Three days after borrowing the textbook, she opened it to chapter seven and noticed a folded envelope tucked between the pages.

Inside were ten crisp hundred-dollar bills.

Hannah counted the money twice.

One thousand dollars.

For several seconds, she simply stared at it.

Her rent was overdue. Her electricity bill was sitting on the kitchen counter, and her car needed new tires before winter.

The money could solve nearly every problem she had that month.

Nobody would know.

The book had been sitting on a public library shelf. The envelope had no name on it, and there was no obvious way to identify its owner.

Hannah slipped the envelope into her backpack and tried to study.

But she couldn't concentrate.

Every time she looked at the textbook, she imagined someone returning to the library, opening the book, and discovering the money was gone.

The next morning, she took the envelope to the librarian.

An older woman named Margaret Ellis examined the book carefully.

"You're the first person to report finding anything like this," she said.

Hannah felt relieved.

"Do you know who owned the book before the library?"

Margaret checked the records.

The textbook had been donated six months earlier by a retired professor named Walter Hayes.

Margaret called the number on his donation form.

A man answered after the third ring.

When Margaret explained the discovery, he went silent.

Then he asked, "Did the envelope contain a note?"

It did.

Hannah had barely noticed the small piece of paper inside, but she unfolded it carefully.

The handwriting read:

"For the student who needs a chance. I once had to choose between buying food and buying books. Someone helped me when I had nothing. If this reaches you, please use it to make your life a little easier. When you can, do the same for someone else."

There was no signature.

Margaret asked whether Walter knew anything about the envelope.

He explained that he had once taught at a community college and had kept the money in the textbook for years.

It was intended as emergency assistance for a student who might discover it.

He had donated the book after moving into a smaller apartment and had forgotten the envelope was still inside.

Walter asked Hannah whether she would be willing to meet him.

They arranged to meet at the library that Saturday.

Walter was seventy-eight, with silver hair and a walking stick. He listened as Hannah explained how she had struggled to pay for college.

Then he asked her a question.

"If you could use that money for anything, what would you do?"

Hannah looked down.

"Pay my rent. Buy my textbooks. Maybe replace my car tires."

Walter smiled.

"Good. Those are exactly the sorts of things that keep people from moving forward."

Then he did something Hannah never expected.

He insisted that she keep the money.

Hannah protested, but Walter explained that the gift had been placed in the book for precisely this reason.

Before leaving, Walter gave her his email address.

As Hannah walked home that afternoon, she couldn't stop thinking about the old professor and the mysterious envelope.

She had received the money, but she was beginning to understand that it meant far more than a thousand dollars.

It was a chance someone had deliberately left behind for a stranger.

And Hannah was determined not to waste it.

text:
The five biggest AI hyperscalers are burning through almost every dollar of free cash flow they generate.   

We aggregated the quarterly SEC cash flow statements for Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle back to 2018.   

Look at the trailing twelve month tape through Q2 2026:
• Operating cash flow generated: $692 billion
• Capital spending (mostly AI data centers): $566 billion
• Remaining free cash flow: $126 billion   

Capex now eats 82% of their operating cash flow. In early 2024, that ratio was 40%.   

Combined free cash flow peaked in Q1 2024 at $247 billion. Today it sits at $126 billion, down 49% even while operating cash flow hit new highs.   

In Q2 2026 alone, those five companies generated $186.4 billion in operating cash and spent $181.5 billion on capex, leaving just $4.8 billion in quarterly free cash flow before financing obligations.

How are they plugging the funding gap:
They are tapping the bond market.   

In the first half of 2026 alone, the group issued $164 billion in net new long term debt. Across the entire seven years from 2018 through 2024 combined, their net new borrowing was just $61 billion.   

For fifteen years, big tech was the ultimate asset light trade. Today, the most heavily weighted stocks in every passive index are transforming into capital intensive, debt funded utilities.   

When companies borrow $164 billion in six months to buy depreciating silicon, the return on that capex and the cost of debt matter more than ever. Stop pricing them on 2019 balance sheet math.

text:
So this is kind of a big thing, and it’s something that people sometimes ask me.  “Why S.U.P.L.E.X?  What does S.U.P.L.E.X. offer in a saturated superhero market that hasn’t been offered before?”  It’s a valid question-the world is full of lazy cape slop, trying to piggyback off the success of the MCU and get a tiny crumb of that multibillion dollar franchise pie.

Most of you probably know by now that S.U.P.L.E.X. started life as a tabletop campaign-one that was fundamentally unserious in nature, as all of my games tend to be.  You can see the tabletop in the bones of the canon, in the quotes, in the players who moved away so their characters became casualties, and in the relationships that appear in the canon as-is, without explanation.  The tabletop is ongoing-my longest running campaign at 15+ years, itself one of my most noteworthy achievements.

But S.U.P.L.E.X. became more than that because of one author whose work I really enjoy and was reading around the time I started The Handbook. That author is Tom Clancy, specifically his series of military reference books that detail different units and their doctrine.  Because S.U.P.L.E.X. is not really a story about superheroes and their dumb antics, even though superheroes and their dumb antics make up most of the plot. S.U.P.L.E.X. is a story of institutions and doctrine, and the people who have to find their way around the systems that make a superhero world possible.  That’s why there are endless references to insurance and logistics and recruitment in the books.  That’s the line that makes S.U.P.L.E.X. take the farcical nature of a superhero world and attempt to determine what it is like to live in that world, and the institutions and doctrines that pop up around it.

The fundamental idea of S.U.P.L.E.X. hasn’t changed from tabletop night one, though.  Because the fundamental question is this: given our own abilities (redneck survivalist D&D nerds) and environment (rural Southern Indiana) how do we create an effective superhero team?

Big hero IP’s like the Justice League or the Avengers don’t really focus on this. (Maybe Damage, Inc does a little bit.)  They don’t focus on the law, or the doctrines, or the training, or the methodology as all of their stories are character driven.  I’m not knocking on them for doing that; this is a no-hater zone.  But S.U.P.L.E.X, while it has character driven stories in it, is fundamentally institution-driven as a narrative.  We see that reflected in everything, from the healing blunts to the recruitment of superhero war orphans into the Child Soldiers Division.  Everything is based off of the creation and refinement of a doctrine that would actually be effective at making the world better. 

Because heroism isn’t about posing in tights (that’s just to get bitches)-it’s about showing up, doing the work, and making sure that you work within the guidelines and rules and environmental constraints that you have.  That’s why some of my biggest, most powerful stories contain no thrown punches-because they are really about the methodology of improving the world with the gifts that you are given. (I have a real problem with writing up meeting transcripts-maybe there’s a little Robert Aspirin in there alongside Tom Clancy.)  Because what’s interesting to me isn’t “Why is this guy the most powerful guy ever?” but “How do you effectively recruit, train and deploy super humans?” 

If there’s a theme to S.U.P.L.E.X. buried beneath the stoner culture memes and dick jokes, there it is. It’s not a deconstructive parody where the gag is how stupid this all is-it’s the concept that real people react in real ways to very absurd threats.  If that intrigues you, I hope you’ll join us.  Maybe you’ll join us at the tabletop.  Maybe you’ll join us with your art and stories, as many of my players have done.  Maybe you’ll join by just clicking like, subscribe and share-God knows I appreciate it from the very bottom of my heart.

It’s been an uphill battle, and it obviously required a lot of work on my part.  But part of S.U.P.L.E.X. will always belong to the players, who took it seriously enough to roll the dice at my table all these years. It is a truly collaborative universe, with me as the stoned degenerate chronicler, and I think it provides something fresh even as the market for superheroes starts to dwindle out, leaving only the truly devoted to play in the sandbox.  Because lots of people are creating flashier and more powerful and more tragic heroes to try to sell you a product, but only I am telling the story of the guy who pumps out the super-septic tank at the training camp.

I’m glad to have you along for the ride.

Building a Career in Robotics?

Denmark Should Be on Your Radar.👇 

A) What Makes Denmark a Robotics Powerhouse?

Denmark has a rich robotics legacy.

From pioneering robotics research conducted in collaboration between Odense University and Odense Steel Shipyard Ltd. (Lindø Shipyard) in the late 1980s, which led to the development of robotic welding systems specifically designed to automate shipbuilding workflows, to the establishment of The Maersk Mc-Kinney Moller Institute in 1997, Odense (Denmark) has been leading the robotics frontier for decades, with an early focus on the maritime industry.

Then came @Universal_Robot . 

Incubated in 2005 by three researchers from the Faculty of Engineering, University of Southern Denmark, the company pioneered collaborative robot arms (cobots) surgically designed to automate modern industrial workflows for automotive giants ranging from Stellantis in Turin, Italy to Nissan in Japan.

Followed by @MobileIndRobots  (MiR), @OnRobot_ , @BlueOceanRobot , @SpinRobotics , Nordbo Robotics, and @SmoothRobotics  ApS.

Today, Denmark is one of Europe's most established robotics hubs.

And this ecosystem continues to scale at an exponential pace.

In June 2026, the Syddansk Universitet - University of Southern Denmark launched its Center for Large Structure Production at the Port of Odense. A major research facility incubated to accelerate the development of robotics solutions for maritime, energy, and construction sectors in the country. 

________

B) Who's Investing in the Odense Robotics Ecosystem?

This ecosystem is being energized by a growing network of prominent investors empowering local robotics startups, including but not limited to EIFO, @join_capital  GmbH, @North_Ventures , @MajInvest , Final Frontier, @ReInvestRobo , Helge Munk Holding, @SupernovaInvest , Odense Robotics StartUp Fund, and @PromusVentures .

Quadsat secured €5M in 2025.
Dropla Tech ApS raised €2.4M in 2025.
BlinkTroll Robotics secured €1.5M in 2025.

________

C) Where Are the Opportunities for Robotics Engineers?

From cobots powering automotive giants like Nissan and Stellantis to high-performance AMRs serving global industrial leaders like Novo Nordisk and Schneider Electric, Odense (Denmark) offers a wide range of opportunities for budding robotics engineers and entrepreneurs.

We'll cover them in detail in Part II of this series. 

Given this trajectory, if you are a student or engineer looking to break into robotics, Denmark should be on your radar.

As of 2024, more than 500 active & planned telecommunication submarine cable systems are estimated to span the globe, connecting continents, markets & households.

https://t.co/FIFDjnnP0i

This infrastructure is indispensable for real-time apps such as financial trading, video conferencing & live streaming. 

https://t.co/hhQncbslWa

Petal transoceanic subsea cable

Funded & operated Meta

Expected to enter service in 2029, the first transoceanic subsea cable @ petabit capacity, & the first to deploy multi-core fiber @ scale. Spanning 7,000 km between France & the United States, Petal will deliver 1 Pbps (1 petabit per second or 1,000 terabits per second), doubling what today’s most advanced subsea cables carry @ this distance w/out a proportional increase in power or physical infrastructure.

Petal will incorporate something called "fan-in/fan-out" tech. As each two-core fiber strand enters a repeater, an optical interface routes the signal from each core into a separate single-core fiber strand so that each can be amplified independently. The amplified signals are then routed back into the two cores of the dual-core fiber before continuing along the cable.

That’s roughly the network capacity required for 75% of the world’s population to stream music @ the same time.*

*Calculation based on a total capacity of 1 Pbps w/ an audio stream bitrate of ~0.16 Mbps (160 kbps) for ≈ 6.25 billion simultaneous streams.

https://t.co/OVBGELmbW1

Petal is a key piece of Meta’s subsea cable investments bringing greater capacity, stronger resiliency, & future-proof infrastructure to Europe as demand for communications & reliable connectivity continues to increase.

Petal is one of many subsea cable investments by Meta in recent years, including Marea in 2018, Amitie in 2023 & Anjana in 2025. Marea, the company's first transatlantic fiber instalment, supports 192 Tbps, meaning Petal will offer more than 5X that capacity.

text:
Chronik and I traded today together which we have not been doing as much as he truly is a part time trader with a job. Short staff forced him to work more.

If you're unaware of Chronik, he has been a coaching student of mine for nearly 2 years come February. 

He's not paid me a dime either. The intentions was established long ago, I want to start a legit prop firm. Not funding, like the shit you guys are use to. I think prop firm is an absolute misuse of what those companies are. 

In my opinion... Okay. For me - Proprietary firms are having access to things you don't have access to as a retail trader. Coaching, accountability, tech, and all sorts of other support.

This is too expensive for one person to pay for as a service in order to survive a multi-year learning curve which also happens in tier 1 props. In those environments you can have a trader still take a year or two - to actually get consistent.

I don't offer coaching, and really never wanted to. The incentive is not worth it.

However we split 50/50 when he finally makes profits. Seems steep, but I take a fuck load of up front risk. I've sunk a tremendous amount of time into him.

He's stuck out this long, I know he will keep riding it out. Some people just dip. So this model is horribly flawed unless you luck out on the student, and obviously there's a shit load of trust on payments. Which as we know trading is full of scumbags.

Sometimes you just take a leap of faith.

No one wrote a handbook on how to get traders to turn the corner, and when other traders brag about their students being consistent - while I've seen indirect success through my teachings (very little by the way) - I'm sure it happens. But I also find that coaching is fucking hard.

I don't have accountability for myself. When we trade together and I fall of the rails, Chronik doesn't call me out. He's sucked into the session as well which becomes a trance like state, and it's hard to snap out of it.

I had initially made tremendous progress with him as he kept one account alive for over 6 months. I mean he flounder fucked in it. But it stayed alive.

We've had issues where he's been so tilted I tell him he's done but he keeps going and has blown accounts like this.

So that's my summary as lots of new subs may not know who this is.

I want to know what it really takes to get someone profitable and maintain it. 

We as a collective in trading have virtually no documentations or running history on this. Maybe success stories and shit. But we lack the actual nuances of the journey. This is my attempt to shed some light on it. 

If we can see him turn the corner, then we have real live understanding of what it took. 

I also believe I can hypnotize someone into success. 

I've been certified in it for some time - which anyone can literally do and a certificate aint shit - but I've practiced it a lot on myself and him. 

This has been the best thing that produces real change and results.

This is why I'll always argue psychology is as important as edge development and must be done together from the start. 

Actively working on his psychological triggers every session fucking works. 

This prop thing is why we built https://t.co/VNVPpVyeYM by the way. 

I need to see where he does well and where he suffers.

There's always stuff you are in control of 100% like taking trades in the best locations, and other emotional triggers.

While markets are random. You can boost your probabilities of success by working real hard on the things you're in control of and making sure your performance is near perfect every session. This alone DOES reflect in the PNL!

Chronik made a big fuck up on blowing an account and when he does, he's not aloud to do one for several months. Only sim.

We are gearing up for his next account. Which Ill document. I have in the past and it's here on X. 

But this next round is us literally going in more prepared after getting fucked up. Haters can hate. But the information through this is of value even if we get fucked up again.

Now I had made the mistake of learning vibe coding over the year and spent too much time building shit and lost focus on myself and Chronik in the psych department, as well as review work. Which this complacency caught up. 

I wasn't being a coach as much as some guy he traded the session with. 

I needed to devlop more will power to pull out of problematic trading as well as systems to monitor him. Often when he starts trading like shit he doesn't tell me and I have no fucking idea. 

There's a prop dash for https://t.co/VNVPpVyeYM that's not released. It was a dead project and never completed. I see his trades come in live and he tags his psych state. 

Currently he streams his PNL live. So I monitor that. Trying to juggle him and myself at the same time.... Its.... Its not fucking easy.

My will power to do the right shit comes from administering my own hypnosis sessions. 

You don't just muster discipline mid session.

It's all done before or after. I have to rewire my neurons through this process to make it a habit. Which is the point of hypnosis in general. We rewire his SPECIFIC PSYCH triggers. 

I can assure you that there's unlimited ways to trade, and there's unlimited potential specific psych triggers.

Being tilted is a broad statement much like the PNLs I added below of Chronik and my session.

This means nothing to you until I explain what happened.

Yesterday I did a fuck load of drills. I had been suffering of execution errors for months and months and months which I have an X post on somewhere explaining this.

I have been focusing on breath work hypnosis. There's different psych tools I employ. This one is the fastest.

I look at all trades that I feel have poor execution in a recorded session on drills and even live. I look at these specific trades and run through this breath work process until the triggering emotion is gone, and I'm content with the price action and feel a sense of calm. 

Looking at the recording and screen of my trade. I'll pause it. And go through the breathing then visualize in pure focus the ideal thing I should of done in this part of the price action, It could be waiting longer and taking nothing here, or just executing a few tick further out. I make sure I see myself doing the right thing while at the same time focusing on ideal emotions.

-Calmness
-Contentment
-Patience

Today I came in more aware of this long review process. Looked at the higher time frame because I seem to forget often.

We literally check listed everything we look at. Because sometimes we forget to look at things we normally look at, and build out deeper context covering EVERYTHING in our systems.

I ended up fading solid fucking areas. Didn't know we could be a trend day. But I played my areas the way I should and took the losses, as they should. 

I didn't over fight. 

1-2 tries on one area and I'm done!

Wait for truly another setup, because I can get churned out hard and fast in the same area. One little area can farm out so much PNL. This is my biggest weakness right now.

The issue is the complacency on working on psych.

IT NEVER ENDS!

Now MOST traders don't do shit for it...

Imagine a video game character with a skill trees or skill stats. 

-Edge is one.
-Psych is another. 

I can't imagine what the difference can be in myself and Chronik if we put in just as much time here as trading? But I KNOW it will make a difference because we have actual recorded results and stats around this shit.

There were 2 areas that were fade worthy on the higher time frame. I took them. 

I took the trades off well for the volatility.

But I also recognized the trend could continue if these were blown out. 

Sometimes intra-day trends are just up legs on a higher time frame range. 

We both did well for fading a trend day, but by not pressing and forcing an opinion on it, and flowing well with the information at hand.

Getting married to ANY BIAS! Is an absolute death blow!

Staying as fluid as possible, but not being overly fluid - just riding that balance point - really paid off. 

In reality you should not take more than 2 losses in a row. At least for us.

We stop the trading session, and review those losses NOW! 

Do the psych work NOW!!!

That way we can pick back up from a fresh place mid session and truly salvage the mother fucker. 

Mid session psych work - fucking works!!!

It saves sessions.

We attempt to use a faster process for it. Not the longer 10-15 minute hypnosis sessions. 

I use to use a lot of loop timers to do mid session psych work. That shit also works which is why it's built into  https://t.co/VNVPpVyeYM - now we plan on making a better version of it. 

We want statistics on how much time are we actually using on psych work. Not doing the breathing part. But the deeper states where the real change occurs.

Does more hours make a difference!? 

Will I guess we will find out....

---

Let's move back into the session. But first. We can see below how my equity curve with the purple line - Shows this recovery from the massive draw down I took on September 30 2026 in one session. I talked about it here: https://t.co/QUgC39E1ur - roughly 10 trading sessions. Was out on vacation last week. 

I'm basically there. 

We also had a little drop that seemed to knock out a ton of work.

Most of everything, is psychological here. I know what to do and how to trade well. No matter what I look at or deal with as far as how charts are displayed - management and being particular about entries and setups will never change and is universal. 

Tooling is simply there to boost clarity, fit with your theory on how markets work, and help you triangulate setups.

But management and proper psych are key. Every tooling, or indicator has some failure at some point, even if the setup is A+

A+ setups never mean 100% win rates. To me A+ in the most clarity you have to get the best setup possible and it works almost as you predicted. You're not caught off guard too much by the noise. Once noise enters your head, you lose clarity and the A+ signal fades.

All setups have clarity boosts assuming they're good setups for you. However the moment clarity fades it's not A+

A+ setups become more A+ the more time you have with them and the more nuances you've seen. 

My A+ hits, if I gave to you will not be A+ for you.

You lack the experience and knowing of the granulars.

Plus context building supports the setups. The entire read on the entire session must be understood to contribute to a setup from being shit to A+

In my opinion, setups should not be stand alone. Narrative and context is key. Multiple factors of support is key!

Today was odd. It's one of those days where the volume did not feel like it mattered in ES and it's full arbitrage. Which ES does arbitrage the actual SPX - Not to be confused with options. - SPX is the official ticker for SP500 

I say this all the time. Pull up charts on SPX ES MES VOO IVV SPY

All the same price action. Different order books and volume. 

I've experimented with combing multiple products, stocks, and options to pinpoint the order flow. Where the real movement takes place. 

SPX doesn't move on order flow as it's a math formula on stocks and their weights.

So all listed symbols I mentioned arb the SPX price.

The way I see it so far, is the volume seems to rotate in and out of each symbol. 

Stock cumulative delta for example - does not at all ever match ES price movement. Where as there are days ES delta is really in sync with ES price movement, despite the occasional divergences.

Delta simply shows the difference between buy and sell orders. So offset. This offset typically wants to rebalance.

Now today - the price seemed to pull the delta. The delta had this very odd lack of response to actual response but lagged at times with price. Price was dragging the delta at times, and moving with no delta response. Now this could mean volume was truly matched and in control. 

But... 

I think some other symbol had a ton of weight on the volume contribution to today's movement.

This is actually how Vest exchange runs their book. They arb with say NQ which is arbing NDX which is moved on stocks.

Vest can fuck their trader - which if you read their fine print they mention how they will take the other side of the trade and not guarantee liquidity. However for the most part their algo will arb NQ price while sometimes their price chart has an odd spike not on NQ where they fucked their customers on a stop.

I digress.

ES is basically like Vest but regulated. Vest will have to pull orders even though there is no order flow in order to stay with NQ. But unlike NQ and ES. Market makers are obligated to leave a minimum amount of liquidity.

Even though it can virtually nothing....

So the algos pulling liquidity to keep the price lock in step and prevent the market makers from having stale quotes, means there's another volume event moving the shit in another order book. 

Which one exactly? I don't know yet. I'm still running science projects. Which all this conspiracy theory is shared in my course modules in detail here at: https://t.co/9d6VzTK1Cg 

Stocks however had by far the most interesting results. Options as well, but more so in the form of just seeing massive orders hit you wont see in futures.

Stocks need to be viewed in volume leg form, which Ill be working on in the near future. Right now volume legs by default should split on candles. If on a high time frame - a range has like 2 candles. One of those massive candles will be putting all of it's volume into either an up or down leg. The volume on that candle should be split from the up leg, to the moment it tests high and roll back over where it should be split to the short leg. This alone is causing accuracy issues with standard zig zag shit.

Easier said then done. I basically have a white board where I hand draw a DOM and order flow events one order at a time and train the AI on as many scenarios as I can think of. Like what happens if the limits widen their spread?

Anyways. Today felt like it was being driven on volume elsewhere. I can't explain it. But watching enough sessions with a DOM and cumulative delta, you can fucking tell. 

I can at least. 

This means volume legs and delta lose the ability to lean into them harder. The typical shit or signals of leaning into heavier volume fail more. 

It was like this yesterday as well.

One day the signals work in specific ways then the next, they're unreliable as fuck. 

This is why you need a bag of tricks. 

Simple price action and ranges give me enough information that with decent fucking management I can lean on them, because after all - The official SPX has those same ranges.

Really making sure we know higher time frame structure here which was the 15m chart as there seemed to be this 2 day range looking thing going on. All those major major pivots as well are key. We pivoted majorly in random spots for a reason. 

Supply flooded in on high sides. 

Remember supply and demand still matter and are the core pillar to why we rotated where we did.

I've talked about this before and this really will be another set of modules on https://t.co/9d6VzTK1Cg - Basically ranges are expanded out spreads. If you don't know the basics of how limit orders are the better price on the spread then market orders... Fuck man. I got youtube videos. Go watch.

HFTs and market makers play these. They're too difficult for us. We need queue advantage, and full automation, as well as latency edge.

Smaller ranges or micro ranges are the next step up on the spread. Still too fast for us. But slow enough for some algos, they don't need to compete for spreads.

As you go up in range sizes, bigger or slower participants start to have more ability to compete.

Volume legs, are like the market orders hitting on the spread. We get an idea of where more pressure exists, or more supply and demand.

The middle of ranges are like markets with wider spreads with no limit orders. Like penny stocks. So the edges are always important.

Ranges are structure. Anything else is slop. Sometimes trend days are legs of a monthly range.

Now on more volatile days. You need more fucking risk. You can't fucking react. The problem is when all this back and forth chop is too fucking fast for you to react and click. Some form of hybrid assist is needed to deal with that. But building that alone can have so many fucking issues, and is a real fucking project. 

So we need to expand our risk. This means we need bigger reward to offset stops.

This means, leaning into the wider ranges. 

At some point I CAN'T COMPETE on smaller ranges, that I could compete on - if volatility was lower.

This was key for today. 

Lean into the best of the best. NO MORE THAN 2 TRIES!

The $50 loss on trade 1 and $25 loss trade 3 were both fat finger mistakes. Not actual attempts.

So out of the 4 non-mistake losses, I tried specific setups on 2 of them once!

This shit should usually work out well and right away. You shouldn't need to keep fucking fighting as this means whatever you're doing is not working and something is changing in the market.

It's like chopping at a golf ball in a sand trap - but you're hitting nothing but sand. 

The delta had initially diverged as if sellers were reloading then ran a rebalance. This is a sign of fuckery on the delta. Basically and early sign of potential unreliability for reloads. 

However it was making massive reclaims that would rebalance and they were doing it near the highs before we leg up. So fading a highly offset delta is always a dangerous game.

Delta rebalances and reloads are just 2 different techniques or reads, on one indicator.

--

Now we had volume pump on the histogram. Which I had fucked with to get better reads from. The way it's setup now, I can see pumps on just the left or right side of V-Flushes.

This can tip off the direction. 

We certainly were getting directional tip offs. But also pockets of slop where it seemed some of the "hot pumps" on the volume where the same traders stopping. They happened in the same rough locations and were the same rough sizes.

Volume however can tip off direction when you get a lot of same direction hot pumping. Basically above average sustained volume. 

Looking for the biggest pockets of hot pumping or throttle pumping, can tip off points of no return. I say that loose as fuck though. Sometimes it holds and we blow back through those before not returning.

Today, it just pumped hard and never returned in a lot of spots.

Now for me I was fading major fucking legs with major volume. The second leg where I took the last 2 losses had 54 and 57 as massive volume legs. Surely a place to slow the price, and it did. If you look at a small enough time frame like a 30s you can see that area stumbled the most on the pure up trend.

The RR on it was so fucking huge I was willing to risk there. After all we are still in a HTF range, and I had no read of pure up trend. 

Now what I know is when my ranges get knocked. Or smaller ranges - this is a sign of a higher time frame play.

We had so much one way throttle pump that when my two major short areas failed, it was worth the flip.

ESPECIALLY MY LAST 2 LONGS!

The volume histogram was building high fucking massive lumps of pressure near new highs on the session. This is a sign of continuation. This is that old school shit where guys use to tell you volume increasing on edges, is a sign of a break!

Histogram is the best method to visualize it. 

For me......

I don't like just hitting out edges on highs. It's such a dangerous game. 

However I told Chronik, this might be one of those trends that has no pullbacks you wait forever for, and by the time it happens it's over.

Those types of trends are a mother fucker to fully be sure of and require you to just sort of jump in. 

Also these types of moves are not the normal. So most of the time tactical fades are working.

Now I left a lot on the table on some of the legs. But I also wanted to bank roll the PNL and make sure I could cover losses and then some, but never being too fucking greedy - because 99% of the time - I get fucked trying to do an extra squeeze for that next 5 points.

The session is narrated and up at https://t.co/9d6VzTK1Cg

I need to pipe in Chronik's mic, but you can hear me telling him all this shit. 

I'm happy with the results for someone who was in the way of the trend, but also trading with it, but not all of it because I wasn't sure.

A lot of the time these fucking things roll in the most random spots not touching other pivots, so it's always a guessing game.

Petal Transoceanic Subsea Cable

Funded & operated by Meta

Expected to enter service in 2029, the first transoceanic subsea cable @ petabit capacity, & the first to deploy multi-core fiber @ scale. Spanning 7,000 km between France & the United States, Petal will deliver 1 Pbps (1 petabit per second or 1,000 terabits per second), doubling what today’s most advanced subsea cables carry @ this distance w/out a proportional increase in power or physical infrastructure.

That’s roughly the network capacity required for 75% of the world’s population to stream music at the same time.*

*Calculation based on a total capacity of 1 Pbps w/ an audio stream bitrate of ~0.16 Mbps (160 kbps) for ≈ 6.25 billion simultaneous streams.

Petal will incorporate something called "fan-in/fan-out" tech. As each two-core fiber strand enters a repeater, an optical interface routes the signal from each core into a separate single-core fiber strand so that each can be amplified independently. The amplified signals are then routed back into the two cores of the dual-core fiber before continuing along the cable.

https://t.co/OVBGELmJLz

Petal is one of many subsea cable investments by Meta in recent years, including Marea in 2018, Amitie in 2023 & Anjana in 2025. Marea, the company's first transatlantic fiber instalment, supports 192 Tbps, meaning Petal will offer more than 5X that capacity.

AFPI economist @JamesBroughel explains why AI data centers offering free Wi-Fi and promising jobs can make residents feel like they're being bought off:

"You would think it’s utility bills or jobs, but often it’s water use, energy use, property values, traffic, the way the data center looks, and noise pollution."

"They’ll offer a big one-time payment to the county, a rec center, or public Wi-Fi in the case of St. Louis. To residents, this can appear like buying them off."

"And when they start talking about creating jobs, people don’t believe it, and for good reason. There aren’t a lot of permanent jobs created by data centers."

"The best thing the companies can do is not operate in secrecy, and address the main concerns: noise, water use, covering the cost of connecting to the grid. These aren’t significant costs to huge tech companies."

text:
What might the brothers Gann and Genann represent?

I would distinguish three possible themes from the narrative.

•Regional identity: Gann and Genann are linked to separate parts of Ireland. Their stories help explain how a single people could be represented as occupying distinct territories.

•Shared authority: Their joint reign offers a literary example of sovereignty shared between brothers. It is an intriguing contrast with stories in which kingship belongs to one exceptional individual.

•The fragility of political order: Their simultaneous deaths from plague show how quickly a royal arrangement can end. The story moves from shared rule to a new succession without presenting either brother as defeated in battle.

Gann and Genann before the Tuatha Dé Danann

The brothers belong to the generation that establishes the Fir Bolg's political order before the arrival of the Tuatha Dé Danann.

In the wider mythological sequence, the Fir Bolg eventually face the newcomers at the First Battle of Mag Tuired. The Tuatha Dé Danann win the battle and take kingship, although accounts differ about what happens to the surviving Fir Bolg.

Gann and Genann therefore belong to the earlier stage of the story: the creation and succession of a human royal order before the conflict that changes Ireland's mythological landscape.

One further point of interest is that an influential scholarly discussion of the Lebor Gabála Érenn suggests Gann and Genann may preserve traces of an older paired figure tradition. That is a scholarly interpretation, not a demonstrated fact about their origins, but it offers an intriguing possibility when examining their joint kingship.

Gann and Genann are not remembered for elaborate heroic adventures. Their significance lies in the way the tradition connects territory, kinship, shared kingship, and succession.

Gann represents the Fir Bolg's northern Munster branch; Genann represents Connacht. Together, they occupy the throne after Rudraige, and their shared reign ends when plague kills them both.

In the broader pattern of Irish mythology, their story helps establish the political world that exists before the Tuatha Dé Danann arrive and challenge the Fir Bolg's claim to Ireland.

text:
Research brief: Ukraine 2014 ("coup" / Euromaidan), the Obama administration, the CIA, and Democrats involved

PROVEN: primary record (official transcript, government document, the audio itself, court record)
REPORTED: credible press
ALLEGED: claim made by a party or advocate, not documented
1. The leaked Nuland–Pyatt call: PROVEN (audio + State Dept non-denial)
What it is: Audio of a call between Asst. Secretary of State Victoria Nuland and U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Geoffrey Pyatt. It was posted to YouTube under the Russian title "Marionettes of Maidan." Date fix: Al Jazeera/AP report it was posted Feb 4, 2014 and went viral on Thursday, Feb 6. Say "leaked in early February 2014" or "surfaced Feb 6." An AP source at State said it sounded like a call from "last week," meaning late Jan/early Feb.

BBC transcript (Feb 7, 2014): https://t.co/qwYEfeGqVi
Al Jazeera/AP on posting date, the Rogozin aide's tweet, and the apology: https://t.co/VIS2OzGPe0
Audio on Wikimedia Commons: https://t.co/Js2jz7fQ7L (Commons tags it "public domain" with source "YouTube." Treat that tag as doubtful and check fair-use rules before you rebroadcast it.)
Key lines, verbatim from BBC's transcript:

Nuland: "I don't think Klitsch should go into the government. I don't think it's necessary, I don't think it's a good idea."Nuland: "I think Yats is the guy who's got the economic experience, the governing experience. He's the... what he needs is Klitsch and Tyahnybok on the outside. He needs to be talking to them four times a week, you know."Nuland: "He's now gotten both Serry and [UN Secretary General] Ban Ki-moon to agree that Serry could come in Monday or Tuesday. So that would be great, I think, to help glue this thing and to have the UN help glue it and, you know, Fuck the EU."Pyatt: "No, exactly. And I think we've got to do something to make it stick together because you can be pretty sure that if it does start to gain altitude, that the Russians will be working behind the scenes to try to torpedo it."Pyatt: "...we want to try to get somebody with an international personality to come out here and help to midwife this thing."Nuland: "So on that piece Geoff, when I wrote the note [Jake] Sullivan's come back to me VFR, saying you need [Joe] Biden and I said probably tomorrow for an atta-boy and to get the deets [details] to stick. So Biden's willing."

(BBC writes "atta-boy" with a hyphen. Its bracketed notes identify "Yats" as Arseniy Yatseniuk, "Klitsch" as Vitali Klitschko, Tyahnybok as Oleh Tyahnybok, Feltman as Jeffrey Feltman (UN), and Serry as Robert Serry (UN). BBC also says "this is a fragment of what may well be a larger phone conversation.")

State Dept non-denial (PROVEN, official transcript): Daily Press Briefing, Feb 6, 2014, spokesperson Jen Psaki: https://t.co/QBNBo9dfYi

Q: "...you believe that this recording is a recording of a real telephone call?" PSAKI: "I didn't say it was inauthentic. I think we can leave it at that." Q: "Okay. So you're allowing for the – you're allowing the fact that it is authentic." PSAKI: "Yes."

In the same briefing Psaki said Nuland "has been in contact with her EU counterparts, and of course, has apologized," called the leak "a new low in Russian tradecraft," and said "It is no secret that Ambassador Pyatt and Assistant Secretary Nuland have been working with the Government of Ukraine, with the opposition... It remains the case that it is up to the Ukrainian people themselves to decide their future."

Follow-up you can state (PROVEN/REPORTED): On Feb 27, 2014 the Rada approved Yatseniuk as prime minister, 371 of 417 MPs registered in the hall (Interfax-Ukraine): https://t.co/yhdb3LXYZq

2. Nuland's "$5 billion" line: PROVEN (official State Dept text)

Remarks at the U.S.-Ukraine Foundation Conference, Washington DC, Dec 13, 2013: https://t.co/egUHRZ2msf

"Since Ukraine's independence in 1991, the United States has supported Ukrainians as they build democratic skills and institutions, as they promote civic participation and good governance, all of which are preconditions for Ukraine to achieve its European aspirations. We've invested over $5 billion to assist Ukraine in these and other goals that will ensure a secure and prosperous and democratic Ukraine."

Context: The figure covers 22 years (1991–2013) and "these and other goals." It is cumulative aid, not a Maidan budget. The State Dept's own FY2013 fact sheet puts total U.S. aid to Ukraine at about $102.6M that year, of which $24.6M was "Governing Justly and Democratically." The rest went to security, health (HIV/TB), economic growth, Chornobyl, and other programs. Fact sheet: https://t.co/fdQla2bM2Q In the same speech Nuland said she was "still jetlagged from my third trip in five weeks to Ukraine," that she made her "first visit to the Maidan on December 5th," and that she "spent more than two hours with President Yanukovych" (BBC dates that meeting to Wed., Dec 11). You can quote all of that. Safe on-screen line: "Nuland: the U.S. 'invested over $5 billion' in Ukraine since 1991." Do not say "$5 billion to overthrow Yanukovych."

3. Nuland and Pyatt handing out food on the Maidan, Dec 11, 2013: REPORTED (wire/press + photos)

BBC, Dec 11, 2013: "Ms Nuland visited Independence Square on Wednesday morning, handing out bread, biscuits and buns, and talking to protesters." The photo caption says Nuland and Pyatt "distributed bread in Independence Square – to protesters and police." https://t.co/iE9ZRbSe5T
Interfax-Ukraine (on the scene, Dec 11, 10:59): "Nuland is treating protesters with cookies, biscuits and bread from a big package... Nuland also approached Interior Forces troops deployed at the square and also offered them cookies, which the soldiers accepted silently." https://t.co/elBAPdCLvC

NPR/AP photo caption: Nuland "offered food to pro-European Union activists as she and U.S. Ambassador... Pyatt... walked through Independence Square... She also offered food to some of the police nearby." (AP photo, Andrew Kravchenko) https://t.co/iHoFVawbRn

Reuters (via the U.S. embassy) confirmed the visit: https://t.co/iG6GvV17Xd

Cookies note: "Cookies" is the popular version. Interfax did use the word, but BBC and the photos show mostly bread and buns, and she handed food to police too. The accurate line is "handed out bread and snacks on the Maidan." Counter-programming risk: critics will point out she fed the riot police as well.
4. U.S. politicians on the Maidan stage, Dec 15, 2013: REPORTED (multiple outlets, with direct quotes)
NPR, Dec 15, 2013: McCain "was accompanied by Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy, of Connecticut." McCain: "To all Ukrainians, America stands with you... The free world is with you, America is with you, I am with you." https://t.co/ToIoz6NnWu
Kyiv Post live blog, Dec 15, 1:50 p.m.: Murphy: "Ukraine's future stands with Europe and the U.S. stands with Ukraine... The way toward change goes through peaceful protests... if you are successful, the U.S. senate will stand with you every step of the way." McCain: "We are here to support your just cause..." https://t.co/8oHR0hcFsi
Both senators were on the Maidan stage, a Democrat and a Republican together. That is a bipartisan story, not only a Democratic one.
Other Democrats and Obama-administration figures

PersonRoleWhat the record showsRatingSourceVP Joe BidenObama's Ukraine point manWhite House readouts of Biden calls to Yanukovych on Feb 4, Feb 18 and Feb 20, 2014. On Feb 20 he "called upon President Yanukovych to immediately pull back all security forces – police, snipers, military and paramilitary units" and said "the United States is prepared to sanction those officials responsible for the violence."PROVENhttps://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/02/04/readout-vice-president-bidens-call-ukrainian-president-viktor-yanukovych · https://t.co/ZeYUd7CT18 · https://t.co/fKzrFHYzEf to Kyiv, Apr 22, 2014, with PM Yatsenyuk"Your former leader had to run in hiding..." He offered U.S. help against "this kleptocracy."PROVENhttps://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/04/22/remarks-press-vice-president-joe-Biden-and-ukrainian-prime-minister-arseBidenNamed in the leaked call"Sullivan's come back to me... saying you need Biden... for an atta-boy... So Biden's willing."PROVEN (audio)BBC transcript aboveHunter BidenBurisma boardCorrection: he joined on May 12, 2014, not in April. Burisma's press release is dated "London, 12 May, 2014." The Senate HSGAC/Finance majority report (Sept 2020) says "on May 12, 2014, Hunter Biden joined Archer on Burisma's board." Devon Archer (his business partner) was announced on Apr 22, 2014, the same day as Biden's Kyiv visit. The report also says Burisma wired $112,758.15 to Archer's Rosemont Seneca Bohai on Apr 15, 2014, and that Archer visited the VP at the White House on Apr 16 (citing RealClearPolitics).PROVEN (corporate release + Senate report). The report's framing is a Republican majority product: REPORTED/ALLEGED as to its conclusions.Burisma release (House record): https://t.co/AR8EMuX9pE · Senate report: https://t.co/R0KaF5JLCK SullivanBiden's national security adviser (BBC's bracket)Named in the call as relaying that Nuland "need[s] Biden."PROVEN (audio)BBC transcriptSec. of State John KerryOn Dec 10–11, 2013: "The United States expresses its disgust with the decision of Ukrainian authorities to meet the peaceful protest... with riot police, bulldozers, and batons" (quoted by BBC). In Kyiv on Mar 4, 2014 he met acting President Turchynov and PM Yatsenyuk and announced "an immediate $1 billion in a loan guarantee."PROVEN / REPORTEDBBC: https://t.co/iE9ZRbSe5T · State Dept Office of the Historian travel log: https://t.co/WHaLy5vzxd · Kerry remarks (GlobalSecurity mirror of State text): https://t.co/3b0oHkLJyb Susan RiceMeet the Press, Feb 23, 2014: Yanukovych "picked up in a very orderly fashion and left the capital, Kiev, just after having signed an agreement..." She said Russian military intervention "would be a grave mistake," and "The United States [is] on the side of the Ukrainian people."PROVEN (NBC transcript)https://t.co/o0LHKB0gaJ ObamaCNN GPS, Feb 1, 2015: Putin "was caught off balance by the protests in the Maidan, and Yanukovych then fleeing after we'd brokered a deal to transition power in Ukraine."PROVEN (CNN transcript)https://t.co/T4HL1ujBH9 Psaki / Jay CarneyState and White House spokespeoplePsaki's non-denial of the call (above). Carney confirmed Brennan's Kyiv trip (below).PROVENabove / below
5. CIA
5a. Brennan's Kyiv visit, April 2014: PROVEN (White House confirmation)
USA Today, Apr 14, 2014: Carney: "we don't normally comment on the CIA director's travel, but given the extraordinary circumstances in this case, and the false claims being leveled by the Russians at the CIA, we can confirm that the director was in Kiev this weekend as part of a trip to Europe." Per AP, "the CIA denies that Brennan encouraged Ukrainian authorities to conduct tactical operations." https://t.co/rY4v1y5so3
CNN transcript (Wolf, Apr 14, 2014) with the same Carney clip: https://t.co/DTx9F29JLo
Timing: the visit came about seven weeks after Yanukovych fell. It is not evidence about the Maidan itself.
5b. NYT, "The Spy War: How the C.I.A. Secretly Helps Ukraine Fight Putin" (Entous & Schwirtz, Feb 25, 2024): REPORTED
https://t.co/c1SmINxXzR (paywalled; I read the Wayback copy: https://t.co/TgywhDuRXi)
"The C.I.A.'s partnership in Ukraine can be traced back to two phone calls on the night of Feb. 24, 2014... Millions of Ukrainians had just overrun the country's pro-Kremlin government and the president, Viktor Yanukovych, and his spy chiefs had fled to Russia."
New SBU chief Valentyn Nalyvaichenko "called the C.I.A. station chief and the local head of MI6... and proposed a three-way partnership. 'That's how it all started.'"
"an unmarked U.S. government plane touched down at an airport in Kyiv carrying John O. Brennan... He told Mr. Nalyvaichenko that the C.I.A. was interested in developing a relationship but only at a pace the agency was comfortable with."
The partnership produced "a C.I.A.-supported network of spy bases constructed in the past eight years that includes 12 secret locations along the Russian border." Around 2016 the CIA began training Unit 2245.
The Times also says Obama advisers were "deeply concerned about provoking Moscow" and imposed restrictive "secret rules." It notes Nalyvaichenko had run "a similar partnership" with the CIA during an earlier stint as spy chief.
Can say: "The NYT reports the CIA partnership began the night Yanukovych's government fell." Can't say: "NYT confirms the CIA ran the Maidan." The article dates the partnership to after the government fell.
5c. CIA involvement in the Maidan itself: ALLEGED (no documentation found)
Putin, Mar 4, 2014: he said the revolution was incited by people "sitting in America doing experiments, like on rats," and that "the western instructors did well." The Guardian fact-check of the same day found "no evidence that either the US or UK have trained opposition forces militarily": https://t.co/PYctVYFbf3 (the Kremlin transcript is at https://t.co/bqV9ggX6YB but would not load from my box, so I did not quote it directly).
Yanukovych accused the CIA of driving the new government's April crackdown in the east, per AP in USA Today above. The CIA denied it.
I found no declassified document, court finding, or credible investigative report showing CIA direction of the Nov 2013–Feb 2014 protests. Rate any "CIA ran the coup" line ALLEGED.
5d. Sniper massacre (Feb 20, 2014): verdict PROVEN; interpretation contested
Verdict (Oct 18, 2023, Sviatoshynskyi District Court, Kyiv), Hromadske report: Oleh Yanishevskyi got life; Pavlo Abroskin and Serhiy Zinchenko got 15 years; Oleksandr Marynchenko got 5 years for abuse of power (already served through pre-trial detention credit); Serhiy Tamtura was acquitted. "All five defendants were exchanged for Ukrainian prisoners in 2019... Yanishevskyi, Zinchenko, and Abroskin... were imprisoned in absentia." The trial ran May 2016–Nov 2022 with 320 hearings and covered 48 killings and 80 attempted killings. https://t.co/RfUFW0erne (The court's own announcement: https://t.co/itVUtqA6Dd. It is JS-rendered, so I could not read the text from my box.)
Ivan Katchanovski (Univ. of Ottawa). Peer-reviewed article: "The 'snipers' massacre' on the Maidan in Ukraine," Cogent Social Sciences, published Oct 16, 2023, DOI https://t.co/YpeHKycNRK (I confirmed the metadata via Crossref; the full text timed out). In his Feb 20, 2024 Canadian Dimension essay he argues the verdict "confirmed that many Maidan activists were shot not by members of... Berkut... but by snipers in the far-right-controlled Hotel Ukraina." He quotes the verdict reaching "a categorical conclusion that on the morning of February 20, 2014, persons with weapons, from which the shots were fired, were in the premises of the Hotel Ukraina," and says it found "nine Maidan protesters were killed and 23 wounded by 'unknown persons'" who were not police. https://t.co/9Sym8UsFgC Rate this: verdict quotes = REPORTED (via Katchanovski's translation); "false flag" conclusion = ALLEGED. He also alleges Soros-funded evidence work and a fabricated forensic match: ALLEGED.
Rebuttal: Cathy Young, The Bulwark: the court found Marynchenko, Abroskin and Zinchenko guilty "in the deaths of 31 of the 48," and "concludes that 40 of the 48 dead protesters were killed by Berkut, while in eight cases other perpetrators cannot be ruled out." She adds that the verdict says shots came "from the direction of" the hotel, not necessarily from inside it. https://t.co/f7mcuBwmJk

Safe line: "A Ukrainian court convicted riot police for most of the killings, but also found that some protesters were shot from the area of the Hotel Ukraina, territory police didn't control." Unsafe: "A court proved the Maidan massacre was a false flag."
6. NED and USAID money before 2014: PROVEN (grantor's own records)
NED (National Endowment for Democracy, a congressionally funded private nonprofit):
NED's Ukraine page as archived Oct 17, 2014 ("Grant descriptions are from the 2013 NED Annual Report") lists 56 grants totaling $2,880,395 (my sum). The largest were NDI $371,000 (building capacity of election monitor Opora for the May 2014 election), CIPE $357,707 (business associations / anti-corruption), and IRI $275,000 (municipal good governance). Others include Telekritika $58,250 (media monitoring), Democratic Initiatives Foundation $41,298, the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union $49,960, Youth Alternative $68,170 (Rada internships), the Institute of the Republic $32,609 (freedom of assembly), and Open Society Foundation–Ukraine $33,980 (monitoring parliament). Several grantees are unnamed. https://t.co/MbgCpPfxW5
The earlier archived page (Mar 3, 2014) lists the prior cycle. Its descriptions refer to the Oct 2012 elections, and I count 64 grants totaling $3,339,250, including NDI $345,000, CIPE $359,945, and IRI $250,000 + $95,000 + $35,000. https://t.co/GlEexRgOse
Nature of grants: voter education, election monitoring, media freedom, human rights, local government accountability, youth internships. None of the listed descriptions funds protests, weapons or "self-defense" units.
USAID / all U.S. aid (State Dept FY2013 fact sheet): total $103.6M (FY2012 actual) and $102.6M (FY2013 est.). "Governing Justly and Democratically" was $28.5M (FY2012) and $24.6M (FY2013). By account, the Economic Support Fund was $57.1M in FY2013, plus USAID and State global health lines. https://t.co/fdQla2bM2Q Can say: "Washington spent tens of millions a year on Ukrainian 'democracy' programs before the Maidan." Can't say: "USAID/NED paid protesters."

In Kyiv on Mar 4, 2014 he met acting President Turchynov and PM Yatsenyuk and announced "an immediate $1 billion in a loan guarantee."PROVEN / REPORTEDBBC: https://t.co/iE9ZRbRGgl · State Dept Office of the Historian travel log: https://t.co/WHaLy5v1HF · Kerry remarks (GlobalSecurity mirror of State text): https://t.co/3b0oHkLbID Susan RiceMeet the Press, Feb 23, 2014: Yanukovych "picked up in a very orderly fashion and left the capital, Kiev, just after having signed an agreement..." She said Russian military intervention "would be a grave mistake," and "The United States [is] on the side of the Ukrainian people."PROVEN (NBC transcript)https://t.co/o0LHKAZIlb ObamaCNN GPS, Feb 1, 2015: Putin "was caught off balance by the protests in the Maidan, and Yanukovych then fleeing after we'd brokered a deal to transition power in Ukraine."PROVEN (CNN transcript)https://t.co/T4HL1uj3RB Psaki / Jay CarneyState and White House spokespeoplePsaki's non-denial of the call (above). 5a. Brennan's Kyiv visit, April 2014: PROVEN (White House confirmation)

CNN transcript (Wolf, Apr 14, 2014) with the same Carney clip: https://t.co/DTx9F29bVQ

5b. NYT, "The Spy War: How the C.I.A. Secretly Helps Ukraine Fight Putin" (Entous & Schwirtz, Feb 25, 2024): REPORTED
https://t.co/c1SmINxpKj (paywalled; I read the Wayback copy: https://t.co/TgywhDuk7K)
"The C.I.A.'s partnership in Ukraine can be traced back to two phone calls on the night of Feb. 24, 2014... Millions of Ukrainians had just overrun the country's pro-Kremlin government and the president, Viktor Yanukovych, and his spy chiefs had fled to Russia."
New SBU chief Valentyn Nalyvaichenko "called the C.I.A. station chief and the local head of MI6... and proposed a three-way partnership. 'That's how it all started.'"
"an unmarked U.S. government plane touched down at an airport in Kyiv carrying John O. Brennan... He told Mr. Nalyvaichenko that the C.I.A. was interested in developing a relationship but only at a pace the agency was comfortable with."
The partnership produced "a C.I.A.-supported network of spy bases constructed in the past eight years that includes 12 secret locations along the Russian border." Around 2016 the CIA began training Unit 2245.
The Times also says Obama advisers were "deeply concerned about provoking Moscow" and imposed restrictive "secret rules." It notes Nalyvaichenko had run "a similar partnership" with the CIA during an earlier stint as spy chief.
Can say: "The NYT reports the CIA partnership began the night Yanukovych's government fell." Can't say: "NYT confirms the CIA ran the Maidan." The article dates the partnership to after the government fell.
5c. CIA involvement in the Maidan itself: ALLEGED (no documentation found)
Putin, Mar 4, 2014: he said the revolution was incited by people "sitting in America doing experiments, like on rats," and that "the western instructors did well." The Guardian fact-check of the same day found "no evidence that either the US or UK have trained opposition forces militarily": https://t.co/PYctVYEDpv (the Kremlin transcript is at https://t.co/bqV9ggWz93 but would not load from my box, so I did not quote it directly).
Yanukovych accused the CIA of driving the new government's April crackdown in the east, per AP in USA Today above. The CIA denied it.
I found no declassified document, court finding, or credible investigative report showing CIA direction of the Nov 2013–Feb 2014 protests. Rate any "CIA ran the coup" line ALLEGED.
5d. Sniper massacre (Feb 20, 2014): verdict PROVEN; interpretation contested
Verdict (Oct 18, 2023, Sviatoshynskyi District Court, Kyiv), Hromadske report: Oleh Yanishevskyi got life; Pavlo Abroskin and Serhiy Zinchenko got 15 years; Oleksandr Marynchenko got 5 years for abuse of power (already served through pre-trial detention credit); Serhiy Tamtura was acquitted. "All five defendants were exchanged for Ukrainian prisoners in 2019... Yanishevskyi, Zinchenko, and Abroskin... were imprisoned in absentia." The trial ran May 2016–Nov 2022 with 320 hearings and covered 48 killings and 80 attempted killings. https://t.co/RfUFW0dTxG (The court's own announcement: https://t.co/itVUtqzyNF. It is JS-rendered, so I could not read the text from my box.)
Ivan Katchanovski (Univ. of Ottawa). Peer-reviewed article: "The 'snipers' massacre' on the Maidan in Ukraine," Cogent Social Sciences, published Oct 16, 2023, DOI https://t.co/YpeHKycg2c (I confirmed the metadata via Crossref; the full text timed out). In his Feb 20, 2024 Canadian Dimension essay he argues the verdict "confirmed that many Maidan activists were shot not by members of... Berkut... but by snipers in the far-right-controlled Hotel Ukraina." He quotes the verdict reaching "a categorical conclusion that on the morning of February 20, 2014, persons with weapons, from which the shots were fired, were in the premises of the Hotel Ukraina," and says it found "nine Maidan protesters were killed and 23 wounded by 'unknown persons'" who were not police. https://t.co/9Sym8Us7r4 Rate this: verdict quotes = REPORTED (via Katchanovski's translation); "false flag" conclusion = ALLEGED. He also alleges Soros-funded evidence work and a fabricated forensic match: ALLEGED.
Rebuttal: Cathy Young, The Bulwark: the court found Marynchenko, Abroskin and Zinchenko guilty "in the deaths of 31 of the 48," and "concludes that 40 of the 48 dead protesters were killed by Berkut, while in eight cases other perpetrators cannot be ruled out." She adds that the verdict says shots came "from the direction of" the hotel, not necessarily from inside it. https://t.co/f7mcuBvOTM

Safe line: "A Ukrainian court convicted riot police for most of the killings, but also found that some protesters were shot from the area of the Hotel Ukraina, territory police didn't control." Unsafe: "A court proved the Maidan massacre was a false flag."
6. NED and USAID money before 2014: PROVEN (grantor's own records)
NED (National Endowment for Democracy, a congressionally funded private nonprofit):
NED's Ukraine page as archived Oct 17, 2014 ("Grant descriptions are from the 2013 NED Annual Report") lists 56 grants totaling $2,880,395 (my sum). The largest were NDI $371,000 (building capacity of election monitor Opora for the May 2014 election), CIPE $357,707 (business associations / anti-corruption), and IRI $275,000 (municipal good governance). Others include Telekritika $58,250 (media monitoring), Democratic Initiatives Foundation $41,298, the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union $49,960, Youth Alternative $68,170 (Rada internships), the Institute of the Republic $32,609 (freedom of assembly), and Open Society Foundation–Ukraine $33,980 (monitoring parliament). Several grantees are unnamed. https://t.co/MbgCpPf06x
The earlier archived page (Mar 3, 2014) lists the prior cycle. Its descriptions refer to the Oct 2012 elections, and I count 64 grants totaling $3,339,250, including NDI $345,000, CIPE $359,945, and IRI $250,000 + $95,000 + $35,000. https://t.co/GlEexRggCG
Nature of grants: voter education, election monitoring, media freedom, human rights, local government accountability, youth internships. None of the listed descriptions funds protests, weapons or "self-defense" units.
USAID / all U.S. aid (State Dept FY2013 fact sheet): total $103.6M (FY2012 actual) and $102.6M (FY2013 est.). "Governing Justly and Democratically" was $28.5M (FY2012) and $24.6M (FY2013). By account, the Economic Support Fund was $57.1M in FY2013, plus USAID and State global health lines. https://t.co/fdQla2bedi Can say: "Washington spent tens of millions a year on Ukrainian 'democracy' programs before the Maidan." Can't say: "USAID/NED paid protesters."
