text:
Two Los Angeles officers jailed a student who had been reading in the library.

It was 1953. James Forman had come outside for air with a book under his arm when the car pulled up, and the officers accused him of a robbery in the area. They took him downtown, locked him up, and let him go three days later without charging him with anything.

Nothing about those three days was written down anywhere. Eight years later he was running the national office of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee out of Atlanta, and he had a telephone line put in for one purpose.

The line ran on a Wide Area Telephone Service account, and it let a field secretary in Mississippi call the office without going through the local exchange.

A worker could phone in an arrest, or harm done to somebody in a county jail, and Atlanta would have it on paper the same day. James Forman's standing instruction to everybody in the field was three words long.

Write it down.

He said it to staff in Mississippi and Alabama and Georgia, to students who came south for one summer and to people who had been organizing their own counties long before he got there. The paper came back to the office and it stayed. The SNCC Legacy Project, run by the organization's surviving members, describes what came of that instruction as a body of documentation that scholars still work from.

SNCC had been running for a year and a half before Forman got near it. It was founded over Easter weekend in April 1960, at a conference at Shaw University in Raleigh that Ella Baker organized with eight hundred dollars she talked Martin Luther King's organization into spending.

What the students had after that was a corner of the SCLC's Atlanta office and whatever money came in the mail. What they did not have was anybody to run it.

Forman took the job in the fall of 1961, a few weeks after turning thirty-three. He was about ten years older than most of the people he was suddenly responsible for.

He had grown up on the South Side of Chicago and spent his first years before that on his grandmother's farm in Marshall County, Mississippi, on land she worked behind a mule. In 1964 he sat down for a recorded interview with Robert Penn Warren and gave the geography before anything else. Marshall County, up in the north of the state, about thirty miles from Oxford, with the mail coming through a little town called Moscow, Tennessee.

He gave the date too. Reference books have printed October 5, 1928, for his birthday, and on the tape he says October 4.

Between the farm and Atlanta there was the Air Force, with a stretch on Okinawa during the Korean War. Los Angeles came after that, then the Veteran's Neuropsychiatric Hospital, then Chicago again in 1954 and Roosevelt University, which he went through in three years as president of the student body.

In 1958 he covered the school desegregation fight in Little Rock for the Chicago Defender. By 1960 he was driving donated food from Chicago down to Fayette County, Tennessee, where Black farmers who had registered to vote were being put off the land they worked.

In August 1961 he was in jail in Monroe, North Carolina, arrested with Freedom Riders who were protesting the segregated facilities there.

The sentence was suspended, and he went to Atlanta.

What he built there was an office in the plainest sense of the word. A payroll, bills paid when they came due, a filing system and a research department.

Clayborne Carson, the historian who wrote the standard history of SNCC, records that Forman took on the mundane administrative chores other staff avoided. Julian Bond, who was working in that office by October 1961, told an interviewer a few years afterward that Forman turned out to be "a fantastic administrator and fund-raiser."

There is a napkin.

It is a paper napkin out of a cafe, and Forman wrote a payroll order across it and sent it to Ruby Doris Robinson, who managed the Atlanta office. Put Miriam Cohen on the payroll, it says, and give her forty dollars for the past four weeks if you have it.

Then the last clause, in the same hand. "But give her some $."

Field secretaries were paid ten dollars a week, less deductions, in the weeks there was money to pay them at all. Forty dollars was four weeks of that.

Forman was not at a desk the whole time. During voter registration work Forman was picked up, held and physically harmed in counties where the people running things would use anything at all to stop it.

In the summer of 1964, SNCC had put hundreds of volunteers into Mississippi and helped build a delegation of Black Mississippians to carry north to the Democratic convention in Atlantic City, where they were offered two seats at large and told to be satisfied with it.

When that was over, Forman and other SNCC workers flew to Guinea at the invitation of the government there.

A week after the troopers met the marchers on the bridge at Selma, he led about six hundred people out of a Baptist church in Montgomery toward the state capitol. They were carrying a petition for Governor George Wallace.

Mounted police rode into them before they got there. It was the same week the President went before Congress and borrowed the movement's own words to announce a voting rights bill.

He was replaced as executive secretary in 1966, and within two years he had left SNCC altogether.

In 1968 he took the title of minister of foreign affairs for the Black Panther Party and threw in with the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, the Detroit organization built out of the auto plants.

On April 26, 1969, in Detroit, he read a document out loud to the National Black Economic Development Conference. The conference adopted it, 187 votes to 63.

The document was the Black Manifesto, and it named a sum. Five hundred million dollars from the white churches and synagogues of the United States, which the manifesto worked out as fifteen dollars for every Black person in the country.

The money was already spent on paper. A land bank in the South for farmers who had been put off their land, four television networks, a university, all of it itemized in the document before a cent of it existed.

Eight days after Detroit he walked into the Riverside Church in Manhattan on a Sunday morning.

The clergy were processing in. Forman went up the steps to the chancel, read the demands into the middle of the service, and about two thirds of the congregation walked out of the building with the minister among them.

Riverside stands on the edge of Harlem in a building John D. Rockefeller Jr. paid for. Forman named its share as sixty percent of its annual income.

Two days after that he posted the manifesto on the door of the Lutheran Church in America headquarters and told the Lutherans their share was fifty million. On May 13, 1969, he sat down in front of the Episcopal Church's presiding bishop and asked for sixty million dollars and sixty percent of the income from everything the church owned.

Riverside was in court inside the week, making any further interruption of its worship a matter for a judge. The mayor of New York offered a police cordon around the building and the church turned it down. By the middle of May the FBI and the Justice Department had opened investigations into the conference.

Then came the counting.

At the end of August 1969, four months after Detroit, Time reported that about twenty-two thousand dollars had reached the conference. The demand had been five hundred million.

The standard encyclopedia account of the manifesto puts the total the churches eventually gave at somewhere near half a million dollars, about two hundred thousand of it from that one congregation. Against what was asked for, that is a dollar in a thousand.

The same hand had once written out a worker's back pay on a napkin and made sure it got honored.

The money that did move went into programs the churches ran themselves. The Manhattan church he had interrupted started a Fund for Social Justice, went after four hundred and fifty thousand dollars over three years for the poor of its own neighborhood, and finished nearly a hundred thousand short of that.

Forman kept writing. In 1969 he published a book about one student, Sammy Younge Jr., killed in 1966, and the title called Younge the first Black college student to die in the Black liberation movement.

Three years after that came his own account of the decade, The Making of Black Revolutionaries. Of 1962 and 1963 he wrote that "accumulating experiences with Southern 'law and order' were turning me into a full-fledged revolutionary."

He went back to school in his fifties, took a master's degree at Cornell in 1980 and a doctorate two years after that, and published the dissertation as a book.

He moved to Washington in 1981. He founded the Unemployment and Poverty Action Council and ran it, and he started a wire service of his own, the Black America News Service, to put out the news that the other wires were not carrying.

The cancer was found in 1991. In July 2004, thirteen years into it and weak, he took a train from Washington up to Boston during the Democratic convention and helped throw bags of tea into the harbor, because the District he lived in had no vote in Congress.

He died on January 10, 2005, at a hospice in Washington, at seventy-six.

His sons gave his papers to the Library of Congress between 2007 and 2009. Correspondence, memoranda, diaries, appointment books, calendars and subject files, catalogued and open to anybody who walks in and asks for a container number.

The finding aid alone runs fifty pages. The earliest paper in the collection is dated 1848.

Seventy-nine thousand items. Two hundred and fifty-five boxes and just over a hundred linear feet of it, left behind by the man whose instruction to everybody else was to write it down.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXKqi
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text: Every day, the men and women of @phillypolice put themselves on the line to protect and serve the people of Philadelphia – and Officer Shane Seiber was one of those brave men serving his city.   Though I did not know Officer Seiber personally, his service and impact on those around him was evident in the memories that were shared and in the stories that were offered. From his time in the United State Air Force to the Philadelphia Police Department, Officer Seiber answered the call time and time again to protect his fellow Americans and keep his community safe.   My heart and prayers go out to his family, friends, and fellow officers who are mourning this deep and terrible loss.   May his memory bring you comfort and forever be a blessing.

text:
Today, I joined fallen Officer Shane Seiber’s family, his loved ones, his @PhillyPolice brothers and sisters, and the entire City of Philadelphia in honoring his memory and life of service. 

Officer Seiber was a true public servant, and he was the best of us. He cared deeply about making others’ lives better — and he demonstrated that by choosing to live a life of service. He served two tours in Iraq with the United States Air Force — and even after he returned to civilian life, he continued his commitment to serving others when he decided to become a police officer with the Philadelphia Police Department. 

As I’ve listened to stories about Shane from some of the officers who served with him, it struck me how his kindness shone through in every memory they shared. To them, he was known as “Colgate” for his big smile that could light up any room. He was a team player — someone who you could always count on to have your back. 

For 10 years, Shane put on the uniform and the badge every day, kissed his family goodbye, and left home to protect and serve his neighbors. While his life was cut far too short, we all have a collective responsibility to come together and remember his life of service and the ultimate sacrifice he made to keep his community safe. 

Policing is a noble profession, and those who take on the incredibly difficult task of protecting our communities deserve our profound gratitude and deep respect.

Lori and I join this community in praying for Shane’s wife Lisa, their two kids — Finn and Emily — his mother Michelle, his stepfather, Nelson, his brothers John and Max, and his sister Sophia — along with all of Shane’s family and everyone who loved him. 

May God offer you comfort and strength in this time of mourning, and may Officer Shane Seiber’s memory forever be a blessing.

text:
You were once far off from the covenants of promise with no hope and without God in the world.

The dividing wall of hostility kept you alienated from the commonwealth of Israel.

Christ Jesus has broken down that barrier by his blood and reconciled all into one body.

This is the message of Ephesians the blueprint of unity in the household of God.

Ephesians 2 Inspires Catholics to Embrace Unity and Grow in Holiness

The passage from Ephesians chapter two reminds readers that they have been brought near through Christ and are now part of a living structure built for God. This message offers steady encouragement for those who strive to live well yet sometimes fall short in their efforts. By focusing on reconciliation and belonging the words help shift attention away from past divisions and toward the ongoing work of becoming a holy dwelling. Faithful Catholics can draw practical strength from this vision as they seek to avoid sin and move forward with hope each day.

How Does Remembering Our Past Separation Lead to Greater Gratitude Today

The reading begins by noting the former state of being without Christ and having no hope while far from the covenants. This description serves as a gentle reminder rather than a source of discouragement because it highlights the change that has already taken place. When believers recall how they once stood apart they can appreciate more deeply the nearness now available through the blood of Christ. Such reflection encourages daily choices that honor this gift instead of returning to old patterns of isolation or conflict. The positive shift from alienation to connection provides motivation to resist temptations that pull people back into division.

What Does the Breaking Down of Walls Reveal About Peace in Everyday Life

The text continues by explaining that Christ is our peace who has made both groups into one and broken down the dividing wall of hostility. This image of unity shows how former barriers no longer need to define relationships or personal conduct. Catholics who face moments of anger or separation can turn to this truth to choose reconciliation over continued strife. The process of abolishing commandments that created separation points to a new humanity formed in Christ where peace becomes the foundation for actions. By dwelling on this reconciled state readers find support for habits that build harmony at home and in communities rather than allowing small offenses to grow into sin.

How Does Access Through the Spirit Strengthen Our Connection to God

The reading next describes how Christ proclaimed peace to those far off and near so that both have access in one Spirit to the Father. This shared access underscores that no one needs to feel like an outsider when approaching prayer or the sacraments. For those working to lead a holy life this assurance offers comfort on days when efforts seem insufficient because the Spirit remains the constant link. It encourages consistent practices such as regular participation in the Eucharist that reinforce belonging and reduce the pull toward self reliance or despair. The result is a steadier path away from sin and toward deeper trust in the ongoing presence of God.

In What Ways Can We See Ourselves as Part of a Growing Holy Temple

The final verses present believers as citizens with the saints and members of the household of God built on the foundation of apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone. This picture of a joined structure that grows into a holy temple in the Lord emphasizes gradual formation rather than instant perfection. Catholics striving for holiness can view their daily attempts as contributions to this building process where setbacks do not remove them from the foundation. The idea of being built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God invites reflection on how personal growth supports the wider community of faith. Such a perspective fosters patience with oneself and others while inspiring choices that align with this sacred purpose over time.

The overall message of the passage centers on the reality of being brought near and formed into something sacred through Christ. This outlook provides ongoing uplift for faithful people who desire to avoid sin by focusing on unity and belonging instead of past failures. As the structure continues to grow each person finds renewed reason to participate actively in that holy work.

Per Grok: 
"That post is a mix of distorted reporting, unproven claims, and outright falsehoods. Here's a point-by-point breakdown based on the available record.

The post claims Trump’s “own wife” told girls not to be alone with him at Mar-a-Lago parties. This refers to secondhand accounts involving his then-wife Marla Maples (they divorced in 1999). A New York Times/Daily Beast-style report describes Maples allegedly warning the mother of a 14-year-old model at a 1994 party to keep the girl away from the men there (including her husband). Maples has denied specifically saying that about Trump. Separate WSJ reporting has her describing Epstein as “off” or “wrong” to staff in the mid-1990s and not wanting time with him. These are decades-old, disputed anecdotes from the social scene of the era—not evidence that Trump abused anyone. No Epstein victim has publicly accused Trump of sexual misconduct with them.⁠

On “shipping in under 15 year old girls and offer[ing] them drinks”: Mar-a-Lago hosted parties with young models in the 1990s (including reports of underage teens at some events), champagne was offered, and Epstein was a frequent guest. One documented example is a 1992 “calendar girls” event where Epstein was the only other male guest. Virginia Giuffre was recruited by Maxwell from the Mar-a-Lago spa as a teen around 2000. Trump has said he banned Epstein for being a creep and for poaching spa staff (he has referred to Epstein “stealing” employees, including Giuffre). Contemporaneous and later reporting shows Trump and Epstein socialized in Palm Beach and New York circles into the early 2000s before the break. That social overlap is real; evidence that Trump participated in or facilitated Epstein’s crimes is not. Multiple reviews of the released files have not produced a smoking-gun allegation against him from victims.⁠

The Bondi claim is false. Attorney General Pam Bondi (and the DOJ under the Epstein Files Transparency Act) oversaw the release of roughly 3–3.5 million pages. Critics (including some survivors and Democrats) have said more material exists (estimates around 6 million total pages in some accounts), with the remainder described as duplicative, privileged, or already reviewed—not that Bondi confirmed the unreleased portion is “horrific” and will “toast” Trump. Bondi has faced criticism over redactions, timing, and process (and was later removed from the post), but the released material has not yielded the decisive evidence against Trump that the post assumes is sitting in the vault. If it existed in clear form, the political incentives on all sides would have surfaced it long ago.⁠  

For context on the original post this was replying to: the 2006 Palm Beach police chief account (Michael Reiter) is documented in an FBI interview summary released in the files. Reiter said Trump called to thank police for stopping Epstein, called Maxwell “evil,” said he had thrown Epstein out of Mar-a-Lago, and described once leaving when teens were present. Epstein’s political giving skewed heavily Democratic (including to the DNC, which kept some funds after his 2008 conviction). And Democratic Delegate Stacey Plaskett did exchange texts with the already-convicted Epstein during the 2019 Michael Cohen hearing, receiving real-time tips that aligned with her questions.⁠

Trump and Epstein had a documented social relationship in the 1990s–early 2000s that ended before Epstein’s Florida case. The files and reporting continue to show that. They do not show Trump as a participant in the trafficking. The post’s leap from old party anecdotes and incomplete file releases to “he’s toast” is not supported by the evidence that has actually come out"

THE ELEPHANT THAT WAS HANGED FOR MURDER

On September 11, 1916, in Kingsport, Tennessee, a circus elephant named Mary killed a man.

Mary was a 5-ton Asian elephant with the Sparks World Famous Shows circus. She was the star. For 20 years she had done tricks.

Her new keeper that day was Walter Eldridge, who had no experience with elephants. Witnesses said he hit her behind the ear with a hook to make her do a trick. She got angry, grabbed him with her trunk, threw him against a drink stand, and stepped on his head.

The town panicked and shouted, "Kill the elephant."

The circus owner, Charlie Sparks, knew if Mary lived no town would let his circus in again. He had to show she was punished.

He tried to shoot her. Bullets bounced off. Towns refused.

The town of Erwin, Tennessee offered to help. Erwin had a crane used to lift railroad cars, a 100-ton Derrick car.

On September 13, 1916, 2,500 people came to watch. They chained Mary's leg to the crane and lifted her. The chain broke. She fell and broke her hip. They put a heavier chain on and lifted her again.

They hanged an elephant with a railroad crane in front of a crowd.

A photographer took a picture. It is still in the Erwin library.

Today Erwin says they did it to protect people. Sparks circus was bankrupt within a year anyway.

text:
$NP Q3 2026 earnings: Neptune earns more per policy, but its plan halves growth

Neptune sold a record amount of flood insurance and kept more of each premium dollar, but its own plan has growth slowing sharply. Revenue rose 34% because the insurers behind its policies paid the company a higher commission on each one it placed. Neptune raised its 2026 target again and set a first target for 2027; by our math both leave growth in the mid-teens.

• Revenue: $𝟱𝟵.𝟲𝗠 (+34% from a year ago)
• Adjusted EBITDA margin: 𝟲𝟭.𝟳% (60.2% a year ago)
• Full-year revenue outlook: 𝗥𝗮𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗱 $𝟱𝗠 ($204M, about 28% growth)
• First 2027 revenue outlook: $𝟮𝟯𝟴𝗠 (17% above the 2026 plan)

⚖️ 𝗩𝗲𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse, because the company has now put a number on the slowdown it had only implied: about 17% growth next year, after the Palomar policy transfer that lifted sales for a year ended in the quarter. The good news: a higher commission rate lifted margins, Neptune repaid $25 million of debt, and the August plan proved cautious.

The question now is whether the 2027 plan is as cautious as this year's turned out to be. Either Neptune keeps lifting its targets through the year, or the Palomar transfer and renewal losses were doing more of the work than the record quarter shows. The fourth quarter, the first without Palomar sales, gives the first reading.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲

🟢🟢 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘄 𝗣𝗮𝘆 𝗡𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲 𝗔 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻
Neptune does not insure anyone itself. It sells flood policies written by 45 insurance companies and keeps a commission on each premium dollar it places. That commission rate is the main lever on its revenue, because the fees per policy hardly change. Neptune said the quarter benefited from "increased commission income as a percent of written premium".

By our math the gap between what insurers pay Neptune and what Neptune pays the agents who sell its policies widened by almost two percentage points of premium in a year. That is why the adjusted profit margin, which leaves out stock pay and one-offs, rose even though overhead grew faster than sales.

• Commission income: 34.6% of written premium, from 33.4% a year ago and 33.5% last quarter
• Agent commissions: 13.1% of written premium, from 13.6% a year ago; Neptune called this "normalized commission expense as a percent of written premium"
• Agent commissions as a share of revenue: 29.2%, down 2.0 points
• Adjusted EBITDA margin: 61.7%, up 1.5 points

This matters because every extra point of commission rate is almost pure profit: the insurers pay it and no new cost comes with it. The step arrived faster than the gradual gain management described after renewing its two largest programs in June, so the better terms show in full this quarter. The remaining programs renew in October and December.

What to watch: commission income as a share of written premium in the fourth quarter, after the October and December renewals. A rate above 34.6% would mean the June step began a trend rather than a one-off reset.

🟢 𝗡𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝗗𝗲𝗯𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗢𝗳 𝗕𝘂𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲𝘀
Three months ago Neptune had drawn almost all of its credit line, partly to fund share buybacks, and its balance sheet still shows a stockholders' deficit from last year's preferred dividend. This quarter it bought no shares and used operating cash to repay debt.

• Debt: $215 million, from $240 million at June 30
• Credit line unused: $45 million, from $20 million
• Net leverage: 1.7 times adjusted EBITDA, from 2.1 times

This matters because a company one year past its listing should not borrow to retire stock. Neptune said it will "balance debt reduction with opportunistic share repurchases", so the stated policy is unchanged, but this quarter the cash went to debt and interest expense fell 35% from a year ago.

What to watch: the debt balance and any buyback in the fourth quarter. Another quarter of repayment with no purchases would mean the June buyback belonged to the private-equity share sale rather than to a new habit.

🟢 𝗡𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲'𝘀 𝗔𝘂𝗴𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗖𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗔𝗴𝗮𝗶𝗻
Neptune gives a full-year revenue target and leaves investors to work out the quarters. By our math the target it set in August pointed to about 20% growth in the second half. The third quarter came in at 34%, so the plan was cautious, and Neptune lifted the full-year target to $204 million.

Without the raise, the August target would have left about $46 million for the fourth quarter, a rise of only 5%, so part of the increase simply recognises what the third quarter delivered. It is the third raise this year, and the moves have been steady rather than shrinking.

• Full-year target by vintage: $186–189 million, then $195 million, then $199 million, now $204 million
• Size of each move: +$7.5 million, +$4 million, +$5 million

A beat against its own plan says the plan was conservative, not that the slowdown in next year's target is wrong, because Neptune sets each plan knowing what it has already sold. What to watch: the fourth quarter against the roughly $51 million the new plan implies. A beat of this quarter's size would mean the 2027 target carries the same caution.

🟢 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁
Four drivers of the standing case got no new numbers, because Neptune reports them on the call or in the quarterly filing rather than in the release. Each is listed with the reading that would move it.

• AI in engineering: Neptune said "AI is allowing our engineering team to accomplish substantially more without a corresponding increase in headcount"; it released 14 versions of Triton, its pricing and underwriting software, against 23 last quarter, and gave no output figure.
• Agent activation: more than 55,000 agents had accounts at June; the release gives no update, and the second phase of Atlas+, the AI sales assistant that management said would arrive this quarter, is not mentioned.
• Product breadth: 11 products, from 9 at year-end, with earthquake cover the newest; premium by product is not broken out.
• Capacity: 45 insurers back the programs, unchanged from June, with coverage above $150 billion from $122 billion at year-end; the October and December renewals will show the terms.

🐻 𝗕𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲

🔴🔴 𝗡𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲'𝘀 𝗢𝘄𝗻 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗛𝗮𝘀 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗛𝗮𝗹𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗡𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿
Neptune says it sees "significant opportunity ahead" and talks of compounding growth. Its first plan for 2027 says revenue of $238 million, or 17% growth. This year's plan works out to about 28%. By our math the fourth quarter already runs at the lower pace: the raised 2026 target leaves about $51 million, 16% above a year ago.

Two things explain part of the step-down. The Palomar policies that Neptune has been moving onto its own book since October 2025 finished transferring, and Neptune said the extra sales "concluded in Q3". The fourth quarter also compares against last autumn's 43-day federal shutdown, when the government flood program could not write new policies and agents turned to Neptune.

But those two effects do not explain all of it, because premium in force, the yearly premium on every active policy, grew almost as fast as revenue and is the base for next year's renewals. Either Neptune has set a cautious plan, as it did twice this year, or growth without Palomar is well below the headline, and it has never disclosed that rate.

What to watch: fourth-quarter revenue growth, the first period with no Palomar sales in it. A rate near the 16% the plan implies would mean the slowdown is in the business, not in the plan.

🔴 𝗙𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗥𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗹 𝗗𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗘𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿
Neptune's revenue depends on policyholders renewing, because each policy lasts a year and Triton re-prices it at renewal. Revenue retention, the share of last year's policy revenue that comes back on renewal, was 89% over the last twelve months. It was 92% in 2025 and has edged down each quarter since.

The two measures behind it, how many policyholders accept a renewal offer and how much premium those renewals carry, appear only in the quarterly filing. Last quarter premium retention fell almost 8 points from a year earlier because Neptune offered smaller price increases, so the in-force book compounds more slowly than its size suggests.

What to watch: premium retention in the filing for this quarter. A rate still near 92% would mean the smaller renewal increases are a lasting choice, and new sales must do more of the work each year.

🔴 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗜𝘀 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗧𝘄𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗔𝘀 𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗔𝘀 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝗲𝘀
Neptune lists "continued emphasis on operating leverage" among the reasons profit rose. The expense lines say otherwise. General and administrative cost, the overhead of running the company, rose 82% from a year ago, more than twice the pace of revenue, and employee pay rose 30%.

• General and administrative: 6.5% of revenue, from 4.8%, up 1.7 points
• Employee pay: 3.6% of revenue, about unchanged
• Stock pay, left out of adjusted profit: 11.8% of revenue

Neptune blamed "increased expenses related to public company costs and technology development", which is fair one year past a listing. But by our math the overhead growth took about 1.7 points off the margin, so the entire gain came from the commission rate, and stock pay is a real cost that the adjusted figures leave out.

What to watch: general and administrative cost in the fourth quarter. A figure still rising faster than revenue would mean the public-company step-up is not a one-year effect and the 61% margin target rests on the commission rate alone.

🔴 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿
Five standing risks got no new reading, because the release carries no call commentary and the quarterly filing is not yet out. Each is listed with the disclosure that would move it.

• Dependence on the insurers that carry the risk: the lifetime loss ratio still reads 19.5% as of June 30; a quiet hurricane season means it faced no test, and the October and December program renewals will show the terms.
• State scrutiny of AI pricing: no comment on the Texas insurance regulator's bulletin or on who oversees Atlas+; the call transcript is where it would appear.
• FEMA flood-map modernisation, the largest lever in the company's own story: no update; any timetable from the agency would move the case.
• Housing market: Neptune again cited the slow real estate market as a drag on selling; home-sales data, not Neptune's, settle it.
• New private-flood competitors: not mentioned; a disclosed loss of agents or policies would be the reading.

👓 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗲𝘀

𝗔 𝗤𝘂𝗶𝗲𝘁 𝗛𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗦𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴
Flood insurance sells best when storms are in the news. Neptune said the quarter carried a "residual slowdown as a result of below-average 2026 Atlantic hurricane season" and an "ongoing slow real estate market reducing selling opportunities". Working the other way, agents moved business to Neptune "driven in part by NFIP uncertainty", the doubt over the federal flood program's future.

— • — • —

💲 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗞𝗣𝗜𝘀

𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗶𝘂𝗺 𝗶𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟰𝟱𝟬.𝟯 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇒ stable
Up 31.7% from a year ago to a record, and up $31 million from June against $24 million in the same quarter last year. Premium in force is the yearly premium on all active policies, so it is the base for next year's renewal commissions. Growth has held near 32% for three readings while policies in force grew 29%, so the average policy carries slightly more premium.

𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗵 𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄 (𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟲𝟵.𝟯 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇗ accelerating
Up 78% from $38.9 million a year earlier, when the figure absorbed listing costs. By our math the quarter alone brought in about $25.9 million, more than net income, because stock pay is a charge that costs no cash. That cash funded the quarter's debt repayment with room to spare.

𝗘𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝘅 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): 𝟯𝟬.𝟮%  ⇗ accelerating
Rose from 25.6% a year ago. Tax expense grew 89% on pretax income up 60%, so a growing share of the profit gain stops at the tax line. Neptune uses a 27.6% rate for its adjusted figures and says the GAAP rate carries items that are not deductible or get special treatment.

𝗗𝗶𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): 𝟭𝟰𝟲.𝟰 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇒ stable
Up 0.1% from last quarter. Restricted stock vesting added 1.4 million shares at quarter end, with 0.5 million withheld to cover employees' taxes. Neptune bought back no shares. A further 3.8 million unvested units remain, so dilution continues at a slow pace unless buybacks resume.

— • — • —

🔮 𝗚𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲

𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲: $𝟮𝟬𝟰 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $199 million
Raised. The plan now has 2026 revenue of $204 million. That is about 28% growth, and by our math it leaves about $51 million for the fourth quarter. That is 16% above a year ago, well below this quarter's pace, because the fourth quarter compares against last autumn's shutdown and the Palomar sales have ended. Third raise this year: +$7.5M, +$4M, +$5M.

𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗔𝗱𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗘𝗕𝗜𝗧𝗗𝗔 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻: 𝗜𝗻 𝗲𝘅𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝟲𝟭%  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from 60% to 61%
Raised. The plan now has the adjusted EBITDA margin, profit before interest, tax, amortisation and stock pay as a share of revenue, above 61% for the year. By our math a 61% year needs a fourth-quarter margin of about 62.4%, higher than any quarter so far, so the plan assumes the commission-rate gain holds while costs stay flat on lower seasonal revenue.

𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲: $𝟮𝟯𝟴 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇘ decelerating
New. The first target for 2027 is $238 million, 17% above this year's plan. That is roughly half this year's growth rate. Neptune has lifted its annual target three times in the past year, and if the pattern holds, by our math 2027 revenue would end near $259 million. But the starting point for 2026 was 25% growth and the starting point for 2027 is 17%.

𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳 𝗔𝗱𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗘𝗕𝗜𝗧𝗗𝗔 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻: 𝟲𝟭%  ⇒ stable
New. The plan keeps the adjusted EBITDA margin at 61% for 2027, the same level as this year's floor, so Neptune expects profit to grow at the pace of revenue rather than faster. By our math that is about $145 million of adjusted EBITDA. The plan assumes no further gain from the commission rate and no relief on the public-company overhead.

— • — • —

❓ 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗣𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗿 𝗮𝗱𝗱, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝘁?
The transferred Palomar policies lifted sales for a year and ended this quarter. Neptune has never disclosed their premium or revenue, so nobody outside the company can tell whether the 2027 plan is cautious or simply organic.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗷𝘂𝗺𝗽 𝗮 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁?
Commission income reached 34.6% of written premium from 33.5% last quarter, far more than the gradual gains management described. Readers need to know whether this is program terms, product mix or a one-off true-up before counting on it.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗶𝘂𝗺 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿?
Revenue retention is down three points from 2025, and premium retention fell almost 8 points last quarter. The filing will show whether smaller renewal increases are still the cause and whether policy retention held at 86%.

𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗮𝘁 𝗙𝗘𝗠𝗔 𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝗙𝗜𝗣?
Management has said earlier plans assume nothing from the federal flood program. If the 2027 target also assumes nothing, flood-map modernisation and NFIP uncertainty are upside; if it assumes something, the 17% is less cautious than it looks.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗔𝘁𝗹𝗮𝘀+, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗽𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿?
The second phase of the AI sales assistant was due this quarter. The release gives no agent-account count, no usage figure and no binding rate, so the distribution leg of the case is unreadable until the call transcript or filing arrives.

text:
Outdated CPR training is putting women’s lives at risk.

Women who suffer cardiac arrest outside hospital are significantly less likely to survive than men, and one overlooked reason is that CPR training almost never accounts for female anatomy.

A Duke University analysis across 47 U.S. states found women are 14% less likely to receive bystander CPR. In the UK, the gap is similar: only 68% of women get CPR from bystanders compared to 73% of men, with many people citing fear of inappropriate touching or concern about injuring a woman’s chest.

The problem is compounded by the tools we train on. A global survey revealed that roughly 95% of CPR manikins are designed with flat chests; only one widely available model includes visible breasts. As a result, most trainees never practice the slight technique adjustments needed for women and often hesitate in real emergencies.

Research published in the Journal of Emergency Medical Services offers hope: when trainees used manikins equipped with realistic silicone breasts, they were almost twice as likely to feel confident performing chest compressions on a woman.

Experts say updating training manikins to represent both male and female anatomy could eliminate hesitation, close the gender survival gap, and save thousands of lives.

text:
Recall that the House bill proposed by Rep. Pallone (D-NJ) (HR 10788 introduced 10/8/26) to "reform" the federal No Surprises Act (NSA) would statutorily bar anyone from challenging the "qualifying payment amount" (QPA or initial payment by the health plan) calculations in court.

Instead, presumably the physician, hospital and supporting community would have to rely on audits by CMS of the QPA.

As mentioned here last week, there have been over 20+ audits pending by CMS of the QPA calculations for 3-4 years and one had been issued. That one CMS audit found that the health plan had incorrectly calculated the QPA.

Now we have 2 more QPA audits--CareSource offers fully insured group health insurance coverage and the School Employees Retirement System, Ohio (Ohio SERS) is a self-funded nonfederal gov't plan that uses Aetna as its TPA.

Two CMS/CCIIO audits illustrate distinct QPA risks: CareSource substituted usual-and-customary rates for contracted-rate medians, an express violation; Ohio SERS excluded negotiated rates associated with contracts that generated no claims, an issue commonly described as “ghost rates,” but CCIIO classified it only as an observation following TMA III litigation.

The physician, hospital and supporting advocacy community has contended for years since the implementation of the NSA on 1/1/22 that the QPAs were not calculated in compliance with law including the +28% inflationary mandate required by the NSA and regulations.  These audits are now independent verification of those contentions.

So, presumably, had the Ohio SERS audit been done after the TMA III en banc US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruling in August, 2026, ruling and new regulations by CMS, that ghost rates could not be included in the QPA, hypothetically then that finding in Ohio SERS could have been an express violation as well.

Both entities were also cited for failing to provide required NSA notices and disclosures (referred to as QPA disclosures).

So, the health plans are now 0-3 in QPA audits but Mr. Pallone would have us wait years under his bill for audits to be completed while the health plans have unilateral and unfettered ability to set and implement the QPAs as they see fit with little to no consequence for their non-compliance--sounds like a "health plans win/we lose" situation.

$20 MILLION IN ALLEGED FRAUD. NOW THE RHODE ISLAND DEMOCRATIC PARTY CHAIR HAS RESIGNED. 

Yesterday, I highlighted the $20 million fraud scandal involving Michael Perik, husband of Rhode Island Democratic Party Chair Liz Beretta-Perik.

Today, she resigned.

On October 8, Ohio officials announced an indictment against Michael Perik in connection with an alleged scheme involving $20 million in funds intended for students at Eastern Gateway Community College, including federal Pell Grants and state money.

Perik faces 12 felony charges, including racketeering, bribery, money laundering, and aggravated theft. He has pleaded not guilty.

Here's how the scheme allegedly worked.

Eastern Gateway offered a "Free College Benefit" program for union members, their families, and even their friends. Enrollment exploded from 8,500 students to more than 60,000.

Companies controlled by Michael Perik allegedly gained improper control over enrollment, attendance verification, and financial aid processes.

Prosecutors allege millions in education funding were improperly diverted through the operation.

And here's where it gets interesting for Rhode Island.

Michael Perik has donated more than $105,000 to political candidates, mostly Democrats, plus another $24,000 to the Rhode Island Democratic Party.

And guess who received $2,900 in campaign contributions from Michael Perik? My opponent, Seth Magaziner.

Now Liz Beretta-Perik, the chair of the Rhode Island Democratic Party, has resigned.

To be clear, Liz has not been charged with a crime, and Michael Perik has pleaded not guilty. But her resignation doesn't erase legitimate questions about political donations, influence, and accountability.

Seth Magaziner once said, "No one should ever have to guess who their elected officials are working for." I agree, Seth.

So let's ask the question.

WHO ARE RHODE ISLAND'S POLITICIANS REALLY WORKING FOR?

Rhode Islanders are struggling with high taxes, rising costs, and an economy that keeps falling behind. 

Meanwhile, politically connected individuals are making headlines for all the wrong reasons.

We need transparency, accountability, and leadership that puts taxpayers ahead of political insiders.

The Atlanta Journal: Officer W. F. Anderson at the Mary Phagan Coroner's Inquest: How Three Atlanta Newspapers Told Different Stories

The Atlanta Journal, The Atlanta Georgian, and The Atlanta Constitution

April 30–May 1, 1913

Coroner Paul Victor Donehoo

On Wednesday, April 30, 1913, Atlanta police officer W. F. Anderson became the first witness to testify at the coroner's inquest into the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan. The hearing was conducted by Fulton County Coroner Paul Victor Donehoo, who was trying to establish how Mary died and what evidence the police had gathered during their first visit to the National Pencil Company.

Anderson was an important witness because he was one of the first officers to enter the factory basement after night watchman Newt Lee reported finding Mary's body early Sunday morning, April 27, 1913. Anderson also received Lee's original telephone call to police headquarters, making him one of the first people to hear what the watchman reported.

Three major Atlanta newspapers covered Anderson's testimony: The Atlanta Journal, The Atlanta Georgian, and The Atlanta Constitution. Although they were reporting on the same hearing, they did not tell the story quite the same way. Each newspaper selected different details, and some of those differences are worth examining because they concern the physical evidence found in the basement (AJ, 2; AG, 3; AC, 4).

The Atlanta Journal Questions Newt Lee's Story

On Wednesday, April 30, The Atlanta Journal published an account of the inquest under the headline "Negro Watchman Tells Story of Finding Girl's Body and Questions Fail to Shake Him."

One of the biggest problems concerned the position of Mary's body.

Newt Lee claimed that when he first discovered Mary, she was lying on her back, with her face upward and her head pointing toward the rear of the building.

But Anderson and the other responding officers described finding her lying face downward, with her head pointing toward the front of the building.

That was a serious difference. If Lee was telling the truth about what he originally saw, someone might have moved the body between the time he discovered it and the time the police arrived.

Of course, another possibility was that Lee had become confused about the position. The newspaper could not establish which account was correct, but the disagreement immediately raised questions about what had happened in the basement.

The Journal also focused on another problem with Lee's story: the small lantern he was carrying.

Anderson described the lantern as smoky and weak, saying it gave very little light. According to his account, the lantern illuminated only about twelve to fifteen feet.

Lee had described noticing Mary's body from roughly twenty to thirty feet away, while standing near the basement toilet.

Anderson questioned how Lee could recognize a body at that distance, especially with a partition partly blocking his view.

The officers had stronger flashlights, yet they still had difficulty seeing the body until they moved closer.

This was an important question because investigators needed to know exactly what Lee could see from where he claimed to be standing.

The difference between seeing something lying on the floor and recognizing it as a dead person was something the attorneys would later examine during Frank's murder trial (AJ, 2).

The Atlanta Georgian Gives More Details About the Basement

The Atlanta Georgian reported Anderson's testimony in an article titled "Went Down Scuttle Hole on Ladder to Reach Body."

Its account gives us a better picture of what the officers encountered when they entered the factory.

Anderson explained that the police went through a trapdoor and climbed down a ladder into the basement. The area contained a boiler, elevator shaft, toilet, and a partition that blocked part of the view.

Mary's body was found near the end of the partition, approximately six feet from an outside wall (AG, 3).

These details help us understand the questions about Lee's lantern.

The basement was poorly lit, the partition blocked part of the room, and the body was lying in an area that could be difficult to see from the toilet.

The Georgian also gave more attention to the condition of Mary's body and clothing.

Anderson described a torn stocking, a missing shoe, bruises, and dirt and sawdust around her face. He also described the cord and cloth tied tightly around her neck.

These were important observations because they helped establish the condition of the body when police first arrived.

Anderson also identified one of the handwritten notes found near Mary's body. The newspaper described it as being written on yellow paper.

The notes eventually became important evidence during Frank's murder trial because prosecutors argued that Jim Conley had written them under Frank's direction. Frank's defense disputed that explanation.

The Georgian also reported that Anderson noticed a damaged fastening on the rear basement door.

Another detail deserves attention. Anderson acknowledged that the first responding officers did not search the second floor during their initial visit.

That means his observations were largely limited to the basement and the evidence discovered there.

It would be a mistake to treat his first visit as a complete investigation of the entire factory. Other investigators later examined the second floor and reported suspected bloodstains and strands of hair near machinery.

The Newspapers Disagree About Mary's Missing Shoe

One difference between the Journal and Georgian concerns where Mary's missing shoe was found.

The Georgian reported Anderson as describing the left shoe and hat near Mary's body.

The Journal placed the left slipper near the elevator in its account of the evidence (AJ, 2; AG, 3).

Those are two different locations.

This is important because investigators were trying to determine whether Mary's body had been dragged through the basement after the murder.

The location of her shoe could help explain where she had been moved and what happened along the way.

Was one newspaper mistaken? Did the reporters confuse the location where the shoe was discovered with the place where it was later placed? Or were they describing different observations made by different officers?

The original testimony needs to be checked carefully before deciding which account is correct.

This is one reason I believe it is important to compare the newspapers instead of relying upon only one version of the story.

The Atlanta Constitution Offers Another Explanation

On Thursday, May 1, The Atlanta Constitution published its account of the April 30 inquest under the headline "Newt Lee Tells His Story During Morning Session."

Like the other newspapers, the Constitution discussed the disagreement about the position of Mary's body.

But its reporter explored another possibility.

What if the murderer was still hiding somewhere in the basement when Newt Lee went downstairs?

Under that theory, Lee might have discovered Mary while the killer was still nearby. The person responsible could then have moved through the basement or escaped after hearing the watchman.

The newspaper even discussed the possibility that the murderer intended to burn Mary's body in the factory furnace (AC, 4).

These were theories, and the article did not establish that any of them actually happened.

What makes the report interesting is how differently the newspapers handled the same disagreement.

The Journal drew attention to problems with Lee's account, while the Constitution explored how Lee might have been telling the truth even though the responding officers found the body in another position.

The Constitution also described Lee as holding to his story during questioning.

That is worth remembering because Lee was an early suspect, and investigators were still trying to determine whether his account could be trusted.

Anderson Tried to Telephone Leo Frank

Another part of Anderson's testimony concerned his attempts to contact Leo Frank after police discovered Mary's body.

Anderson said he tried to telephone Frank early Sunday morning but received no answer.

He also attempted to contact other factory officials, including Herbert Haas and Sigmund Montag.

The Georgian reported the attempts to reach factory officials, while the Constitution gave particular attention to the difficulty police had contacting Frank (AG, 3; AC, 4).

This was important because Frank was the superintendent of the National Pencil Company, where Mary had worked and where her body had been found.

The police naturally wanted to speak with him as soon as possible.

However, Anderson could only testify about his attempts to make contact. An unanswered telephone did not prove whether Frank heard it, was sleeping, or was unavailable for another reason.

That distinction is important when examining the evidence against Frank. Anderson's testimony established that police tried to reach the superintendent and failed. The reason the telephone was not answered required additional evidence.

Anderson's August Trial Testimony Adds an Important Detail

Anderson testified again during Frank's murder trial on Saturday, August 2, 1913.

This time, defense attorney Luther Zeigler Rosser questioned him about the lantern and what Newt Lee could have seen in the dark basement.

Anderson's answers helped explain something that was not always clear in the earlier newspaper reports.

At the coroner's inquest, Anderson had questioned whether Lee could recognize Mary's body from the distance he described.

During the trial, however, Anderson acknowledged that a person might still see the general shape of an object without knowing exactly what it was.

He explained:

"You could see the bulk of anything that far" (BOE, 5).

That statement is important.

Seeing a dark shape lying on the floor is one thing. Recognizing that shape as the body of a dead girl is something else.

The August 2 trial coverage also described an experiment in which officers placed a box and sacks near the spot where Mary's body had been found.

Using a lantern, they tested whether the objects could be seen from farther away.

The experiment suggested that the general outline could be visible, even if the person looking could not clearly identify the object (AJ, 6).

This helps explain Anderson's earlier testimony.

He was questioning Lee's ability to recognize the body from where he claimed to be standing. The later testimony showed that the issue was more complicated than simply saying Lee could see nothing.

Whether the experiment accurately reproduced the conditions of the early morning discovery remains another question.

Another Disagreement About the Condition of Mary's Body

The newspapers also reported differences concerning the condition of Mary's body when police arrived.

The Constitution described Anderson as saying there was still some warmth in the body and that blood was flowing from certain wounds.

Other officers, including Sergeant Robert J. Brown, described the body as cold and stiff (AC, 4; AJ, 2).

This disagreement is worth examining because investigators were trying to estimate when Mary had died.

However, police officers were describing what they believed they observed. They were not conducting a medical examination to establish the time of death.

Different officers might have touched different parts of the body or used different words to describe what they saw and felt.

The exact time of death required medical evidence, and even that evidence had limits.

It would be a mistake to treat Anderson's observations as proof of a precise time when Mary was murdered.

Why Comparing These Newspapers Is Important

The three Atlanta newspapers agree on the basic events.

Anderson received Newt Lee's telephone report, responded to the National Pencil Company, entered the basement with other police officers, and observed Mary's body and the surrounding evidence.

All three newspapers reported problems with the conditions in the basement, particularly the poor lighting and the disagreement about the body's position.

But each newspaper gave readers something different.

The Atlanta Journal focused heavily on the questions surrounding Lee's story, particularly what he could see and why his description of the body differed from the officers' observations.

The Atlanta Georgian gave more details about the basement layout, Mary's clothing, the injuries described by Anderson, and the physical evidence found nearby.

The Atlanta Constitution discussed those same problems while considering whether someone else might have been hiding in the basement when Lee discovered the body.

These differences show why newspaper accounts need to be compared carefully.

A reporter might leave out an important question, shorten an answer, or spend more time discussing a theory about what happened.

That does not automatically make the reporting dishonest. It means the reader needs to separate what the witness actually said from what the newspaper thought his testimony meant.

Anderson's later trial testimony is especially useful because it allows us to compare the original inquest reporting with statements made under further questioning.

Why Officer Anderson Deserves More Attention

Officer W. F. Anderson was one of the first men to respond to the discovery of Mary Phagan's body. He received Newt Lee's telephone call, entered the basement, examined the scene, and described important physical evidence during the coroner's inquest.

He also testified about the weak lantern, the position of Mary's body, the handwritten notes, and his attempts to contact Leo Frank.

These observations became part of the evidence used to examine what happened inside the National Pencil Company.

Anderson was an early witness who could tell investigators what he personally saw before the factory had been subjected to days of questioning, searches, and public attention.

His testimony raised questions about Newt Lee's account, but it did not establish who murdered Mary.

What makes Anderson particularly interesting is how the different newspapers handled his testimony.

The Journal raised questions about Lee's story. The Georgian gave more details about the scene. The Constitution explored other explanations for the differences between Lee's statements and the officers' observations.

Reading all three accounts gives us a much fuller picture than relying on a single newspaper.

For anyone studying the Mary Phagan murder case, that is the value of Anderson's testimony. He helped establish what the police found during those first hours, while the newspapers show how that evidence was being reported and interpreted almost immediately.

The best way to understand his testimony is to compare the original inquest reports with what he later said during Frank's murder trial, paying close attention to the places where the accounts agree and where they differ.

text:
Juror Atticus Haygood Henslee Confronts Leo Frank's Defense as Prosecutor Hugh Manson Dorsey Prepares to Fight the New Trial Motion

The Atlanta Constitution
Sunday, October 12, 1913
Page 21, Column 1
On Sunday, October 12, 1913, The Atlanta Constitution reported that Atticus Haygood Henslee, one of the twelve jurors who convicted Leo Frank of murdering 13-year-old Mary Phagan, had traveled to Valdosta, Georgia, to meet with Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey. Henslee was defending himself against accusations made by Frank's attorneys, Luther Zeigler Rosser and Reuben R. Arnold, who claimed he had entered the murder trial with his mind already made up about Frank's guilt (AC, 1).
The newspaper described Henslee as the center of a bitter dispute that had developed during the previous ten days. Frank's defense was attempting to overturn the unanimous guilty verdict returned on Monday, August 25, 1913, by accusing individual jurors of prejudice.

Henslee had become one of its principal targets.

The October 12 article reported that Henslee spent part of Saturday, October 11, meeting privately with Dorsey, Assistant Solicitor E. A. Stephens, and a court reporter identified as Spurlin. The purpose was to take Henslee's sworn statements answering the accusations collected by the defense.

Henslee was traveling through southern Georgia on business for a Barnesville buggy company. He also had family connections in Valdosta through his brother-in-law, O. W. Franklin, a United States commissioner.

His meeting with Dorsey was important because the prosecution was preparing a detailed response to the defense's efforts to undermine the original jury.

What Frank's Defense Accused Henslee of Saying

The accusations were serious, and some were especially inflammatory.

On Saturday, October 4, 1913, The Atlanta Journal published details of affidavits collected by Frank's attorneys. Eight individuals were reported to have accused Henslee of expressing opinions about Frank's guilt before the murder trial began (AJ, 2).

Three men from Sparta, Georgia, Shi Gray, John M. Holmes, and a third witness surnamed Johnson, claimed Henslee had expressed a firm belief that Frank was guilty during a conversation in late June 1913.

Holmes placed the conversation on Friday, June 27. He also claimed Henslee had mentioned being summoned for jury service and the possibility of sitting on Frank's jury.

This became one of the most important details in the dispute because the defense was accusing Henslee of knowing he might serve as a juror while already expressing a firm opinion about Frank's guilt.

Other witnesses made similar accusations.

C. P. Stough of Atlanta claimed Henslee expressed the belief that Frank was guilty while they were riding together on a streetcar. Stough also alleged that Henslee expressed a desire to see Frank hanged.

In Albany, Georgia, R. L. Gremer and Mack Farkas claimed Henslee had expressed his belief in Frank's guilt during a conversation associated with Farkas's business.

Julian A. Lehman alleged that Henslee had made especially harsh remarks about Frank while traveling by train between Atlanta and Experiment, Georgia. According to Lehman's account, Henslee had declared Frank guilty and suggested that he deserved to have his neck broken.

Perhaps the most damaging accusation came from Samuel Aron, who claimed he overheard Henslee making hostile remarks at the Elks Club in Atlanta shortly after Frank's indictment.

Aron attributed the following statement to Henslee:

"I am glad that they indicted that Jew. The people ought to lynch him."

Aron also alleged that Henslee expressed a determination to vote for Frank's execution if selected for jury service (AJ, 2).

These accusations were the foundation of the defense's claim that Henslee had been prejudiced.

If Henslee had actually made the statements before the trial, they could have raised serious questions about his ability to judge Frank impartially.

However, the accusations were disputed. Frank's attorneys still had to establish when the conversations occurred, whether the witnesses remembered the remarks accurately, and whether Henslee had entered the jury box with a fixed opinion.

The number of affidavits alone did not establish that every accusation was true.

Henslee Denies the Defense's Charges

Henslee rejected the accusations and insisted that he had entered the trial with an impartial mind.

His explanation was particularly important because he did not deny ever discussing the Mary Phagan murder.

According to The Atlanta Constitution on October 12, Henslee acknowledged expressing the general belief that whoever committed such a crime deserved to be hanged.

However, he denied having expressed a settled opinion about Frank's guilt before the trial.

Henslee maintained that the witnesses from Sparta and other communities were mistaken about the timing of conversations they attributed to him.

He insisted that any strong statements he made about Frank's guilt occurred after the trial, when he had already heard the evidence and participated in the verdict (AC, 1).

This was an important part of his defense.

There was a substantial difference between a man expressing the general belief that Mary's murderer deserved punishment and a juror declaring that Frank was guilty before hearing the testimony.

There was also a difference between expressing an opinion after the trial and entering the jury box with that opinion already fixed.

Frank's attorneys needed to establish the latter.

Henslee maintained that they had failed to do so.

The Sparta Witnesses and the Problem With the Dates

The accusations involving the three Sparta witnesses were especially important because their accounts depended upon when the alleged conversation occurred.

John M. Holmes claimed the discussion happened on June 27, 1913, and that Henslee had spoken as though he knew he might serve on Frank's jury.

Henslee disputed the chronology.

He maintained that he did not learn of his jury summons until July 25, three days before Frank's trial began.

If Henslee's account of receiving the summons was correct, it raised a serious problem with the claim that he had spoken in June as though he already knew he had been selected or summoned.

The defense could still argue that Henslee had expressed an opinion about Frank's guilt in June. However, the jury-summons detail became much harder to reconcile with Henslee's version of events.

This was precisely the kind of conflict Judge Leonard Strickland Roan would have to examine.

The defense was presenting sworn statements made after the verdict about conversations allegedly held months earlier. The prosecution was challenging the witnesses' memories of those conversations and the dates on which they supposedly occurred (AG, 3).

A mistaken date would not automatically disprove every word attributed to Henslee, but it could seriously weaken a witness's reliability.

Dorsey Builds a Case Against the Defense's Accusations

Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey was preparing to challenge the accusations rather than allow them to stand unanswered.

The October 12 article explained that Dorsey and Stephens had been working long hours in Valdosta preparing the state's response to Frank's motion for a new trial.

The prosecution's task extended beyond obtaining Henslee's denials. Dorsey needed to examine the defense's witnesses, investigate their statements, and gather evidence supporting the integrity of the original trial.

By October 21, the prosecution had obtained affidavits from fellow jurors and other witnesses challenging the defense's allegations.

Some statements supported the character and impartiality of Henslee and fellow juror Marcellus Johenning. Others questioned the reliability of individuals who had accused them (AJ, 4).

Dorsey also challenged the defense's claim that jurors had been influenced by cheering and demonstrations outside the courtroom.

The prosecution gathered statements from jurors and court officers maintaining that the verdict had been reached from the evidence introduced during the trial.

These responses are important because the defense's affidavits were often presented in newspaper headlines as sensational new developments.

However, the subsequent rebuttals deserve the same attention.

The defense's accusations were only one side of the evidence. Dorsey's investigation produced conflicting statements that Judge Roan had to evaluate.

Henslee's Doubtful Vote Creates Another Problem for the Defense

One particularly interesting development concerned Henslee's conduct during jury deliberations.

According to affidavits published on October 21, several fellow jurors confirmed that Henslee had initially cast a doubtful ballot when the jury began considering Frank's guilt.

Henslee explained that he wanted the evidence discussed thoroughly because a guilty verdict could result in Frank's execution.

The other jurors reported that further discussion followed before the jury reached its unanimous decision (AJ, 4).

This raised another question about the defense's portrayal of Henslee.

Frank's attorneys were accusing him of entering the trial determined to convict. Yet the prosecution produced evidence that Henslee had initially withheld his agreement with the other jurors.

That conduct was difficult to reconcile with the strongest version of the accusation that Henslee was simply determined to convict Frank as quickly as possible.

It did not prove that Henslee had never made a prejudicial remark before the trial. Nevertheless, it was evidence supporting the prosecution's argument that he had taken his responsibilities seriously.

The defense could dispute the importance of the doubtful ballot, but dismissing it as a trick required evidence of a deliberate deception.

The Defense's Evidence Also Required Careful Examination

Not every contradiction favored Henslee.

The defense later produced business and hotel records showing that he had been in Albany on July 8, 1913, despite a broader denial in his account of his travels.

A sworn statement by W. W. Little, head clerk at the New Albany Hotel, identified Henslee's registration on July 8 and assigned room number 79 (NTR, 5).

This evidence raised a legitimate question about the accuracy of Henslee's recollection.

However, proving that a traveling salesman was in Albany on a particular date did not automatically prove that he made the prejudicial statements attributed to him.

The hotel record established his presence. It could not establish the words of a conversation.

The defense was entitled to use the travel discrepancy to challenge Henslee's credibility. The prosecution was equally entitled to challenge the dates, identifications, and recollections offered by the defense's witnesses.

Both sides had to be judged by the evidence.

Dorsey Criticizes the Defense's Investigation

On Tuesday, October 28, 1913, The Atlanta Journal reported Dorsey's arguments against the motion for a new trial.

Dorsey was particularly critical of the defense's campaign to gather affidavits against Henslee.

He argued that Frank's attorneys had searched throughout Georgia for statements that could be used against members of the jury, while failing to establish that the alleged conversations amounted to legally sufficient proof of prejudice.

Dorsey questioned why additional witnesses had not been produced to corroborate certain conversations supposedly made in the presence of other people.

He also challenged the defense's attempts to portray the jury and the surrounding community as prejudiced against Frank because of his Jewish identity (AJ, 6).

These were arguments made by the prosecutor, rather than independent findings about every accusation. Nevertheless, they reveal how directly Dorsey challenged the defense's case.

His position was that the defense had gathered numerous allegations, but the quantity of affidavits could not replace a careful examination of their reliability.

Judge Roan and the Georgia Supreme Court Reject the Challenge

On Friday, October 31, 1913, Judge Leonard Strickland Roan denied Frank's motion for a new trial.

His decision left the original guilty verdict standing.

Frank's attorneys appealed to the Supreme Court of Georgia, which issued its decision on Tuesday, February 17, 1914.

The court upheld Judge Roan by a vote of four to two.

The published opinion, Frank v. State, 141 Georgia Reports 243, addressed the accusations against Henslee under the seventy-third ground of Frank's motion.

The court acknowledged that the defense had presented evidence tending to show that Henslee made statements indicating prejudice before the trial.

However, the court also recognized that Henslee had denied those accusations under oath and maintained that he had served impartially.

The majority explained that Judge Roan had the responsibility to evaluate the conflicting evidence.

The Supreme Court concluded that Roan had not abused his discretion in rejecting the challenge.

It reached the same conclusion concerning the accusations against Marcellus Johenning (GSC, 7).

This was an important legal defeat for Frank's defense.

The allegations had been collected, presented, answered, and considered by the trial judge. The Supreme Court then reviewed the dispute and refused to overturn Roan's determination.

The court did not declare that every defense witness had lied. Its decision was narrower: the conflicting evidence did not establish an abuse of discretion by Judge Roan.

Why the October 12 Article Is Important

The October 12, 1913 report provides an important account of a juror defending his reputation while Frank's attorneys were attempting to overturn the murder conviction.

Henslee was not an anonymous figure accused without an opportunity to respond. He met with Dorsey, submitted sworn statements, disputed the dates of alleged conversations, and maintained that he had entered the jury box without prejudice.

Frank's defense made serious accusations, including claims of violent remarks and hostility toward Frank's Jewish identity. Those accusations deserved examination, but they were not automatically established facts simply because witnesses signed affidavits.

The prosecution investigated the accusations, gathered conflicting evidence, and challenged the credibility of the defense's witnesses.

Judge Roan considered the competing evidence and denied the motion. The Georgia Supreme Court upheld his decision.

The October 12 article is especially valuable because it shows Henslee actively participating in his defense against the allegations rather than allowing the newspaper accusations to go unanswered.

For anyone studying the Mary Phagan murder case, the complete historical record must include what Frank's defense alleged, what Henslee denied, what Dorsey presented in response, and what the courts actually decided.

The defense had every right to investigate possible misconduct, but it also carried the responsibility of proving its claims.

In the end, the accusations against Henslee were not sufficient to overturn the original jury verdict.

That legal result deserves just as much attention as the accusations that preceded it.

Henslee Confers With Hugh Dorsey

Solicitor General Is Now Preparing for Leo M. Frank's Hearing on Retrial Petition.

Valdosta, Ga., October 11. (Special.) Juror A. H. Henslee, who has been the storm center in the Frank case during the last ten days, and who is so bitterly assailed by the defense in the motion for a new trial, was in the city today in conference with Solicitor Hugh Dorsey, who is here preparing the state's answers to the motion.

Mr. Henslee was closeted late this afternoon with Messrs. Dorsey, E. A. Stephens and Spurlin, the latter official court reporter in this circuit, who was taking depositions from the ex-juror. These depositions, it is understood, related to the statements regarding the case made by the ex-juror and covered the affidavits against him filed by citizens of Sparta.

Many of the alleged facts in these affidavits are denied outright by Mr. Henslee. Previously Mr. Henslee had stated that he was merely making his usual ninety days' trip through this section as representative of a Barnesville buggy company, and had stopped over to transact business for his house and incidentally to visit his brother-in-law, O. W. Franklin, United States commissioner here.

Henslee reiterated his former statements as to his impartial state of mind when he went to the Frank jury, and again claimed that the Sparta citizens and others who had attacked him in their affidavits were mistaken as to the time of the alleged conversations.

He said he had not discussed Frank's guilt or innocence until after the trial. He claims that the only statements he made about the case before the trial which could possibly be construed as inimical to Frank, was that the man who would commit such a crime should be hanged, but that he went into the jury box entirely unprejudiced.

Solicitor Dorsey and his assistant, Attorney Stephens, do not hope to complete their answer to the motion for a new trial before next Saturday and say that it is doubtful if they can be ready by that time. They have been working every day from an early hour in the morning until long after dark, but do not expect to complete their work under the two weeks originally contemplated by the solicitor.

An order postponing, at Solicitor Hugh Dorsey's request, the hearing of the motion for a new trial for Leo M. Frank, was filed yesterday with Deputy Clerk John H. Jones. It was signed by Judge L. S. Roan, and set the hearing for next Saturday.

Solicitor Dorsey and E. A. Stephens, his assistant, are still in Valdosta, where they expect to spend the greater part of the week continuing their work on the answer to the petition of the defense.

The solicitor and Mr. Stephens were given an entertainment last week by several prominent Valdosta attorneys. The affair, which was a stag supper, was held at Ocean Grove club, about 15 miles from Valdosta.

Reference
